### [1] [MeshFM: 2D Features Are All You Need for 3D Shape Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27592)
*Jinfan Zhou,Richard Liu,Itai Lang,Rana Hanocka*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MeshFM is a feedforward framework that distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D features for meshes, using a two-stage training strategy (feature field optimization followed by network regression) with no 3D annotation required, achieving performance on par with 3D-supervised methods on part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation while being robust to extreme rotations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To extract rich 3D features from mesh inputs efficiently without requiring per-instance optimization during inference or 3D annotations, leveraging the powerful representations already learned by 2D visual foundation models.

Method: A two-stage training strategy: (1) optimize a 3D feature field supervised only by 2D feature distillation from visual foundation models; (2) train a feedforward network to regress this feature field directly, enabling fast inference. No 3D annotation is used, and training includes robustness to extreme input rotations.

Result: Extensive experiments show MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, performs on par with methods trained with explicit 3D supervision across part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation, without task-specific fine-tuning, while remaining robust to extreme object rotations.

Conclusion: 2D foundation model features can be effectively distilled into 3D via a feedforward network, providing a supervision-free (in 3D) and inference-efficient alternative to optimization-based or 3D-annotated approaches for general 3D feature extraction.

Abstract: We present MeshFM, an efficient feedforward framework for extracting rich features from 3D inputs. Our method distills 2D features from visual foundation models into 3D. We train a feedforward network to directly predict 3D features without requiring optimization during inference. The approach utilizes a two-stage training strategy. First, we optimize a feature field in 3D using only 2D feature supervision. Second, we train a network to regress this feature field. The entire procedure requires no 3D annotation, instead relying on the powerful information in 2D foundation models. We demonstrate that our learned features can be immediately applied to downstream tasks, including part segmentation, dense correspondence, and mesh deformation. Extensive experiments show that MeshFM, trained solely with 2D supervision, performs on par with methods trained explicitly with 3D supervision, even without task-specific fine-tuning. Moreover, our model is trained to be robust to extreme rotations of the input objects. Project page: https://threedle.github.io/MeshFM/

</details>


### [2] [S-Avatar: Diffusion-Guided Gaussian Head Avatars from a Single Image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28164)
*Hail Song,Seokhwan Yang,Jiwon Yang,Woojin Cho,Woontack Woo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: S-Avatar is a method for generating photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a three-stage pipeline: diffusion-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting generation from a single image, FLAME parametric head model alignment, and a binding template that encodes spatial relationships to enable real-time animation. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-image head avatar reconstruction is crucial for lifelike VR applications, but existing approaches struggle to preserve 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints. The paper aims to address this limitation while enabling real-time animation.

Method: The method uses a three-stage pipeline: (1) diffusion-based Gaussian splat generation module to synthesize a high-resolution 3DGS directly from a single image, (2) alignment of the parametric head model FLAME with the generated 3DGS by optimizing its parameters and spatial transformations, and (3) construction of a binding template encoding spatial relationships between initial splats and FLAME, allowing real-time deformation of 3DGS for dynamic head avatar rendering.

Result: Evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency.

Conclusion: By combining diffusion-guided canonical 3DGS generation with FLAME-based control, the method achieves efficient and accurate reconstruction with enhanced 3D consistency, representing a significant advance in accessible avatar creation applicable to VR/AR applications.

Abstract: We propose S-Avatar, a novel method for generating photorealistic 3D head avatars from a single image using a diffusion-guided 3D model generation module and strategies for animating 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). While single-image head avatar reconstruction is crucial for lifelike Virtual Reality (VR) applications, existing approaches often struggle to preserve 3D consistency under unseen viewpoints. S-Avatar addresses this limitation through a three-stage pipeline. First, a high-resolution 3DGS is synthesized directly from a single image using a diffusion-based Gaussian splat generation module. Next, the parametric head model FLAME is aligned with the generated 3DGS by optimizing its parameters and spatial transformations. Finally, to adapt the 3DGS to FLAME variations, we construct a binding template that encodes the spatial relationship between the initial splats and FLAME. The dynamic 3D head avatar can then be rendered in real time by deforming the 3DGS with the binding template. By combining diffusion-guided canonical 3DGS generation with FLAME-based control, our method achieves efficient and accurate reconstruction with enhanced 3D consistency. Evaluations on public datasets demonstrate that S-Avatar outperforms state-of-the-art methods in novel-view and expression generation, achieving superior realism and consistency. Consequently, our approach represents a significant advance in accessible avatar creation, applicable to a wide range of VR/AR applications. The project page is available at https://github.com/hailsong/savatar.

</details>


### [3] [Theatre Chapbooks At Scale: A Statistical Comparative Analysis of Typography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27266)
*Diego Belzarena,Seginus Mowlavi,Paula Casariego Castiñeira,Alejandra Ulla Lorenzo,Gregory Randall,Jean-Michel Morel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A statistical methodology quantifies typeface similarity between historical printed books using character prototypes derived from clustering and alignment of automatically extracted character images, with an a contrario framework to assess significance. Applied to 17th-century Spanish theatre chapbooks, it enabled automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types, leading to new printer attributions and revisions of former ones after expert validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Philological analysis of historical printed books requires identifying which printer produced which book through typeface comparison, but systematic visual inspection is infeasible at scale. A computational tool that quantifies typeface similarity could accelerate and scale this analysis.

Method: Character prototypes are derived from clustering and aligning automatically extracted character images from printed books. A typeface distance is defined between any two books based on these prototypes. An a contrario statistical framework is developed to interpret the significance of the computed distances, enabling automatic comparison of Roman and Italic typefaces across books.

Result: Applied to a corpus of 17th-century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks exceeding human visual inspection capacity. After human expert validation, the method led to new printer attributions being discovered and former printer attributions being revised, demonstrating its practical philological value.

Conclusion: The method successfully enables digital bibliography at a larger scale than previously possible, providing a validated tool that accelerates and expands philological typeface analysis of historical printed books.

Abstract: We propose a statistical methodology that quantifies the similarity of typefaces between printed historical books. This provides a tool that accelerates philological analysis. Using character prototypes derived from clustering and aligning automatically extracted character images, the method defines a typeface distance between any two books. To produce actionable outputs, we develop an a contrario statistical framework to interpret the significance of the computed typeface distances. We apply the method to the philological study of 17 th -century Spanish printed theatre chapbooks in a quantity that exceeds the capabilities of systematic visual inspection by human experts. Our method enables the automatic comparison of Roman and Italic types extracted from different books. After validation by human experts, our method has led to new printer attributions being discovered, and former printer attributions being revised. This success strongly suggests that our method has the potential to enable digital bibliography on a larger scale than was previously possible.

</details>


### [4] [PanDent: Toward Comprehensive Tooth-Level Structure-Language Consistency in Dental Radiology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27378)
*Xiaohan Li,Xinyu Liu,Chang Liu,Sum Wing Au Yeung,Jun Liu,Yixuan Yuan,Hui Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PanDent is a large-scale, clinically grounded benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography, comprising 9,524 OPGs with expert-validated tooth-level annotations and clinically consistent radiology reports. Experiments show current MLLMs generate fluent but clinically inconsistent reports with errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis, while fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency and diagnostic accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate evaluation of MLLMs in dental panoramic radiography is hindered by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation of orthopantomograms (OPGs). Existing benchmarks do not provide the granular tooth-level supervision needed to assess clinical reasoning quality in dental AI.

Method: The authors construct PanDent, a benchmark of 9,524 high-quality OPGs with comprehensive structured annotations from experienced dentists, further validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist. Clinically consistent radiology reports are generated from expert-validated findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. Experiments are conducted across diverse MLLMs including proprietary SOTA models, open-source general-domain models, and medical-specific models.

Result: Current MLLMs can generate fluent radiology reports but fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, exhibiting substantial errors in fine-grained tooth localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, enhancing visual localization accuracy and diagnostic correctness, bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation.

Conclusion: PanDent serves as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and provides a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI, demonstrating that fine-grained expert-validated supervision can substantially improve MLLM performance in dental radiograph interpretation.

Abstract: Accurate evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in dental panoramic radiography (orthopantomogram, OPG) is limited by the lack of fine-grained, clinically reliable benchmarks that reflect expert interpretation. This work introduces PanDent, a large-scale, clinically grounded OPG benchmark built upon fine-grained, expert-validated tooth-level annotations. The dataset comprises 9,524 high-quality OPGs, each associated with comprehensive structured annotations produced by experienced dentists and further validated by an oral and maxillofacial radiologist, providing clinically reliable supervision for tooth-level diagnosis and reasoning. Clinically consistent radiology reports are constructed from expert-validated findings using clinician-defined reporting logic, establishing explicit correspondence between structured clinical evidence and free-text descriptions. This design enables evaluation of whether MLLMs generate reports that are not only linguistically coherent but also clinically consistent with expert-validated tooth-level findings. Experiments are conducted on diverse MLLMs, including state-of-the-art (SOTA) proprietary models, general-domain open-source models, and medical-specific models. Results show that current MLLMs can generate fluent reports, yet fail to produce clinically consistent descriptions, exhibiting substantial errors in fine-grained localization and tooth-level diagnosis. Fine-tuning on PanDent significantly improves structure-language consistency, substantially enhancing visual localization accuracy and diagnostic correctness, and bringing model outputs closer to expert dental interpretation. These results establish PanDent as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating tooth-level clinical reasoning in MLLMs and a valuable resource for clinically grounded dental AI.

</details>


### [5] [OVEarth-Bench: Evaluating Category Breadth and Query Diversity for Open-Vocabulary Earth Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27278)
*Kaiyu Li,Zepeng Xin,Zixuan Jiang,Jing Fu,Lanxuan Xue,Lingyu Zhang,Xiangyong Cao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OVEarth-Bench is a new benchmark for open-vocabulary Earth observation that extends existing evaluation in two directions: broader hierarchical category coverage (with both positive and negative expressions) and greater query diversity (vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries). The benchmark supports mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. Evaluation shows current methods remain limited, MLLM-based methods perform best overall, and EO-specific methods generally underperform general models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing open-vocabulary Earth observation benchmarks typically cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms, failing to reflect real-world complexity. There is a need for a more comprehensive benchmark that spans broad hierarchical categories and diverse query types to enable reliable and realistic evaluation of open-vocabulary EO models.

Method: The authors introduce OVEarth-Bench, extending evaluation along two dimensions: (1) category breadth via broad hierarchical category coverage including both positive and negative expressions, and (2) query diversity via vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports both mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol, and evaluates a broad set of general and EO-specific methods.

Result: Three key findings: (1) current methods show limited performance, though broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods. The data and evaluation package are publicly released.

Conclusion: The findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation. OVEarth-Bench serves as a foundation for this direction.

Abstract: Open-vocabulary Earth observation (EO) aims to localize geospatial concepts specified in natural language rather than a fixed label set. Existing benchmarks, however, usually cover narrow category vocabularies or limited query forms. To fill this gap, we introduce OVEarth-Bench, which extends existing evaluation in two directions: category breadth, through broad hierarchical category coverage with positive and negative expressions, and query diversity, through vocabulary, referring, and reasoning queries. The benchmark supports mask and box localization under a unified zero-shot protocol. We evaluate a broad set of general and EO-specific methods. The evaluation reveals that: (1) the performance of current methods remains limited, while broader category coverage yields more stable model rankings; (2) MLLM-based methods achieve the strongest overall performance; and (3) EO-specific methods generally underperform general models and rarely match the strongest methods. These findings provide guidance for future open-vocabulary EO method design and highlight the importance of developing more realistic, diverse, high-quality, and large-scale benchmarks for reliable evaluation. Our data and evaluation package are released at https://earth-insights.github.io/OVEarth-bench.

</details>


### [6] [VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27292)
*Jonas Grebe,Hossein Shakibania,Tobias Braun,Marcus Rohrbach,Anna Rohrbach*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VETO is a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts joint-attention blocks in modern image-editing models, protecting source images from unauthorized recontextualization and editing. The authors also introduce VetoBench, a new benchmark evaluating defenses on both conventional localized edits and broader contextual shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern image-editing models like FLUX.2 have expanded capabilities beyond localized edits to full recontextualization of objects and identities, broadening the space of potential misuse. Existing anti-edit defenses target the semantic bottleneck of reference-image encoding in legacy diffusion pipelines, but newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, circumventing these protections. The need for a defense adapted to modern architectures and a benchmark that tests broader contextual shifts motivates this work.

Method: The authors propose VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts the internal joint-attention mechanism through which modern models read the source image. They also introduce VetoBench, a benchmark that evaluates defenses on both conventional localized edits and broader contextual shifts/recontextualizations.

Result: Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

Conclusion: VETO effectively adapts anti-edit defense to modern joint-attention-based editing architectures, and VetoBench provides a more comprehensive evaluation framework spanning both localized and recontextualization-based edits.

Abstract: The rise of powerful, accessible image-editing models such as FLUX.2 has brought high-fidelity editing within broad reach. Their capabilities now extend beyond localized modifications to extracting and recontextualizing objects and identities in entirely new scenes. By allowing prompt and generation tokens to attend directly to reference-image tokens, modern models blur the boundary between conventional editing and text-to-image synthesis. This expanded generative freedom also broadens the space of potential misuse, as harmful transformations are no longer confined to a predictable set of localized edits. Existing anti-edit defenses are designed to disrupt the semantic bottleneck of the reference-image encoding in legacy diffusion pipelines. However, newer editors distill reference information through joint-attention blocks, thereby often circumventing these protections. We therefore introduce VETO, a subtle anti-edit cloak that disrupts this inner mechanism through which modern models read the source image. Additionally, as existing editing benchmarks leave comprehensive recontextualizations largely untested, we introduce VetoBench, which evaluates defenses not only on conventional localized edits but also on broader contextual shifts. Across two contemporary editing models and three benchmarks, VETO consistently outperforms existing defenses while providing a stronger protection-fidelity trade-off.

</details>


### [7] [Theia: Large-Scale Multimodal Captioning and Automated Validation of the Incidents1M Dataset for Data-Free Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28269)
*Simone Giano,Lorenzo Severini,Alessandro Galdelli,Adriano Mancini*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a methodology to construct and automatically validate a large-scale multimodal disaster response dataset by recovering 100,000 images from the vision-only Incidents1M dataset, generating captions with two Qwen3.5 architectures (4B dense and 35B MoE), and validating them via an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline (Qwen3.5-9B). The approach achieves 78.65/100 semantic agreement across 173,179 label pairs, with high precision (77.6%) and low recall (46.0%), revealing conservative captioning and exposing human annotation inconsistencies in the original ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal datasets for disaster management either lack descriptive text entirely (Incidents1M) or suffer from severe text-image semantic misalignment (CrisisMMD). High-quality multimodal data is critical for Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD) of Vision-Language Models in critical domains like disaster response, yet no such dataset currently exists.

Method: The authors (1) recover 100,000 images from the vision-only Incidents1M dataset, (2) generate high-fidelity captions using two Qwen3.5 models (a 4B dense and a 35B MoE), and (3) introduce an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge validation pipeline using Qwen3.5-9B, where the original image is intentionally obscured to simulate the modality gap experienced by a student model during DFKD.

Result: Across 173,179 label pairs, the two captioning architectures show high semantic agreement (78.65/100). The automated evaluation reveals conservative captioning behaviour with high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%), which minimizes false positive noise. The evaluation also exposes underlying human annotation inconsistencies in the original Incidents1M ground truth.

Conclusion: This work provides a scalable, LLM-validated multimodal dataset and a reproducible framework that advances cross-modal knowledge distillation in disaster response, addressing the critical gap of reliable text-image semantic alignment for VLM deployment in high-stakes domains.

Abstract: The deployment of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in critical domains like disaster management requires high-quality multimodal datasets, especially for transferring knowledge via Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (DFKD). However, existing datasets in this domain either entirely lack descriptive text, such as Incidents1M, or suffer from severe text-image semantic misalignment, such as CrisisMMD. In this work, we present a novel methodology to construct and automatically validate a large-scale multimodal dataset for disaster response. Starting from the vision-only Incidents1M, we successfully recovered 100,000 images and generated high-fidelity textual descriptions using two distinct Qwen3.5 architectures: a 4B dense model and a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model. To ensure the generated captions provide reliable semantic anchoring for DFKD, we introduce an image-blind LLM-as-a-Judge validation pipeline leveraging Qwen3.5-9B. By intentionally obscuring the original image from the judge, this evaluator accurately simulates the modality gap of the student model during data-free distillation. Our evaluation across 173,179 label pairs demonstrates a high semantic agreement (78.65/100) between the two architectures. Furthermore, the automated evaluation reveals a conservative captioning behaviour, characterized by a high Precision (77.6%) and low Recall (46.0%). This minimizes the false positive noise, while simultaneously exposing underlying human annotation inconsistencies in the original ground truth. This work provides a scalable, LLM-validated multimodal dataset and a reproducible framework to advance cross-modal knowledge distillation.

</details>


### [8] [Bunraku: Turning a Single Illustration into an Editable Live2D Character](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27348)
*Junhao Chen,Jingjia Mao,Dayong Li,Chenghai Li,Saining Zhang,Zhihao Li,Hao Zhao,Yufei Wang,Ruqi Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first system that generates all structured information required by a Live2D runtime from a single illustration: ordered RGBA layers, per-layer deformation meshes, and parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets. Stage 1 performs layered diffusion-based decomposition under a Live2D-aware taxonomy, and Stage 2 jointly predicts keypose displacement fields across all layers using a transformer where every vertex is a token. Joint prediction is the largest gain (scaling the network 112x yields none), achieving a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). The system also enables re-texturing a layer via natural language while reusing mesh and animation, and introduces Live2D-Bench benchmark plus an 8,884-model corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Authoring a Live2D model is extremely labor-intensive, requiring weeks of manual layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing. Despite the format's widespread use in virtual streaming, mobile games, and interactive characters, no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end, motivating the need for a system that can generate the full Live2D asset pipeline from a single illustration.

Method: The method has two stages. Stage 1 casts layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh for each layer from its alpha channel, then predicts the keypose displacement field of all layers jointly using a transformer where every vertex of every layer is a token, self-attention spans layer boundaries, and each displacement is factorized into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude.

Result: On 50 held-out characters under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 attains a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Joint prediction is the largest gain, while scaling the network 112x yields no improvement. The system also enables zero-modification re-texturing of a clothing layer from natural-language instructions while reusing mesh and predicted animation byte-for-byte.

Conclusion: Joint prediction across layers (rather than independent prediction) is what yields a coherent character rather than separately plausible parts, and is the key architectural insight. The paper contributes the first end-to-end Live2D generation system, the Live2D-Bench standardized benchmark, and a large 8,884-model corpus with layer and animation supervision.

Abstract: Live2D is the dominant 2D character-animation format for anime characters and virtual avatars, representing each character as a stack of RGBA layers driven by per-layer mesh deformation. Despite its wide use in virtual streaming, mobile games, and interactive characters, authoring a Live2D model still demands weeks of manual layer separation, occlusion completion, mesh placement, and keyframing, and no prior generative method produces such a structured asset end-to-end. We present the first system that, from a single illustration, generates all the structured information a Live2D runtime consumes: ordered RGBA layers, a deformation mesh per layer, and the parameter-driven keypose vertex offsets that make the character move. Stage 1 casts layered decomposition as a layered diffusion process under a Live2D-aware organ-level taxonomy, producing an ordered RGBA stack with hidden-region completion. Stage 2 builds a content-conforming triangle mesh for each layer from its alpha channel alone, then predicts the keypose displacement field of all layers jointly: every vertex of every layer is one token, self-attention spans layer boundaries, and each displacement is factorised into a bounded direction and a log-magnitude. Joint rather than independent prediction is what makes the result a coherent character instead of separately plausible parts, and is our largest gain; scaling the network 112x yields none. On 50 held-out characters, under true generation with no teacher forcing, Stage 2 attains a per-vertex direction cosine of 0.768 (median 0.828). Because a layer's mesh derives from its alpha channel, a clothing layer can be re-textured from a natural-language instruction while the mesh and predicted animation are reused byte-for-byte. We further contribute Live2D-Bench, the first standardized benchmark for the task, and an 8,884-model Live2D corpus with layer and animation supervision.

</details>


### [9] [Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation for Unpaired Cross-Modal Medical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27357)
*Dillan Imans,Phuoc-Nguyen Bui,Duc-Tai Le,Hyunseung Choo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SSCD is a cross-modal knowledge distillation method for unpaired medical images that aligns teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook, enabling knowledge transfer without requiring paired samples or comparable raw features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-modal knowledge distillation in medical imaging faces the challenge of unpaired modalities collected from different patient cohorts with geometrically incompatible feature spaces, making instance-level distillation invalid and direct feature matching unreliable.

Method: SSCD compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook, representing each image as a distribution over a common modality-agnostic vocabulary. Knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions globally and class-conditionally across modalities without paired samples. The codebook is evolved online via exponential moving average, with diversity maintained through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. At inference, only the student encoder and classifier remain.

Result: On OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves student performance from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines.

Conclusion: Shared discrete codebook distillation effectively enables cross-modal knowledge transfer in unpaired medical imaging settings, achieving state-of-the-art results while discarding teacher-side and codebook modules at inference time for efficient deployment.

Abstract: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can transfer diagnostic knowledge from a strong but costly teacher modality to a cheaper and more deployable student modality. In medical image analysis, however, the two modalities are often unpaired: they are collected from different patient cohorts and occupy geometrically incompatible feature spaces. This makes instance-level distillation invalid and direct feature matching unreliable. To address these challenges, we propose Shared Semantic Codebook Distillation (SSCD), which compares teacher and student representations through a shared discrete codebook. Each image is represented as a distribution over a common, modality-agnostic vocabulary, and knowledge is transferred by aligning these distributions across modalities, both globally and class-conditionally, without requiring paired samples or directly comparable raw features. The codebook is evolved online by exponential moving average and kept diverse through entropy regularization and dead-code restart. At inference, all teacher-side and codebook modules are discarded, leaving only the student encoder and classifier. On two heterogeneous unpaired settings, OCT-to-fundus retinal disease classification and CT-to-chest-X-ray pneumonia classification, SSCD improves the student from 64.5 to 70.2 macro-F1 and from 73.8 to 76.3 macro-F1, respectively, outperforming all evaluated distillation baselines on both settings. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/DillanImans/SSCD-unpaired-distillation

</details>


### [10] [VideoCoCo: Code-as-CoT for Physically-Consistent Video Generation via an Agentic Dual-Engine System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27380)
*Haodong Li,Tianfei Ren,Xiaoxiao Ma,Chunmei Qing,Zhen Fang,Sipeng He,Ziyu Guo,Haoyu Wu,Juanxi Tian,Yihang Zou,Ruichuan An,Dongzhi Jiang,Boxue Yang,Ji Xie,Xu Huang,Wenhao Yan,Jialv Zou,Zhengrong Yue,Yaxin Luo,Xiaotong Li,Yuzhu Wang,Junyan Ye,Jinjing Zhao,Zehui Chen,Lin Chen,Renye Yan,Feng Zhao,Pheng-Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VideoCoCo is an agentic dual-engine framework that uses executable Blender code as a process-level chain of thought for physically consistent text-to-video generation. A coding agent synthesizes Blender programs specifying scene dynamics, which are executed to produce deterministic spatiotemporal drafts, then transformed into photorealistic video by a generative editor. It achieves state-of-the-art results on PhyGenBench (0.558) and VBench-2.0 (77.88).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-video models struggle with physically consistent dynamics because temporal evolution must be inferred from compressed text prompts. Existing chain-of-thought approaches use intermediate plans or visual states that are non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control complete spatiotemporal processes.

Method: VideoCoCo employs a dual-engine framework: (1) a coding agent generates executable Blender code serving as a process-level chain of thought that explicitly specifies the scene and temporal evolution; (2) the Blender simulation engine executes the code to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft; (3) a generative video engine transforms the draft into a photorealistic video via draft-conditioned editing. A curated dataset, VideoCoCo-3K, of draft-instruction-target triplets is constructed to adapt the video editor to simulated drafts.

Result: VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks.

Conclusion: Executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation, decomposing process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization.

Abstract: Text-to-video models have achieved remarkable visual quality, yet they still struggle to generate physically consistent dynamics because the temporal evolution of a scene must be inferred implicitly from a highly compressed text prompt. Existing chain-of-thought approaches introduce intermediate plans or visual states, but these representations are typically non-executable or temporally sparse, limiting their ability to instantiate and control the complete spatiotemporal process. To address this limitation, we introduce VideoCoCo, an agentic dual-engine framework in which executable Blender code serves as a process-level chain of thought. Given a text prompt, a coding agent synthesizes a Blender program that explicitly specifies the scene and its temporal evolution. The executable simulation engine runs the program to produce a deterministic spatiotemporal draft, which is subsequently transformed into a photorealistic video by a generative video engine through draft-conditioned editing. This decomposition separates process-level reasoning from high-fidelity visual realization. To adapt the video editor to simulated drafts, we construct VideoCoCo-3K, a curated dataset of draft-instruction-target triplets. VideoCoCo improves the OmniWeaving baseline from 0.475 to 0.558 on PhyGenBench and from 52.18 to 77.88 on VBench-2.0, achieving the best average score on both benchmarks. These results demonstrate that executable code provides an effective, controllable, and inspectable intermediate representation for physically consistent video generation.

</details>


### [11] [IGME: Efficient Chained Method Ensemble for Transferable Semantic Segmentation Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27465)
*Mengqi He,Jing Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes IGME, an efficient single-source transferable adversarial attack method for semantic segmentation that chains differentiable attack components to share source-model gradient computation, and uses integrated-gradient-style path-averaged directions for stability, achieving competitive transferability with faster runtime than ensemble attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transferable adversarial attacks on semantic segmentation are computationally expensive, especially when using ensemble attacks that require multiple surrogate models. There is a need for a more efficient single-source alternative that still achieves competitive transferability.

Method: The method formulates transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, sharing the expensive source-model gradient computation. To mitigate update instability from chained composition, an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction is used as an empirical stabilization heuristic.

Result: IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model, evaluated on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a carefully designed single-source attack with shared gradient computation and path-averaged stabilization can effectively trade off transferability and efficiency for semantic segmentation attacks, offering a practical alternative to ensemble-based methods.

Abstract: Semantic segmentation models are vulnerable to transferable adversarial perturbations, yet evaluating transfer attacks on dense prediction models can be computationally expensive. Existing ensemble attacks often rely on multiple surrogate models, increasing the computation cost, even harder for segmentation. This paper studies an efficient single-source alternative for transferable attacks on semantic segmentation. We formulate transferable attack composition as a chained computation over differentiable attack components, allowing the expensive source-model gradient computation to be shared. To reduce the update instability introduced by chained composition, we further use an integrated-gradient-style path-averaged direction as an empirical stabilization heuristic. Experiments on Pascal VOC and Cityscapes evaluate the resulting transferability efficiency trade-off across CNN- and transformer-based segmentation models. IGME achieves competitive transferability compared with single-source baselines and favorable runtime compared with model-ensemble attacks, while requiring access to only one source model.

</details>


### [12] [ProgFormer: Hierarchical Voxel Diffusion Transformer for Longitudinal Brain MRI Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27537)
*Dexuan Ding,Yuankai Qi,Luping Zhou,Jian Yang,Quan Z. Sheng,Ming-Hsuan Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ProgFormer is a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction, featuring a coarse pathway for overall volumetric prediction and a fine pathway for voxel-level refinement, jointly estimating a velocity field via conditional flow matching directly in voxel space without a separate autoencoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Longitudinal brain MRI prediction is challenging because changes are subtle and localized, while most brain structure is stable over time. Existing latent-space methods suffer from information loss in compression-reconstruction, and direct voxel-space methods use a unified prediction pathway where subtle local changes become overshadowed by dominant stable structures.

Method: ProgFormer uses a two-pathway hierarchical Diffusion Transformer in voxel space: (1) a coarse pathway performs primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens, modeling overall brain structure and longitudinal context; (2) a fine pathway uses coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. Both pathways jointly estimate a velocity field in voxel space via conditional flow matching, and the future scan is generated from Gaussian noise through Euler steps integrating the velocity field, enabling end-to-end prediction without a learned image autoencoder.

Result: Extensive experiments on three benchmarks (ADNI, AIBL, OASIS) under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favorable performance compared to several state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: ProgFormer effectively addresses the trade-off between preserving global brain consistency and detecting fine-grained disease progression by decoupling global and local modeling into coarse and fine pathways, all within voxel space to avoid latent information loss.

Abstract: Predicting future structural MRI of a brain is challenging because longitudinal changes are often subtle and confined to specific anatomical regions, while most subject-specific brain structure remains stable over time. An effective model should therefore preserve global brain structural consistency while remaining sensitive to fine-grained disease progression. Existing latent-space-based methods improve computational efficiency, but suffer from information loss during their compression-reconstruction procedure. In contrast, direct voxel-space methods avoid latent reconstruction but commonly use a unified prediction pathway to model brain structure and progression-related changes. Subtle local changes may therefore be overshadowed by the dominant stable brain structure. To address these challenges, we propose ProgFormer, a hierarchical voxel-space Diffusion Transformer for longitudinal brain MRI prediction. ProgFormer uses a coarse pathway to perform the primary volumetric prediction from 3D patch tokens. This pathway models overall brain structure and longitudinal context. The fine pathway then uses the coarse representations as spatio-temporal grounding for voxel-level refinement within individual patches. The two pathways jointly estimate a velocity field directly in voxel space through conditional flow matching, enabling end-to-end prediction without a separately learned image autoencoder. The predicted future scan is then generated from Gaussian noise by integrating the estimated velocity field over a sequence of Euler steps. Extensive experimental results on three widely used benchmarks, ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS, under both pairwise and trajectory settings demonstrate favourable performance compared against several state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [13] [Drawing-Recode: Annotation Grounding for Parametric CAD Code Generation from Raster 2D CAD Drawings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27558)
*Mingi Kim,Yongjun Kim,Hyungki Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Drawing-Recode is a framework that recovers Parametric CAD sequences (as CAD code) from raster 2D CAD drawings by extracting geometric features via an image encoder, recognizing dimensional annotations with a text recognition module, and explicitly grounding annotations to geometry using cross-attention and an Annotation Grounding Loss before feeding features into an LLM to generate CAD code in the SPCC format.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for recovering parametric CAD sequences from legacy raster 2D CAD drawings either process only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and none explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, thereby failing to exploit dimensional constraints for 3D parametric CAD recovery.

Method: Drawing-Recode uses an image encoder to extract geometric features from raster drawings, a text recognition module to recognize dimensional annotations, and cross-attention with a proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL) to explicitly ground annotations to geometric features. These grounded features are fed into an LLM to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format.

Result: Experiments show that Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions.

Conclusion: Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings, supporting part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

Abstract: Recovering Parametric CAD sequences from raster-format 2D Computer-Aided Design (CAD) drawings accumulated prior to digital transformation is important for part reproduction and manufacturing process automation. However, existing studies either process only vector drawings or are limited to specific domains, and fail to explicitly connect dimensional annotations to geometric information, limiting their use of dimensional information for 3D Parametric CAD sequences recovery. We propose Drawing-Recode, a framework that generates Parametric CAD sequences as CAD code from raster 2D CAD drawings. Drawing-Recode extracts geometric features via an image encoder and recognizes annotations through a separate text recognition module, then explicitly grounds annotations to geometric information using cross-attention and our proposed Annotation Grounding Loss (AGL). The resulting features are fed into a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate CAD code in the Structured Parametric CAD Code (SPCC) format. Experiments show that Drawing-Recode outperforms existing baselines and remains robust on scanned drawings resembling industrial conditions. We expect Drawing-Recode contributes to digitizing raster 2D CAD drawings in industrial settings and to part reproduction and manufacturing automation.

</details>


### [14] [Inference-Time Agentic Decision Rules Beat Longer Evolving Search for Multi-Image Medical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27564)
*Site Li,Jianyi Hao,Xiaofeng Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper studies MedFrameQA, a multi-image medical VQA task, showing that agentic decision-making—not prompt length—is the core challenge. Through a controlled comparison of five inference-time aggregation strategies with identical optimization budgets, the simple 'order-vote' policy achieves 57.89±0.65% accuracy, significantly outperforming both the fixed baseline (52.73%) and the more complex order-rerank variant (55.79%). Crucially, doubling the evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit (final-test accuracy actually drops to 56.02%), suggesting that defining the correct agentic decision rule matters more than expanding optimization search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a gap in multi-image medical VQA: while prior work treats multi-image problems primarily as a prompt-length or context-window challenge, the authors argue it is fundamentally an agentic decision-making problem requiring evidence aggregation across ordered images, robustness to answer-order perturbations, and resilience to noisy search-time feedback.

Method: The authors construct MedFrameQA and perform a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies (including order-vote, order-rerank, and a fixed baseline), all optimized with the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration. Experiments are conducted on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test) with five independent repeated runs, and significance is assessed via paired bootstrap analysis.

Result: The order-vote policy is the strongest strategy, achieving 57.89±0.65% final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline (52.73±0.42%) and the order-rerank variant (55.79±0.43%). Extending the evolutionary budget from 50 to 100 generations does not improve generalization: holdout improves marginally but final-test accuracy drops from 57.89% to 56.02%.

Conclusion: For multi-image medical reasoning, selecting the correct agentic decision rule (a simple robust aggregator) is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget. Simple, order-robust aggregation policies generalize better than both fixed baselines and more complex but brittle variants.

Abstract: Multi-image medical VQA is not merely a prompt-length problem; it is a fundamental challenge of agentic decision-making. Medical vision-language agents must aggregate evidence across ordered images, remain robust to answer-order perturbations, and avoid overfitting to noisy search-time feedback. We study MedFrameQA through a controlled comparison of five inference-time agentic strategies, optimized using the same high-budget ShinkaEvolve configuration and evaluated on a reproducible internal frozen split (1,331 evolution, 665 holdout, 855 final test). Across five independent repeated runs, the strongest method emerges as the simplest robust aggregator: the \textbf{order-vote} policy achieves $57.89 \pm 0.65\%$ final-test accuracy, significantly outperforming the fixed baseline ($52.73 \pm 0.42\%$) and the more complex, albeit brittle, order-rerank variant ($55.79 \pm 0.43\%$). Paired bootstrap analysis confirms these significant gains. Extending the evolutionary search budget from 50 to 100 generations yields no generalization benefit: while holdout performance marginally increases, final-test accuracy drops from $57.89\%$ to $56.02\%$. Our findings suggest that for multi-image medical reasoning, defining the correct agentic decision rule is substantially more impactful than expanding the optimization search budget.

</details>


### [15] [Objective-Aligned Direct Answer SFT for Robust Multi-Frame Medical VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27566)
*Site Li,Jianyi Hao,Xiaofeng Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: On MedFrameQA, direct decoder-only answer supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of MedGemma-1.5-4B is the strongest robust adaptation family, outperforming more complex approaches (controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, staged continuation) when evaluated under fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The multi-frame medical VQA community increasingly favors complex adaptation mechanisms (controller-style inference, localization reranking, hard-negative mixing, staged continuation). The authors hypothesize that simpler methods tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective are actually the most robust, but this competing hypothesis has not been rigorously tested under controlled evaluation conditions.

Method: Comparative evaluation of multiple adaptation families on MedFrameQA: controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Experiments are controlled across fixed splits, matched computational budgets, repeated seeds, and post-hoc calibration. Transfer is also tested on Qwen2.5-VL-3B as a secondary backbone.

Result: Direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B substantially improves held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining stable across repeated seeds and matched controls. Post-hoc calibration repairs confidence estimation without harming accuracy, and the approach transfers to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

Conclusion: Objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family for MedFrameQA, not complex auxiliary mechanisms. The paper calls for the community to focus on fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity, establishing a strong minimalist baseline.

Abstract: Multi-frame medical VQA appears to reward increasingly complex adaptation: controller-style inference, localization-aware reranking, static hard-negative mixing, and staged continuation all appear plausible from first principles. We test a simpler competing hypothesis on MedFrameQA: methods that remain tightly aligned with the benchmark's final answer objective should be the strongest \emph{robust} adaptation family once evaluation is controlled across fixed splits, matched budgets, repeated seeds, and calibration. We compare controller-based methods, scaffold evolution, static mixed supervision, continuation-heavy variants, and direct answer-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The strongest robust family is direct decoder-only answer SFT on MedGemma-1.5-4B. Empirically, this family yields substantial improvements in held-out report accuracy over frozen baselines while remaining remarkably stable across repeated seeds and matched controls, ensuring our claims reflect true family-level robustness rather than an isolated hyperparameter peak. Furthermore, post-hoc calibration effectively repairs confidence estimation without compromising accuracy, and the core approach transfers consistently to secondary backbones like Qwen2.5-VL-3B. The main result is therefore not that a complex auxiliary mechanism wins, but that objective-aligned direct answer SFT is the strongest robust adaptation family we found for MedFrameQA. By establishing this strong, minimalist baseline, we hope to redirect community focus toward fundamentally robust optimization rather than architectural complexity.

</details>


### [16] [ZMIS-SAM: Segment Anything Model Enhanced with Wavelet Transform for Zooplankton Microscopy Image Instance Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27585)
*Dekun Yuan,Zhongwei Li,Zheng Qiao,Jie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ZMIS-SAM is a novel instance segmentation model combining Segment Anything Model (SAM) with wavelet transforms, featuring three core modules (ZM-ViT, NFAM, WM2FE) to address zooplankton-specific challenges such as inaccurate classification, discontinuous slender appendage segmentation, and incomplete boundary segmentation. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on zooplankton datasets and strong cross-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SAM performs poorly on microscopic zooplankton image segmentation due to the lack of domain-specific knowledge and inherent challenges like semi-transparent slender appendages, discontinuous boundaries, and intensity variations in microscopic imagery.

Method: The framework integrates three innovations: (1) ZM-ViT enhances SAM's zooplankton morphology and intensity distribution modeling via two lightweight adapters; (2) NFAM (Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module) merges general-purpose and domain-specific features for continuous segmentation of semi-transparent appendages; (3) WM2FE (Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement) recovers high-frequency details for refined boundary completion.

Result: Extensive experiments show ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on zooplankton datasets and demonstrates strong generalization across multiple public cross-domain datasets.

Conclusion: By injecting zooplankton-specific knowledge into SAM's general-purpose segmentation capabilities and leveraging wavelet-based multi-scale feature enhancement, the proposed model effectively resolves the identified challenges and sets a new benchmark for marine zooplankton instance segmentation.

Abstract: As primary consumers in the marine food chain, zooplankton play a crucial role in maintaining marine ecological balance. However, the Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibits limited performance in microscopic image instance segmentation due to its lack of zooplankton-specific domain knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a novel instance segmentation model based on SAM and wavelet transform (ZMIS-SAM), effectively tackling issues such as inaccurate classification, discontinuous segmentation of slender appendages, and incomplete boundary segmentation. Our framework incorporates three core innovations: ZM-ViT enhances SAM's capability to model zooplankton morphology and image intensity distributions through two lightweight adapters, the Neighboring Feature Aggregation Module (NFAM) improves continuous segmentation of semi-transparent slender appendages by integrating general-purpose and domain-specific features, and the Wavelet-based Multi-scale Multi-directional Feature Enhancement (WM2FE) module effectively recovers high-frequency details to refine boundary segmentation completeness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZMIS-SAM achieves state-of-the-art instance segmentation performance on the zooplankton dataset and exhibits strong generalization capability across multiple public cross-domain datasets.

</details>


### [17] [MPIE-Bench: Benchmarking Anatomically Plausible Multi-Person Interaction Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27616)
*Jiajia Lin,Mingxuan Du,Tuowen Zhou,Benfeng Xu,Hongtao Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample video-mined benchmark for multi-person image editing, and MPIE-Eval, a mesh-based evaluation scoring anatomy and interaction geometry. Shows current editors and VLM judges fail at multi-person contact scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing text-to-image and personalized editing models struggle with multi-person contact actions (e.g., embrace, carry, grapple), producing fused limbs and interpenetrating bodies. Current evaluations overlook these anatomical/geometric issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists saturate while errors remain obvious to humans.

Method: Builds MPIE-Bench from video-mined editing triplets (405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, 4 contact densities C0-C3). Proposes MPIE-Eval using frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction to score two axes: Anatomy (every human-like mass explained by complete reconstructed bodies) and Interaction (penetration and surface distance match the requested contact).

Result: Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72, with no single editor strong on both. VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study shows both axes track human judgement better than zero-shot VLM judge; rankings hold under ablations of weights and thresholds.

Conclusion: Existing editors fail at multi-person contact generation despite high VLM checklist scores; mesh-based evaluation provides more reliable and human-aligned assessment of multi-person anatomy and interaction geometry.

Abstract: Text-to-image and personalized editing models now synthesize high-fidelity single-subject images with ease. Yet placing multiple named people into shared contact actions such as embrace, carry, or grapple still exposes major failures: fused limbs, invented extremities, and interpenetrating bodies. Existing evaluations largely overlook these anatomical and geometric issues, and VLM-as-a-judge checklists often saturate on Interaction while the errors remain obvious to humans. We introduce MPIE-Bench, a 2,500-sample benchmark of video-mined editing triplets spanning 405 scenes, 14 interaction categories, and four contact densities (C0-C3). We also propose MPIE-Eval, whose two new axes score contact-time geometry from a frozen public multi-person mesh reconstruction. Anatomy asks whether every human-like mass is explained by a complete set of reconstructed bodies, and Interaction asks whether the penetration and surface distance between those bodies match the contact the instruction asked for. Across ten editors, mesh Anatomy tops out at 0.65 and mesh Interaction at 0.72 on two different models, so no single editor is strong on both, while VLM checklists rate the same images above 0.95. A five-rater study confirms that both axes track human judgement more closely than a zero-shot VLM judge, and the rankings hold under ablation of every weight and threshold.

</details>


### [18] [MedXplore: Towards Reliable and Unbiased Generalized Category Discovery in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27620)
*Jianwei He,Kailin Lyu,Junhao Dong,Long Xiao,Wenjie Hou,Jingze Lu,Di Wu,Lin Shu,Jie Hao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MedXplore is a unified framework for Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) in medical imaging that jointly optimizes perceptual and decision levels via Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) and Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM), achieving an average 8.5% improvement in All accuracy and reducing false-old errors from 14.50% to 0.80% on Kvasir.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most deep learning methods in medical imaging rely on large-scale annotations and a closed-world assumption that rarely holds in clinical practice. While GCD has advanced on natural images, it remains largely underexplored in medical imaging, leaving a gap in discovering both known and novel categories from unlabeled medical data.

Method: MedXplore optimizes from two levels: (1) Perceptual level - Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to highlight local abnormal signals relative to global context and provide reliable semantic anchors for patch consistency learning; (2) Decision level - Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average 8.5% gain in All accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On Kvasir, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50% to 0.80%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.

Conclusion: The two modules together improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias, providing a reliable and unbiased medical GCD solution that effectively addresses the gap in applying GCD to medical imaging.

Abstract: Deep learning has shown strong potential in medical image analysis, but most existing methods rely on large-scale annotations and a closed-world assumption that rarely holds in clinical practice. Although Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) has advanced rapidly on natural images, it remains underexplored in medical imaging. To address this issue, we propose MedXplore, a unified framework for reliable and unbiased medical GCD, optimizing from both perceptual and decision levels. Specifically, at the perceptual level, taking a frequency domain perspective, Frequency-SNR Adaptive Attention and Consistency (FAAC) performs learnable full-spectrum filtering and global-local energy contrast activation to not only highlight local abnormal signals relative to the global context, but also provide reliable semantic anchors for patch consistency learning. At the decision level, Adaptive Cosine-Angular Margin (ACAM) adjusts angular margins using semantic difficulty and feature confidence to balance intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Together, the two modules improve lesion-sensitive representation learning and mitigate old-class bias. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show an average \textbf{8.5\%} gain in \textit{All} accuracy over the strongest competing methods. On Kvasir, MedXplore reduces false-old errors from 14.50\% to 0.80\%, demonstrating strong robustness under severe old-new ambiguity.

</details>


### [19] [BlindPSNR: A No-Reference Fidelity Predictor for Low-Light Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27628)
*Mingzhe Lyu,Jinqiang Cui,Hong Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BlindPSNR is a lightweight no-reference network that predicts ground-truth PSNR for low-light image enhancement without a reference image, enabling automatic selection of enhancement parameters. It fuses the enhanced image with the degraded input via windowed cross-attention and uses heteroscedastic regression, achieving 89.5% top-1 selection accuracy versus 54.4% for scalar regression baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-light image enhancement methods rely on tunable parameters that are typically fixed, leading to performance degradation across different scenes. Manual parameter selection is time-consuming, and while PSNR is the natural fidelity criterion for automating this selection, it requires a ground-truth reference that is typically unavailable. Existing NR-IQA methods target perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity and completely fail (0% top-1 accuracy) on parameter selection tasks.

Method: BlindPSNR leverages paired training data where ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a teacher network. The architecture is a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention, and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression.

Result: BlindPSNR achieves 89.5% top-1 parameter selection accuracy compared to 54.4% for a scalar-regression baseline, reducing regret from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB. It also generalizes to unseen datasets with Spearman rank correlation coefficients of 0.61-0.67. All seven existing NR-IQA baselines achieve 0% top-1 accuracy on the benchmark.

Conclusion: BlindPSNR demonstrates that no-reference PSNR prediction is feasible and highly effective for automating parameter selection in low-light image enhancement, significantly outperforming perceptual quality-based alternatives and generalizing across unseen datasets.

Abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) methods involve tunable parameters that are typically fixed, often leading to performance degradation when applied across scenes. Manually selecting the best configuration, however, can be time-consuming and not always practical. Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) is the natural fidelity criterion for automating parameter selection, yet it requires a ground-truth reference that is typically unavailable. To our knowledge, no learning-based method addresses no-reference PSNR prediction for low-light image enhancement; the natural surrogate, no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA), targets perceptual quality rather than signal fidelity, and all seven baselines we test achieve 0% top-1 selection accuracy on our benchmark. With paired training data, the ground-truth PSNR is analytically computable, providing exact supervision without a separate teacher network. Building on this, we propose BlindPSNR, a lightweight no-reference network that fuses the enhanced image with the degraded low-light input via windowed cross-attention and estimates PSNR through heteroscedastic regression. While a scalar-regression baseline achieves top-1 accuracy of 54.4%, BlindPSNR raises this to 89.5% with regret dropping from 1.62 dB to 0.026 dB, and generalizes to unseen datasets (SRCC = 0.61-0.67).

</details>


### [20] [4DHumanDiff: Direct Text-to-4DGS Generation for Consistent 360-Degree Dynamic Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27634)
*Renlong Wu,Haoran Chen,Yuxiang Wei,Xiaowei Jin,Wangmeng Zuo,Hui Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: 4DHumanDiff is a diffusion framework that directly generates 360-degree dynamic human assets as 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) from text prompts, bypassing video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction. It uses a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention, a 60,000-pair text-to-4DGS dataset, 2D regularization, and training-free 4D interpolation to achieve consistent dynamic human generation in under one minute with 10x faster inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for generating 4D dynamic human assets from text typically synthesize monocular/multi-view videos first then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and suffers from incomplete geometry and view-inconsistent renderings. The goal is to directly generate high-fidelity 360-degree dynamic humans in a unified, efficient framework.

Method: A diffusion framework that models the structured 4D Gaussian Splatting representation space end-to-end, using a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation. It includes a large-scale text-to-4DGS dataset (60,000 pairs), 2D regularization for improved rendering quality, and training-free 4D interpolation for enhanced motion smoothness.

Result: The model generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency compared to prior approaches, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.

Conclusion: Directly generating 4D Gaussian Splatting representations with diffusion models is a viable and efficient alternative to video-then-reconstruction pipelines, enabling fast, view-consistent, and temporally coherent dynamic human asset generation from text.

Abstract: Generating high-quality 360-degree dynamic human assets from text prompts is challenging. Existing methods usually synthesize monocular or multi-view videos first and then fit a 4D representation, which is expensive and often causes incomplete geometry or view-inconsistent renderings. We present 4DHumanDiff, a diffusion framework that directly generates dynamic humans represented by 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) from text prompts. By modeling the structured 4D representation space end-to-end, 4DHumanDiff avoids video pre-generation and per-scene reconstruction, making it better suited for view-consistent and temporally coherent asset generation. The model uses a 3D U-Net backbone with temporal attention for motion-aware generation. We further construct a large-scale text-to-4DGS dataset with 60,000 high-quality pairs, and introduce 2D regularization and training-free 4D interpolation to improve rendering quality and motion smoothness. Experiments show that 4DHumanDiff generates consistent 360-degree dynamic humans within one minute, achieves better temporal and multi-view consistency, and reduces inference time by more than 10x.

</details>


### [21] [MMOOC: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Out-of-Context Evaluation in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27637)
*Wenjie Zhu,Yabin Zhang,Wenjun Zeng,Lei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark with over 41K image-question pairs designed to evaluate Multimodal Large Language Models' (MLLMs) ability to both refuse truly out-of-context (OOC) questions with subject-level context shifts while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions with non-subject context shifts. The benchmark spans three question formats, eight shift types, and six visual scenarios, with experiments showing current MLLMs struggle to balance answerability and refusal under shifted contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks primarily target OOC or visually unanswerable questions but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shifts. A reliable MLLM should refuse truly OOC questions while still answering Shifted IC questions, yet this balanced capability has not been properly benchmarked.

Method: The authors construct MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark containing 41K+ image-question pairs covering both answerable Shifted IC cases and unanswerable OOC cases across three question formats, eight shift types, and six visual scenarios. Data quality is ensured via MLLM-based filtering and human verification. Evaluation uses Accuracy and Refusal Rate, plus a novel LLM-as-a-Judge metric for assessing reasoning correctness.

Result: Experiments on diverse MLLMs show current models still struggle to balance answerability and refusal under shifted contexts. Key failure patterns are analyzed, and post-training is shown to improve robustness.

Conclusion: Current MLLMs have difficulty maintaining the appropriate balance between answering and refusing under shifted contexts, and the MMOOC benchmark provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating and improving this capability. The benchmark will be publicly released.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of vision-language tasks, but often fail under imperfect or shifted contexts. A reliable MLLM should refuse truly out-of-context (OOC) questions with subject-level context shifts while still answering shifted in-context (Shifted IC) questions with non-subject context shifts. Existing benchmarks mainly target OOC or visually unanswerable questions, but overlook answerable Shifted IC cases and cover limited OOC shifts. To fill this gap, we present MMOOC, a large-scale benchmark for evaluating refusal and robust answering abilities of MLLMs. MMOOC contains over 41K image-question pairs, including answerable Shifted IC cases and unanswerable OOC cases, spanning three question formats, eight shift types and six visual scenarios, with data quality ensured through MLLM-based filtering and human verification. We evaluate model responses using Accuracy and Refusal Rate, and further introduce an LLM-as-a-Judge metric to assess the correctness of model reasoning. Experiments on diverse MLLMs show that current models still struggle to balance answer-ability and refusal under shifted contexts. We further analyze key failure patterns and show that post-training can improve robustness. MMOOC will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [22] [Learning Color Grading, No Photo Sharing: Federated Aesthetic Preference Learning for Personalized Image Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27659)
*Chuanzhi Xu,Ziyuan Tao,Jean Julien KNell,Yanrong Chen,Haolan Guo,Xuanhua Yin,Adnan Mahmood,Weidong Cai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedPAIE is a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework for user-adaptive color grading. It trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs—all without centralizing raw photos or ratings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized image enhancement must reflect individual aesthetic taste, but learning such preferences relies on private photos and ratings unsuitable for centralized collection. The task requires inferring preference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback and translating it into natural color transformations on resource-constrained devices.

Method: FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance.

Result: Training remains lightweight: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity.

Conclusion: FedPAIE connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches, achieving effective personalization while keeping computation and data privacy constraints satisfied.

Abstract: Personalized image enhancement should reflect individual aesthetic taste, yet learning such preferences commonly depends on private photos and ratings that are unsuitable for centralized collection. The task must infer preference from sparse, heterogeneous feedback and translate it into natural-looking color transformations on resource-constrained user devices. We introduce FedPAIE, a federated personalized aesthetic image enhancement framework for user-adaptive color grading without centralizing raw photos or ratings. FedPAIE trains a lightweight dual-cue aesthetic scorer, calibrates it into a personalized scorer on a small local support set, and freezes it to guide regularized adaptation of a lightweight CLUT enhancer from unpaired local photographs. Fidelity constraints and an excess-gap penalty regularize scorer-guided adaptation to limit proxy-score over-optimization while preserving content and natural appearance. Training remains lightweight throughout the pipeline: scorer learning updates at most 0.787M parameters, enhancer adaptation updates 0.265M, and inference retains only a 0.293M-parameter personalized enhancer. Experiments on MIT-Adobe FiveK and Flickr-AES demonstrate effective open-world personalization and a favorable balance between user preference and image fidelity. FedPAIE thus connects decentralized preference learning with efficient personalized image transformation without requiring paired user retouches.

</details>


### [23] [Witness Evidence Portfolios: Single-Prefill Risk Detection for Closed Multimodal Answers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27667)
*Fexiang Liu,Shiye Wang,Qiang Qiu,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WEP is an inference-time risk detection method for MLLMs that estimates layer-by-layer which visual contributions support or contradict a predicted candidate answer, summarizes them via question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration, and fuses a sparse top-k route portfolio with candidate confidence to decide whether an answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Confidence scores from MLLMs capture candidate margins but not the provenance or distribution of the signed visual readouts underlying those margins. Reliable deployment requires knowing whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or escalated, and existing confidence signals are insufficient for this decision.

Method: WEP uses the white-box prefill path to estimate, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes contributions via two interpretable route families (question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration), uses nested grouped validation to select the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, and fuses this with candidate confidence. It requires no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier.

Result: Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model-dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs.

Conclusion: WEP provides an effective, perturbation-free, white-box inference-time risk detection method for closed-answer MLLM systems, improving reliability decisions over confidence-only baselines using only a labeled calibration slice.

Abstract: Reliable deployment of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) requires deciding whether a confident visual answer should be trusted, reviewed, or routed to a stronger system.
