Confidence scores capture candidate margins, but not where the estimated signed visual readouts associated with those margins come from or how they are distributed. We study inference-time risk detection for closed visual answers using the same white-box prefill path that produces the answer. Witness Evidence Portfolios (WEP) first estimates, layer by layer, which visual contributions support or contradict the predicted candidate. It summarizes these contributions through two interpretable route families: question-related evidence provenance and signed evidence concentration. Nested grouped validation chooses the more reliable family and a sparse top-k route portfolio, which is fused with candidate confidence. WEP needs no image perturbation, decoding change, backward pass, or external verifier. Across three MLLMs and four binary-answer benchmarks, WEP improves mean error AP by 0.134. All 12 model--dataset gains are positive, and image-cluster bootstrap intervals are strictly positive on 10 pairs. WEP targets white-box closed-answer systems and uses a labeled calibration slice.

</details>


### [24] [JigShape: Evaluating Visual-Geometric Reasoning in VLMs through Jigsaw Puzzles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27670)
*Shawn Li,Wei Yang,Jike Zhong,Jiate Li,Jiawei Yang,You Qin,Ryan Rossi,Franck Dernoncourt,Roger Zimmermann,Yue Wang,Zhengzhong Tu,Vicente Ordonez,Mohit Bansal,Yue Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a jigsaw puzzle benchmark called \ours{} featuring tab-and-blank interlocking pieces that provide unambiguous ground truth even in texture-repeated regions. Across 95K instances from 4×4 to 16×16 grids, zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning (only GPT-5.5 exceeds random on 4×4), and all models collapse on larger grids—a "scaling cliff" revealing current architectures cannot maintain constraint satisfaction as puzzle size increases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing jigsaw puzzle benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions, making it difficult to assess whether models truly reason about geometric constraints versus relying on visual content alone.

Method: The authors design a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking jigsaw pieces, where geometric constraints (the interlocking shapes) provide strong local compatibility requirements that, combined with visual content, yield unambiguous ground truth. They create 95K instances across four grid densities (4×4 to 16×16) and evaluate five frontier VLMs in zero-shot settings, plus supervised fine-tuned models.

Result: Only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4×4 puzzles; all others perform at chance level in zero-shot. Supervised fine-tuning achieves >97% on 4×4, but all models collapse on larger grids: GPT-5.5 drops from 70% to near-random on 8×8, and fine-tuned models fall below 5% on 12×12.

Conclusion: Current vision-language model architectures exhibit a "scaling cliff"—they cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of puzzle pieces increases. This establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

Abstract: Jigsaw puzzle solving requires jointly reasoning about visual content and geometric constraints, yet existing benchmarks use rectangular cuts that create ambiguous ground truth in texture-repeated regions. We introduce \textit{\ours{}}, a benchmark with tab-and-blank interlocking pieces where geometric constraints provide strong local compatibility requirements that, combined with visual content, yield unambiguous ground truth. Across 95K instances at four grid densities (4$\times$4 to 16$\times$16), we find that \textbf{zero-shot VLMs largely lack geometric reasoning}: only one of five frontier models (GPT-5.5) exceeds random baseline on 4$\times$4 puzzles, while all others perform at chance level. While supervised fine-tuning achieves $>$97\% on 4$\times$4, \textbf{all models collapse on larger grids}: GPT-5.5 drops from 70\% to near-random on 8$\times$8, and even fine-tuned models fall below 5\% on 12$\times$12. This ``scaling cliff'' suggests current architectures cannot maintain consistent constraint satisfaction as the number of pieces increases. \ours{} establishes scalable geometric reasoning as an open challenge for vision-language models.

</details>


### [25] [RefineSVG: Visual Feedback-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Image-to-SVG Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27699)
*Shaobo Liu,Feiqiao Mao,Shuaishuai Zhou,Yan Zhan,Weiqi Tan,Zhiqiong Lu,Zhengping Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RefineSVG is a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that improves multimodal large language models' (MLLMs) image-to-SVG generation by using an external rendering engine to compare rendered output with the target image, generating a Diff-Map correction signal that drives targeted self-correction, supported by an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary, progressive training pipeline, and agentic reinforcement learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based SVG generation methods rely on single-pass open-loop inference where the model sees the input only once and generates thousands of SVG tokens without intermediate verification, leading to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images. This necessitates a closed-loop self-correction mechanism.

Method: RefineSVG invokes an external rendering engine after initial SVG generation to compare the rendered output against the target image, producing a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) that is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal. The method introduces an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary compressing token sequences by over 52%, and uses a progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning.

Result: Extensive experiments show that RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.

Conclusion: The closed-loop render-observe-correct paradigm with visual residual feedback significantly improves high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation, demonstrating the value of intermediate verification for MLLM-based structured output generation.

Abstract: We propose RefineSVG, a single-step closed-loop visual feedback framework that enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform high-fidelity image-to-SVG generation through self-correction. Existing MLLM-based approaches rely on single-pass open-loop inference, where the model receives visual input only once and must generate thousands of SVG code tokens without intermediate verification. This paradigm inevitably leads to geometric drift, error accumulation, and visual hallucination on complex images. RefineSVG overcomes this limitation by invoking an external rendering engine after an initial SVG generation pass to compare the rendered output against the target image. The comparison yields a multi-dimensional visual residual map (Diff-Map) that is fed back to the model as a ReAct-style correction signal, driving a targeted correction step. To support this render-observe-correct interaction, we further introduce an SVG-oriented semantic vocabulary that compresses token sequences by over 52%. A progressive training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampling cold-start data construction, and end-to-end agentic reinforcement learning aligns the model with closed-loop visual correction. Extensive experiments show that RefineSVG consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity, structural accuracy, and code efficiency.Code is available at https://github.com/liuxiaobo66/RefineSVG.

</details>


### [26] [Calibrate Before Reason: Robust Visual Token Reduction against Semantic Drift in VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27700)
*Jiasheng Li,Zhong Ji,Yan Zhang,Huihui Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CaRe is a training-free framework for visual token reduction in VLMs that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning, using perturbation-robust calibration anchoring and confidence-gated token calibration to preserve semantic fidelity while pruning up to 94.4% of visual tokens with only 3.6% performance loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large VLMs suffer from prohibitive inference overhead due to long sequences of visual tokens. Existing visual token reduction methods improve efficiency by pruning/compressing redundant tokens but fail to examine whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original, leading to severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding.

Method: CaRe introduces the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' and consists of two modules: (1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; and (2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors.

Result: CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, it retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance, delivering up to 2.30x faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.

Conclusion: Calibrating compact visual representations before reasoning is a training-free and effective way to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs while achieving significant efficiency gains, demonstrating that token reduction methods should not only focus on compression but also on maintaining semantic consistency.

Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) suffer from prohibitive inference overhead due to long sequences of visual tokens. However, existing visual token reduction methods mainly improve efficiency by pruning or compressing redundant tokens without examining whether the resulting representation remains semantically consistent with the original representation. Mapping the original N-token visual sequence to K tokens may discard, dilute, or misassign critical visual cues, triggering severe semantic drift that deviates the VLM's understanding. In this paper, we first introduce the principle of 'Calibrate Before Reason' to visual token reduction and propose CaRe, a training-free robust framework that calibrates compact visual representations before reasoning to preserve semantic fidelity in VLMs. CaRe consists of two mutually complementary modules: 1) Perturbation-Robust Calibration Anchoring, which identifies calibration anchors with stable model-side influence under multi-directional perturbations; 2) Confidence-Gated Token Calibration, which extracts reliable calibration signals from unselected tokens and injects them into anchors. Extensive evaluations across diverse VLM architectures and benchmarks verify that CaRe outperforms state-of-the-art token reduction baselines. While pruning 94.4% of visual tokens, our method retains 96.4% of the original full-token performance, delivering up to 2.30 times faster end-to-end inference speed relative to unpruned vanilla models.

</details>


### [27] [PrintAnything: Learning an Intermediate Representation for 3D printing G-code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27729)
*Sangmin Hong,Daniel Sungho Jung,Heewon Kim,Kyoung Mu Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PrintAnything is a novel framework that directly generates executable 3D printing G-code from point clouds, bypassing mesh reconstruction entirely. It introduces a slice-wise point projection strategy to convert unstructured point clouds into layer-aligned 2D representations and a Geometric plan (G-plan) map (occupancy, region, and flow maps) that encodes geometry and extrusion properties, enabling a fully mesh-free 3D printing pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most 3D printing pipelines require watertight meshes as input, preventing direct use of point clouds (a fundamental 3D representation). Mesh reconstruction from point clouds often produces geometric artifacts and topological inconsistencies that are difficult to repair and may cause printing failures.

Method: The framework proposes: (1) a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with the layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling; and (2) a Geometric plan (G-plan) map, a compact 2D representation comprising occupancy, region, and flow maps that encode geometric and extrusion properties needed for toolpath synthesis. These enable direct G-code generation from point clouds without mesh reconstruction.

Result: The proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, enabling a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing. Code is publicly available.

Conclusion: PrintAnything demonstrates that direct point-cloud-to-G-code generation is feasible, eliminating mesh dependency in the 3D printing pipeline and overcoming artifacts associated with mesh reconstruction.

Abstract: Point clouds are one of the most fundamental and widely used 3D representations, serving as the most basic geometric representation of 3D shapes. Nevertheless, most existing 3D printing pipelines require a watertight mesh as input, preventing the direct use of point clouds for fabrication. A common workaround is to reconstruct meshes from point clouds; however, the resulting meshes often contain geometric artifacts, such as incorrect faces or topological inconsistencies, that are difficult to repair and may lead to printing failures. To overcome these limitations, we propose PrintAnything, a novel framework that learns to produce executable 3D printing G-code directly from 3D point clouds without requiring mesh reconstruction. To enable point clouds to serve as direct input for slice-wise toolpath generation, we introduce a slice-wise point projection strategy that transforms unstructured 3D point clouds into slice-aligned 2D representations consistent with layer-by-layer nature of fused deposition modeling in 3D printing. To eliminate mesh dependency and provide a unified representation that bridges point clouds and G-code, we propose Geometric plan (G-plan) map, a compact 2D representation composed of occupancy, region, and flow maps that encode the geometric and extrusion properties required for toolpath synthesis in 3D printing. As a result, our proposed method accurately generates printable G-code directly from point clouds, enabling a practical and fully mesh-free pipeline for 3D printing. The code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/Sangminhong/PrintAnything}{https://github.com/Sangminhong/PrintAnything}.

</details>


### [28] [Articulated Object Reconstruction from Rest-State Observation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27749)
*Daeun Lee,Jaeah Lee,Woosung Kim,Haebeom Jung,Jaesik Park*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces a rest-state formulation for reconstructing articulated objects (3D geometry + kinematic structure) from a single closed configuration, using explicit mesh intermediates for cross-model fusion and video-diffusion-synthesized articulation hypotheses validated via geometric consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for articulated object reconstruction require observable motion from multiple articulation states, which is restrictive. This work aims to recover both geometry and kinematic structures from a single closed configuration—an ill-posed problem that needs geometry, semantics, and motion priors to compensate for missing motion cues.

Method: The framework uses an explicit mesh as an intermediate representation for cross-model verification and fusion, reconciling noisy outputs from vision-language and segmentation models into spatially consistent part structures. To estimate joint parameters without observed motion, it leverages a video diffusion model to synthesize articulation hypotheses, which are then validated through geometric consistency.

Result: The approach achieves accurate part decomposition and physically plausible articulation, performing competitively with motion-observing reconstruction-based, generation-based, and modular pretrained-model baselines.

Conclusion: Articulated object reconstruction is feasible from a single closed configuration using rest-state formulation with priors, yielding competitive performance against methods that observe motion.

Abstract: Building interactive digital twins requires recovering both 3D geometry and the kinematic structures that govern how objects articulate. Yet existing methods for articulated object reconstruction require explicitly observable motion from multiple articulation states. We introduce a rest-state formulation that reconstructs articulated objects from a single closed configuration, an inherently ill-posed setting where geometry, semantics, and motion priors compensate for the absence of motion cues. Our framework adopts an explicit mesh as an intermediate representation for cross-model verification and fusion, reconciling noisy outputs from vision-language and segmentation models into spatially consistent part structures. To estimate joint parameters without observed motion, we use a video diffusion model to synthesize articulation hypotheses and validate them through geometric consistency. Our approach achieves accurate part decomposition and physically plausible articulation, performing competitively with motion-observing reconstruction-based, generation-based, and modular pretrained-model baselines.

</details>


### [29] [EgoGVAE: Ego-body Mesh Reconstruction via Guided Variational Autoencoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27755)
*Jaehun Jung,Wonjun Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a fast method for full-body mesh reconstruction from head pose only, using a variational autoencoder as a guidance network whose latent distribution regularizes a head-to-motion network, enabling one-step inference that is over 50x faster than diffusion-based approaches while improving reconstruction performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recovering full-body mesh from head pose alone is essential for head-mounted device and smart glass applications, but existing head-conditioned generative models rely on costly diffusion-based iterative processes that are time-consuming. A faster yet accurate alternative is needed.

Method: The method uses a guidance network (a variational autoencoder trained on full-body poses) to enforce similarity between its latent distribution and that of a head-to-motion network. By aligning these latent distributions, latent features sampled from the head-to-motion network can be reliably decoded into natural full-body poses using only head pose input, via a one-step sampling scheme.

Result: The proposed method achieves inference over 50 times faster than diffusion-based approaches due to one-step sampling, while improving ego-body mesh reconstruction performance on benchmark datasets.

Conclusion: A simple VAE-guided latent distribution alignment enables fast and accurate full-body mesh reconstruction from head pose, offering an efficient alternative to diffusion-based generative methods for head-mounted device applications.

Abstract: We address the problem of recovering the full-body mesh from only the head pose. This task has become essential for various applications based on head-mounted devices or smart glasses. The challenge of this task lies in estimating the pose information of unobserved body parts based solely on a single joint (i.e., head) trajectory. Several studies have begun to adopt head-conditioned generative models, however, such previous methods are costly and time-consuming due to the diffusion-based iterative process. As an alternative, we propose a simple yet novel method that leverages the latent space of the guidance network, which is designed as a variational autoencoder taking full-body poses as inputs. By enforcing latent distributions of this guidance network and our head-to-motion network to be similar, latent features sampled from the 'guided' distribution, i.e., distribution learned in our head-to-motion network, can be reliably decoded for natural representations of full-body poses even only with the head pose. One important advantage of the proposed method is that one-step sampling scheme achieves remarkably fast inference (more than 50 times faster) compared to diffusion-based approaches. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that the proposed method efficiently improves the performance of ego-body mesh reconstruction.

</details>


### [30] [DS@GT ARC at ImageCLEFmedical 2026: Architectural Diversity for Concept Detection and Foundation-Model Scaling for Caption Prediction in Medical Image Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27763)
*Bowen Wang,Youwen Zhang,Ritesh Mehta*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DS@GT's ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026 system: for Task 1, a three-way ensemble (ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, DenseNet-169) with Honest Threshold Tuning ranked 1st (F1 0.5790), while a training-free KNN retrieval pipeline nearly matched it (F1 0.5780); for Task 2, a fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B ranked 3rd (0.3571), alongside fine-tuned BLIP and zero-shot MedGemma-4B runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026 benchmark on ROCOv2, tackling both Concept Detection (UMLS CUI assignment) and Caption Prediction, while studying cost-performance tradeoffs between fine-tuned ensembles, training-free retrieval, and large language models across different scales.

Method: Task 1: three-way late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, and DenseNet-169 with a regularized "Honest Threshold Tuning" procedure to prevent validation overfitting on rare concepts; plus a training-free KNN retrieval pipeline over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings. Task 2: fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B, fully fine-tuned BLIP with custom Vizwins merging, and zero-shot MedGemma-4B with PubMed-style prompting.

Result: Task 1: ensemble ranked 1st with primary F1 0.5790 and secondary F1 0.9657; KNN retrieval achieved primary F1 0.5780 and secondary F1 0.9599. Task 2: Gemma-3 27B ranked 3rd with 0.3571, fine-tuned BLIP 0.3564, zero-shot MedGemma-4B 0.3186.

Conclusion: The team achieved top rank in Concept Detection while demonstrating that a training-free KNN approach can nearly match a fine-tuned ensemble at a fraction of the cost; for captioning, spanning model scales from 4B to 27B showed competitive performance with fine-tuned large language models and multimodal architectures.

Abstract: We describe the DS@GT submissions to the ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026 challenge, which continues a long-running benchmark on the ROCOv2 dataset with two tracks: Concept Detection (Task 1), assigning UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs) to radiology images, and Caption Prediction (Task 2), generating natural-language captions. For Task 1, our primary submission was a three-way late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, and DenseNet-169 with a regularized ''Honest Threshold Tuning'' procedure designed to avoid validation overfitting on rare concepts; this submission ranked first on the official submission with a primary $F_1$ of $0.5790$ and a secondary $F_1$ of $0.9657$. In parallel, we submitted a training-free KNN retrieval pipeline over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings, which reached a primary $F_1$ of $0.5780$ and a secondary $F_1$ of $0.9599$-essentially matching the fine-tuned ensemble on the primary track at a fraction of the cost. For Task 2, our submissions included a fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B model (overall $0.3571$, ranking third in the official submission), a fully fine-tuned BLIP pipeline with custom Vizwins merging ($0.3564$), and a zero-shot MedGemma-4B run with a PubMed-style prompt ($0.3186$), spanning a wide range of model scales and training costs. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/imageclef-caption-2026.

</details>


### [31] [Private Face Recognition Training Dataset Publication via Identity-Decoupled and Geometry-Preserving Face Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27764)
*Shuhuan Chen,Xiangyu Zhu,Weisong Zhao,Siran Peng,Tianshuo Zhang,Haoyuan Zhang,Haichao Shi,Xiao-Yu Zhang,Zhen Lei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes Private Face Distillation, a framework that decouples source-identity semantics from recognition-useful proxy identity geometry to enable privacy-preserving face recognition training dataset publication. It achieves stronger utility than baselines while reducing source-identity linkability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Publishing private face recognition training datasets is privacy-sensitive because faces expose identity information. Existing protected proxy approaches face an "identity paradox": identity cues making released faces useful for recognition are the same cues making them linkable to real individuals. Removing cues too aggressively destroys class structure for recognition learning, while preserving them too faithfully increases linkability.

Method: The proposed Private Face Distillation framework has two key components: (1) Orthogonal Geometry Preservation, which constructs decoupled proxy identities from private identity representations while maintaining hyperspherical geometry, and (2) Relational Topology Alignment, which preserves identity relations for recognition learning. The core insight is separating source-aligned identity semantics (to be suppressed) from recognition-useful proxy identity geometry (to be preserved).

Result: On IJB-C surveillance, Private Face Distillation improves TAR@FAR=1e-3 by 3.94% over the baseline while reducing source-identity linkability. Experiments across multiple domain-shifted FR scenarios show stronger utility than evaluated publication baselines.

Conclusion: Private FR training dataset publication should decouple source-identity correspondence while preserving proxy identity geometry, as demonstrated by the success of Private Face Distillation.

Abstract: Publishing private face recognition~(FR) training datasets is privacy-sensitive because faces expose identity information. Private FR training dataset publication mitigates this risk by releasing protected proxies as substitutes for private training faces. However, training FR models with such data introduces an identity paradox: \emph{the identity cues that make released faces useful for recognition supervision are also the cues that make them linkable to real individuals.} A protected face should be decoupled from the original identity, yet still behave as a reliable identity sample for training. Removing these cues too aggressively may destroy the class structure needed for recognition learning, whereas preserving them too faithfully may increase source-identity linkability. We argue that this paradox stems from conflating source-aligned identity semantics with recognition-useful proxy identity geometry. The former should be suppressed to reduce linkage to private individuals, while the latter should be preserved for FR learning. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{Private Face Distillation}, an identity-decoupling and geometry-preserving framework. It uses Orthogonal Geometry Preservation to construct decoupled proxy identities from private identity representations while maintaining hyperspherical geometry, and Relational Topology Alignment to preserve identity relations for recognition learning. Experiments across multiple domain-shifted FR scenarios show that Private Face Distillation achieves stronger utility than the evaluated publication baselines. On IJB-C surveillance, it improves $\mathrm{TAR}@\mathrm{FAR}{=}1\text{e-}{3}$ by 3.94\% over the baseline while reducing source-identity linkability. These results suggest that private FR training dataset publication should decouple source-identity correspondence while preserving proxy identity geometry.

</details>


### [32] [CXR-Retrieve: Compositional Text-to-Image Retrieval in Chest Radiography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27779)
*Tomer Erez,Moshe Kimhi,Chaim Baskin,Ehud Rivlin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CXR-Retrieve is a structured benchmark for compositional chest X-ray text-to-image retrieval, containing 5,159 test images and 145 textual queries covering single and conjunction findings with positive and negative constraints. The paper also proposes a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective that models both which findings are mentioned and how they are clinically asserted, improving Precision@5 over CXR-CLIP by 8.5 points on two-pathology conjunctions and 22.0 points on negation queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large chest radiography archives are hard to search because studies are paired with free-text reports rather than structured annotations. Existing biomedical vision-language models are optimized for report-to-image matching, which creates an objective mismatch when satisfying short clinical queries involving conjunctions and negations (e.g., "atelectasis and no pneumonia")—a model may retrieve images matching query words while failing the full clinical constraint.

Method: The paper introduces CXR-Retrieve, a benchmark built from the official test-split of MIMIC-CXR-JPG with 5,159 test images and 145 textual queries spanning single and conjunction findings, both positive and negative. Relevance is defined by whether an image satisfies all asserted pathology constraints rather than matching a paired report. The paper further proposes a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective that attracts image-text pairs with compatible asserted pathology constraints (including shared confirmed absences) while repelling contradictory pairs, starting from the CXR-CLIP checkpoint.

Result: The proposed label-aware contrastive fine-tuning improves Precision@5 over CXR-CLIP by 8.5 percentage points on two-pathology conjunctions and by 22.0 percentage points on negation queries.

Conclusion: Reliable chest X-ray retrieval requires training objectives that model not only which findings are mentioned in a query, but also how they are clinically asserted (e.g., presence vs. absence). The benchmark and training objective address the objective mismatch in current biomedical vision-language models for compositional clinical retrieval.

Abstract: Large chest radiography archives are difficult to search because most studies are paired only with free-text reports rather than structured clinical annotations. Vision-language models offer a natural interface for text-to-image retrieval, but current biomedical models are primarily optimized for report-to-image matching rather than for satisfying short clinical search queries. This creates an objective mismatch: a model may retrieve images related to words in the query while failing to satisfy the full clinical constraint, especially for conjunctions and negations such as ``atelectasis and no pneumonia.''
  We introduce CXR-Retrieve, a structured benchmark for compositional chest X-ray text-to-image retrieval. The benchmark contains 5,159 test images from the official test-split of MIMIC-CXR-JPG and 145 textual queries spanning single and conjunction findings, both positive and negative. Relevance is defined by whether a retrieved image satisfies all asserted pathology constraints, rather than by whether it matches a paired report.
  We further propose a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective for clinical retrieval. Our method attracts image-text pairs with compatible asserted pathology constraints, including shared confirmed absences, while explicitly repelling contradictory pairs. Starting from the in-domain CXR-CLIP checkpoint, our method improves Precision@5 over CXR-CLIP by 8.5 percentage points on two-pathology conjunctions and by 22.0 percentage points on negation queries. These results show that reliable chest X-ray retrieval requires training objectives that model not only which findings are mentioned, but also how they are clinically asserted.

</details>


### [33] [FDDWAN: A Frequency-Decoupled Diffusion Network for Watermarking Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27800)
*Chunpeng Wang,Yuxin Li,Xiaoyu Wang,Jidong Yang,Suo Gao,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FDDWAN is a coarse-to-fine framework for invisible watermark removal that decomposes watermarked images via wavelet transforms and uses residual diffusion refinement to achieve a better trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing invisible watermark removal methods fail to accurately capture watermark-bearing features, resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity.

Method: FDDWAN consists of two stages: (1) WFPAM decomposes the watermarked image into low- and high-frequency subbands using wavelets and applies frequency-specific attack strategies; (2) FRDAM models and selectively refines residual distributions in the frequency domain via a diffusion process, directing refinement toward remaining watermark-related discrepancies while minimizing content modifications.

Result: Experiments on CelebA and ImageNet across four representative watermarking schemes demonstrate that FDDWAN achieves a more favorable trade-off between watermark removal effectiveness and visual fidelity than conventional and learning-based attack methods.

Conclusion: The frequency-decoupled coarse-to-fine approach enables more precise watermark-bearing feature capture, leading to superior watermark removal with better preserved perceptual image quality.

Abstract: Existing invisible watermark removal methods often struggle to accurately capture the watermark-bearing features, leading to an unfavorable trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity. In this paper, we propose the Frequency-Decoupled Diffusion Watermark Attack Network (FDDWAN), a coarse-to-fine framework that performs watermark removal through wavelet-domain decomposition and residual diffusion refinement. In the initial stage, the Wavelet-based Frequency-domain Preliminary Attack Module (WFPAM) decomposes the watermarked image into low- and high-frequency subbands and applies frequency-specific attack strategies tailored to their respective contributions to watermark robustness and perceptual quality. In the next stage, the Frequency-domain Residual Diffusion Attack Module (FRDAM) separately models the residual distributions between the preliminarily attacked outputs and the corresponding watermark-free references during training. Rather than reconstructing the entire image, FRDAM selectively refines frequency-domain residuals, directing the diffusion process toward the remaining watermark related discrepancies while minimizing modifications to image content. Extensive experiments on CelebA and ImageNet across four representative watermarking schemes demonstrate that FDDWAN achieves a more favorable trade-off between watermark removal effectiveness and visual fidelity than conventional and learning-based attack methods.

</details>


### [34] [LoMeVQA: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Longitudinal Medical VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27806)
*Zhilin Wu,Zhangkai Ni,Chengmei Yang,Longzhen Yang,Yihang Liu,Ying Wen,Lianghua He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces LoMeVQA, a comprehensive benchmark with 206K longitudinal visual question answering pairs for temporal medical image analysis, covering five tasks. The authors also propose MedLong-8B, an MLLM that achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks, and provide detailed analyses of failure modes in temporal medical reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), longitudinal medical visual reasoning—understanding how a patient's condition evolves across multiple imaging examinations over successive visits—remains largely underexplored. Modeling temporal information is critical for reliable assessment of disease progression and treatment response.

Method: The authors build LoMeVQA via an automated pipeline that (1) organizes patient records chronologically, (2) extracts clinically meaningful entities using a medical knowledge graph, and (3) models temporal evolution of those entities to guide large language models in generating high-quality longitudinal VQA pairs. Five tasks are covered: progress classification, progress description, progress report generation, differential region grounding, and differential region description. They also introduce MedLong-8B to address identified shortcomings.

Result: Extensive evaluations show that both general-purpose and medical-domain MLLMs perform poorly on LoMeVQA, revealing substantial limitations in temporal reasoning. MedLong-8B achieves state-of-the-art performance across all five tasks.

Conclusion: The benchmark exposes key shortcomings in existing MLLMs for temporal medical reasoning and demonstrates that MedLong-8B can significantly improve performance. The detailed analyses uncover critical failure modes and provide insights for advancing longitudinal medical visual reasoning. Data is publicly released.

Abstract: In clinical practice, patients often undergo multiple imaging examinations over successive visits, yielding longitudinal data. Modeling such temporal information is crucial for reliable assessment of disease progression and treatment response. However, despite the rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), longitudinal medical visual reasoning remains largely underexplored. To fill this gap, we propose LoMeVQA, a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 206K longitudinal visual question answering (VQA) pairs for temporal medical image analysis. LoMeVQA covers five tasks: progress classification, progress description, progress report generation, differential region grounding, and differential region description. To construct the dataset, we develop an automated pipeline that (1) organizes patient records chronologically, (2) extracts clinically meaningful entities via a medical knowledge graph, and (3) models their temporal evolution to guide large language models in generating high-quality longitudinal VQA pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that both general-purpose and medical-domain MLLMs perform poorly on LoMeVQA, revealing substantial limitations in temporal reasoning. To address these limitations, we introduce MedLong-8B, which achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct detailed analyses that uncover key failure modes and shed light on how to improve longitudinal medical visual reasoning. Our data is available at: https://github.com/pepperbubble/LoMeVQA

</details>


### [35] [SPFM-Net: Semantic-Prior-Guided Frequency-Constrained Mamba for Invisible Watermark Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27811)
*Chunpeng Wang,Yanan Shi,Zhiqiu Xia,Jidong Yang,Suo Gao,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPFM-Net is a semantic-prior-guided and frequency-constrained Mamba framework for invisible watermark attacks, combining high-ratio masking, a partially fine-tuned Masked Autoencoder, a Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module, and a Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling unit to remove watermarks while preserving perceptual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing watermark attacks rely on predefined signal-processing operations or locally constrained restoration networks, which fail to capture long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals, resulting in poor trade-offs between removal effectiveness and visual fidelity.

Method: SPFM-Net employs high-ratio masking to disrupt spatial coherence of watermark signals, a partially fine-tuned pretrained Masked Autoencoder for semantically consistent reconstruction while suppressing watermark information, a Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module for multi-receptive-field watermark residual aggregation, a lightweight Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling unit for long-range watermark feature separation, and a multi-level spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain objective for optimization.

Result: Extensive experiments across spatial-domain, transform-domain, orthogonal moment-based, and deep learning-based watermarking schemes demonstrate that SPFM-Net achieves a favorable trade-off between watermark attack effectiveness and perceptual fidelity.

Conclusion: SPFM-Net effectively captures long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals and achieves superior watermark removal while preserving visual quality, validated across diverse watermarking schemes.

Abstract: Existing watermark attacks typically rely on predefined signal-processing operations or locally constrained restoration networks, making it difficult to capture the long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals and resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between removal effectiveness and visual fidelity. In this paper, we propose SPFM-Net, a semantic-prior-guided and frequency-constrained Mamba framework for invisible watermark attack. SPFM-Net first employs high-ratio masking to disrupt the spatial coherence of invisible watermark signals, and then utilizes a partially fine-tuned pretrained Masked Autoencoder to reconstruct semantically consistent image from sparse observations while suppressing watermark-related information. A Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module subsequently aggregates watermark-related residual features across multiple receptive fields, while adaptively suppressing responses from watermark-irrelevant regions. To further capture the long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals, a lightweight Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling (GSFM) unit is introduced to separate watermark-related features from natural image content and suppress the remaining watermark traces. In addition, SPFM-Net is optimized using a multi-level objective that jointly imposes spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain constraints, enabling effective watermark suppression while preserving perceptual quality. Extensive experiments on representative spatial-domain, transform-domain, orthogonal moment-based, and deep learning-based watermarking schemes demonstrate that SPFM-Net achieves a favorable trade-off between watermark attack effectiveness and perceptual fidelity.

</details>


### [36] [Hallucinations Leave a Grounding Signature:Verifier-Guided Decoding for Selective Object Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27823)
*Lei Yang,Xinze Liu,Dayan Wu,Ding Wang,Hengjie Zhu,Zihao Zhang,Tianzhu Hu,Hanqi Wu,Peng Fu,Zheng Lin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Verifier-Guided Decoding (VGD), a decoding framework for large vision-language models that uses an Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS)—a distributed signed attention pattern encoding reliable object-level visual grounding evidence—to detect hallucinated object mentions during generation. VGD employs a lightweight verifier that inspects each emerging object mention, rolls back the KV cache for high-risk mentions, suppresses the object and its synonyms, and regenerates the affected continuation. This selective intervention reduces object hallucination while preserving visual understanding and grounded object coverage, achieving state-of-the-art results on CHAIR and AMBER-G benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large vision-language models frequently hallucinate objects absent from images. Existing mitigation methods lack reliable object-level grounding diagnostics, leading to coarse-grained interventions that impair visual understanding, shorten responses, and reduce coverage of genuinely grounded objects. The key challenge is detecting whether each emerging object mention is supported by reliable visual evidence during generation, since output confidence reflects next-token plausibility rather than actual visual support.

Method: The paper proposes VGD, a decoding framework built on the discovery that a distributed signed attention pattern (Intrinsic Grounding Signature, IGS) encodes missing diagnostic evidence for confident hallucinations. A lightweight verifier examines each emerging object mention, rolls back the KV cache when the mention is identified as high risk, suppresses the object and its synonyms, and regenerates the affected continuation. The intervention is applied selectively only to object mentions identified as high risk.

Result: On CHAIR and AMBER-G benchmarks, VGD achieves state-of-the-art object hallucination reduction: at @rec90 it cuts AMBER-G CHAIR by 43.6% while retaining 99.6% of grounded-object coverage, and reduces CHAIR-MSCOCO CHAIR_i/CHAIR_s by 37.0%/30.4% without shortening captions.

Conclusion: VGD demonstrates that selective, object-level intervention guided by intrinsic attention signatures can effectively mitigate hallucination while preserving the model's original visual understanding and grounded object coverage, addressing the limitations of prior coarse-grained mitigation approaches.

Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects that are absent from an image. Despite recent progress, existing mitigation methods still lack reliable object-level grounding diagnostics and therefore tend to apply coarse-grained interventions, which can impair visual understanding, shorten responses, and reduce coverage of genuinely grounded objects. The key challenge is thus to detect, during generation, whether each emerging object mention is supported by reliable visual evidence, so that hallucination can be mitigated selectively. Yet output confidence reflects next-token plausibility rather than visual support, allowing language priors to make absent objects appear certain. We show that the missing diagnostic evidence is encoded in an Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS), a distributed signed attention pattern that remains informative for such confident hallucinations. Based on IGS, we propose Verifier-Guided Decoding (VGD), a decoding framework in which a lightweight verifier examines each emerging object mention, rolls back the KV cache when the mention is identified as high risk, suppresses the object and its synonyms, and regenerates the affected continuation. Because VGD intervenes only on object mentions identified as high risk, it reduces object hallucination while preserving the model's original visual understanding and grounded object coverage. Experiments on CHAIR and AMBER-G show that VGD achieves state-of-the-art object hallucination reduction: at @rec90, it cuts AMBER-G CHAIR by 43.6\% while retaining 99.6\% of grounded-object coverage, and reduces CHAIR-MSCOCO CHAIR$_i$/CHAIR$_s$ by 37.0\%/30.4\% without shortening captions.

</details>


### [37] [Thinking Once Is Enough: Intermediate-Layer Evidence Routing for High-Resolution VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27830)
*Zhongkuan Mao,Xianjie Liu,Tianyu Meng,Yidong Wang,Wenzhuo Zhao,Ronghao Xian,Yao Jiang,Fei Shen,Junfeng Fang,Yong Dai,Yi Zhang,Keren Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Thinking-Once is a training-free, single-visual-pass evidence-routing method for high-resolution visual question answering. It reconstructs question-conditioned attention within an intermediate-layer routing window, preserving core entity tokens and compact background context, and routes this already-encoded evidence to later layers without extra visual encoding. Across five base models, it improves or matches baseline performance on V*Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K while reducing peak memory by ~4GB, and outperforms 11 open-source HR-VQA baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper argues that HR-VQA is often incorrectly treated as a problem of insufficient evidence acquisition, where models must repeatedly crop, re-encode, or search images. The authors show this view is incomplete: fine-grained evidence often already survives visual encoding and is identifiable and influential within an intermediate-layer routing window, but is later diluted before answer generation. This motivates a method that routes already-encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring new visual inputs.

Method: Thinking-Once is a training-free, single-visual-pass method that reconstructs question-conditioned attention at an intermediate-layer routing window. It preserves core entity tokens and compact background context, then routes this evidence to later layers without performing additional visual encoding passes.

Result: Across five base models, Thinking-Once consistently improves or matches the corresponding base setting, increasing average scores on V*Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K by +3.1, +3.0, and +2.7 points respectively, while reducing average peak memory by about 4GB. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B it improves the three benchmarks by +9.9, +4.6, and +5.5 points, raising the cross-benchmark mean from 72.5 to 79.1. With ZwZ-8B it reaches a mean score of 82.7. Against 11 open-source baselines it achieves the best or tied-best score on all three benchmark averages, and compared with DeepScan reduces V*Bench inference time by 97.2% while improving cross-benchmark mean from 77.8 to 79.1.

Conclusion: The results show that HR-VQA performance can be improved by routing already encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring new visual inputs, challenging the prevailing assumption that HR-VQA failures stem primarily from insufficient evidence acquisition. The method is training-free, reduces memory and inference cost, and achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks and base models.

Abstract: High-resolution visual question answering (HR-VQA) is often treated as a problem of insufficient evidence acquisition, where failing multimodal large language models must inspect images again through cropping, re-encoding, or multi-round search. We show that this view is incomplete: in many cases, fine-grained evidence has already survived visual encoding and become identifiable and influential within an intermediate-layer routing window, but is later diluted before answer generation. We propose Thinking-Once, a \textbf{training-free, single-visual-pass} evidence-routing method that reconstructs question-conditioned attention at this window, preserves core entity tokens and compact background context, and routes this evidence to later layers without extra visual encoding. Across five base models, Thinking-Once consistently improves or matches the corresponding base setting, increasing the average scores on V$^*$Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K by \textit{+3.1}, \textit{+3.0}, and \textit{+2.7} points while reducing the average peak memory by about 4,GB. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it improves the three benchmarks by \textit{+9.9}, \textit{+4.6}, and \textit{+5.5} points, raising the cross-benchmark mean from 72.5 to 79.1. With the ZwZ-8B base model, Thinking-Once reaches a mean score of 82.7. Against 11 open-source HR-VQA baselines, it obtains the best or tied-best score on all three benchmark averages and the best overall mean; for example, compared with DeepScan, it reduces V$^*$Bench inference time by \textbf{97.2\%} while improving the cross-benchmark mean from 77.8 to 79.1. These results show that HR-VQA can be improved by routing already encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring new visual inputs. Code is available in the appendix.

</details>


### [38] [SAFViT: Spatial Attention Fusion Gating for Vision Transformer-Based Nucleus Segmentation and Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27835)
*Harshit Mittal,Arash Rabbani*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) Gating module that replaces standard skip connections in a CellViT-based segmentation model. SAF gates concatenate encoder and upsampled decoder features, compress them via pointwise convolutions with ReLU, and apply channel-wise softmax to produce per-pixel trust heatmaps summing to unity. This improves minority "Dead" class detection and achieves the highest mPQ (0.471) on PanNuke, driven by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 over the ungated baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard direct skip connections in encoder-decoder architectures treat all spatial locations equally, passing redundant and potentially conflicting information to the decoder. Existing gating mechanisms only filter encoder information and neglect the benefit of global contextual information from the decoder.

Method: Proposes a Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) Gating module that replaces conventional skip connections in a CellViT-based model. Each SAF gate concatenates encoder skip features with upsampled decoder features, compresses them through two pointwise convolutions with an intermediate ReLU, and applies a channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel heatmap of trust that sums to unity at each spatial location.

Result: SAF Gating achieves the highest mPQ (0.471) on PanNuke, compared against six gating alternatives (no gating, attention gates, squeeze-and-excitation, CBAM, cross-attention, attentional feature fusion). The gain is driven primarily by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 score compared to the ungated CellViT baseline.

Conclusion: Lesion-level gating that accounts for decoder context enables the network to learn where each source is most trustworthy, improving minority class detection and overall panoptic quality. SAF Gating is validated on PanNuke and MoNuSeg datasets as a superior alternative to existing gating mechanisms.

Abstract: Accurate cell segmentation and classification are foundational to digital pathology, enabling quantitative tissue analysis for diagnosis and treatment planning. Encoder-decoder architectures that fuse multi-scale features through skip connections have become the dominant paradigm for this task, yet standard direct skip connections treat every spatial location equally, which leads to redundant and potentially conflicting information reaching the decoder. To overcome this problem, various gating mechanisms have been introduced, but most of them operate solely on filtering encoder information, neglecting the benefit of global contextual information from the decoder. This study proposes replacing conventional skip connections in a CellViT-based model with a novel Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) Gating module. Each SAF gate concatenates the encoder skip and upsampled decoder features, compresses them through two pointwise convolutions with an intermediate ReLU, and applies a channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel "heatmap of trust" that sums to unity at every spatial location, allowing the network to learn where each source is most trustworthy. The resulting fused features improve the model's ability to detect the minority "Dead" class, which in turn enhances the multi-class panoptic quality (mPQ) on the PanNuke dataset. SAF Gating is compared against six gating alternatives including no gating, attention gates, squeeze-and-excitation, CBAM, cross-attention, and attentional feature fusion on PanNuke and MoNuSeg datasets. SAF Gating achieves the highest mPQ (0.471), a gain driven primarily by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 score compared to ungated CellViT baseline.

</details>


### [39] [FeatFix: Reuse What You Verify through Local Exact-Feature Correction for Faster Cached Diffusion Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27842)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Qianli Ma,Fanshuai Meng,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FeatFix is a training-free acceleration method for diffusion model inference that reuses exact features computed during verification at sparse layer-timestep sites, replacing the draft block output to reset local residuals and reduce downstream feature error, achieving up to 6.70x speedup over Vanilla while maintaining competitive output quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models produce high-quality outputs but are computationally expensive due to iterative denoising. Existing training-free accelerators cache or forecast intermediate features, sometimes computing exact block features for verification, but these exact features are typically discarded after measuring discrepancy. The authors observe that these exact features can be reused for correction rather than being thrown away.

Method: FeatFix operates at a fixed sparse set of layer-timestep sites. At each selected site, it replaces the complete draft block output with the exact output computed from the same incoming state — avoiding token- or channel-level partial replacement and full-timestep recomputation. The key insight is that forwarding the exact feature at the verification site resets the local draft residual and reduces downstream feature error.

Result: Experiments across four image and video backbones show FeatFix consistently accelerates generation, achieving a speedup of up to 6.70x over Vanilla while maintaining competitive output quality.

Conclusion: The previously computed verification feature can be effectively reused for local correction rather than discarded, providing a simple and effective training-free acceleration strategy for cached diffusion inference.

Abstract: Diffusion models are widely used to generate high-quality images and videos, but their iterative denoising process remains computationally intensive. A growing class of training-free accelerators reduces this cost by reusing cached intermediate features or forecasting future ones. To control draft drift, these methods sometimes compute an exact block feature for verification. Yet the resulting exact feature is typically used only to measure discrepancy or guide a later decision and is then discarded. We find that this previously computed feature can instead be reused for correction. Forwarding it at the verification site resets the local draft residual and reduces downstream feature error. Based on this observation, we introduce FeatFix, a local exact-feature correction method for cached diffusion inference. FeatFix operates at a fixed sparse set of layer--timestep sites. At each selected site, it replaces the complete draft block output with the exact output computed from the same incoming state, avoiding token- or channel-level partial replacement and full-timestep recomputation. Experiments across four image and video backbones show that FeatFix consistently accelerates generation, achieving a speedup of up to $6.70\times$ over Vanilla while maintaining competitive output quality.

</details>


### [40] [VCP-DCN: Beyond Visual Concealed Property via Depth Collaborative Network for Camouflaged Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27843)
*Songsong Duan,Xi Yang,Nannan Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes VCP-DCN, a depth collaborative network for Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) that mines distinguishable multi-modality features beyond visual concealed prototypes in the depth domain. It progressively performs multi-modality alignment (via Separable Prototype Embedding with prototype contrastive learning), interaction (via Multi-modality Dual Attention with local response maps), and fusion (via Depth Adaptive Injection with a decision-making mechanism) to improve COD performance on three authoritative datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing COD methods that use depth maps rely on complementary RGB-D feature learning but ignore modality-specific characteristics of concealed objects in the depth domain, limiting detection performance.

Method: VCP-DCN consists of three progressive stages: (1) Alignment: a Separable Prototype Embedding (SPE) module learns modality-consistency and modality-specific RGB/depth prototype tokens via prototype contrastive learning; (2) Interaction: a Multi-modality Dual Attention (MDA) module enhances cross-modal feature representation using local response maps between modality-consistency prototype tokens and visual tokens; (3) Fusion: a Depth Adaptive Injection (DAI) module adaptively measures the contribution of RGB/depth features via a decision-making mechanism that computes similarity distances between modality-specific and modality-consistency prototype tokens.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of VCP-DCN on three authoritative COD datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-stage depth collaborative framework with prototype-based alignment, interaction, and adaptive fusion effectively leverages both modality-consistency and modality-specific features for camouflaged object detection.

Abstract: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to identify and segment camouflaged objects in complex environments, which are often concealed because their color and texture are similar to the background. Several existing COD methods introduce depth maps to boost detection performance via learning complementary RGB-D features, ignoring modality-specific characteristics of concealed objects in the depth domain. To address this issue, we propose a depth collaborative network, called VCP-DCN, to mine distinguishable multi-modality features beyond visual concealed prototype in depth domain. Specifically, VCP-DCN progressively performs multi-modality alignment, interaction, and fusion for the COD task. In the \textbf{alignment} stage, we propose a Separable Prototype Embedding (SPE) module to learn modality-consistency and modality-specific RGB/depth prototype tokens through prototype contrastive learning. Furthermore, we develop a Multi-modality Dual Attention (MDA) module to enhance the cross-modal feature representation through local response maps between modality-consistency RGB/depth prototype tokens and visual tokens on the \textbf{interaction} stage. Finally, we design a Depth Adaptive Injection (DAI) module to adaptively measure contribution of RGB/depth features with a decision-making mechanism, which calculates similarity distance between RGB/depth modality-specific prototype tokens and modality-consistency ones on the \textbf{fusion} stage. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our VCP-DCN on three authoritative datasets.

</details>


### [41] [Benchmarking Foundation and Large Language Models for Few-Shot Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27856)
*Jinghong Liu,Yuchuan Deng,Fanping Liu,Meng Huang,Xirong Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FAME is a unified benchmark for evaluating few-shot medical image segmentation (FS-MIS) methods, covering 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories. It evaluates models under zero-shot and ten-shot settings with target-absence recognition and generalization assessments, revealing that direct visual adaptation outperforms prompt-based strategies, support examples help only when effectively utilized, and semantic transfer is harder than imaging-domain adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing FS-MIS solutions span diverse paradigms (specialists, SAM-based, CLIP-based, MLLM-based) but are evaluated under inconsistent settings, leaving their relative effectiveness unclear. A unified benchmark is needed to provide fair, comprehensive comparison and understanding.

Method: The authors construct FAME, a large-scale benchmark with 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories. Models are evaluated under zero-shot and ten-shot settings, with additional assessments of target-absence recognition and generalization under covariate and semantic shifts, covering four categories of methods: specialists, SAM-based, CLIP-based, and MLLM-based.

Result: Three key findings: (1) effective few-shot segmentation depends on how models exploit support examples, with direct visual adaptation generally outperforming prompt-based strategies; (2) increasing support examples improves performance only when models can effectively utilize them; (3) semantic transfer is substantially more challenging than imaging-domain adaptation, and strong localization ability does not necessarily imply reliable target-absence recognition.

Conclusion: FAME provides a comprehensive understanding of current FS-MIS solutions and aims to facilitate the development of more effective and reliable few-shot medical segmentation methods by establishing a unified evaluation standard.

Abstract: Few-shot medical image segmentation (FS-MIS) aims to segment novel regions of interest (ROIs) from a few annotated support examples. Despite rapid progress, existing FS-MIS solutions span diverse paradigms but are evaluated under inconsistent settings, leaving their relative effectiveness unclear. We introduce FAME, a unified benchmark for evaluating FS-MIS solutions, covering specialists, SAM-based methods, CLIP-based methods, and MLLM-based methods. FAME contains 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories, and evaluates models under zero-shot and ten-shot settings with additional assessment of target-absence recognition and generalization under covariate and semantic shifts. Our evaluation reveals several findings. First, effective few-shot segmentation depends on how models exploit support examples: direct visual adaptation generally outperforms prompt-based strategies. Second, increasing support examples improves performance only when models can effectively utilize them. Third, semantic transfer remains substantially more challenging than imaging-domain adaptation, and strong localization ability does not necessarily imply reliable target-absence recognition. We hope FAME provides a comprehensive understanding of current FS-MIS solutions and facilitates the development of more effective and reliable few-shot medical segmentation methods.

</details>


### [42] [EEG-EditBench: Probing Visual Information in EEG-Image Retrieval Models with Controlled Image Edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27857)
*Kaifan Zhang,Lihuo He,Yuqi Ji,Junjie Ke,Lukun Wu,Tianhao You,Xinbo Gao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark built from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images containing 2,137 controlled image edits (object identity, attributes, background, object presence) to evaluate whether EEG-to-image retrieval models can distinguish subtle visual variations beyond coarse semantic differences. Testing eight representative models reveals that strong standard retrieval performance does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation, with fine-grained attribute changes being the most challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard EEG-to-image retrieval benchmarks use semantically diverse candidate sets, allowing models to succeed by capturing coarse category-level information without truly understanding the specific visual content viewed. The authors question whether these models can still distinguish a viewed image from a minimally edited version (e.g., the same scene with a cheetah replaced by a dog), motivating the need for a diagnostic benchmark that probes fine-grained visual discrimination.

Method: The authors construct EEG-EditBench from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, creating 2,137 quality-controlled edits across four edit types: object identity, object attributes, background, and object presence. They evaluate eight representative EEG visual decoding models on this benchmark and compare against standard retrieval performance.

Result: Results show that strong standard retrieval accuracy does not consistently transfer to the edit-based evaluation. Fine-grained attribute modifications present the greatest challenge for all evaluated models, revealing behavior that is hidden by aggregate retrieval accuracy metrics.

Conclusion: EEG-EditBench provides a controlled diagnostic basis for understanding what visual information EEG-to-image retrieval models actually preserve, exposing limitations in fine-grained visual discrimination that standard benchmarks overlook. The code and dataset are publicly released to facilitate further study.

Abstract: Recent EEG-to-image retrieval models have achieved strong performance in identifying viewed images from semantically diverse candidates. Yet such success does not reveal what visual information supports the match. A model may readily identify a cheetah among tools, plants, and vehicles, but can it still distinguish the viewed cheetah from the same scene with the cheetah replaced by a dog? Motivated by this question, we introduce EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines this question through controlled edits of object identity, attributes, background, and object presence. Built from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, EEG-EditBench contains 2,137 quality-controlled edits and evaluates eight representative EEG visual decoding models. Our results show that strong standard retrieval does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation, with fine-grained attribute changes presenting the greatest challenge. EEG-EditBench reveals model behavior hidden by aggregate retrieval accuracy and provides a controlled basis for studying what visual information EEG-image models preserve. The code and complete dataset are publicly available.

</details>


### [43] [Learning to Understand Body Language from Flight through Robust 3D Avatar Placing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27865)
*Dragos Costea,Alina Marcu,Cristina Lazar,Marius Leordeanu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset that grounds human motion and communicative intents in real 4K UAV footage by placing animated avatars into unmodified drone scenes with metrically correct position, scale, and orientation maintained across camera motion, enabled by a lightweight geometric world model using semantic anchors and streaming monocular depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is essential for socially intelligent aerial robots, but the training data for this task barely exists. There is a need for a dataset that grounds human motion in real UAV footage with correct 3D placement.

Method: Avatars manifesting ten communicative intents are placed into unmodified 4K drone scenes. A lightweight geometric world model of the local scene is built using semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D via streaming monocular depth. A placement point is predicted as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights, and re-rendered under an SVD-fitted ground rotation to maintain metrically correct position, scale and orientation over hundreds of frames of camera motion.

Result: Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data lifts mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted, and generated motion alike, with gains confirmed on two in-the-wild scenes.

Conclusion: The Drones2BodyLanguage dataset effectively addresses the data scarcity problem for long-range human motion and intent perception in aerial robotics, providing a scalable way to ground animated human motion in real UAV footage and significantly improving intent recognition accuracy across diverse architectures and motion types.

Abstract: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is a prerequisite for socially intelligent aerial robots, yet the data to learn it barely exists. We introduce Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset grounding human motion in real UAV footage: avatars manifesting ten communicative intents are placed into unmodified 4K drone scenes with metrically correct position, scale and orientation, maintained over hundreds of frames of camera motion. Enabling it is a lightweight geometric world model of the local scene - semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D through streaming monocular depth - in which a placement point is predicted as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights, and re-rendered under an SVD-fitted ground rotation. Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data lifts mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted and generated motion alike, with gains confirmed on two in-the-wild scenes.

</details>


### [44] [DECODE: Tackling Representation and Decision Degradation in Continual AI-Generated Image Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27882)
*Zihao Cai,Xinghan Li,Ruiyan Yang,Xue Song,Haijun Shan,Jingjing Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DECODE is a decoupled continual learning framework for AI-generated image detection that jointly addresses representation- and decision-level forgetting (termed "Dual Degradation") via Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA), achieving 99.36% average accuracy with 0.39% forgetting across 19 generative domains and 95.36% accuracy on 11 unseen generators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual learning methods for AI-generated image detection primarily stabilize feature representations, implicitly treating forgetting as a representation-level problem. The authors show this perspective is incomplete: even when representations remain discriminative, the decision boundary can progressively drift as the classification head is continually optimized on new domains, creating a compound failure mode called Dual Degradation.

Method: DECODE is a decoupled continual detection framework with two key components: (1) Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations across generative domains, and (2) Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without manual hyperparameter tuning.

Result: On 19 generative domains, DECODE achieves 99.36% average accuracy with only 0.39% forgetting, and further generalizes to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

Conclusion: Decision-level forgetting is a critical yet overlooked factor in continual AI-generated image detection. By explicitly addressing both representation- and decision-level degradation in a decoupled manner, DECODE demonstrates near-perfect retention and strong generalization to unseen generators, highlighting the importance of handling the compound nature of catastrophic forgetting in forensic tasks.

Abstract: As generative models continue to evolve, AI-generated image detectors must incrementally adapt to emerging generative domains while preserving knowledge acquired from previous ones. This continual learning setting is particularly challenging because forensic traces are often subtle and generator-specific, making detectors highly vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods primarily address this problem by stabilizing feature representations, implicitly treating forgetting as a representation-level issue. In this paper, we show that this perspective is incomplete. We demonstrate that even when feature representations remain discriminative, the decision boundary can progressively drift as the classification head is continually optimized on new domains. These two effects jointly give rise to a compound failure mode, termed Dual Degradation. To overcome this challenge, we propose DECODE, a decoupled continual detection framework that jointly mitigates representation- and decision-level forgetting. Specifically, we introduce Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without manual hyperparameter tuning. Extensive experiments on 19 generative domains show that DECODE achieves an average accuracy of 99.36% with only 0.39% forgetting, while further generalizing to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

</details>


### [45] [Unifying Adversarially Robust Model Experts in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27897)
*Nguyen Duc Thai,Junhao Dong,Sua Qi Rong,Hua Yu,Yew-Soon Ong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes CARE, a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework that maintains multiple specialized robust model experts, enables knowledge exchange via embedding-space alignment, and consolidates them into a single unified model that inherits complementary robustness properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Different adversarial fine-tuning strategies produce specialized models with distinct robustness characteristics, each thriving in some evaluation settings but failing in others, limiting their defensive capabilities against adversarial attacks on vision-language models like CLIP.

Method: CARE (Collaborative Adversarial Robustness fine-tuning using Embedding alignment) maintains multiple experts during training, allows knowledge exchange through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates learned knowledge into a single unified robust model while preserving individual specializations.

Result: Experiments on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks show CARE outperforms individually learned model experts, demonstrating effectiveness across complementary robustness behaviors.

Conclusion: Collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness in vision-language models.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, posing a serious problem for real-life applications and deployment. Adversarial fine-tuning emerges as a prominent defense method; however, different fine-tuning strategies often produce specialized models with distinct robustness characteristics. Each fine-tuned model in turn thrives in some evaluation settings but falters on others, limiting their defensive capabilities. We refer to these specialized fine-tuned models as robust model experts and propose a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework: CARE - Collaborative Adversarial Robustness fine-tuning using Embedding alignment. CARE maintains multiple experts during training, enables knowledge exchange through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates the learned knowledge into a single unified robust model. Experts benefit from one another while preserving their individual specializations, enabling the final model to inherit complementary robustness properties. In this paper, we demonstrate CARE on two different adversarial fine-tuning strategies with complementary robustness behaviors. Extensive experiments on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks display the effectiveness of our approach, with CARE being able to outperform individually learned model experts. The results suggest that collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness.

</details>


### [46] [CoRE-UIR: Prior-guided common and residual experts for efficient all-in-one remote sensing image restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27898)
*Zaiyan Zhang,Qiangqiang Yuan,Jie Li,Ziyang Lihe,Yu Wan,Yuzeng Chen,Xin Su,Liangpei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV
