TL;DR: CoRE-UIR is a universal image restoration framework for UAV/satellite remote sensing images that decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert and low-rank residual experts within a Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE), supplemented by Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) using frozen CLIP features and Global Feature Modulation (GFM). It also introduces MDVD-108K, a large-scale multi-degradation UAV dataset. CoRE-UIR improves average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83x faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% compared to the strongest baseline (BaryIR).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote sensing images from UAVs and satellites suffer from co-occurring degradations (adverse weather, illumination variation, imaging artifacts) that induce both global distribution shifts and local structural corruption. Existing All-in-One restoration methods face weak/implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy from full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping behaviors, motivating a more efficient unified framework.

Method: CoRE-UIR employs a prior-guided global-local framework built on the Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE), which explicitly decomposes restoration capacity into: (1) a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration, and (2) low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation. Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) adapts frozen CLIP features into explicit restoration-oriented priors, and Global Feature Modulation (GFM) aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. The paper also constructs MDVD-108K, a large-scale UAV restoration dataset covering single and compound degradations, plus a real-world test set.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show CoRE-UIR improves overall average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83x faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline BaryIR, achieving a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluations on downstream tasks and unseen degradation confirm generalizability.

Conclusion: CoRE-UIR demonstrates that explicitly decomposing restoration capacity into common and low-rank residual experts, combined with CLIP-derived degradation priors and global feature modulation, yields superior quality-efficiency performance for universal image restoration in remote sensing. The dataset and code are released for further research.

Abstract: Remote sensing images acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellites are often degraded by adverse weather, illumination variation, and imaging artifacts, which may co-occur and jointly induce global distribution shifts and local structural corruption. Although All-in-One image restoration offers an appealing unified alternative to task-specific pipelines, existing methods still suffer from weak or implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy caused by full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping restoration behaviors. We propose CoRE-UIR (Common and Residual Experts for Universal Image Restoration), a prior-guided global-local framework centered on the Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE). CoRE explicitly decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation, enabling adaptive specialization without redundant expert replication. Built on this design, Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) adapts frozen CLIP features into an explicit restoration-oriented prior, while Global Feature Modulation (GFM) aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. We also construct MDVD-108K (Multi-Degradation VisDrone), a large-scale UAV restoration dataset covering both single and compound degradations, together with a real-world test set. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show that CoRE-UIR improves the overall average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83$\times$ faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline, BaryIR, thereby maintaining a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluations on downstream tasks and unseen degradation also validate the generalizability of CoRE-UIR. The code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/zzaiyan/CoRE-UIR.

</details>


### [47] [One Patch Is Enough: Reinforcement-Optimized Visual Token Grounding for MLLM-Based Scene Text Spotting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27902)
*Rui Tang,Wentao Yang,Peirong Zhang,Yongxin Shi,Shun Zhang,Huiguo He,Lianwen Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPaTS is a vision-centric single-patch text spotting framework for MLLMs that routes each text instance through one anchor visual token and recovers geometry via full-image refinement, outperforming frontier closed-source and OCR MLLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous multi-patch visual-token grounding paradigms in MLLMs introduce redundant noise and localization ambiguity for scene text spotting, particularly for dense or small text instances, hindering precision alignment between textual recognition and spatial localization.

Method: SPaTS routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token and recovers geometry via full-image refinement. It introduces: (1) SPaSO, a reinforcement learning framework for discrete visual-token selection using patch-level rewards without oracle labels; (2) DEA, which decouples feature magnitude and direction to suppress unstable norm bias; (3) PED, which fuses the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attends over the full-image feature map for geometry-aware boundary regression.

Result: Extensive experiments show SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs on scene text spotting benchmarks.

Conclusion: The single-patch anchor routing paradigm with reinforcement learning-based token selection and geometry-aware decoding offers a superior alternative to multi-patch grounding for text spotting in MLLMs. Code will be released.

Abstract: Scene text spotting requires high-precision alignment between textual recognition and spatial localization. While visual-token grounding has emerged as a promising formulation for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the previous multi-patch paradigm often introduces redundant noise and localization ambiguity, particularly for dense or small text instances. To address this, we propose Single-Patch Text Spotting (SPaTS), a vision-centric framework that routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token and then recovers geometry via full-image refinement. To accurately identify this anchor without oracle labels, we introduce Single-Patch Selective Optimization (SPaSO), a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes discrete visual-token selection using patch-level rewards. To further improve representation robustness and localization precision, we introduce Directional Embedding Alignment (DEA) to suppress unstable norm bias by decoupling feature magnitude and direction, and Patch-Enhanced Decoding (PED) to fuse the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attend over the full-image feature map for geometry-aware boundary regression beyond coordinate-space surrogates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs. Code will be released soon.

</details>


### [48] [ARD-REFSM: Enhancing Reflection Symmetry Detection with Asymmetric Denoising and Rotation Equivariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27927)
*Dongfu Yin,Rourou Su,Cong Zhao,Fei Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reflection symmetry detection method combining an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module to suppress background clutter and a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module for rotation-equivariant feature consistency, along with a new benchmark dataset GMSYM. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four standard datasets and GMSYM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reflection symmetry detection is challenging because asymmetric regions introduce background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, and conventional CNNs lack rotation equivariance, causing inconsistent feature representations under rotational transformations.

Method: The method comprises two key modules: (1) an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module that suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, and (2) a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module using a dual-input framework that leverages rotation loss to maximize consistency between score maps of original and rotated images, enabling precise prediction of rotation-equivariant symmetry axes. Additionally, a new benchmark dataset GMSYM categorizes images into diverse scenarios with various interferences.

Result: Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and the proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.

Conclusion: The proposed ARD and REFSM modules effectively address asymmetric interference and rotation equivariance limitations in reflection symmetry detection, and the GMSYM benchmark provides a more comprehensive evaluation setup, with the method achieving superior accuracy and robustness across all datasets.

Abstract: Reflection symmetry detection remains challenging due to interference from asymmetric regions and arbitrary orientations of symmetric patterns. Asymmetric regions introduce background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, whereas conventional convolutional neural networks lack rotation equivariance, leading to inconsistent feature representations under rotational transformations. To address these issues, we propose an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module and a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module. The ARD module suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, while the REFSM module enhances rotation equivariance through feature similarity matching between original and rotated images. Specifically, our dual-input REFSM framework leverages rotation loss to maximize consistency between the score maps of original and rotated images, thereby enabling precise prediction of rotation-equivariant symmetry axes. Furthermore, we introduce GMSYM, a new benchmark dataset that categorizes images into diverse scenarios and incorporates various interferences to address the limitations of existing reflection symmetry detection benchmarks. Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and our proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.

</details>


### [49] [LAST: The Last Query Token Guides Visual Token Pruning for Edge-Cloud Collaborative MLLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27952)
*Feng Yang,Xinrui Ju,Keyang Zhang,Xiandong Meng,Rongqun Lin,Howard Leung,Shiqi Wang,Haoliang Li,Chris Xing Tian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LAST is a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative multimodal LLM inference. It uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy, deriving importance signals from the last query token's attention to visual tokens, enabling query-aware pruning before cloud transmission. LAST retains 12.5% of visual tokens while preserving 95.4% of full-token accuracy across 11 multimodal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense visual-token sequences in multimodal foundation models increase cloud-side inference costs in edge-cloud collaborative settings. Existing pruning methods are limited: vision-driven approaches are query-agnostic, query-guided methods depend on the target MLLM's internal states (unavailable before transmission), and compact guidance models often require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation.

Method: LAST employs a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token attends to the full visual sequence and entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or costly multi-position attention aggregation. LAST retains a diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed token budget.

Result: Evaluated on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets, LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance, preserving 95.4% of full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

Conclusion: LAST demonstrates that training-free, query-dependent visual token pruning is feasible at the edge using a compact guidance VLM and the last query token's attention signal, achieving strong performance retention with minimal overhead and reduced cloud inference cost.

Abstract: Multimodal foundation models are reshaping edge-cloud visual intelligence from task-specific feature pipelines into token-based interfaces, where edge devices encode visual inputs into tokens for a general-purpose cloud MLLM. However, dense visual-token sequences increase cloud-side inference costs. Existing pruning methods mainly target centralized inference: vision-driven methods can operate before cloud execution but are typically query-agnostic, whereas query-guided methods often rely on internal states of the target MLLM and cannot determine token relevance before transmission. Compact guidance models offer an alternative, but existing designs may require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation. We propose LAST, a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative MLLM inference. LAST uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token can attend to the full visual sequence and the entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or costly aggregation over multiple query positions. LAST then retains a diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed token budget. We evaluate LAST on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets against pruning methods with different guidance strategies. Experiments show that LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance, preserving 95.4% of the full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of the visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

</details>


### [50] [FiRE: Enhancing MLLMs with Fine-Grained Context Learning for Complex Image Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27959)
*Bohan Hou,Haoqiang Lin,Xuemeng Song,Haokun Wen,Meng Liu,Yupeng Hu,Xiangyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes a fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline and a two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning strategy to enhance MLLM-based image retrieval, achieving superior zero-shot performance across five complex retrieval datasets with a lightweight backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM-based image retrieval approaches overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives, limiting their performance on complex tasks such as long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR).

Method: (1) An automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline that generates a comprehensive CIR dataset with fine-grained image captions and modification text; (2) a novel two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning strategy that decouples the fine-tuning into fine-grained context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning and fine-grained retrieval-oriented fine-tuning to sequentially enhance context understanding and query-target alignment.

Result: Extensive experiments across five datasets covering diverse complex image retrieval tasks demonstrate significant superiority over existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, achieved even with a more lightweight MLLM backbone compared to prior methods.

Conclusion: Fine-grained context modeling combined with disentangled, stage-wise fine-tuning objectives effectively improves MLLM-based retrieval performance on complex tasks, offering a more efficient and accurate alternative to existing entangled fine-tuning paradigms.

Abstract: Due to their strong generalizable multimodal processing and reasoning capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant potential as universal image retrievers, effectively addressing diverse real-world image retrieval tasks. Nevertheless, pioneering studies, while promising, overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives in enhancing MLLMs' retrieval performance, particularly for complex tasks such as long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR). Therefore, in this work, we propose an automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline and a novel two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning strategy. The dataset generation pipeline produces a comprehensive CIR dataset with fine-grained image captions and modification text, facilitating fine-grained context modeling. Beyond the previously entangled fine-tuning paradigm, our approach separates the fine-tuning process into two distinct stages: (1) fine-grained context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning and (2) fine-grained retrieval-oriented fine-tuning. These stages aim to sequentially enhance the model's context understanding and query-target alignment capabilities, thereby improving retrieval performance. Extensive experiments across five datasets encompassing diverse and complex image retrieval tasks demonstrate the remarkable superiority of our method over existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, even with a more lightweight MLLM backbone compared to those methods.

</details>


### [51] [FootprintNet: State-Transition-Guided Dynamic Footprint Learning for Multi-temporal Remote Sensing Change Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27969)
*Haotian Zhang,Hao Chen,Han Guo,Zhengxia Zou,Zhenwei Shi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD) for detecting building-change dynamic footprints (temporal intervals of change) from multi-temporal remote sensing imagery. The authors propose FootprintNet, which models building-change processes as interactions between latent states and actions with state-action transition constraints, and introduces the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) metric to evaluate temporal proximity between predictions and labels. Experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU datasets show FootprintNet outperforms state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing remote sensing multi-temporal change detection methods typically assign a single change category per spatial location over the entire observation period, implicitly assuming each location undergoes only one change. This limits their ability to characterize regions with recurrent change, which are closely related to human activities such as repeated construction, demolition, or renovation.

Method: (1) UBDD framework: identifies building-change dynamic footprints (temporal intervals of change) from multi-temporal imagery and produces pixel-wise classification masks. (2) Multi-change class: an independent class for regions undergoing two or more changes, enabling unified modeling of single- and multi-change processes. (3) FootprintNet: abstracts building-change processes as latent state-action interactions with transition constraints for causally coherent change trajectories, and exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast across boundary sides. (4) BCDS metric: evaluates predictions based on preservation of change semantics and temporal offsets from corresponding labels.

Result: Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU datasets demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in building change dynamics detection.

Conclusion: The proposed UBDD paradigm and FootprintNet effectively overcome the single-change assumption limitation of existing MTCD methods, enabling accurate detection of both single and recurrent building changes over time. The BCDS metric provides a more meaningful evaluation of temporal footprint predictions. The code is publicly available.

Abstract: Despite substantial progress in remote sensing multi-temporal change detection (MTCD), most existing MTCD methods still represent the dynamic process at each spatial location over the entire observation period using a single change category associated with the final observation. This implicit single-change assumption limits their ability to characterize regions of recurrent change closely related to human activities. To address this limitation, we introduce Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD), which identifies building-change dynamic footprints, i.e., the temporal intervals in which changes occur, from multi-temporal imagery and produces pixel-wise classification masks. For regions undergoing two or more changes, UBDD introduces an independent multi-change class for unified representation, thereby enabling unified modeling of single- and multi-change processes. Furthermore, we propose FootprintNet, which abstracts building-change processes as interactions between latent states and actions, and imposes state-action transition constraints to guide the learning of causally coherent change trajectories. It further exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast across boundary sides, thereby improving the discrimination among different dynamic footprints and enabling accurate detection of dynamic footprints. Moreover, we introduce the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) to address the inability of conventional metrics to reflect the temporal proximity between predicted footprints and labels. It evaluates predictions according to their preservation of change semantics and temporal offsets from the corresponding labels. Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/zmoka-zht/FootprintNet.

</details>


### [52] [Now You Have My Healthy Attention: A U-DiT for Brain-MRI Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27974)
*Danilo Danese,Angela Lombardi,Tommaso Di Noia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper presents a U-DiT-based deterministic regression model for brain MRI inpainting in the ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis task. The network uses downsampled global self-attention with 3D rotary position embeddings, constrains occluded tokens to attend only to healthy known tokens with a contralateral bias, and incorporates a mirrored-hemisphere prior. It achieves mean SSIM of 0.864, PSNR of 24.7 dB, and MSE of 4.6e-3 on the BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To produce anatomically plausible completions of healthy brain tissue within masked regions of T1-weighted MRI, providing tumor-free anatomical references for downstream analysis. Since the task is scored by distortion metrics, the authors aim to build a regression model with inductive biases specifically tailored to inpainting.

Method: A U-DiT architecture (volumetric encoder-decoder with downsampled global self-attention using 3D rotary position embeddings) that uses convolutions and skip connections to preserve high-frequency detail. Two key inductive biases: (1) attention masking so void tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens of the same volume with a learned contralateral-homologue bias; (2) a contralateral-symmetry input supplying the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior.

Result: On the BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard (219 cases), the model achieves mean healthy-region SSIM of 0.864, PSNR of 24.7 dB, and MSE of 4.6e-3.

Conclusion: The authors analyze the residual smoothness inherent to distortion-optimal regression and discuss implications for anatomical realism, suggesting that while distortion metrics are optimized, further attention may be needed to ensure anatomically realistic outputs beyond what regression-optimal solutions provide.

Abstract: The ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis (Inpainting) task asks for the anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue within a masked region of a T1-weighted MRI, providing a tumor-free anatomical reference for downstream analysis. As the task is scored by distortion metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE), we build a deterministic regression model and focus on giving it inductive biases tailored to inpainting. Our network follows the U-DiT principle of performing self-attention on a downsampled token grid: a volumetric encoder-decoder imports long-range context through a downsampled global self-attention block with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings, while convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two ideas drive our results. First, we constrain the attention so that occluded ("void") tokens attend only to known-healthy tokens of the same volume, with a learned bias toward each query's contralateral homologue, forcing the completion to be inferred from observed anatomy rather than from other unknown regions. Second, we add a contralateral-symmetry input that supplies the mirrored healthy hemisphere as a patient-specific prior; since the brain is approximately bilaterally symmetric and lesions are typically unilateral, this prior improves the distortion metrics at matched structural similarity. On the official BraTS-2026 validation leaderboard our submission reaches a mean healthy-region SSIM of $0.864$, PSNR of $24.7$\,dB and MSE of $4.6{\times}10^{-3}$ over $219$ cases. We further analyse the residual smoothness inherent to distortion-optimal regression and discuss its implications for anatomical realism.

</details>


### [53] [ViP-Rig: Visual-Prompted Controllable Rigging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27982)
*Zihan Qin,Mingze Sun,Yifan Mao,Jialei Xu,Jingfeng Guo,Changrong Hu,Wenbo Zhao,Junjun Jiang,Xianming Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ViP-Rig is a visual-prompted rigging framework that injects features from user-drawn 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones, supporting both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing to control skeleton structure and skinning behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigging is inherently task-dependent, requiring different skeletons and deformation behaviors across animation tasks. Existing automatic methods offer limited explicit control over resulting skeletons and deformation behavior, whereas artists typically inspect and repeatedly edit initial rigs to meet specific requirements.

Method: ViP-Rig consists of two stages: (1) Skeleton Generation, where a Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding processes the skeletal sketch into compact conditioning tokens injected into a frozen pretrained autoregressive generator via gated adapters to control joint placement and branching structure; (2) Skinning Prediction, where a rigidity map is processed with the same visual encoding and tokens are symmetrically injected into point and joint streams of a frozen pretrained skinning backbone to modulate point-joint compatibility and skinning weights.

Result: Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show ViP-Rig more accurately recovers target skeletons and skinning weights than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results demonstrate explicit and localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.

Conclusion: ViP-Rig provides a novel visual-prompt-based approach to rigging that enables explicit user control over both skeleton generation and skinning prediction while preserving the geometric priors of frozen pretrained backbones.

Abstract: Rigging is inherently task-dependent because the same mesh may require different skeletons and deformation behaviors across animation tasks. In practice, artists often inspect an initial rig and repeatedly edit its skeletal structure and deformation behavior to meet specific animation requirements. Existing automatic methods primarily generate a plausible rig from geometry, offering limited explicit control over the resulting skeleton and deformation behavior. In this work, we present ViP-Rig, a visual-prompted framework that supports both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing by injecting features extracted from user-drawn or edited 2D skeletal and rigidity prompts into frozen pretrained backbones. Specifically, ViP-Rig consists of two stages, Skeleton Generation and Skinning Prediction. In the first stage, the skeletal sketch is processed by the Dense-to-Compact Visual Prompt Encoding to produce compact, fixed-length conditioning tokens. The resulting tokens are injected into a frozen pretrained autoregressive generator through gated adapters to control joint placement and branching structure while preserving the generator's geometric prior. In the second stage, the rigidity map is processed using the same visual encoding design, while the pretrained skinning backbone remains frozen. The resulting tokens are symmetrically injected into the point and joint streams to modulate point-joint compatibility and the resulting skinning weights. Experiments on Articulation-XL2.0 and zero-shot evaluation on ModelsResource show that ViP-Rig more accurately recovers target skeletons and skinning weights than geometry-conditioned baselines under prompt-guided evaluation. Qualitative results further demonstrate explicit and localized control in both prompt-first rigging and result-guided editing.

</details>


### [54] [Deep learning-based hierarchical insect classification using camera trap imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28005)
*Zaki Mahfoud,Juan A. Chiavassa,Simon Walther,Florian Haselbeck,Ehsan Yaghoubi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model for automated insect biodiversity monitoring from camera-trap images, using a manually curated dataset of ~1 million images annotated with a five-level, 34-class taxonomy, achieving 80-99% per-level accuracy across the hierarchy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Declining insect populations demand reliable biodiversity monitoring, but current approaches lack standardised data and rely on costly, time-consuming manual identification by expert entomologists. There is an urgent need for scalable, automated monitoring solutions.

Method: The authors curated a long-tailed dataset of ~1 million insect images from 1,801 camera-trap videos, annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. They adapted a hierarchical classification model to a variable-depth hierarchy with class-balanced weighting, leveraging biological taxonomy to extract granularity-specific features. The model makes hierarchy-consistent predictions down to the deepest taxonomic level meeting a confidence threshold (T=0.6).

Result: The hierarchical model improves on non-hierarchical classifiers, achieving 80-99% per-level accuracy across all five levels of the hierarchy on test data, while producing hierarchy-consistent predictions.

Conclusion: The proposed hierarchical deep learning approach demonstrates that leveraging biological taxonomy with confidence-gated predictions enables automated, scalable insect biodiversity monitoring that outperforms flat classifiers and handles highly imbalanced, long-tailed data.

Abstract: Declining insect populations make reliable biodiversity monitoring increasingly urgent, yet monitoring of insect biodiversity is hampered by a lack of standardised data and by costly and time-consuming manual identification by expert entomologists. Deep learning-based image classifiers, processing data from automated non-lethal camera traps, have the potential to transform and scale insect biodiversity monitoring. However, challenges remain in acquiring expert-annotated datasets, developing model architectures that generalise well across diverse taxonomic levels and training models on highly imbalanced data. Hierarchical data also benefits from designing models that default to higher-confidence, coarser-level predictions, when uncertain about finer taxonomic levels. In this paper we address these challenges with a deep learning-based hierarchical classification model. First, we present a manually curated, long-tailed dataset of around one million images of insects, extracted from 1,801 camera-trap video recordings and annotated with a five-level, 34-class hierarchy. Further, we adapt a hierarchical classification model architecture to a five-level variable-depth hierarchy, with class-balanced weighting. Our model improves on non-hierarchical classifiers by leveraging biological taxonomy to extract granularity-specific visual features and makes hierarchy-consistent predictions to the deepest taxonomic level that meets a confidence threshold (T = 0.6). Our model achieved a per-level accuracy of 80-99% on test data, across five levels of hierarchy. Furthermore ...

</details>


### [55] [Beyond Classification: Pathology Foundation Models as Detection Encoders for Mitotic Figures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28007)
*Sweta Banerjee,Alireza Teimoury,Nils Porsche,Alexandra K. Stoll,Viktoria Weiss,Niklas Hargarter,Jonas Ammeling,Thomas Conrad,Christoph Stroblberger,Christopher Kaltnecker,Robert Klopfleisch,Christof A. Bertram,Katharina Breininger,Marc Aubreville*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether current pathology foundation models (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) can serve as backbones for dense object detection of mitotic figures, comparing their performance against a ResNet50 end-to-end baseline across three detector types (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR) on MIDOG++ and TUPAC16 datasets. Results show H-optimus-0 and Virchow achieve competitive performance, suggesting current FMs are suitable for mitotic figure detection and offer modest robustness advantages out-of-domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pathology foundation models have demonstrated effectiveness for classification tasks including mitotic figure classification, but it remains unclear whether their latent spaces provide features that are sufficiently discriminant and spatially resolved to serve as backbones for dense object detection paradigms. This work seeks to answer this question empirically.

Method: The authors evaluate six current pathology foundation models (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) as backbone feature extractors combined with three detector representatives—RetinaNet (single-stage), Faster R-CNN (dual-stage), and Deformable DETR (self-attention-based). They benchmark these on the multi-domain MIDOG++ dataset and TUPAC16 as an out-of-domain case, comparing against a fully end-to-end trained ResNet50 baseline.

Result: The H-optimus-0 and Virchow foundation models yielded competitive detection performance compared to the end-to-end trained baseline, indicating that the latent spaces of current image-level self-supervised pathology FMs are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection. These models also demonstrated slightly stronger robustness on the out-of-domain TUPAC16 test case.

Conclusion: Current pathology foundation models trained on image-level self-supervision can be effectively leveraged as backbones for dense mitotic figure detection across different detector architectures, with H-optimus-0 and Virchow showing the most promising results, including marginally better out-of-domain generalization.

Abstract: Pathology foundation models (FMs) are models trained on vast amounts of typically unlabeled data and have been shown to yield regularized latent spaces that can be used effectively in downstream classification tasks. This is also true for the classification of mitotic figures vs. other cells. However, it is so far unclear if the latent space of current FMs provides features that are discriminant and spatially suitably resolved to also serve as a backbone for dense object detection paradigms. In this work, we investigate this question for common current pathology FMs (UNI, UNI2-h, Virchow, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, H-optimus-1) and compare their performance against a fully end-to-end trained baseline based on a ResNet50 architecture. We combine FM backbones with representatives of single stage, dual stage and self-attention-based detectors (RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, Deformable DETR respectively) on the multi-domain MIDOG++ dataset, and on the TUPAC16 dataset as an out-of-domain case. We show that the H-optimus-0 and Virchow models yielded competitive performance, indicating that the latent spaces of current FMs, all trained on image-level self-supervision, are suitable for direct mitotic figure detection and may be slightly more robust on our out-of-domain test case. All code is made available publicly at https://github.com/DeepMicroscopy/FM4MFdet.

</details>


### [56] [ENCORE: Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement for Learned Video Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28020)
*Shuhan Ye,Hongbin Yu,Chenqi Kong,Pingchuan Ma,Chong Wang,Jun Wan,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ENCORE is an event-assisted complementary motion refinement framework for learned video compression that uses event cameras to capture fine-grained intensity changes between RGB frames, decomposes aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations, calibrates event-specific responses, and routes energy-aware motion corrections to refine RGB flow, achieving up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings on BS-ERGB.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing learned video codecs estimate motion from discretely sampled RGB frames only, making them vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras provide complementary asynchronous intensity-change evidence between RGB timestamps that can improve inter-frame motion modeling.

Method: ENCORE consists of three components: (1) Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) decomposes aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations; (2) Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) identifies active and novel event-specific responses relative to RGB, suppresses weak/redundant evidence, and predicts candidate flow corrections; (3) Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly corrections refine the RGB flow. Events serve only as auxiliary modality for motion modeling; RGB remains the only coding and reconstruction target.

Result: Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED datasets demonstrate consistent gains across datasets and GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings, with clear improvements retained on the other two datasets.

Conclusion: Event-assisted complementary motion refinement effectively addresses the limitations of RGB-only motion estimation in learned video compression, yielding consistent rate-distortion improvements across multiple datasets while keeping RGB as the sole coding target.

Abstract: Learned video compression relies on accurate temporal modeling to remove redundancy between adjacent frames. However, most existing codecs infer motion solely from discretely sampled RGB frames, making their estimates vulnerable to fast motion, blur, occlusion, weak texture, low illumination, and abrupt brightness changes. Event cameras asynchronously capture fine-grained intensity changes between RGB timestamps and therefore provide complementary evidence about inter-frame dynamics. We propose ENCORE, an Event-Assisted Complementary Motion Refinement framework for learned video compression. ENCORE first employs Complementary Motion Representation (CMR) to decompose aligned RGB-event features into common and modality-specific motion representations. Spatial Energy and Redundancy-Informed Calibration (SERIC) then identifies event-specific responses that are active and novel relative to RGB, suppresses weak or redundant evidence, and predicts a candidate flow correction. Finally, Energy-Aware Routing (EAR) determines where and how strongly the correction should refine the RGB flow. Events serve solely as an auxiliary modality for motion modeling, while RGB remains the only coding and reconstruction target. Experiments on BS-ERGB, HQ-EVFI, and CED demonstrate consistent gains across datasets and GOP lengths. On BS-ERGB, ENCORE achieves up to 20.80% PSNR-RGB and 22.14% MS-SSIM-RGB BD-rate savings, while retaining clear improvements on the other two datasets.

</details>


### [57] [Split and Drive: Dual-Axis Disentanglement for Real-Time Gaussian Head Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28032)
*MD Wahiduzzaman Khan,Mingshan Jia,Xiaolin Zhang,En Yu,Kaska Musial-Gabrys*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SpiD (Split and Drive) is a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework that generates photorealistic animatable head avatars by disentangling along two axes: a compute axis that internalizes per-frame driving (eliminating external tracking dependency) and a feature axis that decomposes the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches for geometrically distinct facial regions. It achieves state-of-the-art quality with the fastest end-to-end inference on a single GPU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting head avatar methods rely on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements, and they use unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting expressiveness and rendering fidelity. The goal is to create photorealistic animatable head avatars from a single image without these limitations.

Method: SpiD is built on two disentanglement axes: (1) the compute axis internalizes per-frame driving to remove external tracking dependency at inference time, and (2) the feature axis splits the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain (e.g., separate regions such as eyes, mouth, and skin/overall head).

Result: Extensive experiments show SpiD achieves consistently strong performance against state-of-the-art methods while attaining the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU, with the full driving pipeline included in the measurement.

Conclusion: SpiD demonstrates that disentangling computation (driving) and representation (facial features) enables single-image Gaussian head avatars that are both more expressive and faster at inference, without relying on external tracking systems.

Abstract: Creating photorealistic animatable head avatars from a single image remains a fundamental challenge in digital human synthesis. While recent 3D Gaussian Splatting methods have achieved promising results, they rely on external tracking pipelines whose latency is excluded from inference measurements. Furthermore, they adopt unified representations that entangle geometrically distinct facial regions, limiting both expressiveness and rendering fidelity. We propose SpiD (Split and Drive), a single-image Gaussian head avatar framework built on two disentanglement axes. The compute axis internalizes per-frame driving, eliminating external tracking dependency at inference. The feature axis decomposes the avatar into three specialized Gaussian branches, each modeling a geometrically distinct facial domain. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistently strong performance against state-of-the-art methods while achieving the fastest inference speed among all compared methods on a single GPU with the complete driving pipeline included.

</details>


### [58] [TongueReenact: Geometry-Anchored Tongue Synthesis for Face Reenactment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28039)
*MD Wahiduzzaman Khan,Mingshan Jia,Xiaolin Zhang,En Yu,Kaska Musial-Gabrys*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment, using a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline to create a tongue segmentation model without curated annotations, and a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis with adaptive mask dilation. It achieves over 2x improvement on all tongue-specific metrics and validates results with a VLM-based evaluation protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing face reenactment systems achieve impressive pose and expression transfer using geometry-driven representations but largely ignore tongue dynamics, resulting in anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive motions.

Method: The framework comprises (1) a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without curated annotations, and (2) a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis with adaptive mask dilation to ensure seamless mouth boundary transitions.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. A VLM-based evaluation protocol replicates expert annotation at scale, confirming perceptual superiority across all ablation variants.

Conclusion: The proposed approaches effectively address the previously overlooked tongue dynamics in face reenactment, achieving anatomically consistent and perceptually superior tongue synthesis, validated by both quantitative metrics and automated expert-level evaluation.

Abstract: Modern face reenactment systems achieve impressive pose and expression transfer using geometry-driven representations. However, they largely ignore tongue dynamics, leading to anatomically inconsistent mouth interiors during speech and expressive motions. We introduce the first framework for cross-identity tongue dynamics transfer in face reenactment. We propose a foundation-model-assisted bootstrapping pipeline that produces a dedicated tongue segmentation model for in-the-wild reenactment without curated annotations. We further introduce a spatially constrained latent masked diffusion model for realistic tongue synthesis, with adaptive mask dilation for seamless mouth boundary transitions. Extensive experiments demonstrate improvements of more than two times over all baselines on every tongue-specific metric. We additionally propose a VLM-based evaluation protocol that replicates expert annotation at scale, confirming perceptual superiority across all ablation variants.

</details>


### [59] [Temporal Concentration from Rollout Errors: Implicit Preference Optimization for Text-to-Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28058)
*Henglin Liu,Fangyuan Kong,Jing Wang,Yizhou Lin,Nisha Huang,Chang Liu,Xintao Wang,Pengfei Wan,Kun Gai,Xiu Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: cIPO is a post-training framework for video diffusion models that derives implicit preference signals from the denoising process (reconstruction vs. original video) and concentrates optimization on high temporal reconstruction error segments, addressing temporally sparse artifacts like motion collapse and object flickering without requiring human annotations or external reward models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporally sparse artifacts such as motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation remain a major barrier to perceptual realism in diffusion-based video generation. Existing preference alignment methods (e.g., DPO) struggle due to (1) the preference attribution bottleneck—offline human annotations are costly and fail to capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are rollout-aware but unstable/biased—and (2) temporal credit misallocation, where uniform supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments where artifacts occur.

Method: cIPO derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, treating the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This captures inference-time errors without human annotations or external reward models. It then computes frame-level (temporal) reconstruction errors between original and reconstructed videos to identify when failures occur, and concentrates optimization on high-error segments for precise correction of failure-prone regions.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference with temporally concentrated optimization.

Conclusion: Implicit preference signals derived from reconstruction error, combined with temporally concentrated optimization, provide an effective and efficient alternative to costly human annotations or unstable reward models for aligning video diffusion models, overcoming both the preference attribution bottleneck and temporal credit misallocation.

Abstract: Recent advances in preference alignment for diffusion-based video generation, particularly via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), have significantly improved visual quality. However, temporally sparse artifacts such as motion collapse, object flickering, and color oversaturation remain a major barrier to perceptual realism. Existing methods struggle with these issues due to two key limitations: (1) the preference attribution bottleneck, where offline human annotations are costly and fail to accurately capture learning dynamics, while online reward signals are rollout-aware but often unstable and biased; and (2) temporal credit misallocation, where uniformly applied supervision cannot effectively target the brief segments in which artifacts occur. To address these challenges, we propose concentrated Implicit Preference Optimization (cIPO), a post-training framework for video diffusion models. cIPO derives implicit preference signals directly from the denoising process: given a real video, the model adds forward noise and reconstructs it via iterative denoising, treating the original as the preferred sample and the reconstruction as the dispreferred one. This formulation captures inference-time errors without requiring human annotations or external reward models. Moreover, frame-level discrepancies between original and reconstructed videos reveal when failures occur. cIPO leverages this by computing temporal reconstruction errors and concentrating optimization on high-error segments, enabling more precise correction of failure-prone regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that cIPO consistently enhances video authenticity and temporal coherence across multiple datasets, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of implicit preference with temporally concentrated optimization.

</details>


### [60] [Landmark shape spaces with induced metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28064)
*Sarang Joshi,Peter W. Michor,Stefan Sommer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper unifies Kendall's landmark shape spaces (rigid motions factored out, scale fixed) with landmark configuration spaces carrying right-invariant Sobolev metrics from the diffeomorphism group by introducing the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space is exactly the rigid motions. This creates new shape spaces that prevent landmark collisions, define metrics independent of landmark count, preserve local rigid transformations, remove global rigid motions, and fix scale. Numerical methods for matching and geodesic computation are also presented.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To combine the advantages of two distinct approaches to landmark shape analysis: Kendall's shape spaces (which factor out global rigid motions and fix scale but suffer from degenerate metrics) and Sobolev metrics from the diffeomorphism group (which provide regularity and prevent collisions but do not naturally factor out shape invariances).

Method: The authors define a particular Sobolev-type operator, the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space consists exactly of rigid motions. They show how this operator descends to enable the desired geometry on landmark configurations, and develop numerical approaches for solving matching problems and computing geodesics.

Result: The resulting landmark shape spaces achieve all defining properties of both approaches: regularity of the descending metric prevents landmark collisions, the metric is defined in the ambient space independent of the number of landmarks, local rigid transformations are preserved, global rigid motions are removed, and scale is fixed.

Conclusion: The construction allows landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics to be used in applications while retaining the shape invariances characteristic of Kendall's shape spaces, providing a unified framework that bridges the two previously separate approaches.

Abstract: We present a unification of Kendall's landmark shape spaces, where rigid motions are factored out and scale fixed on landmark configurations equipped with Euclidean geometry, with landmark configuration spaces carrying Riemannian metrics descending from right-invariant Sobolev metrics on the diffeomorphism group. The resulting new landmark shape spaces achieve the defining properties of both approaches: The regularity of the descending metric prevents landmarks from colliding, the metric is defined in the ambient space independent of the number of landmarks, local rigid transformations are preserved, global rigid motions are removed, and scale fixed. To achieve this, we define a particular Sobolev-type operator, the screened elasticity operator, whose null-space consists exactly of the rigid motions, we show how this operator descends to achieve the desired geometry, and we present approaches to solving matching problems and computing geodesics numerically. The resulting construction allows the use of landmark configuration spaces with sufficiently regular metrics in applications while retaining the shape invariances that are a hallmark of Kendall's shape spaces.

</details>


### [61] [BladeYOLO: Wind Turbine Blade Defect Detection with Limited Annotations and Weak-Saliency Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28065)
*Yabin Xu,Fangtao Zhang,Fan Wang,Zhan Wang,Honghua Chen,Mingqiang Wei,Haoran Xie,Sam Kwong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BladeYOLO is a defect detection framework for wind turbine blades that integrates a DINOv3-pretrained Vision Transformer backbone into YOLOv12-L, along with a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module and a lightweight Style-Injector module, achieving superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset and outperforming the best competitor by 3.5% mAP50 and 2.5% mAP50-95 on a public dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wind turbine blade defect detection in real-world scenarios is highly challenging due to limited on-site training data, small-scale and low-contrast defects, and difficulty distinguishing defects from complex backgrounds, which limits the robustness of existing detectors.

Method: BladeYOLO builds on YOLOv12-L by: (1) integrating a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights to transfer large-scale generic visual priors; (2) developing a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module comprising a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency structural cues and a Cross-Mamba module for propagating high-level semantic guidance to shallow features; and (3) introducing a lightweight Style-Injector module that captures environment-related style information via Fourier decomposition and injects it into selected ViT self-attention layers.

Result: BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset, shows favorable performance under reduced training annotations in annotation-budget experiments, and demonstrates cross-dataset robustness on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset, where it outperforms the best competing method by 3.5% in mAP50 and 2.5% in mAP50-95.

Conclusion: The proposed BladeYOLO framework effectively addresses the challenges of limited data and subtle defect characteristics in wind turbine blade inspection by combining self-supervised ViT transfer learning, multi-scale detail enhancement with Mamba-guided semantic propagation, and Fourier-based style injection, yielding state-of-the-art detection performance and cross-dataset robustness.

Abstract: Wind turbine blade defect detection remains highly challenging in real-world inspection scenarios due to limited on-site data and the subtle visual characteristics of defects. In practice, blade defects are often small-scale, low-contrast, and difficult to distinguish from complex backgrounds, which significantly limits the robustness of existing detectors. To address these challenges, we propose BladeYOLO, a defect detection framework for wind turbine blades. Specifically, we integrate a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone initialized with DINOv3 self-supervised pre-trained weights into YOLOv12-L, enabling the transfer of large-scale generic visual priors to blade defect detection and improving feature representation under limited training annotations. To enhance the perception of subtle defects, we further develop a Mamba-guided Weak-Defect Enhancement module, which consists of a Detail-Enhanced Multi-scale Branch for preserving high-frequency structural cues and a Cross-Mamba module for progressively propagating high-level semantic guidance to shallow features. In addition, we introduce a lightweight Style-Injector module that captures environment-related style information via Fourier decomposition and injects it into selected ViT self-attention layers, thereby improving robustness against environment-induced appearance variations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BladeYOLO achieves superior performance on the WTBlade-Defect dataset, with additional annotation-budget experiments showing its favorable performance under reduced training annotations. Evaluation on the public Wind Surface Defect dataset further provides supportive evidence for the cross-dataset robustness of BladeYOLO. In particular, on this public dataset, BladeYOLO outperforms the best competing method by 3.5\% in mAP$_{50}$ and 2.5\% in mAP$_{50-95}$.

</details>


### [62] [mmRadarTwin: A Measurement-Calibrated Signal-Level Digital Twin Platform for Indoor mmWave Radar](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28108)
*Jianyi Zhou,Chenghao Zhang,Yanli Li,Dong Yuan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: mmRadarTwin is a signal-level, path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar that links real FMCW radar measurements with an Unreal Engine scene simulation through a shared processing interface, achieving 70.8% recall of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions across 154 poses in an office deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indoor mmWave radar perception is difficult to reproduce because measured range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, material response, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools expose rendering, channel, or path-level quantities, while radar sensing requires complex signal products that can be processed and compared in the same domain as real FMCW measurements.

Method: mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator writes complex multi-channel receive grids and exports per-path contribution records identifying actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support of each simulated return. Evaluation uses a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware in an office deployment across 154 measured poses spanning 22 radar locations.

Result: The physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view, while exposing residuals caused by weak or missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms.

Conclusion: Rather than claiming complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, mmRadarTwin establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.

Abstract: Indoor mmWave radar perception is difficult to reproduce because measured range-angle responses depend on scene geometry, material response, multipath, hardware conventions, and signal processing. Existing ray-tracing and digital-twin tools often expose rendering, channel, or path-level quantities, while radar sensing requires complex signal products that can be processed and compared in the same domain as real FMCW measurements. We present mmRadarTwin, a signal-level and path-attributed digital-twin platform for indoor mmWave radar. mmRadarTwin links a real radar measurement branch with an Unreal Engine scene-simulation branch through a shared receive-channel and range-angle processing interface. The simulator writes complex multi-channel receive grids and exports per-path contribution records that identify the actor, material tag, propagation event, and output-bin support of each simulated return. We evaluate mmRadarTwin in an office deployment using a commodity monostatic mmWave radar and mobile scene-capture hardware. Across 154 measured poses spanning 22 radar locations, the current physics-only path-basis simulator recalls 70.8% of measurement-active geometry-supported response regions in the central usable field of view while exposing residuals caused by weak or missing path support, shifted responses, unsupported anchors, and missing physical mechanisms. Rather than claiming complete radar-map reconstruction or cross-room generalization, mmRadarTwin establishes a practical systems workflow for constructing, comparing, and diagnosing indoor radar digital twins.

</details>


### [63] [Towards Practical Algorithm Selection for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation in Medical Imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28125)
*Yiheng Xiong,Luisa Gallée,Daniel Santak Wolf,Heiko Hillenhagen,Michael Götz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A label-free criterion for jointly selecting the best UDA algorithm and hyperparameters by scoring candidate models against a two-level agreement reference built from multiple label-free selection signals, validated on brain MRI and chest X-ray datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In clinical practice, choosing the best UDA algorithm and its hyperparameters is difficult because the unlabeled target domain prevents direct evaluation, making algorithm/hyperparameter selection unclear.

Method: The approach constructs a two-level agreement reference without target labels: (1) multiple label-free selection signals each nominate a model within each algorithm; (2) nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to form a reference prediction per target sample. Each candidate is scored by agreement with this reference, and the highest-scoring candidate is selected for deployment.

Result: Evaluated on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios, the method outperforms other selection methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools.

Conclusion: The proposed approach advances practical, label-free algorithm and hyperparameter selection for clinical deployment of UDA.

Abstract: Numerous unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) algori-thms exist, but for clinical practice, selecting the best-suited one along with proper hyperparameters often remains unclear, as the unlabeled deployment (target) domain prevents direct evaluation. We propose a label-free criterion that jointly selects the algorithm and hyperparameters for UDA. Given a pool of candidate models from multiple algorithms trained with different hyperparameters, our approach scores each candidate against an agreement reference, and selects the one with the highest score. The agreement reference is constructed in two levels without using target labels. First, we leverage multiple label-free selection signals, using each to nominate a model within every algorithm. Second, the nominated models are aggregated across algorithms to form a reference prediction for each unlabeled target sample. The candidate whose predictions agree most with this reference is then selected for deployment. Experimental results on four brain MRI and four chest X-ray datasets across seven clinically relevant transfer scenarios show that our method achieves better selection performance than other methods and remains effective across different algorithm pools. Our approach takes a step towards practical, label-free algorithm selection for clinical deployment of UDA.

</details>


### [64] [Face and Voice Cross-modal Association with Learning Convex Feature Embedding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28129)
*Taewan Kim,Jiwoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a cross-modal feature embedding method for face-voice association that learns embeddings within a convex hull and incorporates cross-modal attention to reduce false positives and false negatives. Evaluated on VoxCeleb, it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on verification, matching, and retrieval tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous cross-modal face-voice association methods address cross-modal discrimination but underestimate inter-modal feature heterogeneity between audio and video, leading to many false positives and false negatives.

Method: The method trains cross-modal features by ensuring another feature exists between them, causing voice and face features of the same person to be embedded within a convex hull. Cross-modal attention mechanisms are combined with convex embedding techniques to minimize inter-class discrepancies and attenuate false positives/negatives.

Result: Exhaustive evaluation on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks demonstrates notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: Combining convex embedding with cross-modal attention effectively handles cross-modal heterogeneity and significantly improves face-voice association performance beyond current methods.

Abstract: Face-and-voice association learning is one of the most challenging tasks in deep learning. In this paper, we propose a simple but powerful cross-modal feature embedding method for the association of faces and voices. Previous work has studied cross-modal association tasks to establish the correlation between voice clips and facial images. These works have addressed cross-modal discrimination but underestimate the importance of handling heterogeneity in inter-modal features between audio and video, resulting in a lot of false positives and false negatives. To tackle the problem, the proposed method learns the embeddings of cross-modal features by making another feature exist between cross-modal features, facilitating the voice and face features of the same person to be embedded in a convex hull. Moreover, the incorporation of cross-modal attention mechanisms with convex embedding techniques represents a highly effective strategy for the attenuation of false positives and false negatives, accomplished via the minimization of inter-class discrepancies. We exhaustively evaluated our method for cross-modal verification, matching, and retrieval tasks on the large-scale VoxCeleb dataset. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves notable improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [65] [Collaborative Feature Aggregation for Face Super-Resolution and Robust Re-Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28130)
*Juheon Hwang,Taewan Kim,Jiwoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A novel collaborative face super-resolution and person re-identification framework using transformer-based feature aggregation across multi-sequence or multi-view facial images, paired with a cascade SR network for progressive restoration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional face super-resolution methods suffer from blurring and distortion when recovering faces from low-quality images, and existing image/video-based SR approaches using landmarks or segmentation face similar challenges. The paper aims to overcome these limitations by leveraging multiple correlated facial observations across time or viewpoints.

Method: The approach introduces a transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method that unifies identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view facial data, enabling multiple sequences of an individual to contribute to estimating common facial features. A cascade SR network progressively restores high-resolution face images with gradual facial feature unification, and the unified identity representation is used for person re-identification.

Result: Exhaustive experiments show the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both face super-resolution and person re-identification tasks, with consistent improvements in accuracy under severe image degradation.

Conclusion: Joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs is effective in enhancing downstream visual recognition tasks, demonstrating the benefit of collaborative multi-view/multi-sequence facial processing.

Abstract: We propose a novel collaborative approach for face super-resolution (SR) and robust person re-identification from sequential or multi-view facial images. Traditional SR methods often suffer from blurring and distortion in faces recovered from poor-quality images due to low resolution. Image- and video-based facial SR methods using facial landmarks or segmentation also have similar challenges. To overcome these limitations, we leverage multiple correlated facial observations, across time or viewpoints, by introducing a transformer-based collaborative feature aggregation method that unifies identity features from multi-sequence or multi-view data. This allows faces in multiple sequences of an individual to contribute to accurately estimating common facial features. Furthermore, we propose a cascade SR network to progressively restore the high-resolution image of the target's face with gradual facial feature unification. The unified identity representation is further utilized in person re-identification scenarios, enabling accurate matching even under severe image degradation. The exhaustive experimental results and comparisons show that our method outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating consistent improvements in both face super-resolution and re-identification performance. Our work highlights the effectiveness of joint identity reconstruction and progressive image restoration from multiple facial inputs in enhancing downstream visual recognition tasks.

</details>


### [66] [Convolutional Neural Shading for High-Quality 3D Reconstruction from Multi-View Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28132)
*Juheon Hwang,Taewan Kim,Heeseok Oh,Jiwoo Kang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes Convolutional Neural Shading (CNS), a novel pipeline for reconstructing high-quality 3D shapes from multi-view images. It uses a convolutional neural shader to capture local geometric variations beyond single-point information (positions and normals), and introduces a fine-detail displacement network that leverages spatial context to reduce surface irregularities at image boundaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural differentiable rendering methods for 3D reconstruction rely on single-point geometric information (e.g., positions and normals), which limits their ability to capture detailed local geometry, especially in dark and textureless regions.

Method: The method consists of two key components: (1) a convolutional neural shader that captures local variations using spatial convolution rather than single-point information, improving geometry prediction in challenging regions; and (2) a fine-detail displacement network that utilizes spatial information of surface geometry to learn fine displacement details by correlating neighboring values in rendering coordinates, mitigating surface irregularities at image boundaries.

Result: Extensive experiments show significant quality improvements in both reconstructed 3D shapes and rendered images compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: CNS demonstrates that incorporating local spatial context via convolutional neural shading and displacement learning effectively overcomes the limitations of single-point-based neural rendering, yielding more accurate 3D reconstructions.

Abstract: We propose a convolutional neural shading (CNS), a novel pipeline to reconstruct high-quality 3D shapes from multi-view images. Several recent studies have used neural radiance fields and other neural differentiable rendering methods to understand 3D geometry. However, these approaches rely on single-point geometric information, such as positions and normals of the surface, leading to a lack of detailed local geometry. Our approach addresses the inherent limitations of single-point information by leveraging a neural shader to capture variations even in dark and textureless regions with a convolutional neural shader, resulting in far more accurate geometry predictions. Additionally, our method mitigates surface irregularities at image boundaries by introducing a fine-detail displacement network, which utilizes spatial information of surface geometry and learns fine displacement details by correlating neighboring values in the rendering coordinates. Through extensive experiments, our proposed method has demonstrated significant quality improvements in the reconstructed shapes and rendered images over current state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [67] [What Makes Deep Learning Work for Traditional Chinese Medicine Tongue Diagnosis? A Comprehensive Ablation Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28148)
*Longxia Gao,Linan Wang,Yuhe Han,Junze Geng,Meng Zhang,Hanqing Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A systematic ablation study on deep learning for automated tongue diagnosis in TCM, testing 20+ model versions across architectures, losses, augmentations, and training strategies. Best weighted-F1 of 0.7761 on 11K samples and 0.6625 on 976 samples, yielding six generalizable design principles for multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite deep learning showing promise for automated tongue diagnosis in TCM, the design space (architectures, losses, augmentations, training strategies) remains underexplored. A systematic evaluation is needed to identify optimal design choices.

Method: Conducted a systematic ablation study spanning 20+ model versions under rigorous 5-fold cross-validation. Compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies on two datasets: TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples.

Result: Best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625 (ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble); best 11,101-sample model reached weighted-F1 of 0.7761. Key findings: ConvNeXt-Tiny is most parameter-efficient; BCE outperforms Asymmetric Loss by +2.7%; restrained color augmentation is critical; weak-group ensemble provides +2.1% over probability averaging; data scaling yields +20.6% improvement; expanding from 13 to 45 labels caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22).

Conclusion: The study establishes six key design principles for tongue diagnosis models that generalize to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance, providing a systematic reference for future work in this domain.

Abstract: Deep learning has shown promise for automated tongue diagnosis in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), yet the design space remains underexplored. We conducted a systematic ablation study spanning 20+ model versions under rigorous 5-fold cross-validation on TongueDx2 (5,109 images, 976 expert-annotated) and a merged dataset of 11,101 samples. We compared six backbone architectures, four loss functions, five augmentation strategies, and six training strategies. The best 976-sample model achieved weighted-F1 of 0.6625 using ConvNeXt-Tiny with restrained augmentation and weak-group ensemble, while the best 11,101-sample model reached weighted-F1 of 0.7761. Six key design principles emerged: (1) ConvNeXt-Tiny offers optimal parameter efficiency; (2) BCE substantially outperforms Asymmetric Loss (+2.7%); (3) restrained color augmentation is critical; (4) weak-group ensemble replacement (+2.1%) outperforms probability averaging; (5) data scaling yielded +20.6% improvement; (6) expanding from 13 to 45 label dimensions caused catastrophic collapse (0.78 to 0.22). These principles are generalizable to multi-label medical image classification with class imbalance.

</details>


### [68] [OPLD: On-Policy Latent Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28154)
*Shoutai Zhu,Tianyang Xu,Bin Sun,Mingyuan Xu,Yu Liu,Qinzhen Guo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes OPLD (On-Policy Latent Distillation), a framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from privileged multimodal Chain-of-Thought into latent reasoning representations, outperforming existing latent reasoning methods on multiple multimodal benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interleaved multimodal CoT methods rely on externally defined reasoning traces and visual operations, limiting flexible abstract visual thinking. Current visual-latent methods supervise latent states via alignment with compressed auxiliary visual features, treating them as proxies for visual observations rather than active reasoning states—capturing evidence but failing to internalize the abstract reasoning process.

Method: OPLD transfers the reasoning capability induced by privileged multimodal CoT into latent reasoning representations via on-policy latent distillation, supervising latent representations at the reasoning-process level rather than conventional feature-level alignment.

Result: Extensive experiments on diverse multimodal benchmarks show OPLD consistently outperforms existing latent reasoning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
