### [110] [SKY-Piano: A Multimodal Piano Performance Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27296)
*Joonhyung Bae,Dawon Park,Taegyun Kwon,Yoon-Seok Choi,Hyeon Hur,Satoshi Obata,Shigeru Kai,Yohei Wada,Yu Takahashi,Akira Maezawa,Jaebum Park,Jonghwa Park,Juhan Nam*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SKY-Piano is a multimodal piano performance dataset containing 11 hours of synchronized recordings (motion, multi-view video, audio, MIDI, MusicXML scores) from 19 pianists (7 professional, 12 amateur), with flagged and imputed motion data, body-segment kinematics, an interactive browser, a fingering annotation tool, and a MIDI-to-motion generation baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Music information retrieval research on piano performance increasingly requires diverse modalities of data beyond just audio and MIDI, but comprehensive multimodal piano datasets that include synchronized motion, video, audio, MIDI, and scores from pianists of varying expertise are lacking.

Method: The dataset comprises 11 hours of performance recordings from 7 professional and 12 amateur pianists covering a shared core repertoire selected based on playing technique, difficulty, and performer expertise. Motion data includes hand and body motion released in both flagged and imputed forms, along with Visual3D body-segment kinematics and synchronized modalities. A fingering annotation model/tool derives pseudo-fingering annotations from MIDI and motion data, and a fine-tuning experiment demonstrates MIDI-to-motion generation as a use case. An interactive web browser facilitates data exploration.

Result: The paper presents the complete SKY-Piano dataset with synchronized multimodal data, provides an interactive browsing interface, introduces a fingering annotation tool, and demonstrates a MIDI-to-motion generation fine-tuning experiment as a downstream use case.

Conclusion: SKY-Piano addresses the need for multimodal piano performance data by offering a rich, synchronized dataset from pianists of different skill levels, enabling research in areas such as motion generation, fingering analysis, and cross-modal learning.

Abstract: Music information retrieval research on piano performance increasingly involves diverse modalities of data and annotations beyond audio and MIDI. We present SKY-Piano, a multimodal piano performance dataset that includes 11 hours of performance recordings of motion, multi-view video, audio, MIDI from 7 professional and 12 amateur pianists along with MusicXML scores. The performance pieces were selected considering playing technique, difficulty, and performer expertise on a shared core repertoire. The motion data include both hand and body motion, released in both flagged form, where samples lost to marker occlusion are marked as unreliable, and imputed form, where those gaps are reconstructed, together with Visual3D body-segment kinematics and other time-synchronized modalities. To easily browse different modalities of data at a glance, we provide an interactive web browser. In addition, we developed a fingering annotation model and tool for deriving pseudo fingering annotations from the MIDI and motion data. Lastly, we present MIDI-to-motion generation through a fine-tuning experiment as a use case of the dataset.

</details>


### [111] [Enhancing Law-Enforcement Audio Transcription: A LoRA-Based Adaptation of Whisper for BWC Footage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27245)
*Vivek Senthil,Zhiqiang Tao,Ernest Fokoué*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a framework for adapting OpenAI's Whisper speech recognition to police Body-Worn Camera footage using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) via LoRA, enabling accurate transcription on consumer-grade hardware through 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing. The transcribed audio is integrated into a symbolic reasoning pipeline with a domain-specific ontology, achieving a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate for evidence-linked incident graphs to advance procedural justice and transparency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Law enforcement agencies hold petabytes of BWC footage that remain largely unutilized for accountability or systemic review due to the prohibitive labor costs of manual transcription. The "visibility paradox" describes this gap between data availability and actionable insight, motivating the need for automated, accurate transcription adapted to the policing acoustic environment.

Method: The method involves adapting OpenAI Whisper via Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to handle policing-specific acoustic challenges (high-stress scenarios, sirens, radio interference). The fine-tuning is made feasible on consumer-grade hardware (4GB GTX GPU) using 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing. Transcriptions are then processed through a symbolic reasoning pipeline with a domain-specific ontology to generate evidence-linked incident graphs from raw audio.

Result: The adapted model overcomes the significant performance degradation of zero-shot Whisper on police audio and achieves a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate when integrating transcriptions into the domain ontology for incident graph construction.

Conclusion: PEFT-based Whisper adaptation is a viable, low-cost approach for processing police BWC footage at scale on consumer hardware, converting raw audio into structured, evidence-linked representations that can advance procedural justice and transparency in policing.

Abstract: Modern policing faces a "visibility paradox" where law enforcement agencies possess petabytes of Body-Worn Camera (BWC) footage that remains largely unutilized for accountability or systemic review due to the prohibitive labor costs of manual transcription. This research presents a framework for adapting the OpenAI Whisper architecture to the unique acoustic and linguistic challenges of the policing environment. By employing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), we address the significant performance degradation observed in zero-shot models when confronted with high-stress scenarios, sirens, and radio interference. Crucially, we demonstrate that this adaptation is feasible on consumer-grade hardware (Acer Nitro local machine with NVIDIA 4GB GTX GPU) using 8-bit quantization and gradient checkpointing. We further integrate these transcriptions into a symbolic reasoning pipeline using a domain-specific ontology to transform raw audio into evidence-linked incident graphs, achieving a 93.7% lexicon mapping rate for the advancement of procedural justice and transparency.

</details>


### [112] [Does EEG Foundation Models Transfer to Speech? A Benchmark on Overt and Imagined Speech Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27268)
*Owais Mujtaba Khanday,Mohamed Baha Ben Ticha,Sanae Belfrouh,Marc Ouellet,Jose A. Gonzalez-Lopez*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: First systematic benchmark of EEG foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against convolutional baselines for speech decoding shows pretrained foundation models provide no consistent advantage over a small 16K-parameter CNN across two speech corpora, suggesting current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not transfer to speech decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While EEG foundation models pretrained on thousands of hours have shown gains in other BCI tasks (motor imagery, seizure detection, sleep staging, emotion recognition), their utility for speech decoding—the most demanding non-invasive BCI application—has not been tested.

Method: A unified preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol is used to compare two EEG foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against three established convolutional baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) on two speech decoding corpora: UGR-MINDVOICE (overt and covert Iberian Spanish) and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (imagined speech).

Result: Large-scale EEG pretraining yields no consistent improvement over a 16K-parameter CNN baseline on speech decoding tasks, indicating a lack of transfer from general-purpose EEG pretraining to speech production tasks.

Conclusion: Current general-purpose EEG foundation model pretraining does not yet transfer to speech decoding, motivating the development of speech-specific EEG foundation models.

Abstract: EEG foundation models pretrained on thousands of hours have shown large gains over task-specific networks for motor imagery, seizure detection, sleep staging, and emotion recognition, but their transfer to speech decoding-arguably the most demanding non-invasive BCI application-remains untested. We present the first systematic benchmark of EEG foundation models against strong convolutional baselines for speech decoding, using two corpora: UGR-MINDVOICE (overt and covert Iberian Spanish) and BCI Competition 2020 Track 3 (imagined speech). We compare two foundation models (LaBraM, EEGMamba) against three established baselines (EEGNet, ShallowFBCSPNet, EEGConformer) under a unified preprocessing and fine-tuning protocol. Large-scale EEG pretraining yields no consistent advantage over a 16K-parameter CNN on speech tasks, indicating that current general-purpose EEG pretraining does not yet transfer to speech production and motivating speech-specific foundation models.

</details>


### [113] [Cocktail-Talker: Multi-Speaker Dialog Modeling in Noisy Social Environments with Turn Action GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27756)
*Xilin Jiang,Riki Shimizu,Sukru Samet Dindar,Junkai Wu,Zhongweiyang Xu,Nima Mesgarani*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: The paper introduces Cocktail-Talker, a speech LLM framework for multi-speaker spoken dialog modeling in noisy social environments. It uses three action tokens (<|respond|>, <|listen|>, <|ignore|>) to decide whether to respond, listen, or stay silent, and is trained with supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning. Training data is prepared via Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based pipeline that simulates realistic multi-speaker dialogs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world social conversations are ambiguous and noisy: multiple speakers may participate, utterances may not be directed to the assistant, and background noise is common. Traditional spoken dialog systems assume clean, dyadic turn-taking interactions, which fails to capture these complex scenarios. The assistant needs to decide not only what to say but also whether to speak at all.

Method: Cocktail-Talker is a speech LLM framework that models assistant behavior using three action tokens (<|respond|>, <|listen|>, <|ignore|>) placed before a response or silence. It is trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning to generate the correct action token and, only in <|respond|> mode, a speech response. Training data is generated by Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based data pipeline that simulates realistic multi-speaker dialogs with speaker roles across diverse social settings.

Result: The paper presents the framework and data pipeline as components toward more natural and selective spoken dialog systems in complex social environments, though specific experimental results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: Together, Cocktail-Talker and Cocktail-DialogGen take a step toward spoken dialog systems that interact more naturally and selectively in complex social environments with multiple speakers and background noise.

Abstract: Spoken dialog systems are typically designed for clean, dyadic interactions in which a single user and an assistant take turns speaking. Real-world social conversations, however, are often more ambiguous: multiple speakers may participate in the same conversation amid irrelevant speech and background noise. Each utterance may be directed to the assistant, addressed to another speaker, or completely irrelevant. In such settings, the assistant must decide not only what to say, but also whether to speak at all. In this paper, we introduce Cocktail-Talker, a speech LLM framework for multi-speaker spoken dialog modeling in noisy social environments. We model the assistant's behavior with three action tokens: <|respond|>, <|listen|>, and <|ignore|>, placed before a response or silence. Cocktail-Talker is trained via supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning to generate the appropriate action token and, only in <|respond|> mode, a speech response. To prepare the training data, we develop Cocktail-DialogGen, an LLM-based data pipeline that simulates realistic multi-speaker dialogs with speaker roles across diverse social settings. Together, these components take a step toward spoken dialog systems that interact more naturally and selectively in complex social environments.

</details>


### [114] [Improved Robustness in AI-Generated Music Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27454)
*Emile Dugelay,Thomas Barand,Baptiste Campeas,Aurélien Laouar,Darius Afchar,Romain Hennequin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses the robustness problem of AI music generator detectors, which fail under audio manipulations like speed modification or pitch shifting. The authors propose a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline using log-STFT remapping, a learned cross-correlation filter with max-pooling for shift invariance, and a hybrid loss that supervises both binary detection and artifact-peak localization, achieving robustness by design and interpretability via speed-change factor estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI music detectors exploit spectral artifacts with near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks but collapse under simple audio manipulations such as speed modification or pitch shifting. This robustness gap motivates the need for a detection method that is invariant to frequency scaling by design rather than relying on post-hoc augmentation.

Method: The method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via log-STFT remapping, applies a single learned cross-correlation filter combined with max-pooling to achieve shift invariance at inference time, and trains with a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization while regularizing boundary weights.

Result: The detector is robust to speed change by design, maintains detection accuracy under audio manipulations, and provides interpretable outputs including both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

Conclusion: Frequency-scaling-invariant detection can be built into the architecture itself, addressing the robustness problem without sacrificing interpretability, while also enabling speed-change factor estimation as a byproduct.

Abstract: AI music generators leave predictable spectral artifacts determined by their architecture. Existing detectors exploit these artifacts with near-perfect accuracy on raw generated tracks, but their performance collapses under simple audio manipulations, such as speed modification or pitch shifting. We address this open robustness problem by introducing a frequency-scaling-invariant detection pipeline that aims to prevent this kind of attack by design. Our method maps audio onto a log-frequency axis via a log-STFT remapping. A single learned cross-correlation filter, combined with max-pooling, provides shift invariance at inference time. Training uses a hybrid loss that jointly supervises binary detection and artifact-peak localization, regularizing boundary weights. Because robustness to speed change is built in by design, the detector is also interpretable: it outputs both a binary decision and an estimate of the applied speed-change factor.

</details>


### [115] [VocalRender: Score-Native Singing Voice Synthesis for Real-World Composition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27768)
*Yukun Chen,Tianrui Wang,Zhaoxi Mu,Xinyu Yang,EngSiong Chng*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: VocalRender is a score-native singing voice synthesis system that directly generates singing from lyrics, pitches, note values, and tempo using an interleaved lyric-note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model, eliminating the need for explicit duration prediction. Trained on 2,300 hours of data, it achieves strong intelligibility, melody control, and speaker similarity, outperforming baselines by 0.42 CMOS in naturalness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing singing voice synthesis systems require predefined durations, explicit duration prediction, or time-aligned acoustic guidance, which limits compatibility with practical composition workflows. The authors aim to remove these constraints to enable direct synthesis from score-level inputs.

Method: The system uses an interleaved lyric-note representation combined with an autoregressive diffusion model that generates continuous acoustic latents while simultaneously predicting output length, removing the need for explicit duration prediction. It is trained on a 2,300-hour singing dataset.

Result: VocalRender achieves strong intelligibility, melody control, and high speaker similarity on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. It outperforms the strongest baseline by 0.42 CMOS points in naturalness.

Conclusion: The score-native architecture is effective for singing synthesis, demonstrating that eliminating explicit duration prediction is feasible and yields superior naturalness while maintaining strong control and similarity metrics.

Abstract: Existing singing voice synthesis systems often require predefined durations, explicit duration prediction, or time-aligned acoustic guidance, which limits their compatibility with practical composition workflows. We propose VocalRender, a score-native system that directly synthesizes singing from lyrics, pitches, symbolic note values, and tempo. It uses an interleaved lyric--note representation and an autoregressive diffusion model to generate continuous acoustic latents while predicting the output length, eliminating the need for explicit duration prediction. Trained on a 2,300-hour singing dataset, VocalRender achieves strong intelligibility, strong melody control, and high speaker similarity across both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Notably, it outperforms the strongest baseline by $0.42$ points in naturalness CMOS, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed score-native architecture.

</details>


### [116] [CrowdioSet and PaRIRset: Two Datasets Towards Live Music Source Separation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27828)
*Enric Gusó,Xavier Serra*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper addresses the poor generalization of Music Source Separation (MSS) models to live music recordings by proposing two novel datasets: CrowdioSet (4800 real ambience tracks plus synthetic sing-alongs for vocals) for audio denoising, and PaRIRset (stereo impulse responses from 40 professional concert venues) for simulating live acoustics. Training with these datasets improves MSS performance on live recordings in both objective and subjective evaluations, with all resources made publicly available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MSS models are trained exclusively on studio recordings and fail to generalize to live music because they ignore venue acoustics, speaker system responses, and audience noise. This gap limits real-world applicability of source separation.

Method: The authors create two datasets: (1) CrowdioSet, comprising 4800 real ambience tracks from Freesound and synthetic sing-along vocals generated via zero-shot singing voice conversion for MUSDB18 and MOISESDB, enabling audio denoising; (2) PaRIRset, a stereo impulse response dataset captured across 40 professional concert venues using a microphone array. Both datasets are used to train MSS models.

Result: CrowdioSet enables effective denoising of live recordings, yielding superior objective and subjective separation results. Adding PaRIRset RIRs improves MSS model performance compared to using real RIRs from speech enhancement tasks alone.

Conclusion: Training MSS models with the proposed CrowdioSet and PaRIRset datasets bridges the domain gap between studio and live recordings, improving source separation quality in live scenarios. All datasets, code, and model weights are released to the public.

Abstract: Most Music Source Separation (MSS) models do not generalize well to live music recordings because they are trained on studio recordings alone, disregarding the venue acoustics, the speaker system's response and audience noise. We propose to bridge this gap by providing and training a model on two novel datasets. First, we present CrowdioSet: a noise dataset comprising 4800 real ambience tracks from Freesound and synthetic sing-alongs for the vocals in MUSDB18 and MOISESDB datasets, generated from zero-shot singing voice conversions. CrowdioSet enables effective audio denoising for live recordings, resulting in superior separation both in objective and subjective evaluations. Second, we introduce PaRIRset, a stereo impulse response dataset captured across 40 professional concert venues using a microphone array. Our results show that adding PaRIRset RIRs increases the performance of a MSS model compared to using real RIRs from Speech Enhancement tasks alone. We make the examples, code, model weights, PaRIRset, and CrowdioSet freely available to the public.

</details>


### [117] [Integrating Contextual Embeddings into Evaluation of Expressive MIDI Piano Performances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27909)
*Dmitrii Gavrilev,Ilya Borovik,Vladimir Viro*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces Pereval, an open-source library for evaluating expressive MIDI piano performances using both traditional attribute-scoped metrics and deep feature metrics based on self-supervised symbolic music models (Aria and CLaMP3). The authors show that contextual embeddings from these models serve as perceptual proxies with human-rating agreement on par with traditional metrics, and adapt Kernel Audio Distance to symbolic music for measuring conditional distributional similarity without requiring note alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances relies on per-note attribute statistics (timing, velocity, duration) that ignore inter-note dependencies and cannot fully capture performance similarity. Additionally, the wide variety of expressive attributes in generative applications makes it difficult to aggregate into a single scalar metric for model selection.

Method: The authors reexamine attribute-scoped metrics and explore perceptual properties of contextual embeddings from two self-supervised symbolic music models (Aria and CLaMP3). They conduct a listening study to validate these models as perceptual proxies, and adapt Kernel Audio Distance (KAD) to the symbolic music domain to measure conditional distributional similarity, comparing against Pearson correlation and reconstruction error using kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings.

Result: Listening study results show the self-supervised symbolic music models achieve per-sample human rating agreement on par with traditional metrics. Kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations, unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error.

Conclusion: The authors release Pereval, an open-source library integrating performance evaluation utilities including both attribute-scoped and deep feature metrics, providing a reproducible framework for evaluating expressive MIDI piano performances.

Abstract: Objective evaluation of expressive MIDI piano performances typically relies on attribute statistics such as timing, velocity, and duration of individual notes. However, these methods often disregard dependencies between notes, which poses a potential limitation in assessing the similarity between two sets of performances. In generative applications, the wide variety of expressive attributes makes it difficult to aggregate them into a single scalar metric for model selection. In this work, we reexamine attribute-scoped metrics and explore the perceptual properties of contextual embeddings from self-supervised symbolic music models, Aria and CLaMP3. Results from our listening study indicate that these models can be used as perceptual proxies, showing agreement with per-sample human ratings on par with traditional metrics. To measure conditional distributional similarity, we adapt Kernel Audio Distance to the symbolic music domain. Unlike Pearson correlation and reconstruction error, kernel-based methods on contextual embeddings do not require note alignment and are sensitive to contextual perturbations. To facilitate reproducibility, we release Pereval, an open-source library that integrates performance evaluation utilities, including both attribute-scoped and deep feature metrics.

</details>


### [118] [Teffic-Audio: Tell Fact from Fiction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28351)
*Wan Lin,Li Wang,Jindong Wang,Kunyu Feng,Zhizheng Wu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Teffic-Audio is a general speech deepfake detection system using a Conformer-based encoder with multi-head attentive statistics pooling and binary classification. Instead of architectural complexity, it improves generalization via a training recipe with multi-source data, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation. Trained only on open-source data, it achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on the 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, surpassing all public systems on the leaderboard, with the lowest EER on five individual test sets and a favorable performance-complexity trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech deepfake detection faces increasingly heterogeneous spoofing mechanisms (speech synthesis, voice conversion, vocoder reconstruction, neural-codec resynthesis) compounded by variability in source speech, recording environments, and transmission channels. This variability makes robust generalization across heterogeneous conditions essential for practical detection systems, motivating a general-purpose solution rather than a task-specific one.

Method: Teffic-Audio uses a straightforward detector architecture: a Conformer-based speech encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Generalization is achieved through the training recipe rather than architectural complexity, incorporating multi-source data integration, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation. It is trained only on open-source data.

Result: Teffic-Audio achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on the 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, outperforming all currently public systems on the leaderboard. It obtains the lowest EER on five individual test sets and demonstrates a favorable performance-complexity trade-off compared with larger leading systems.

Conclusion: Teffic-Audio provides a strong, practical reference system for general speech deepfake detection, demonstrating that effective generalization can be achieved through careful training strategy rather than architectural complexity, and offering a competitive performance-complexity balance.

Abstract: Speech deepfake detection has expanded in scope with increasingly heterogeneous spoofing mechanisms, including speech synthesis, voice conversion, vocoder reconstruction, and neural-codec resynthesis. The resulting spoofing artifacts can be further shaped by variability in source speech, recording environments, and transmission channels. This variability makes robust generalization across heterogeneous conditions a central requirement for practical detection systems. This report presents Teffic-Audio, a general speech deepfake detection system designed for comprehensive evaluation environment. Teffic-Audio adopts a straightforward detector architecture consisting of a Conformer-based speech encoder, multi-head attentive statistics pooling, and a binary classifier. Rather than relying on additional architectural complexity, the system improves generalization through its training recipe, which integrates multi-source data, attack- and source-balanced sampling, and diverse audio augmentation. Trained only with open-source data, Teffic-Audio achieves a pooled EER of 1.454% on the 14 test sets of Speech-DF-Arena, outperforming all currently public systems on the leaderboard. It also obtains the lowest EER on five individual test sets and shows a favorable performance-complexity trade-off compared with larger leading systems. Overall, Teffic-Audio provides a strong and practical reference system for general speech deepfake detection.

</details>

### [119] [Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27251)
*Kart-leong Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms (Tiny Recursive Model, Depth Recursive transformer, and simple recursive transformer) as surrogate models for engineering design, demonstrating that recursive weight-sharing architectures with additional compute rather than additional parameters provide a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off for small, low-dimensional engineering datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional transformer architectures are over-parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where expensive simulation data is limited. Excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting, unnecessary memory and compute overhead, motivating architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters.

Method: The paper performs a systematic, hardware-aware comparison of three recursive transformer paradigms: (a) Tiny Recursive Model, (b) a proposed Depth Recursive transformer, and (c) a simple recursive transformer. These are evaluated on metrics including Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank, parameter count, and FLOPs, across two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of semiconductor packages under FEA, and iterative Laplace PDE numerical solving for capacitance field.

Result: The recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling, validated on both engineering tasks.

Conclusion: Recursive transformer architectures, which allocate more compute per parameter rather than adding parameters, are recommended for resource-constrained engineering surrogate modeling scenarios, offering practical design guidelines for architecture selection.

Abstract: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

</details>


### [120] [Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27260)
*Zhen Zhang,Jielei Chu,Bin Liu,Tianrui Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) as a new source of forgetting in multimodal continual learning, quantifies it via an MCD score, and proposes CMCDR—a regularization method with replay-based and replay-free variants—that preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual VQA validate its effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MMCL methods focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity to mitigate forgetting, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks—a decision-level shift termed Modality Contribution Drift (MCD).

Method: The authors define the MCD score combining contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. They propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), with a replay-based version using modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples to constrain contribution changes, and a replay-free version using current-task samples as probes to distill the frozen model's old-task contribution responses.

Result: Theoretical and empirical analyses explain why existing MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate MCD. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

Conclusion: Preserving the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks—rather than only aligning representations—is essential for mitigating forgetting in multimodal continual learning, and CMCDR achieves this effectively in both exemplar-available and exemplar-free settings.

Abstract: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

</details>


### [121] [DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27263)
*Dennis Thumm,Billy Tim Anthony,Ying Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DoTime is an open, scalable, theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as a PyPI package with four frozen evaluation suites. It introduces capabilities absent from prior generators including continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs, non-stationary dynamics, and deterministic intervention profiles. It also demonstrates the generator's suitability as a prior for a causal foundation model, showing that interventional training yields a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over observational models of identical capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served in high-stakes domains like healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. There is a need for a scalable, general-purpose benchmark that supports interventional and counterfactual estimation with exact ground truth.

Method: The paper develops DoTime, a generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models with interventions featuring: continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics via switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp/sinusoidal intervention profiles. The suites include 100,000 trajectories spanning eight named identification structures with paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM and shared-noise counterfactuals. Reference baselines with an evaluation harness are provided, testing an interventional prior-fitted network (PFN) against an observational model of identical capacity across three seeds per arm.

Result: Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network exhibits a positive direction-accuracy gap relative to the observational model of identical capacity in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested, providing empirical support for the falsifiable claim that interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage.

Conclusion: DoTime fills the gap in interventional and counterfactual causal inference benchmarks for time series by providing a scalable, theoretically grounded generator with rich intervention capabilities and exact ground truth. The empirical results demonstrate the value of interventional training data for time-series causal models, positioning DoTime as a suitable prior for causal foundation model development.

Abstract: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

</details>


### [122] [PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27265)
*Shengtian Yang,Yewen Li,Peng Jiang,Zhiyi Lyu,Bo An,Peng Jiang,Qingpeng Cai,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PlatformBid is the first comprehensive auto-bidding benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective, integrating SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions. It defines three realistic competition settings and evaluates existing auto-bidding methods, while introducing BidFlow, a flow-matching-based bidding method that handles dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou show a +0.68% target cost improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional auto-bidding algorithms only focus on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions against competitors. However, modern ad platforms now internally integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions, meaning the goal should also include platform revenue maximization. There is a lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks, and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research motivates this work.

Method: The paper proposes PlatformBid, a comprehensive benchmark from a unified ad platform perspective, defining three representative settings: homogeneous competition (identical algorithms), heterogeneous competition (diverse algorithmic strategies), and promotional competition (budget surges during events like Black Friday). It systematically evaluates classical control, RL-based, and generative methods, and proposes BidFlow, a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching for expressive policy representation in dynamic environments.

Result: BidFlow effectively handles dynamic competitive environments across the three benchmark settings. Online experiments on Kuaishou demonstrate a +0.68% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

Conclusion: PlatformBid serves as the first comprehensive platform-centric benchmark for auto-bidding, and BidFlow demonstrates the effectiveness of flow-matching in this domain, with offline-online consistency confirmed through real-world deployment evidence.

Abstract: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

</details>


### [123] [Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27269)
*Weiye Shi,Fanxu Meng,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses the problem that converting MHA/GQA models to multi-head latent attention (MLA) for cache efficiency substantially degrades speculative decoding acceptance rates due to attention-function errors introduced by low-rank factorization and RoPE handling. The authors propose an end-to-end functional reconstruction method that optimizes each converted MLA module to reproduce the original MHA/GQA module's post-output-projection responses on calibration hidden states, without needing verifier logits or supervision. Evaluated across 192 configurations (4 Llama/Qwen pairs, TransMLA/MHA2MLA, HF/vLLM, 4 tasks), the method materially improves acceptance in 37/64 task cells, leaves 26 unchanged, and decreases only 1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLA offers significant cache efficiency benefits for long-context inference, but most capable open checkpoints use MHA/GQA, requiring conversion. While direct conversion works for standalone generation, it sharply reduces draft-token acceptance in speculative decoding because attention-function errors from low-rank factorization and RoPE handling disrupt the agreement between draft proposals and target verification.

Method: The authors formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Their end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. The method is converter-agnostic, preserves the converted cache and inference graph, and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision.

Result: Across 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen pairs, two converters (TransMLA and MHA2MLA), two backends (HF and vLLM), and four 200-prompt tasks, functional reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one, using a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance.

Conclusion: Functional reconstruction of MLA attention modules is an effective post-conversion procedure that substantially improves speculative decoding acceptance rates when converting MHA/GQA checkpoints to MLA, while preserving the cache and inference graph benefits of the conversion.

Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

</details>


### [124] [QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28415)
*Zhoushun Yu,Xiaoyu Hu,Xiangyu Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QQWorld replaces the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective in latent world models with a quantile-quantile (QQ) matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. A cross-batch extension enlarges the ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, improving Gaussian alignment, thinning latent tails, and boosting planning success rates across four control environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent world models (e.g., LeWorldModel) rely on regularizing latents toward an isotropic Gaussian for efficient planning, but the Epps-Pulley objective's corrective gradients vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled, which degrades downstream planning performance.

Method: QQWorld replaces the EP objective with a quantile-quantile matching objective that aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, preserving corrective gradients in the tails. It further introduces cross-batch QQ, which uses detached samples from prior batches to enlarge the effective ranking pool, and provides a bias-variance trade-off characterization.

Result: Across four control environments, QQWorld improves the average planning success rate over LeWM while consistently achieving better Gaussian alignment (shorter latent tails).

Conclusion: Quantile-quantile matching is a more effective regularizer than Epps-Pulley for enforcing Gaussianity in latent world models, particularly for tail behavior, leading to improved planning performance.

Abstract: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

</details>


### [125] [RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27271)
*Huihao Jing,Haozhe Cui,Wenbin Hu,Shaojin Chen,Haochen Shi,Changxuan Fan,Yuxuan Liu,Hanyu Yang,Sirui Zhang,Ziyi Chen,Haoran Li,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback) trains code agents to not only pass tests but also produce faster correct implementations by converting execution outcomes into a staged reward: failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by relative improvement from baseline toward an expert reference. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench improves correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most code model training signals stop at correctness, overlooking runtime efficiency. Two correct programs can pass identical tests yet differ drastically in performance. Since runtime is a fragile reward (only meaningful for correct programs, varies across tasks, and gives little signal when most samples fail to compile), there is a need to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations during training rather than treating efficiency solely as an evaluation metric.

Method: RLPF converts execution outcomes into a staged reward signal. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress (e.g., how far they get in compilation/running), providing useful feedback before correctness is achieved. Correct programs are ranked by their relative runtime improvement from a baseline toward an expert reference, providing performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. This composite reward is used to fine-tune code agents via reinforcement learning.

Result: Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and improves relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%. The resulting model is competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Ablation studies show model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and the full composite reward outperforms correctness-only or runtime-only baselines.

Conclusion: Code agents can be trained not only to pass tests but also to optimize the programs they write, suggesting that execution feedback should encompass performance, not just correctness, as a first-class training signal.

Abstract: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

</details>


### [126] [SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27273)
*Jinliang Gao,Ning Yang,Hai Wang,Baili Xiao,Pin Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization) is a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure based on representation-space structure, improving convergence across SFT, DPO, and GRPO without excluding training samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements focus mainly on sample selection or training schedules. However, data organization is treated as a static preprocessing step where embedding-based grouping creates fixed partitions, failing to adapt to evolving sample exposure during optimization. This causes all samples to receive similar exposure despite different optimization needs, resulting in redundant updates for some samples and under-optimization for others.

Method: SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead. Within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal. Across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. It is a plug-and-play framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism.

Result: Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid training phase. It produces more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

Conclusion: SDO demonstrates that dynamically organizing data according to representation-space structure with exposure-driven feedback improves training efficiency and outcome balance across multiple post-training paradigms, offering a lightweight and effective alternative to static data preprocessing.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

</details>


### [127] [Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27274)
*Zhiyuan Ma,Zeyuan Li,Zhiyi Lu,Jiacheng Hao,Youlang Du,Zhen Jiang,Xinche Zhang,Yuhao Sun,Sen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework for EEG-based disease diagnosis that decouples instance-level representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains an encoder via self-supervised alignment of temporally nearby windows and within-subject sub-bags without inherited labels, while Stage 2 trains an attention-based MIL aggregator with subject-level supervision only. It achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings (76.57% overall, +4.28 pp over the strongest baseline) across three EEG datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard EEG pipelines segment recordings into instances, inherit subject labels, and train instance-level classifiers, falsely assuming all instances carry equally reliable diagnostic evidence. MIL avoids inherited labels but struggles because EEG datasets have far fewer subjects than instances, limiting representation quality in end-to-end MIL. The authors propose a framework that learns from abundant instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

Method: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags, using variance and covariance regularization to prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only at the subject level, and limits representation drift via feature retention.

Result: Across three EEG disease datasets and five backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 4.28 percentage points. Analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, higher sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved diagnostic-class separation.

Conclusion: Aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances (without assigning disease labels to individual instances) is key to effective EEG-based disease diagnosis. The findings underscore the importance of decoupling instance representation learning from subject-level supervision in low-subject, high-instance regimes.

Abstract: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

</details>


### [128] [Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27275)
*Jiwon Jang,Kisu Yang,Heuiseok Lim,Hyunwoo Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training 4-bit quantization looks lossless on standard task-reward metrics for multi-turn tool-calling agents, but this is a masking artifact: it amplifies existing failure patterns (e.g., tool-name hallucination) by up to 2.5x in volume without creating new failure types. The benchmark's ten-error budget hides this damage; shrinking to two errors re-exposes a 17-point score gap, and targeted error-repair prompts remove the damage exactly where it lives. The authors recommend reporting per-channel error rates and success under a shrinking budget alongside task reward.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 4-bit post-training quantization is widely claimed to be nearly lossless, but this claim has not been tested for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where quantization's effects now matter most. The paper aims to test whether the lossless claim holds when looking beyond standard aggregate metrics at process-level diagnostics.

Method: Evaluated two open-weight model families (dense and MoE variants) across two domains on τ²-bench, covering eight cells with 456 episodes each at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights. Used standard metric comparisons with multiple-comparison correction and equivalence testing, analyzed the process-level failure patterns (error types, volumes, rank correlations across precisions), tested a masking hypothesis by shrinking the error budget from ten to two, and applied a targeted error-repair prompt for verification.

Result: Quantization shows no statistically significant score change on the standard metric in any cell (equivalence bounds at ±7.5 points in the worst cell). However, quantization amplifies existing failures (up to 2.5x in volume, +17.6 points per task) without creating new failure types (rank correlation ≥0.94, 0.18% novel events). The flat score is explained by the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbing extra failures; shrinking to two errors reveals a 17-point gap specifically in the cell with added error volume. A targeted error-repair prompt removes the damage exactly and only where it lives.

Conclusion: The widely reported lossless claim for 4-bit quantization is an artifact of metric masking in benchmarks with large error budgets. Quantization does damage processes—amplifying existing failure modes—but standard task rewards conceal it. Benchmarks should report per-channel error rates and success under a shrinking budget alongside task reward, since both diagnostics come from logs already collected.

Abstract: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

</details>


### [129] [RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27775)
*Jaehyuk Lee,Yeajin Lee,Dayeon Shin,Donghun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RIPPLE is a method that generates inter-channel phase (rather than recovering it) using a rectified flow refined from a Griffin–Lim-based phase prior, improving inter-channel phase coherence in multi-channel waveform generation across ambisonics and seismic domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-channel waveform generation delegates phase recovery to channel-independent modules, which cannot produce the inter-channel phase relationships that carry physical information in spatial audio and seismograms. Moreover, magnitude-based metrics are insensitive to collapses in inter-channel phase coherence, making such losses invisible and allowing pipelines to discard physical information while still scoring well.

Method: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin–Lim as a phase prior rather than a final estimator. It initializes from the source phase to preserve inter-channel structure, then uses a rectified flow to refine the phase toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss.

Result: RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on coherence metrics in both first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation. In the seismic task, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the 57.3° random expectation, while learned phase reduces it to 33.8°.

Conclusion: Phase should be generated, not recovered, for multi-channel waveform synthesis. Learned inter-channel phase generation significantly improves physical coherence metrics in downstream analyses across physically unrelated domains.

Abstract: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

</details>


### [130] [The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27281)
*Lei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Language model capabilities form only when all parts of a multi-part circuit align in a single stochastic attempt; this joint-alignment step with no partial credit is the rate-limiting barrier. The paper provides empirical fingerprints (missing-part scaling), a rate equation read in forward/backward directions, identifies the failure mode (query-key slice corruption), and proves the mechanism in a controlled model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to explain why capabilities in language models suddenly appear ("ignite") rather than gradually improving. They hypothesize that a capability only emerges when the final parts of its underlying circuit align in one stochastic attempt—a joint, all-or-nothing event—and that this no-partial-credit alignment constitutes the rate-limiting step of capability formation.

Method: The authors identify two fingerprints of joint alignment: (1) circuit-shortcut-free experiments where the wait time scales with the number of missing parts rather than circuit size; (2) Pythia ablation studies across seven capabilities and three scales showing single-part ablation leaves median 17% capability versus 50-83% predicted by partial credit (p=2e-10). They derive a rate equation (sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K) - destruction), read in three preregistered ways with frozen constants, and run forward (capability ignition above a concentration floor, datable arrival from precursor) and backward (learnability delay growing until critical step, invisible to standard monitors) experiments. They locate the damage in query-key slices, isolate a re-initialization cure, and prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model, finally replacing SGD noise with fluctuation-dissipation annealing.

Result: Forward predictions: capability ignites at chosen steps once mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), with arrival datable to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward predictions: delay to learn withheld capability grows until a critical step beyond which it never ignites, while validation loss falls smoothly (standard monitors blind). Query-key slice re-initialization restores learnability (6/6) while value slices do not (0/6). Mechanism proven in a controlled gated-attention model. Results cover conjunction circuits in transformers up to 1.4B parameters.

Conclusion: Capability formation is gated by a joint alignment of circuit parts in a single stochastic attempt—a rare event with an all-or-nothing payoff. This predicts sharp ignition thresholds, blind spots in standard training monitors, and specific interventions (re-initializing query-key slices). The mechanism is installed via fluctuation-dissipation annealing to schedule circuit formation, validated empirically and theoretically up to 1.4B-parameter transformers.

Abstract: A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

</details>


### [131] [Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27283)
*Chao Peng,Zhiheng Lyu,Peijie Dong,Hande Dong,Qiang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This position paper argues that to claim a "long-horizon failure," benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages, using a metric called the "horizon residual" (the log-ratio between baseline prediction and actual success). This comparison must use the same agent configuration and pre-specified choices for stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets, though targeted experiments are still needed to explain the cause of any residual.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon benchmarks show agents fail more as tasks lengthen, but this observation alone does not explain why failure occurs. Failures could stem from compounding ordinary errors, harder individual decisions, or trajectory-induced degradation (earlier execution making later work harder, e.g., context rot). The paper aims to establish a rigorous methodology for defining and measuring long-horizon failure.

Method: The paper proposes a formal framework: benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction constructed from short, individual stages. The log-ratio between this prediction and actual success is defined as the "horizon residual." The comparison must use the identical agent configuration and pre-specify how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets are selected. The residual indicates deviation from the baseline, but does not itself explain causation.

Result: The paper presents a conceptual framework and metric (horizon residual) rather than empirical results. It clarifies that merely observing increased failure on longer tasks is insufficient; the residual quantifies whether and how much full-rollout behavior deviates from a stage-wise baseline prediction, providing a principled basis for claiming long-horizon failure.

Conclusion: To make valid claims of "long-horizon failure," benchmarks need a pre-specified baseline built from short stages and identical agent configuration; the horizon residual captures the gap between prediction and actual success. However, the residual only identifies that a difference exists—targeted experiments remain necessary to explain the underlying cause (e.g., accumulated context, harder decisions, or compounding errors).
