Abstract: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

</details>


### [132] [TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27289)
*Yu Chang,Anzhe Cheng,Chenwei Wu,Zhuoran Wang,Jiahao Chen,Tamoghna Chattopadhyay,Sophia I. Thomopoulos,Paul M. Thompson,Liyue Shen,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIER-MoE is a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model for multimodal fusion that defines modality reliability as the expected prediction loss of a unimodal predictor, learned from out-of-fold predictions, and combines this risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing while preserving multimodal complementarity via an always-active shared path.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: More evidence from multiple modalities does not always yield better predictions. Existing multimodal models focus on richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion, but the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert.

Method: TIER-MoE defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss a unimodal predictor is expected to incur, learned from out-of-fold predictions from models not trained on the corresponding sample. It combines estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, and uses an always-active shared path to preserve multimodal complementarity.

Result: Evaluated on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification), TIER-MoE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

Conclusion: Risk-guided, sample-adaptive modality reliability estimation combined with subspace expert routing improves multimodal fusion effectiveness over existing approaches, particularly in biomedical applications where modalities may be unreliable, redundant, or mismatched to specialized experts.

Abstract: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

</details>


### [133] [EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27290)
*Lei Zan,Keli Zhang,Shifeng Xie,Jiale Zheng,Zehao Xiao,Zhiwei Dong,Ke Zhang,Ruichu Cai,Malik Tiomoko,Lujia Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoCause is a framework that refines causal graphs for alarm root cause analysis by combining LLM-proposed graph edits (using semantic alarm knowledge) with deterministic validation, iteratively incorporating expert labels from historical incidents. The paper also introduces TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecom network with 485,681 alarm events across 194 alarm types and 5,621 resources. Experiments show EvoCause improves over the PC baseline on synthetic data (Node F1 +11.59, Case EM +9.40, Graph F1 +4.59 percentage points, nSHD -0.2379) and demonstrates that alarm-name semantics contribute to graph refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RCA approaches learn a fixed causal graph from observational logs and predict zero-in-degree alarms as root causes, but these graphs cannot adapt or benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents collected over time. The authors aim to close this feedback loop by incorporating expert labels into graph refinement.

Method: EvoCause uses an LLM to propose semantically plausible graph edits based on expert labels that constrain which alarms should be source nodes, while deterministic code validates node identities and ensures acyclicity. It retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph produces transparent predictions without requiring LLM calls. The authors also construct TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecom network.

Result: On synthetic data, EvoCause (initialized with PC causal discovery) outperforms the unrefined PC baseline: Node F1 improves by 11.59, Case EM by 9.40, and Graph F1 by 4.59 percentage points, while nSHD decreases by 0.2379. On TeleRCA, replacing readable alarm titles with anonymous IDs lowers Node F1 by 6.12 and Case EM by 8.04 percentage points, showing alarm-name semantics are valuable for graph refinement.

Conclusion: EvoCause effectively integrates expert labels into causal graph refinement via LLM-proposed edits with deterministic validation, and semantic alarm names play a significant role in improving RCA performance. The TeleRCA benchmark provides a real-world resource for future work in expert-guided causal graph refinement.

Abstract: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

</details>


### [134] [THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27303)
*Yixin Peng,Diego Collarana,Er Jin,Stefan Decker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: THGFM is a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model with a dual-path architecture combining shared-space and relation type-partitioned temporal attention branches, fused via type-conditioned non-competitive gated sum fusion, and equipped with rotary temporal attention that rotates queries/keys by relative time phases. It consistently outperforms baselines on academic graph benchmarks with up to +12.37% gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for temporal heterogeneous graph learning struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization. They typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel, failing to model both structural heterogeneity and temporal dynamics jointly in a unified framework.

Method: THGFM uses a dual-path architecture: (1) a Shared-Space Temporal Attention branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer, (2) a Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention branch for relation-aware specialization. These are integrated via Dual-Path Relational-Shared Fusion using Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, which assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to each branch without zero-sum competition. A novel Rotary Temporal Attention directly incorporates relative time into attention by rotating queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching.

Result: THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graph benchmarks, delivering a +3.25% six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L2, +1.18% on PF-L1, and +4.24%, +3.73%, +4.61% on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP respectively.

Conclusion: THGFM demonstrates that jointly modeling structural heterogeneity and temporal dynamics through a fused dual-path architecture with time-aware attention mechanisms yields substantial improvements over existing methods on temporal heterogeneous graph learning benchmarks.

Abstract: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

</details>


### [135] [Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27304)
*Supratik Bhowal,Subhrajyoti Basu,Aritra Gir Mahanta,Anik Pal Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoT-Mediate is a behavioral framework that tests whether chain-of-thought reasoning causally mediates predictions in medical VLMs by perturbing single clinical attributes in generated reasoning and measuring whether predictions follow the edits. Experiments on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma with 1,000 VQA-RAD samples show that prefix-forced continuation yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, provenance has model-specific effects, and laterality is the least faithfully tracked attribute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While medical VLMs generate chain-of-thought reasoning before answering clinical questions, it is unclear whether this reasoning actually causally influences the model's predictions or is merely post-hoc rationalization. This question is critical for trust and safety in clinical deployment.

Method: The paper introduces CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework combining (1) a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence against prefix-forced continuation for injecting reasoning, and (2) a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to separate reasoning mediation from sycophancy. The framework edits a single clinically meaningful attribute within the model's own generated reasoning and observes whether the prediction follows the edited reasoning.

Result: On 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each, prefix-forced continuation consistently achieves higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning across both models, while laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute.

Conclusion: The mechanism used to inject reasoning significantly affects measured faithfulness. Contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning, suggesting that medical VLMs may not genuinely reason like humans and their CoT may be less causally reliable than assumed.

Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

</details>


### [136] [ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27308)
*Christopher Warner,Jonas Mago,JR Huml,Beren Millidge*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction, supporting variable sequence lengths up to 30s, arbitrary channel configurations, and partial channel/time-interval reconstruction. It matches or exceeds its predecessor ZUNA1 in performance while being far more flexible, and substantially outperforms standard methods like spherical spline interpolation in MNE. Released open source under Apache 2.0.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a more flexible EEG signal reconstruction model that can handle variable-length sequences, arbitrary channel configurations, and partial reconstructions, overcoming the rigidity of earlier models like ZUNA1 and standard interpolation-based methods.

Method: ZUNA1.1 is a diffusion autoencoder with 380M parameters, designed to reconstruct EEG signals with variable input lengths up to 30 seconds, arbitrary numbers of channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and support for reconstructing temporal sub-intervals within channels or entire channels.

Result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with ZUNA1 while being significantly more flexible across a wider range of reconstruction tasks, and continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising/reconstruction baselines such as spherical spline interpolation used in MNE.

Conclusion: ZUNA1.1 provides a flexible, open-source EEG reconstruction solution that combines competitive performance with broad task adaptability, released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

Abstract: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

</details>


### [137] [Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27350)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies leakage-aware Sybil bot detection on Ethereum by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against tree-based baselines (XGBoost, SVM). The authors propose a Blind-Spot protocol to eliminate label leakage from high-signal smart contracts and a Transaction Grammar representation for wallet behavior. They find that under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while offering lower latency and energy use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning-based Sybil detection methods for Ethereum are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. The authors seek to determine whether sequence models truly outperform simpler tabular models once leakage is removed.

Method: The approach consists of a Blind-Spot protocol to remove shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, combined with a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior that models rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. They compare Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines for Ethereum actor classification.

Result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use. The study also examines whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal.

Conclusion: The paper contributes a leakage-aware framework for Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior, demonstrating that simpler tree-based models are both more accurate and more practical for real-time Sybil detection when label leakage is controlled.

Abstract: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

</details>


### [138] [Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27370)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a training-free, compression-based (gzip NCD) behavioral framework to detect Sybil bots on the EVM blockchain using symbolic Transaction Grammar synthesized from transaction traces, without requiring token transfer edges. It filters high-signal contracts via the Blind-Spot Protocol and builds behavioral graphs for Sybil discovery, validated against supervised baselines, temporal splits, and synthetic camouflage tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sybil attackers impersonate regular users to exploit airdrops or manipulate governance. Existing methods rely on graph construction requiring token transfers between wallets, while ML-based approaches treat the problem as closed-set classification and fail under evolving attack strategies and evasion tactics.

Method: A symbolic Transaction Grammar is synthesized from EVM traces, capturing transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent separately. High-signal contracts are filtered using the Blind-Spot Protocol, and Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. The framework is validated against supervised ML baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests.

Result: The framework outperforms supervised baselines and remains robust under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations. The NCD primitive expands suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links, enabling training-free local discovery in open-world blockchain audits.

Conclusion: The work contributes a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery, positioned as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world audits rather than a formal open-set recognition system.

Abstract: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

</details>


### [139] [Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27372)
*Alexi Gladstone,Heng Ji,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Explorative Modeling (XMs), a new generative modeling paradigm that factors the training loop by exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data and training on the best, rather than factoring the generation procedure like existing approaches. XMs serve as both a new pretraining axis (scaling exploration improves performance by 7-36%) and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm that matches diffusion performance with 16-256x fewer inference steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative models remain the exception to the end-to-end training paradigm that revolutionized discriminative learning (e.g., AlexNet). Existing scalable generative approaches factor the generation procedure into stages to handle multi-modal distributions, which prevents end-to-end generation. The authors aim to address this fundamental limitation.

Method: XMs factor the training loop instead of the generation procedure. During training, they explore K candidate matches between model-generated samples and real data, then train on the best match, causing predictions to commit to specific modes rather than averaging (blurring) across them.

Result: Exploration scaling improves performance across images, video, and language, with gains increasing from 7% to 36% with data scale and 13% to 23% with model scale. XMs achieve 4.1x FLOP efficiency, 6.2x sample efficiency, 47% parameter efficiency, a near-SOTA 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, and enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps.

Conclusion: Explorative Modeling establishes a new pretraining axis (exploration) beyond parameters and data for existing generative models, while also serving as a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm. This addresses the longstanding gap of generative models not being trained end-to-end and demonstrates broad applicability across continuous and discrete domains.

Abstract: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

</details>


### [140] [The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27383)
*Yijiang Pang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper provides the first convergence guarantees for plain vector-form Adam under heavy-tailed stochastic noise (bounded p-th central moment for p∈(1,2]). It generalizes the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise and develops a discounted regret analysis without restrictive parameter coupling. Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points but with suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent rate, which persists even when p=2. With known domain radius to control the online-learner output, the rate improves to match the optimal complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Adam variants achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior under heavy-tailed stochastic gradients (bounded p-th central moment), which is increasingly observed in modern deep learning.

Method: The authors generalize the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise, and develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling. They also consider a variant where the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output.

Result: Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise, but exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity with p-dependent convergence, which persists even in the bounded-variance case (p=2). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity.

Conclusion: The findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes, establishing the first convergence guarantees for plain vector-form Adam in this setting.

Abstract: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

</details>


### [141] [FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27389)
*Bingheng Li,Junyang Cai,Yupeng Zhang,Bistra Dilkina,Jayant Kalagnanam,Dzung T. Phan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FunL2O is the first unified framework that automates feature design in learning-to-optimize (L2O) pipelines via LLM-driven program evolution. Using a FunSearch-style loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions and a fixed evaluation retrains the L2O model to measure downstream performance, it consistently outperforms hand-crafted representations across continuous (LP, QP) and discrete (MIP) optimization tasks with four different LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feature functions that map problem instances to ML model inputs are a critical yet largely overlooked component of L2O pipelines. Existing methods rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual, domain-specific, and difficult to generalize across optimization tasks.

Method: FunL2O employs a FunSearch-style evolutionary loop: an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. The framework is applied to solution prediction, warm-starting (LP/QP), GNN-guided backdoor branching, and Predict-and-Search (MIP tasks).

Result: Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four different LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations, demonstrating the general effectiveness of LLM-driven feature evolution for L2O.

Conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is a general and effective approach to automating representation design in learning-to-optimize, establishing FunL2O as the first unified framework for this purpose.

Abstract: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

</details>


### [142] [ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27404)
*Yixuan Duan,Wei Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECG-InterpBench is a benchmark for systematically evaluating the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations using sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas across six ECG foundation models, five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ECG foundation model benchmarks focus only on downstream predictive performance, offering limited insight into whether internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses.

Method: The benchmark uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments with matched capacity across models. It evaluates six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds (450-cell interpretability atlas with 75 matched six-model comparison blocks). It assesses sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility/coverage of 49 clinical ECG measurements, cross-seed reproducibility, patient-sampling uncertainty, depth/seed variation, and sensitivity to sparsity parameterization.

Result: ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles, with reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identifying different leading models, as confirmed by matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG.

Conclusion: ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability, accompanied by executable code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits.

Abstract: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

</details>


### [143] [Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27418)
*Yuan Guan,Chandler Squires,Timothy Hu,Pradeep Ravikumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Conditional Informer, an encoder-decoder architecture for long-term ship trajectory prediction that formulates trajectory forecasting as a conditional generation task. It introduces a Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel states query environmental contexts (weather) through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates vessel dynamics. A Modality Masking training strategy prevents degradation during sensor fallback, achieving 15.4% improvement in prediction accuracy and reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Transformer-based ship trajectory predictors rely solely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system while ignoring extrinsic factors like weather and static vessel characteristics. Moreover, current multimodal approaches model environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.

Method: The Conditional Informer uses an encoder-decoder architecture with a specialized Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates (but is not generated by) vessel dynamics. A Modality Masking training strategy is introduced to handle intermittency in real-world data and prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback.

Result: Experiments on AIS and ERA5 data show the approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

Conclusion: Conditional generation with directional physical priors and modality masking significantly improves long-term ship trajectory prediction accuracy and robustness under sensor intermittency, demonstrating the importance of explicitly modeling environmental causality rather than treating context as peer features.

Abstract: Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

</details>


### [144] [Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27422)
*Ayushman Singh,Siddharth Aphale*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive critics (bilinear or cosine-bounded scores) are poorly calibrated as value-like objectives for action selection: they suffer from norm drift, score saturation, and in-support misranking, resulting in weakly calibrated or inverted scores in top deciles, whereas Bellman-trained TD-Q provides correct value ordering. Contrastive critics remain useful as compatibility rankers, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contrastive critics are increasingly used as value-like objectives for best-of-K selection, planning, and critic-guided generation, yet it is unclear whether their raw scores constitute a safe, well-ordered objective to maximize.

Method: The paper performs a controlled support decomposition separating raw bilinear regret into norm drift and in-support components; it evaluates cosine-bounded, hybrid, and raw bilinear critics across four OGBench navigation tasks, compares against a Bellman-trained TD-Q with a parameter-matched function-class control, and uses a training/readout decomposition to attribute lost ordering to the cosine training objective. It also runs simulator rollouts to measure realized selection costs.

Result: Cosine bounding does not remove failure; cosine and hybrid critics still select off-support actions and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks and fail to order fixed-query actions by value, while TD-Q succeeds. Simulator rollouts show single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-Q* toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze where the controller self-corrects. The training/readout decomposition shows raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization, implicating the cosine training objective itself.

Conclusion: Candidate maximization of contrastive critics can exploit false positives from norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics are useful as compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

Abstract: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

</details>


### [145] [SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27431)
*Yikun Bai,Binghang Lu,Yikai Liu,Elaheh Akbari,Soheil Kolouri,Linxuan Wang,Ping He,Shuchan Wang,Ruqi Zhang,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SE(3)-MeanFlow is a few-step generative framework for protein backbone design that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to SE(3) Lie group geometry, deriving closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, plus an SE(3) alpha-Flow warm-up objective that eliminates Jacobian-vector products. It matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines with fewer sampling steps, particularly excelling in the few-step regime via rectification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone generation on SE(3)^N produce high-quality results but require computationally expensive inference—hundreds of network evaluations with Lie group exponential maps per sample—which bottlenecks high-throughput design campaigns. A few-step generative framework that retains quality while drastically reducing sampling cost is needed.

Method: SE(3)-MeanFlow works natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and R^3, deriving closed-form average-velocity identities for rotational and translational components, enabling simulation-free training targets. It introduces an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that eliminates the Jacobian-vector product in the rotation branch as a warm-up stage, then switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for remaining pretraining and rectification-based post-training.

Result: In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps. Its advantage widens in the few-step regime where rectification enables it to lead at every matched budget, at a modest cost in diversity.

Conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow demonstrates that few-step generative modeling of protein backbones is achievable on SE(3) geometry through closed-form MeanFlow extensions and alpha-Flow warm-up, offering an efficient alternative to flow-matching models for high-throughput de novo protein design with only modest diversity trade-offs.

Abstract: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

</details>


### [146] [Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27450)
*Chaofan Deng,Linyu Sun,Jaeho Lee,Arijit Raychowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NN-CLEAN is a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network into the iterative CLEAN multipath extraction loop, replacing exhaustive grid search with rapid parallel forward passes while keeping exact mathematical models for residual subtraction. It achieves over 96% estimation accuracy at 5 dB SNR, matching Grid-Search CLEAN baselines while dramatically reducing computational complexity and maintaining near-flat scaling in runtime and memory as batch sizes increase.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms like CLEAN provide high-resolution multipath parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search, while purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and fail to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters.

Method: The proposed NN-CLEAN framework embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. The network replaces the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes, while residual subtraction is delegated to exact mathematical models to ensure physical multipath parameters are isolated without accumulating non-physical errors.

Result: Extensive Monte Carlo simulations show NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the Grid-Search CLEAN baseline while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity. It substantially outperforms subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks, and exhibits near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase.

Conclusion: NN-CLEAN is established as a robust, real-time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems, offering highly efficient parallelization and a favorable accuracy-complexity tradeoff compared to both classical and purely data-driven approaches.

Abstract: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

</details>


### [147] [FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27463)
*Lucas Greff Meneses,Evandro S. Ortigossa,Claudio Silva,Luis Gustavo Nonato*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FADEx is a novel local per-instance feature attribution method for explaining non-linear dimensionality reduction (DR) methods. It uses first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition via weighted least squares to provide DR-method-agnostic local feature attributions and distortion analysis, outperforming existing DR explanation approaches in robustness and reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-linear DR techniques are often opaque transformations themselves, making it difficult to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. Existing DR explanation approaches suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific DR methods, hindering their practical use.

Method: FADEx leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition. It computes local linear models via weighted least squares, which eliminates the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making the approach agnostic to the specific DR method while providing both local feature attributions and distortion analysis.

Result: Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, FADEx demonstrates effectiveness and versatility in explaining DR methods. Results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

Conclusion: FADEx provides a general, DR-method-agnostic framework for local per-instance feature attribution and distortion analysis, addressing key limitations of prior DR explanation methods and offering improved transparency for analyzing high-dimensional data projections.

Abstract: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

</details>


### [148] [Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27479)
*Aryan Mishra,Randy Martinez,Lizhen Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCGR is a group-theoretic graph rewiring method that augments input graphs with a Schreier-Coset graph from a special linear group to mitigate over-squashing in GNNs, providing theoretical guarantees of spectral gap and bounded effective resistance while reducing effective resistance by 5-40% empirically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over-squashing in GNNs constrains long-range information propagation due to structural bottlenecks. Existing graph-rewiring methods introduce prohibitive structural/computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve original graph properties, and massively increase edge counts.

Method: SCGR augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group, providing a group-theoretic approach to rewiring that creates low-resistance bypasses for long-range communication while maintaining original graph properties.

Result: The method provides theoretical guarantees including a spectral gap and bounded effective resistance. Empirical evaluations show SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Conclusion: SCGR offers a theoretically grounded, group-theoretic approach to graph rewiring that effectively alleviates over-squashing in GNNs with measurable improvements in connectivity while preserving accuracy.

Abstract: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

</details>


### [149] [Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27482)
*Kevin Guan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether discrete regimes in temporally drifting data streams can be recovered by fitting a hidden Markov model (HMM) to the chronological trajectory of model weights. Using multimodal misinformation detection (Fakeddit) and sentiment analysis (Yelp), the authors show that classifiers generalize better to data windows sharing the same recovered latent state, and that this within-state transfer advantage survives controls for temporal proximity, exceeds naive equal-size partitions, and remains significant beyond what the data distribution alone explains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporally drifting data streams may shift through discrete regimes rather than evolving continuously. The authors ask whether such underlying regimes can be discovered purely from the weights of models trained on the stream, which would enable detection of meaningful state boundaries for better domain adaptation and model transfer.

Method: Train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows, align their weights, fit a hidden Markov model to the chronologically ordered weight trajectory to recover latent states partitioning the timeline into coherent phases. Validate via within-state transfer advantage, controlling for temporal proximity and comparing against both naive equal-size contiguous partitions and permutation nulls after residualizing class divergence and lag.

Result: On both Fakeddit and Yelp, models generalize better within states than across state boundaries. The advantage survives temporal-proximity controls, modestly exceeds equal-size contiguous partitions, and—after removing class-distribution shifts—still surpasses its permutation null. Effects replicate on both tasks but are attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

Conclusion: Regimes in drifting data streams are recoverable from model-weight trajectories alone, and the recovered states encode structure relevant to transfer that goes beyond raw data-distribution shifts. However, the strength of the signal depends on the temporal stability of the label distribution.

Abstract: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

</details>


### [150] [A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27501)
*Liangyu Wu,Qibin Liu,Alexander Yue,Julia Gonski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NEXUS is a lightweight foundation model (~3M parameters, fully connected autoencoder) pre-trained on unlabeled Large Hadron Collider charged particle track data, that transfers to downstream collider tasks and out-of-domain scientific datasets (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity) with improved accuracy on small labeled datasets, while being computationally simpler than transformers for power-efficient, real-time, and edge applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To bring the benefits of foundation models to scientific domains while overcoming the computational cost of large transformer-based architectures. The authors aim to demonstrate that a lightweight, power-efficient model pre-trained on collider physics data can generalize to other scientific tasks, enabling real-time and edge deployments for scientific experiments.

Method: A fully connected autoencoder with ~3 million parameters is pre-trained without supervision on large-scale LHC collision data represented by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks (kinematic regression and event classification) are built on the pre-trained weights and evaluated against training-from-scratch baselines. Latent space interpretation and transfer to gravitational wave, flood forecasting, and neural activity datasets are used to assess generalization.

Result: Pre-trained NEXUS weights achieve improved accuracy on downstream collider tasks with only small labeled datasets compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The model demonstrates benefits in cross-domain transfer to gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity, and shows computational simplicity relative to transformer approaches at comparable scale.

Conclusion: Lightweight foundation modeling with a small autoencoder can deliver pre-training benefits and cross-domain transfer in scientific applications while remaining computationally efficient enough for power-constrained, real-time, and edge use cases, offering a practical alternative to large transformer-based foundation models.

Abstract: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

</details>


### [151] [Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27507)
*Tingting Mu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents the first rigorous theoretical analysis of sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems. The authors derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results, validated by comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While sparsity in two-factor matrix factorisation has been extensively studied theoretically, rigorous guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain unexplored. This gap hinders the reliable use of tri-factorisation in applications despite its greater modelling flexibility.

Method: The authors establish the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Their analysis relies on a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original tri-factorisation problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, preserving the structural information needed for recovering original factor matrices. From this, they derive recovery guarantees, structural consistency results, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error bounds, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation properties.

Result: The theoretical framework characterises how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the theory and demonstrate close agreement between theoretical results and empirical observations.

Conclusion: The work closes a significant theoretical gap in matrix tri-factorisation by providing rigorous sparsity-induced identifiability guarantees, supported by empirical validation.

Abstract: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

</details>


### [152] [Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27522)
*Alessio Cascione,Mattia Setzu,Cristiano Landi,Paolo Maria Mancarella,Riccardo Guidotti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model that builds predictive models by selecting representative examples (pivots) to compare against input instances, inspired by decision trees and human case-based reasoning. The method supports single and pairs of pivots, works with ensembles, is data modality-agnostic via pre-trained networks, and demonstrates competitive performance across tabular, text, image, and time-series data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many machine learning methods for complex decision-making are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally reason by comparing new cases against few representative examples, the authors aim to design an interpretable predictive model based on selecting such pivots.

Method: The method is a hierarchical pivot selection model inspired by decision trees, using similarity between pivots and input instances. It extends beyond single pivots to include pairs of pivots (as used by proximity and oblique trees) and supports ensembles. It is modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation across different data types.

Result: Experiments on diverse datasets (tabular, text, images, time series) show the approach outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while using a minimal number of pivots.

Conclusion: The proposed hierarchical pivot selection approach provides an effective and interpretable predictive modeling framework that works across data modalities, outperforming other instance selection methods and rivaling state-of-the-art interpretable models with a compact set of pivots.

Abstract: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

</details>


### [153] [Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27529)
*Mansoor Ahmed,Yue-Tsz Fan,Hemanth Venkateswara,Murray Patterson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel for discrete diffusion that expresses correlated denoising steps natively via a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. A single LKF step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling cost as a factorized model, and MDLM is recovered as a special case at M=1. On LM1B and WikiText-103, LKF improves generative perplexity by 2.1x–3.3x over likelihood baselines, grows with M, and at M=8 surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard discrete diffusion and flow-matching models factorize the transition across positions, causing independent token decisions that struggle with coupled targets (e.g., subject-verb agreement) under few-step generation. Existing few-step methods distill or rectify slow teachers, inheriting the teacher's quality ceiling. The authors ask whether correlated steps can be expressed natively to avoid this limitation.

Method: LKF is a flow-map kernel defined as a mixture of M factorized components tied by one shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap; the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. One latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory, giving the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model. MDLM is shown to be a special case at M=1.

Result: On One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 for unconditional text generation, LKF learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The improvement grows with M, and at M=8 LKF surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. Code is publicly available.

Conclusion: LKF demonstrates that correlated denoising steps can be expressed natively in a discrete flow-map model without distillation/rectification or a teacher ceiling, achieving superior few-step text generation quality at the same sampling cost as factorized models, with quality scaling in the number of mixture components M.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent.
