Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

</details>


### [154] [When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27530)
*Xiao Yue,Guangzhi Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether multi-head graph-text retrieval models achieve true semantic routing or merely architectural channelization. Using a controlled version of MV-GTA with verifiable text segments and view-specific graph heads on BBBP and BACE datasets, the authors find that correct routing improves nDCG by 0.305-0.685 over deranged training, and expected graph heads outperform wrong heads by 0.303-0.453. However, they find limited evidence for free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, or statistical equivalence to separately trained specialists.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-text retrieval models typically use a single embedding for both graph and description, even when queries concern only one semantic aspect. Multi-head models can separate these aspects, but a change in query head may alter retrieval regardless of content correctness—demonstrating architectural channelization rather than true semantic routing. The authors aim to resolve when this distinction can be established.

Method: The authors construct a controlled version of MV-GTA with deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. They test causal routing via correct routing versus per-sample derangements, compare expected graph heads against wrong heads, and perform matched three-seed comparisons of joint models against separately trained Single specialists. They also evaluate property paraphrase augmentation and consistency/hard-template extensions.

Result: On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305-0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303-0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across datasets. A joint model achieves mean topology/label/property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877 versus specialists at 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140-0.147. Consistency and hard-template extensions reduce canonical retrieval in some settings.

Conclusion: The evidence supports explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation, but does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction. The model's multi-head behavior should be interpreted as architectural channelization in general, with semantic routing only confirmed under controlled, externally verifiable conditions.

Abstract: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

</details>


### [155] [Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27539)
*Vishwajith Ramesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates exact deletion from persistent language-model memory, showing that deletion feasibility depends on how memory represents records. Addressable influence (e.g., support-vector memory in Gemma 3) can be removed by algebraic decrement, while influence entangled in shared recurrent state (e.g., Kimi Linear) requires checkpointed rewind-and-replay from before the offending write. Experiments demonstrate near-perfect deletion agreement (KL 5.4×10⁻¹⁵) and bit-for-bit recovery with deterministic MLX implementations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The right-to-be-forgotten requires exact deletion of records from pretrained language models, but current methods are approximate and verification is unclear. The authors aim to understand whether exact deletion is feasible and how it depends on the underlying memory representation architecture.

Method: The authors test two distinct deletion mechanisms: (1) algebraic decrement for addressable memory (support-vector memory replacing Gemma 3's global-attention layers at 1B, 4B, 12B scales), verifying against retained-key refit and masked-refit proxies under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks; (2) checkpointed rewind-and-replay for shared recurrent state in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, examining additive writes, diagonal decay, and delta-rule write types, validated on real clinical records up to 18,842 tokens in a deterministic MLX implementation.

Result: At 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree to median KL 5.4×10⁻¹⁵ over 31 support-token deletions with +2.0% perplexity versus a matched fine-tune; masked-refit is indistinguishable from never-ingested floor under all attacks. Utility cost rises to 11.2% at 4B and 44.3% at 12B. In Kimi Linear, additive writes admit fixed decrement, diagonal decay a corrected one, but the delta rule makes 12–49% of record contribution suffix-dependent. Rewind-and-replay matches never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit-for-bit within deterministic MLX.

Conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes. The choice of how memory stores information determines whether precise removal is tractable, enabling exact amendment via replaying corrections.

Abstract: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

</details>


### [156] [Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27546)
*Shuting Luo,Monika Mikhail Kanaan,Cameron Gordon,Anna Leontjeva,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates memory requirements of Tabular Foundation Models (such as TabPFN) and demonstrates that model compression techniques can reduce memory usage by up to 7.6x (nearly 87%) while maintaining similar performance levels, providing practical guidance for efficient deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular Foundation Models have gained attention for their strong in-context learning performance, but their practical deployment considerations—particularly memory requirements—have been largely overlooked. This gap motivated the investigation into memory-efficient deployment strategies.

Method: The authors apply model compression approaches to Tabular Foundation Models (e.g., TabPFN) and evaluate the trade-off between memory reduction and performance retention on tabular machine learning tasks.

Result: Model compression achieves up to 7.6x memory reduction with comparable performance levels, decreasing deployment memory requirements by nearly 87%.

Conclusion: Model compression is an effective approach for significantly reducing the memory footprint of Tabular Foundation Models without substantial performance loss, offering practical guidance for practitioners seeking efficient deployment in real-world settings.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

</details>


### [157] [Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27563)
*Zhengli Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies optimal strategies for entrepreneurial start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting, modeling the firm's state as a diffusion process where the entrepreneur chooses among multiple activities with different costs, drifts, and variances. The authors fully solve the stochastic control problem with multiple controls and characterize the optimal policy via an efficient frontier curve ordering controls by riskiness and cost-effectiveness. Depending on model parameters, different types of efficient frontier curves emerge, leading to qualitatively different optimal policy structures—a novel contribution to stochastic control theory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Start-ups must survive through multiple milestone stages, yet current understanding of how entrepreneurs should allocate efforts among competing activities in such milestone-oriented settings is limited. Existing stochastic control models with multiple (three or more) controls are typically intractable, leaving a significant gap in both entrepreneurship theory and stochastic control methodology.

Method: The firm's state is modeled as a diffusion process. The entrepreneur selects among multiple activities (controls) that differ in cost, drift, and variance. Success occurs when the process reaches an upper boundary; failure occurs at a lower boundary. The authors solve the optimal control problem in continuous time with multiple controls, deriving an explicit characterization through an efficient frontier curve that ranks controls by drift-to-volatility ratio (riskiness) and drift-to-cost ratio (cost-effectiveness).

Result: The optimal policy is completely characterized and uses only controls from a set defined by the efficient frontier curve. Different model parameter regimes yield different types of efficient frontier curves, resulting in qualitatively distinct optimal policy structures. This is the first stochastic control model admitting efficient frontier curves of multiple types.

Conclusion: The work provides start-up firms with intuitive, operational measures (riskiness and cost-effectiveness) to evaluate activities and reveals how optimal strategies change qualitatively across different scenarios. It establishes a foundational framework for entrepreneurial decision-making under milestone constraints and advances stochastic control theory for multi-control problems.

Abstract: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

</details>


### [158] [A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27565)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a montage-agnostic encoder for myoelectric prosthetic control that uses shared weights and physical electrode coordinates instead of channel indices, enabling a single architecture to handle any channel count. Trained across users, it outperforms per-user Hudgins+LDA baselines on DB1 and DB2 but not DB5. The performance margin is insensitive to training subject count (from 9 to 39) once above a stability floor, and the direction of comparison is governed by baseline signal fidelity rather than training pool size. Self-supervised pretraining offers no added benefit once supervised training is adequate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pattern-recognition myoelectric prostheses promise multi-gesture control but remain confined to the laboratory because recognizers trained on one person rarely transfer to another, and useful performance generally requires fresh labeled calibration from each end user. The paper seeks to overcome this cross-user transfer hurdle without montage-specific architectural parameters.

Method: The authors introduce a montage-agnostic encoder that reads each electrode with shared weights and localizes electrodes by their physical coordinates rather than their channel indices, allowing one architecture to ingest any channel count. They train across users and compare against a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier, with ablation studies and a controlled subject-count sweep to isolate contributing factors.

Result: The encoder exceeds the per-user Hudgins+LDA baseline by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, but falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro-F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation. A subject-count sweep shows the margin is nearly flat from 9 to 39 training subjects, meaning the training pool only serves as a stability floor; the direction of comparison tracks the strength of the per-user baseline set by signal fidelity. Self-supervised pretraining showed no benefit once supervised training was adequate.

Conclusion: Cross-user myoelectric control is achievable with a montage-agnostic architecture that avoids recalibration, and the comparison outcome across databases is determined primarily by per-user baseline quality (signal fidelity) rather than training set size. Above a minimum stability floor, more training subjects do not improve margins, and self-supervised pretraining is unnecessary when supervised training is already sufficient.

Abstract: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

</details>


### [159] [Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27568)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic encoder trained for cross-user, cross-montage transfer maintains 0.688 macro-F1 across recording sessions without recalibration, outperforming a per-user LDA pipeline (0.540), and improves via feature-statistic alignment rather than batch-normalisation re-estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pattern-recognition based myoelectric control suffers from day-to-day variability (electrode shift, skin condition, elbow position) causing recognition accuracy to degrade across sessions, yet recalibrating for 20 minutes at every doff/don event is unrealistic in daily practice.

Method: A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained on data from one recording session and applied unchanged to data collected in a different recording session, using ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. Five label-free test-time adaptations are compared, including feature-statistic alignment and batch-normalisation re-estimation.

Result: The encoder retained 0.688 macro-F1 across sessions versus 0.540 for the per-user LDA pipeline, and exceeded both published source-only baselines on the per-window metric. Feature-statistic alignment improved every subject, whereas batch-normalisation re-estimation collapsed the architecture entirely, recovering roughly the equivalent of a single labelled calibration repetition.

Conclusion: A montage-agnostic cross-user encoder can be carried across recording sessions without adjustment, outperforming standard per-user pipelines, and can be further improved by aligning feature statistics at test time, offering a viable path toward practical myoelectric control without frequent recalibration.

Abstract: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

</details>


### [160] [Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27574)
*Yoann Poupart,Aurélie Beynier,Nicolas Maudet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), a reinforcement learning-based method for steering LLM behavior at inference time. PGS accumulates gradients from a temporary behavioral objective over rollouts or demonstrations to construct removable task vectors. It outperforms existing steering methods that fail in a two-route gridworld, and demonstrates composable, transferable behavioral adaptations in chess puzzles and competitive football.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment, revealing a fundamental limitation in current lightweight alternatives for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time.

Method: PGS formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem, accumulating gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector.

Result: PGS is demonstrated to be calibrated and reversible in a two-route gridworld. In chess puzzles, independently fitted PGS vectors combine constructively for compatible tactical objectives. In competitive football, PGS alters specific team behaviors with effects that transfer across opponents.

Conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

Abstract: Activation steering has emerged in large language models as a lightweight alternative for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time. However, we show that existing steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment. To address this limitation, we propose Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), which formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem. PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. We first demonstrate the calibration and reversibility of PGS in a two-route gridworld environment. Using chess puzzles, we then evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors both in isolation and in combination, finding that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively. Finally, in competitive football, we show that PGS can alter specific team behaviors and that its effects transfer across opponents. Together, these results show that policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

</details>


### [161] [MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27581)
*Zhankai Ye,Yukai Jin,Bingyang Wei,Bofan Li,Yusen Wu,Fangyi Li,Shangqian Gao,Xin Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that eliminates the quantization cost of discrete codebooks and the iterative decoding cost of diffusion/AR heads. It uses a single adaptive-length autoencoder to compress motion into a few continuous latent slots, which a language model generates in one draw for text-to-motion and reads back for motion understanding. It achieves state-of-the-art FID on HumanML3D, best CIDEr and BLEU@4, and surpasses discrete-token SOTA on SnapMoGen retrieval and alignment metrics—at a decoding cost of K LM steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified motion-language systems are essential for physical AI, but existing approaches suffer from a quality-cost tradeoff: discrete codebooks limit generation quality, while stronger generators (residual codebooks, masked decoding, long AR rollouts, diffusion chains) incur growing inference costs, and none of this decoding machinery benefits the understanding direction.

Method: MUGEN uses a single adaptive-length autoencoder to compress arbitrary-length motion into a few continuous latent slots as the sole motion representation. A language model generates these slots for text-to-motion and reads them back for understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot extract information from the appropriate transformer depth, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, enabling a single draw to capture text-conditional cross-slot variation.

Result: MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D, raises retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses discrete-token state-of-the-art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen, all at a minimal decoding cost of K LM steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.

Conclusion: A unified motion-language framework can achieve both generation quality and understanding performance without the computational overhead of iterative decoding or discrete codebooks, demonstrating that a compact continuous-latent design with single-draw generation is sufficient and superior.

Abstract: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

</details>


### [162] [Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27591)
*Jinyi Liu,Wei Chen,Pengyu Chen,Xinyi Yuan,Minghe Bai,Guoquan Wu,Jun Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs in LLM inference that constructs channel masks from magnitude rankings of the intermediate state rather than exact values, achieving up to 1.99x end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity while outperforming existing training-free baselines across ten LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward networks dominate memory traffic and computation in LLM inference, making activation sparsification critical. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in channel-selection strategies. While the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, obtaining it requires costly dense computation.

Method: Prox is a two-stage training-free framework. Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask. Stage 2 computes only the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. The key insight is that sparse execution only needs the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be built from magnitude ranking rather than exact values.

Result: Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels across ten LLMs from six model families, achieves up to 1.99x end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

Conclusion: Prox demonstrates that effective channel selection for sparse SwiGLU FFNs can be done in a training-free manner by leveraging magnitude rankings of the intermediate state, enabling significant speedups while maintaining model quality and compatibility with other optimization techniques.

Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

</details>


### [163] [Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27594)
*Pankayaraj Pathmanathan,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a unified adaptive hypernetwork framework for multi-policy compliance in large reasoning models (LRMs). Safety policies serve as inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which produces policy-compliant LoRA weights that can be added to a single LRM to enable on-demand compliance with different policy subsets, avoiding the combinatorial overhead of training separate models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LRMs become personalized for downstream users, different user-specific models must comply with different subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM per policy subset incurs severe combinatorial overhead, while in-context learning methods introduce computational challenges from long context generation. An efficient unified solution is needed.

Method: The proposed framework uses an adaptive hypernetwork where safety policies are treated as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator. The generator learns to produce policy-compliant LoRA weights for the downstream LRM. When these weights are added to the LRM, the model generates responses compliant with the specified policy subsets.

Result: The framework enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance, demonstrated across reasoning models of different sizes and different evaluation datasets.

Conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is an effective and practical approach for multi-policy compliance in LRMs, solving the combinatorial overhead problem while maintaining task performance.

Abstract: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

</details>


### [164] [Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27600)
*Stephen Gould,Anton van den Hengel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a KV cache eviction scheme for LLMs that removes redundant tokens—those that can be well-predicted from more recent tokens—by running a counter-causal attention pass that reuses existing cache contents, with a fast single-layer approximation for efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV caches grow linearly with context length and quickly exhaust GPU memory for long prompts or outputs. Existing compression and eviction strategies aim to reduce memory footprint while preserving generation accuracy, but there is a need for an effective, training-free, in-distribution scoring method for cache eviction.

Method: The authors propose scoring cache entries by running the model on tokens in their original order, reusing existing key/value representations from the cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so each position attends only to future context. Tokens well-predicted from recent tokens are deemed redundant and evicted. A fast single-layer approximation restricts this counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, significantly reducing refresh cost at marginal accuracy loss.

Result: The proposed KV eviction scheme achieves competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods across various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets, with the fast single-layer approximation providing a significant speedup per refresh cycle.

Conclusion: The counter-causal eviction strategy offers a simple, effective, training-free approach to KV cache management that reduces memory footprint and speeds up inference while maintaining or improving generation quality.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

</details>


### [165] [Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27610)
*Haodong Zhu,Yangyang Ren,Yanjing Li,Sheng Xu,Haiguang Liu,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KGPS reformulates prompt selection in RL fine-tuning of LLMs as a dynamic state estimation problem using a Kalman filter, modeling each prompt's latent success rate in logit space with process noise tied to policy update magnitude, enabling adaptive selection of intermediate-difficulty prompts without extra rollouts. It achieves SOTA performance across math, planning, and geometry benchmarks, using 83% fewer rollouts than DS on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B while slightly improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL fine-tuning of LLMs requires selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy, but prompt difficulty evolves non-stationarily during training. Existing online methods face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but assume stationary difficulty, making them unsuitable for RL's non-stationary dynamics.

Method: KGPS models prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem. It represents each prompt's latent success rate in logit space with a linear-Gaussian state-space model, where process noise is coupled to policy update magnitude (uncertainty grows with larger policy changes). A Kalman filter maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while revisiting uncertain ones. The method requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training.

Result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks with multiple RL algorithms show KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B across six math reasoning benchmarks, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while improving average performance by 0.12 points.

Conclusion: KGPS establishes state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods by being adaptive to policy drift while remaining computation-efficient, effectively resolving the accuracy-versus-efficiency trade-off in online prompt selection for RL fine-tuning of LLMs.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

</details>


### [166] [Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27626)
*Wentao Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes OCO-PAoI-Hard, a framework that converts hard peak-AoI deadline constraints in safety-critical IoT systems into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over polyhedral safe sets, guaranteeing zero per-slot deadline violations under adversarial conditions with O(sqrt(T)) regret.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical IoT systems (industrial closed-loop control, V2X, teleoperation) require hard per-slot peak-AoI deadlines, which existing approaches (Whittle-index, deep RL, long-term constrained OCO) only satisfy under restrictive assumptions like stochastic channels or simulator access. A rigorous framework is needed that guarantees zero per-slot violations even under adversarial conditions.

Method: The key insight is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline constraint collapses exactly into an affine half-space constraint on the resource allocation vector, transforming hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization. The method uses a strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop: one Euclidean projection per slot enforces feasibility, a gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate.

Result: The framework achieves zero per-slot modeled-state deadline violations under one-step viability in adversarial settings with O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator. It establishes closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. Experiments on a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel show zero deadline violations across ten seeds while four baselines miss 1.65%-64.0% of slots, with empirical normalized regret below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

Conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard provides the first principled framework for hard real-time AoI deadline enforcement under adversarial conditions, combining geometric insight (polyhedral safe sets) with OCO tools to achieve both feasibility and near-optimal regret, validated empirically against strong baselines.

Abstract: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

</details>


### [167] [First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27632)
*Yang Jiao,Kaixuan Jiao,Kai Yang,Nadjib Aitsaadi,Ilhem Fajjari,Renwei,Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses distributed robust coreset selection by formulating it as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints, and proposes a Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization (F²CTO) method that combines a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm, achieving a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding an ε-stationary point.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the growth of IoT and distributed edge networks, training models on full data is computationally prohibitive, making coreset selection essential. Moreover, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the need for robust models in real-world deployments, an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital yet unexplored.

Method: The paper first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, formulating the problem as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. It then proposes F²CTO, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm to solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner.

Result: F²CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection and the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. It achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) for finding an ε-stationary point, and extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency.

Conclusion: The proposed F²CTO provides the first distributed framework for robust coreset selection, addressing privacy and robustness concerns in distributed edge networks while delivering provable convergence guarantees and demonstrating practical efficacy on continual learning tasks.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

</details>


### [168] [Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27651)
*Jia Bi,Samuel Pinilla,Chenyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OPAL is a framework for deciding whether adaptive experimentation should be enabled at all, using precommitted contracts that require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value after cost. It demonstrates theoretical impossibility boundaries and empirical success on a Cell Painting dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, but existing methods assume adaptation is already permitted. There is a need to decide at a prior level whether adaptation should be enabled, since naive adaptation can lead to poor risk control and negative value.

Method: OPAL introduces a precommitted authorization contract requiring: (1) non-trivial adaptation, (2) controlled target risk, and (3) positive executed value after cost. It establishes an impossibility theorem showing that source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derives a target-calibrated recovery procedure.

Result: On an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities with strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion, and achieved a 5.18% false-activation upper bound below the 7.5% limit. Among six methods, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with risk control.

Conclusion: Authorization constitutes a distinct layer for safe adaptive science, separate from the adaptation methods themselves. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies help distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing OPAL as a principled approach to decide when adaptation should be enabled.

Abstract: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

</details>


### [169] [Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27655)
*Hanting Suo,Yuwen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EEG emotion recognition accuracy depends on the entire evaluation procedure, not just the classifier. Using a DGCNN pathway on SEED and SEED-IV, the authors separate target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, showing that subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer different questions. They find large train-to-held-out-subject accuracy gaps and demonstrate that checkpoint selection, evaluation protocol, and participant rankings are all procedure-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reported accuracy in EEG emotion recognition is often treated as a property of the classifier, but the complete evaluation procedure (target quantity, development procedure, reporting rule) determines the result. The authors aim to disentangle these components and critically examine how protocol choices shape reported performance.

Method: Using one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV, the authors conduct protocol-matched checks, subject-dependent evaluations, repeated test-set checkpoint selection, five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, and held-out participant generalization tests with BCa confidence intervals. They also analyze participant ranking stability across representations and time scales, and test a tail-risk ensemble in a separate final evaluation.

Result: SEED subject-dependent accuracy was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference; SEED-IV's 3.40-point gap remained unresolved. Repeated test-set checkpoint selection raised mean window accuracy from 0.7855 (epoch 80) to 0.8892. Five-fold subject-disjoint validation-selected checkpoints gave 0.9990 (SEED) and 0.9920 (SEED-IV) training-participant trial accuracy, but held-out participant accuracy dropped to 0.5348 on SEED and 0.3954 on SEED-IV. Participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, and the tail-risk ensemble showed no positive gain.

Conclusion: The large train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting but do not isolate subject identity from other confounds. Reporting should explicitly distinguish subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results as answers to different questions, rather than reporting a single accuracy number as a classifier property.

Abstract: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

</details>


### [170] [Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27656)
*Bum Jun Kim,Kohei Hayashi,Shunsuke Kamiya,Masanori Koyama,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), a method for looped Transformers that reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. SCSE retains input dependence through a learned anchor and initial deviation, maps zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance via a zero-deviation mask. SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier across multiple language modeling benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Looped Transformers reuse the same Transformer block over recurrent depth to create a train/test-time compute axis without increasing parameter count. However, the shared block must govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states across trained and extrapolated depths. Moreover, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state, breaking reference preservation.

Method: SCSE retains input dependence through a learned anchor and initial deviation. It allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through a zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation.

Result: SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion. Ablation studies show that the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence are the primary contributors to the gains, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

Conclusion: The paper provides theory showing that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom with potentially harmful, neutral, or beneficial task effects. SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero, yielding consistent improvements across benchmarks.

Abstract: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

</details>


### [171] [Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27660)
*Rishabh Iyer,Truong Pham,Anay Majee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework connecting Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition, characterizing how different SIMs (Total Information and Mutual Information variants) capture intra-class and inter-class geometric/statistical properties, validated by synthetic experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SIMs have shown empirical success in representation learning (e.g., the SCORE framework for supervised contrastive learning), but their geometric and statistical properties are poorly understood. A unified theoretical underpinning is needed to explain why different submodular information measures work and to guide principled selection and design of SIM-based objectives.

Method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework linking SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning. They analyze three Total Information (TI) objectives—Graph Cut TI (within-class variance), LogDet TI (generalized variance/covariance volume), and Facility Location TI (imbalance-aware separation for rare/confusable classes)—and three Mutual Information (MI) objectives—Graph Cut MI (centroid separation/Fisher-style discrimination), LogDet MI (Mahalanobis distance-based covariance-aware separation), and Facility Location MI (nearest-mode representational overlap). They validate these characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.

Result: The theoretical characterizations are validated empirically: across all synthetic settings (varying variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap), the observed behavior closely matches the proposed theory. This provides the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures in the context of representation learning.

Conclusion: The paper delivers the first unified theoretical framework for understanding SIMs in representation learning, mapping each SIM variant to classical statistical concepts. This not only explains their empirical success but also offers principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives.

Abstract: Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

</details>


### [172] [FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27665)
*Zekai Chen,Haodong Lu,Shihao Li,Weiwei Ji,Xunkai Li,Xun Wu,Yinlin Zhu,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedOGL is a semantic-structural memory preservation framework for federated graph learning under open-world conditions, addressing catastrophic forgetting in decentralized multimodal graph streams via client-side replay and distillation with global structural basis projection, plus server-side category prototype sharing. It reduces forgetting degradation by 42.67% over the best baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In federated graph learning, clients must continuously learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting out-of-distribution samples. Catastrophic forgetting in this setting is not merely a classifier-level problem—it manifests through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation, which existing methods fail to holistically address.

Method: FedOGL employs a dual-sided framework: (1) On the client side, it preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, and protects graph-propagation memory by projecting it onto a globally shared structure basis. (2) On the server side, it maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to enable cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.

Result: Extensive experiments show FedOGL reduces catastrophic forgetting-induced performance degradation by 42.67% compared to the best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving downstream task performance.

Conclusion: FedOGL effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in federated open-world multimodal graph learning by jointly addressing classifier-level, structural, and federated memory loss, achieving substantial performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.

Abstract: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

</details>


### [173] [Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27680)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper closes two theoretical gaps in LoRA fine-tuning: it proves a matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) for the excess risk of rank-r LoRA estimators, complementing the existing O(rd/n) upper bound. This yields a rank-selection dichotomy: for constrained ERM, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r* and over-ranking hurts; for nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators, over-ranking is harmless. Theory is verified on synthetic trace regression and real LoRA fine-tuning on DistilBERT/RoBERTa (SST-2, MRPC), showing predicted U-shape validation loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generalization bounds for LoRA only provide upper bounds (O~(√(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n)) without matching lower bounds, and there is no formal answer to the practical question of how to choose the LoRA rank r. These gaps prevent a principled understanding of LoRA's statistical complexity and over-parameterization behavior.

Method: Three results: (1) a local Rademacher argument establishes an O~(rd/n) upper bound on excess risk for the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA when the target has rank at most r; (2) a Fano-type packing argument over the rank-r subspace of R^(d×d) proves a matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n), applicable to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class; (3) synthesizing these bounds yields a rank-selection dichotomy distinguishing constrained ERM from nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators.

Result: For constrained ERM, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r* and over-ranking strictly hurts (O~(rd/n) grows with r). For adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Θ~(r*d/n) regardless of chosen r. Experiments on synthetic trace regression and real LoRA fine-tuning (DistilBERT/RoBERTa on SST-2/MRPC) confirm the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two configurations showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p=0.016).

Conclusion: The paper fully characterizes the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning in the well-specified locally quadratic regime, providing matching upper and lower bounds. It identifies the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as an artifact of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than an inherent property of the LoRA class, offering a formal theoretical basis for rank selection in LoRA.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

</details>


### [174] [Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27681)
*Baoli Hao,Chenxi Hu,Ming Zhong,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) for transient-stability assessment and critical clearing time (CCT) estimation in power systems. ES-PINN aligns its representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics, enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces, and introduces a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin for differentiable CCT boundary approximation. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show consistent improvements over neural-surrogate baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transient-stability assessment is essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages in power systems. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times, making conventional approaches computationally expensive and difficult to scale.

Method: ES-PINN structurally matches its neural representation to the three distinct dynamic phases (pre-fault, fault-on, post-clearing) and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin provides a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, supporting accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction via a distilled readout. A local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error bound is proven, where exact event chaining removes separate state-interface defect terms.

Result: On IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems, ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses confirm effectiveness and computational efficiency.
