Conclusion: The event-structured architecture with exact interface chaining and a differentiable CCT boundary formulation offers an accurate, efficient, and theoretically grounded framework for transient-stability assessment and CCT prediction in power systems.

Abstract: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [175] [NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27710)
*Petra Eerikinharju,Marko Tuononen,Ville Hautamäki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous multidimensional variables, combining a MINE-based mutual information estimator with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators, and demonstrates improved accuracy over KSG-based baselines on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Normalized mutual information is valuable for comparing dependency scores across datasets and applications (e.g., molecular dynamics, interpretable ML), but existing estimators are sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability. A more robust estimator is needed.

Method: The estimator combines two neural components: (1) mutual information is estimated via the Donsker-Varadhan representation (MINE-based), and (2) marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution (MI-NEE-inspired), from which entropy is recovered. The normalized MI is formed from these two estimates.

Result: Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show the proposed neural estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline.

Conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings, offering improved accuracy over k-nearest-neighbor-based approaches.

Abstract: Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

</details>


### [176] [VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27712)
*Angshuman Chakravertty,Rahul Maheshwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VESTIGE is a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns masking probabilities with empirically measured per-position corruption profiles instead of using a uniform distribution. Applied to ancient DNA reconstruction, it outperforms standard MLM across all tested configurations, cuts validation cross-entropy by 13%, and produces high-quality protein reconstructions, demonstrating that spatial redistribution of masking alone yields significant gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MLM fine-tuning assumes reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic by using uniform masking. When degradation is concentrated at predictable positions (e.g., cytosine deamination in aDNA), this assumption fails and the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor at peak damage sites.

Method: VESTIGE replaces the standard MLM collator by aligning the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. For aDNA, per-position C-to-T/G-to-A gradients from mapDamage2 are used; masking rates are rescaled so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% (identical to standard MLM), isolating spatial redistribution as the sole variable. All other model parameters, data, seed, and hyperparameters are held fixed across DNABERT-2 runs.

Result: Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier yields AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows.

Conclusion: VESTIGE demonstrates that knowledge-guided masking distribution alignment is a domain-agnostic principle applicable to any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore). It improves reconstruction quality without adding parameters or architectural changes.

Abstract: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

</details>


### [177] [Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27731)
*Jiaxiang Li,Zhiqi Bu,Shiyun Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the joint effect of learning rate and batch size schedules on deep learning training dynamics through the lens of convex optimization, deriving a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any learning rate schedule and proposing joint scaling laws that outperform static batch size baselines in large language model training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern deep learning typically keeps batch size static throughout training, overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on training dynamics. The paper aims to address this gap by providing a theoretical characterization of how these two hyperparameters jointly influence loss.

Method: The paper studies deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derives a joint characterization of loss in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization enables a closed-form optimal batch size schedule given any prescribed learning rate schedule.

Result: The derived joint scaling laws consistently outperform static batch size baselines, demonstrating that dynamic batch size scheduling significantly improves large language model training performance.

Conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling is significant for large language model training, and the proposed joint scheduling framework provides a principled way to optimize both learning rate and batch size together, leading to better training efficiency than static batch size approaches.

Abstract: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

</details>


### [178] [Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27737)
*Vincent Ryusuke Takahashi,Yoshinari Takeishi,Jun'ichi Takeuchi,Kave Salamatian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper extends Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) by adding a second "clean teacher" model trained only on clean data alongside the existing robust teacher, using cross-layer attention matrices to transfer features from both teachers to the student. The method improves clean accuracy over IBD while maintaining adversarial robustness, and is competitive with state-of-the-art dual-teacher approaches like B-MTARD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing adversarial robustness methods like IBD trade off clean accuracy for robustness, degrading performance on clean inputs. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging both a robust teacher (from adversarial training) and a clean teacher (trained on clean data only) to preserve both clean and adversarial performance.

Method: The method extends the IBD framework by introducing an additional clean teacher model trained solely on clean inputs. Both the clean and robust teachers' features are transferred to the student via a cross-layer attention matrix in the distillation process, allowing the student to learn from complementary representations.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show the proposed method improves clean-sample classification accuracy over original IBD while maintaining similar adversarial accuracy. It is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including B-MTARD, particularly regarding the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. The paper also analyzes how different training settings affect the attention module.

Conclusion: Adding a clean teacher to the IBD framework enables better trade-offs between clean and adversarial accuracy, achieving competitive performance with state-of-the-art dual-teacher distillation methods.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

</details>


### [179] [ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27744)
*Yuxin Chen,Liang Luo,Buyun Zhang,Jian Jiao,Boda Li,Haoyu Wang,Tongyi Tang,Ao Cai,Zijian Shen,Zhengkai Zhang,Wenyi Xie,Ryan Dick,Han Liu,Neng Shi,Bin Yu,Jianbo Xiao,Shuyao Bi,Hongtao Yu,Yuanwei Fang,Zhuoran Zhao,Sijia Chen,Yang Chen,Shuqi Yang,Qianru Li,Zikun Liu,Wei Ling,Sihan Zeng,Longhao Jin,Jiaxin Lu,Yinbin Ma,Jiawei Li,Yichen Ruan,Yong Ler Lee,Birmingham Guan,Zijian Li,Jianbo Sun,Zhengyu Zhang,Zeliang Chen,Xiaohan Wei,Yuchen Hao,GP Musumeci,Venkatesh Ranganathan,Yantao Yao,Chunqiang Tang,Wenlin Chen,Santanu Kolay,Ellie Dingqiao Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ROCS (Request-Oriented Compute Sharing) is a modeling and inference paradigm for recommendation systems that defers request-candidate interactions, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates model components once per request instead of once per candidate, achieving significant inference efficiency gains (up to 3x QPS) while maintaining or improving prediction quality, with production deployment across large-scale systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern recommendation models improve quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints limit scalability. The key insight is that in recommendation inference, each user request is evaluated against many candidates while request-side features are shared across candidates—a property not exploited by current modeling and inference paradigms.

Method: ROCS introduces three components: (1) Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, (2) Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures, and (3) In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) for efficient GPU deployment. The paradigm defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible and evaluates substantial model portions once per request rather than per candidate.

Result: On public benchmarks, ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, it achieves up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation, and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. It has been deployed across large-scale systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, with over two orders of magnitude in inference complexity.

Conclusion: ROCS demonstrates that exploiting the request-candidate sharing property in recommendation inference can substantially improve efficiency without sacrificing prediction quality, and has proven effective at scale in production deployment across diverse recommendation surfaces and stages.

Abstract: Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

</details>


### [180] [DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27761)
*Shubin Ma,Liang Zhao,Chuanye He,Zhenjiao Liu,Liang Zou,Lin Yuanbo Wu,Yu Shao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes DAS-PMVC, a framework for partial multi-view clustering that addresses the partial view alignment problem (PVAP) through dual alignment and structure enhancement, combining anchor graph structure alignment, structure-enhanced feature learning via multi-view graph convolutional networks, and a dual alignment strategy with contrastive learning and the Hungarian algorithm. The framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-view clustering faces the partial view alignment problem (PVAP) where data across different views are misaligned due to limitations in data collection devices. This misalignment leads to view asymmetry and irrelevant samples that degrade clustering performance, and existing methods do not adequately address these challenges.

Method: DAS-PMVC consists of three components: (1) anchor graph structure alignment, which derives sample joint embedding representations from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment in a consistent latent space; (2) structure-enhanced feature learning, which learns view structure information through pretraining and uses multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure; (3) a dual alignment strategy incorporating pretraining-phase anchor graph alignment and training-phase contrastive learning loss with the Hungarian algorithm for further latent feature alignment optimization.

Result: Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing the framework's effectiveness and superiority.

Conclusion: The DAS-PMVC framework effectively mitigates the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples in partial multi-view clustering, achieving superior clustering performance through the combination of view structure consistency and semantic relevance via dual alignment and structure enhancement.

Abstract: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

</details>


### [181] [Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27767)
*Robert Jankowski,Pedro Almagro-Blanco,Marián Boguñá,Melanie Weber,M. Ángeles Serrano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a zero-shot transfer protocol where GNNs are trained on graph replicas scaled down via geometric renormalization (GR), with weights transferred directly to full-resolution graphs without retraining. This preserves predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost, and learned representations remain aligned across scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs become infrastructure-sensitive and computationally expensive at the scale of millions of nodes, raising the question of whether models trained on smaller graph replicas can be deployed directly on full-resolution graphs without retraining.

Method: A zero-shot transfer protocol is proposed in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained via geometric renormalization (GR), and the trained weights are transferred directly to the original full-resolution network. The approach is evaluated across synthetic and real-world networks.

Result: Training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales.

Conclusion: Structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

</details>


### [182] [Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27770)
*Songshuo Lu,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RL-trained policies produce incomplete teachers that only amplify a subset of valid solution modes. The paper proposes an expand-then-compress framework: RGRPO trains a sequence of complementary teachers, and TU-OPD distills them into a single student using reliability gating and per-example quality weighting. The resulting Qwen3-1.7B student outperforms the strongest individual teacher by 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9% on math reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A single RL run can produce a strong reasoner but an incomplete teacher, amplifying only a subset of valid solution modes. The paper argues RL-trained policies should be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold rather than globally reliable supervisors, motivating the need for complementary teachers.

Method: The framework has two stages. (1) Expansion: Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a shared initialization, redirecting each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. (2) Compression: reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes, where only reliable teachers contribute and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by per-example quality. Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over reliable peers to prevent specialist behavior suppression.

Result: On mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, the Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, with relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference.

Conclusion: Stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union. This establishes a simple but powerful principle for RL-based teacher-student distillation.

Abstract: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

</details>


### [183] [LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27787)
*Ken Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LSPO (LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization) is a sampling-time mechanism that recovers the lost gradient in RLVR for mathematical reasoning on "cliff" prompts—those where all sampled rollouts fail, resulting in zero group-normalized advantage. It detects cliff prompts, fits a small LoRA adapter via supervised learning on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls with the base-plus-adapter model, splices successful completions back into the RL batch with importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone while discarding the adapter. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, LSPO beats or ties a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells with up to +10.7 points improvement and an average of +3.8 points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning has a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts where every sampled rollout in a group fails, the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, meaning GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. These are the hardest, most informative prompts for improving reasoning, yet the standard RL mechanism cannot learn from them.

Method: LSPO operates at sampling time each RL step: (1) detect cliff prompts where all rollouts fail; (2) fit a small LoRA adapter via a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions; (3) re-roll the cliff prompts using the base-plus-adapter model; (4) splice the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction; (5) take a GRPO step on the base model alone. The adapter only receives the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, ensuring the final model is base-only.

Result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins, 1 exact tie). Gains reach up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; average improvement over the 16 cells is +3.8 points.

Conclusion: LSPO effectively recovers the lost gradient on cliff prompts, demonstrating consistent improvements over a strong DAPO baseline across all benchmarks and pass@k settings. The importance-sampling correction and base-only final model ensure the method's gains are cleanly attributable to the scaffolding mechanism rather than adapter parameters persisting in the final model.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

</details>


### [184] [Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27797)
*Lennart Fertig,Lukas Kirchdorfer,Tobias Sesterhenn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a controlled benchmark comparing three modeling paradigms for predictive process monitoring (PPM): classical deep sequence models (e.g., LSTM), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models with in-context learning. Results show sequence models consistently outperform others on next-activity prediction, tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, and LLMs generally lag behind despite higher cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While PPM research has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, foundation-model approaches (especially LLMs) are increasingly explored. Tabular foundation models with in-context learning offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM, leaving unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in the evolving landscape.

Method: The paper compares three modeling paradigms—(1) sequence-based deep models trained from scratch, (2) tabular foundation models with in-context learning, and (3) LLMs—both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks.

Result: Sequence models consistently perform best for next-activity prediction, tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks (e.g., remaining time, time to next event), and LLMs usually lag behind despite incurring higher cost.

Conclusion: Classical sequence-based models remain highly competitive in PPM, particularly for next-activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are a viable alternative for temporal prediction tasks, while LLMs are often outperformed by the other paradigms despite higher computational cost.

Abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

</details>


### [185] [Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27807)
*Tianhang Lu,Runtian Ren,Shengcai Liu,Ke Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. It proposes deterministic and randomized algorithms with provable robustness and consistency guarantees, improves the competitive ratio lower bound for randomized online algorithms, and validates findings numerically.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online aggregation with delays on line metrics is a fundamental problem, but existing deterministic algorithms have limitations in competitive performance. The paper aims to leverage machine-learned advice and randomization to achieve better competitive ratios, improving upon the state-of-the-art deterministic Balance benchmark.

Method: The paper introduces a deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm with (4/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (4+λ)-consistency. It then develops a randomized algorithm for the classical adversarial model achieving (e+1)-competitiveness against an oblivious adversary. The two approaches are combined into a randomized learning-augmented algorithm with (e/λ+1/λ²)-robustness and (e+λ)-consistency. Numerical experiments complement the theoretical analysis.

Result: The randomized algorithm achieves (e+1)-competitive ratio, beating the deterministic 5-competitive Balance benchmark and even surpassing the lower bound of 4 for deterministic algorithms. A lower bound of e is established for randomized online algorithms, improving the previous e/(e-1) bound. The algorithms' robustness and consistency trade-offs are formally characterized for all λ∈(0,1].

Conclusion: Randomization provides a significant competitive advantage over deterministic algorithms for online aggregation with delays on a line metric, while learning-augmented approaches offer a flexible robustness-consistency trade-off controllable via the parameter λ.

Abstract: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

</details>


### [186] [Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27904)
*Roel Visser,Isaac Roberts,Barbara Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces contrastive concept importance (CCI), a method that attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to concepts in a visual concept basis, enabling signed, decomposable explanations that answer "why P rather than Q?" questions rather than non-contrastive "why P?" questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard concept-based attribution methods answer non-contrastive "why P?" questions by attributing concepts to a single output class. However, in many real scenarios—such as misclassification, class confusion, or low-margin predictions—the more natural and informative question is "why P rather than Q?". Existing methods do not directly support this contrastive framing.

Method: The authors propose CCI, which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast (foil) class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The scores are signed, indicating which side of the class pair a concept supports, and are decomposable into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This decomposition distinguishes globally important concepts from those that specifically influence class-pair distinctions, and identifies whether effects are shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.

Result: The method is evaluated on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion/deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy comparisons. Results show that CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary concept importance, and that highly contrastive concepts can be assessed against semantic superclass structure to determine if they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

Conclusion: Contrastive concept importance provides a more nuanced and practically relevant form of concept-based explanation by answering "why P rather than Q?" questions, uncovering class-pair-specific model behavior that ordinary concept importance misses, with the ability to distinguish between fine-grained and broad-category influences.

Abstract: Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

</details>


### [187] [Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27905)
*Muhammad Adil Saleem,Syed Ali Raza,Mary-Anne Williams*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether including an instance's predicted class in the RL state representation improves counterfactual explanation (CFE) generation. A class-aware RL method is compared against a class-blind baseline across seven diverse datasets, showing faster convergence, higher reward optimization, reduced episode length, significantly more valid CFEs, and the class feature ranking as one of the most influential predictors in action selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous RL-based CFE generation approaches formulate states exclusively from predictor-derived features in the supervised dataset, potentially limiting exploration efficiency and policy optimality. The authors hypothesize that incorporating the instance's predicted class into the RL state representation can enhance exploration and improve the quality of generated counterfactuals.

Method: The authors propose a class-aware RL method for CFE generation that augments the state representation with the instance's predicted class alongside standard predictor-derived features. They compare it to a class-blind RL baseline (identical except for excluding class information) across seven datasets of varying sizes and domains. Evaluation covers training dynamics (convergence speed, reward optimization, episode length), CFE validity, and feature influence analysis using SHAP and LIME.

Result: Class-aware RL outperforms class-blind RL in convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction during training. It generates significantly more valid CFEs. SHAP and LIME analyses show the class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL action selection across datasets.

Conclusion: Class-awareness in RL state representation is beneficial for CFE generation, leading to clearer and faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets. The results underscore the significance of incorporating predicted class information into RL states for counterfactual explanations.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

</details>


### [188] [S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27913)
*Glenn Anta Bucagu,Thorir Mar Ingolfsson,Yawei Li,Luca Benini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: S-CEReBrO is an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture for continuous EEG monitoring, introducing a Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism that factorizes attention into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory. It processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention, uses 55% of the memory while increasing throughput by 2.1X compared to linear attention, and achieves SOTA on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters after pre-training on >25,000 hours of EEG from >12,000 subjects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer-based architectures for EEG analysis face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. This limits the applicability of foundation models for long-term, continuous EEG monitoring scenarios.

Method: The paper introduces S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), which employs a novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism that factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, ensuring constant KV cache memory since only the active window requires resident attention maps. The model was pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects.

Result: Windowed alternating attention processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. It requires only 55% of the memory of low-rank linear attention on long contexts while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.

Conclusion: This work represents a significant step toward efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring by demonstrating that constant-memory attention can deliver state-of-the-art performance with reduced parameter counts, making continuous streaming EEG analysis practical.

Abstract: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

</details>


### [189] [Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27914)
*Takumi Shioda,Kohei Terashima,Tatsuo Nagai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether frontier reasoning LLMs can achieve competitive multi-zone VAV control from text alone without building-specific training, and whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. GPT-5 achieved the largest electricity reduction (6.2%) but reduced ventilation margin, while TD3 reduced electricity by 4.5% with improved compliance. However, RFT failed to produce sustained improvement: the learned critic's within-state ranking was unreliable despite near-perfect across-time correlation, and 200 RFT steps yielded no improvement. The authors recommend transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model predictive control and reinforcement learning for VAV control typically require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The authors aim to test whether frontier reasoning models can achieve competitive control from text alone, and whether knowledge can be transferred to a locally deployable open-weight model via RFT.

Method: Five controllers were evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator: a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 RL (4.5% reduction), GPT-5 without building-specific training (6.2% reduction), and an open-weight model with RFT. RFT used deterministic rollouts that restore saved states, apply one candidate action, and use TD3 to score actions. The learned critic was audited against these rollouts.

Result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO2 compliance. GPT-5 achieved a 6.2% reduction but reduced ventilation margin. The learned critic had near-perfect across-time correlation (r=0.9998) but unreliable within-state ranking, selecting the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement; the open-weight controller used more electricity than baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions were worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better.

Conclusion: Frontier reasoning models can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training, but value-based RFT transfer to open-weight models is not yet effective. Exact rollout scores reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction, and unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

Abstract: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

</details>


### [190] [ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27924)
*Dongxiu Liu,Haoyi Niu,Peng Cheng,Yuan Gao,Xirui Kang,Sangli Teng,Koushil Sreenath,Xianyuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field in physical time, parameterized by an ODE in representation space. Building on this, ODEWorld is a continuous-time latent world model that addresses representation collapse, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, and reconciles planning-conducive dynamics with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing machine learning world models are confined to discrete-time prediction, which is inefficient for capturing the fundamentally continuous nature of physical space and time dynamics.

Method: PT-Flow learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time, with sequential data dynamics parameterized by an ODE embedded in a structured representation space. Future prediction is recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. ODEWorld extends this with time-variant feature extraction and enforcement of ODE properties on both the representation space and latent velocity field to prevent representation collapse.

Result: ODEWorld achieves high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, and excels in both video generation and robotic control by providing planning-oriented information.

Conclusion: ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, demonstrating that continuous-time latent world models are effective and versatile for both generative and control tasks in the physical world.

Abstract: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

</details>


### [191] [Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27928)
*Xiang Yuan,Kaiqing Lei,Zhenyu Jin,Jun Shu,Deyu Meng,Zongben Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a Bayesian domain weighting method for LLM pre-training that infers optimal domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution using Gamma prior information learned from observations, achieving stable and efficient domain weight learning while consuming substantially less data than existing search-based function-fitting methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The performance of LLMs is strongly influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. Existing approaches either rely on proxy function fitting with strong structural assumptions (e.g., rank invariance, scaling laws) that are often violated and introduce estimation bias, or directly optimize weighting schemes from data but suffer from unstable optimization trajectories and prohibitive computational overhead. There is a need for a method that balances accuracy, stability, and efficiency.

Method: The proposed method is a Bayesian domain weighting approach that infers domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution, incorporating Gamma prior information learned from observational data to guide the inference process.

Result: Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves stable and efficient domain weights learning, identifies optimal mixtures, and consumes substantially less data than search-based function-fitting approaches, thereby revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

Conclusion: The Bayesian domain weighting method effectively addresses the limitations of both proxy-function-based and direct optimization-based approaches, offering a scalable and data-efficient solution for discovering optimal domain mixtures in LLM pre-training.

Abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

</details>


### [192] [TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27940)
*Cheng Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TriShield is a three-layer deterministic defense against the NeuroImprint privacy backdoor attack in federated LLM fine-tuning, achieving 0% reconstruction success with zero model utility loss and no additional communication rounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated fine-tuning of LLMs enables collaborative training without exposing raw data, but the NeuroImprint attack allows a malicious parameter server to reconstruct 59%-79% of client training data by corrupting PEFT adapters with memorization neurons. Existing defenses like LDP and gradient clipping either fail or impose unacceptable utility degradation, motivating a defense that is both effective and utility-preserving.

Method: TriShield consists of three layers: (1) a Parameter Artifact Detector that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a Stateful Virtual Iteration mechanism forcing Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection operator that projects local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, eliminating gradient components that carry private memorization.

Result: Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B show TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to 0% across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy with less than 5% additional GPU computation overhead. Theoretically, after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is proven to be zero.

Conclusion: TriShield provides a deterministic, theoretically grounded defense against NeuroImprint-style gradient-based reconstruction attacks in federated LLM fine-tuning, achieving complete protection with zero utility loss and minimal computational overhead, offering a viable alternative to stochastic defenses like LDP.

Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

</details>


### [193] [AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27953)
*Shengda Gu,Kai Li,Xinyi Ke,Haobo Fu,Yifan Zhang,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoPref is the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in neural combinatorial optimization, factorizing objectives into pairwise loss and set-aware weighting programs, and using staged conditional search with behavioral gates to efficiently discover superior objectives that outperform hand-designed baselines across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing preference-based neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) methods use manually specified, one-size-fits-all objective formulations that conflate two distinct design choices: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. This limits performance and scalability across diverse problem types.

Method: AutoPref factorizes the preference objective into (1) a pairwise loss program defining the learning signal and (2) a set-aware weighting program determining each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space that subsumes existing preference objectives. A staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates filters inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation to make the search tractable.

Result: AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, demonstrating superior performance across various problem scales.

Conclusion: Automated objective discovery via LLM-guided programmatic search is a scalable and effective alternative to manual preference-objective design in NCO, generalizing across diverse combinatorial optimization problems.

Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

</details>


### [194] [What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27966)
*Dongxiao He,Siqi Liu,Jitao Zhao,Yawen Li,Yi Wang,Di Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces SliGFM, a graph foundation model that unifies heterogeneous node features across domains by ordering feature dimensions via topological smoothness and encoding them with a shared sliding-window transformer, guided by four desiderata for effective cross-domain feature unification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to unifying heterogeneous node features in graph foundation models typically project features into a fixed-dimensional space, implicitly assuming dimensional uniformity equals effective feature unification. This is insufficient because dimensional consistency alone does not guarantee preservation of informative semantics or capture transferable cross-domain patterns.

Method: SliGFM distills four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification (formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility). It orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and applies a shared sliding-window feature encoder to transform heterogeneous features into ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. A smoothness-aware transformer captures relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, and a generative reconstruction objective preserves original feature information.

Result: The paper proposes SliGFM as a graph foundation model addressing the conceptual gap in feature unification, providing a principled framework based on topological smoothness ordering and sliding-window encoding with generative reconstruction.

Conclusion: SliGFM offers a principled alternative to naive fixed-dimensional projection by ensuring formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility in graph foundation model feature unification.

Abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

</details>


### [195] [Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27968)
*Efstratios Zaradoukas,Davide Gabrielli,Bardh Prenkaj,Gjergji Kasneci*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reward decomposition framework for machine unlearning in the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) paradigm, introducing two new reward functions—an exponential reward based on forbidden-concept occurrence counts and a PageRank-inspired reward weighting penalties by semantic importance—that outperform sparse binary rewards by up to 3× faster convergence on the RWKU benchmark while preserving general model utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RLVR-based unlearning methods use sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal—indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided—which limits convergence speed. The paper aims to decouple verifiability from sparsity in reward design to improve unlearning efficiency.

Method: The paper introduces a principled reward decomposition framework that separates verifiability from sparsity within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. Two new reward functions are proposed: (1) an exponential reward providing graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and (2) a PageRank-inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance.

Result: Experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark show that both proposed reward functions consistently outperform the binary reward setting, achieving similar forgetting performance up to 3× faster while preserving general model utility.

Conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency, offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

Abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

</details>


### [196] [TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27973)
*Cong Li,Peixi Peng,Yisen Zhao,Xinyu Hu,Shudong Liu,Zhan Su,Zhuojian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAPO is a unified training framework for LLM agents that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision, using action-conditioned next-observation prediction on a shared backbone to exploit dense environmental feedback during online interaction.
