It consistently improves task performance on WebShop and ALFWorld over pure RL baselines without extra data, sampling, or inference overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL post-training methods for LLM agents rely on sparse task rewards, failing to leverage dense supervisory signals naturally available from environmental feedback after each action. Theoretical work suggests predictive knowledge of environmental consequences is key for generalization in multi-step goal-oriented tasks, motivating the use of transition dynamics as additional supervision.

Method: TAPO alternates between standard RL policy optimization and transition supervision. It repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction loss on a shared backbone model, jointly enhancing the model's understanding of environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while optimizing the policy. It is designed as a lightweight, plug-and-play module compatible with existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no expert data, extra sampling, or inference overhead.

Result: Systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld across foundation models of varying scales integrated with different policy optimization algorithms show TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

Conclusion: Incorporating transition-aware supervision via action-conditioned next-observation prediction during online RL training significantly enhances LLM agent performance in multi-step goal-oriented tasks, offering an effective and efficient complement to reward-based policy optimization.

Abstract: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

</details>


### [197] [Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27975)
*Kağan Akman,Naci Saldi,Serdar Yüksel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper derives finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions, using a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation to interpret training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. Bounds are obtained via quantization, concentration inequalities, and Lipschitz stability, then extended to distributionally robust control connecting to Wasserstein DRO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide theoretical guarantees on the generalization performance of Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions, an area lacking finite-sample bounds that account for the recursive structure of the training dynamics.

Method: The authors view datasets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, reformulating training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. They analyze a quantized model (quantizing state, action, and measure-state spaces), derive finite-sample generalization bounds via concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces and a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function, and transfer these bounds to the base model with an explicit approximation error. The machinery is then applied to yield a distributionally robust control formulation tied to Wasserstein DRO.

Result: Explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for the quantized Transformer model, transferred to the original model with quantified approximation error. Additionally, a connection is established between Transformer generalization and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

Conclusion: The doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation provides a rigorous pathway to finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers with dynamic programming recursions, and naturally bridges to distributionally robust optimization frameworks for further theoretical and practical insights.

Abstract: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

</details>


### [198] [It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27987)
*Florian Fervers,Sebastian Bullinger,Christoph Bodensteiner,Michael Arens*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces einx, a universal notation for tensor operations based on vectorization. It uses declarative, pointful expressions defined by analogy with loop notation to represent the vectorization of tensor operations, reducing large Numpy-like APIs to a small set of elementary operations with consistent rules, and provides a Python implementation that integrates with existing tensor frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Numpy-like notation used by predominant tensor frameworks is difficult to read/write and prone to shape errors due to inconsistent rules across a large collection of operations. Existing alternatives like einsum and einops are restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.

Method: The paper revisits vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, using it to lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations plus their vectorization. Based on this, einx is introduced as a universal notation using declarative, pointful expressions defined by analogy with loop notation, representing vectorized tensor operations.

Result: einx reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and provides a clean, readable, and writable representation in code. A Python implementation is provided that integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks.

Conclusion: Vectorization provides a universal foundation for defining and reasoning about tensor operations, and einx demonstrates this by offering a simpler, more consistent, and more expressive notation for tensor programming compared to existing approaches.

Abstract: Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

</details>


### [199] [Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28019)
*Solal Vernier,Ivan Can Arisoy,Merwan Barlier,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a user foundation model for open-web real-time bidding (RTB), where user identity is fragmented and non-persistent unlike stable-identity e-commerce settings. The model pre-trains a Transformer encoder using masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories, then fine-tunes for click prediction. The pre-training pipeline is optimized via an LLM-as-optimizer paradigm that searches over reviewable code-level edits. The learned representations improve multiple production tasks: +1.197% RIG on bid win-rate, +1.354% RIG on CTR ranker, and a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial user foundation models typically assume stable persistent user identities, but open-web RTB operates on fragmented, non-persistent user identities with limited browsing history depending on privacy choices. A large portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records are short, disjointed sessions typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving sequential structure unexploited.

Method: The authors pre-train a Transformer encoder with two objectives: masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories. The encoder is then fine-tuned on the click prediction task. The pre-training pipeline is optimized using an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting.

Result: The encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker. A 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC, with 80% CI excluding zero on both metrics.

Conclusion: User foundation models based on self-supervised learning over browsing histories are viable and effective on the open web, despite fragmented and non-persistent user identities. The learned sequential representations improve multiple downstream production tasks, and the LLM-as-optimizer pipeline provides a practical mechanism for optimizing industrial pre-training infrastructures.

Abstract: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

</details>


### [200] [Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28022)
*Yuran Wang,Zekun Wang,Bohan Zeng,Ruixu Zhang,Wenxuan Liu,Liu Yang,Yifan Dai,Yang Shi,Bozhou Li,Chengzhuo Tong,Daili Hua,Yuanxing Zhang,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Flux-OPD, an online preference distillation paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision for LLM training in open-ended domains. By decomposing the reverse KL objective, it reveals that students are distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers and identifies a conflict term measuring disagreement among teachers. Flux-OPD leverages this decomposition to inject contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, weighting corrections by the conflict indicator, outperforming existing OPD paradigms on open-ended tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences hard to formalize as supervision. Contexts can convey preferences but provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision leads to unstable distillation targets and conflicting distributions, requiring stabilization and conflict-downweighting mechanisms.

Method: The paper decomposes the reverse KL objective to analyze the effect of contexts, revealing two insights: (1) the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and (2) the objective contains a conflict term measuring teacher disagreements. Based on this, Flux-OPD treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator.

Result: Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, demonstrating improved performance and highlighting the potential of combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

Conclusion: Flux-OPD effectively captures task preferences in open-ended domains via evolving-context supervision with stabilized targets and conflict-weighted corrections, offering a promising direction for combining teacher supervision with dynamic contexts in LLM preference distillation.

Abstract: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

</details>


### [201] [Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28026)
*Xingjian Wu,Junlin Liu,Xingchen Liu,Xuhang Zhu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces CRPO (Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization), which reformulates agentic On-Policy Self-Distillation from a contrastive learning perspective to address exposure bias in multi-turn LLM agentic settings, outperforming existing RL and self-distillation baselines across 13 benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD provides dense logit-level supervision but suffers from exposure bias due to privileged self-teacher information, leading to reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions in multi-turn agentic settings.

Method: CRPO reformulates agentic OPSD as contrastive learning by using predictive entropy to distinguish positive positions (reflective exploration) from negative positions (exposure bias), then performs group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.

Result: Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks show CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, with improved training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

Conclusion: CRPO effectively mitigates exposure bias in agentic self-distillation via contrastive learning, enhancing training stability and generalization for long-horizon reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

</details>


### [202] [Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28035)
*Tianen Shen,Zhengyu Li,Yutong Li,Xiangfei Qiu,Xingjian Wu,Bin Yang,Jilin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WrapFlow is a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular multivariate time series forecasting that combines Continuous-Time Tokenization (gap-aware encoding of raw observation events) with a standard Transformer backbone for temporal dependency modeling, and introduces a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching training paradigm to learn conditional residual vector fields around base predictions—achieving state-of-the-art results without the computational burden of numerical ODE solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Irregular multivariate time series are common in healthcare, activity recognition, and environmental sensing, but existing approaches either rely on discretization preprocessing that disrupts continuous-time semantics, or use ODE-based continuous-time models that require specialized architectures and incur high computational overhead from numerical solvers.

Method: WrapFlow has two key components: (1) Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens, processed by a standard Transformer backbone; (2) a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching that learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions, avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training, requiring only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance in irregular time series forecasting.

Conclusion: WrapFlow provides an effective continuous-time modeling solution for irregular time series that avoids both the semantic distortion of discretization and the computational overhead of ODE-solver-based approaches, combining easy integration with standard Transformer architectures and efficient simulation-free training.

Abstract: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [203] [Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28036)
*Rémy Vallot,Florian de Vuyst,Thibault Dairay,Mathilde Mougeot*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy that leverages learned features from parameter-space sampling and precomputed solutions to accelerate convergence of Newton's method for systems of nonlinear equations. It constructs complementary reduced spaces (solution and corrective search direction), uses regression for surrogate approximation, then applies a residual-minimizing GMRES-based correction before high-fidelity Newton iteration, yielding quantifiable speedups on PDE problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Newton's method converges faster with better initial guesses, but obtaining good initial guesses for large-scale nonlinear systems remains challenging. The authors aim to systematically construct high-quality initial guesses using learned reduced-space features from precomputed solutions, reducing both iteration count and CPU time.

Method: A two-stage strategy: (1) discrete Newton trajectories are used to build two reduced spaces — a solution feature space from converged states and a corrective search direction feature space from intermediate Newton increments; (2) for an unseen parameter, a regression model predicts a surrogate solution, followed by a residual-minimizing correction computed via a dedicated GMRES-based approach involving a small least-squares problem. The corrected state serves as the initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method.

Result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems demonstrate quantifiable speedups in both Newton iteration count and overall CPU time compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are achieved, and the corrective step is computationally inexpensive (only residual evaluations and a small least-squares solve).

Conclusion: The two-stage learned-initialization strategy is weakly intrusive, generic, and applicable to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems, offering a practical path to accelerating Newton-based solvers through a combination of reduced-order modeling and cheap residual-based corrections.

Abstract: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

</details>


### [204] [ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28037)
*Xingjian Wu,Xuhang Zhu,Xingchen Liu,Junlin Liu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ClawTrack is a dual-assessment benchmark for LLM-based agents that evaluates both task outcomes (Task Score) and reasoning processes (Process Score) across 320 tasks, 8 domains, and 25+ mock services. Using 12,541 rubric items across four reasoning dimensions, the authors evaluate 21 models over 16,000+ trials, finding that process scoring reveals lucky successes hidden by outcome-only evaluation, identifies result verification as a systematic bottleneck, remains robust across judge LLMs, and enables process-based trajectory filtering that improves post-training across model scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based agents only evaluate final outcomes, which cannot distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, creating an evaluation gap in complex, multi-step workflows.

Method: ClawTrack introduces a dual-assessment framework with a Task Score (measuring what an agent achieves) and a Process Score (measuring how it achieves it). A Process Grader evaluates each reasoning turn along four dimensions—goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification—anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. The benchmark includes 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services.

Result: Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, the study finds that process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filter out lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation, reveal that the four dimensions are complementary with result verification as the systematic bottleneck, remain robust across different judge LLMs, and yield consistent post-training improvements via process-based trajectory filtering across model scales.

Conclusion: ClawTrack demonstrates that process-level evaluation is essential for diagnosing agent reasoning deficiencies and improving models, with process-based trajectory filtering providing a scalable path to post-training improvement.

Abstract: As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

</details>


### [205] [GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28073)
*Yiming Xu,Jihua Kang,Chunsai Du,Qifan Zhang,Wangqiu Zhou,Yiting Wu,Tianqi Li,Qi Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GVR-Coder is a framework that generates logically coherent, visually appealing SVG diagrams from lengthy professional texts through curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning, explicit layout constraint injection, reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, and a generate-verify-repair agent loop, supported by a new DocMeetSVG-100K dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-SVG generation is hindered by three challenges: scarcity of datasets for complex logic-rich diagrams, absence of explicit layout priors leading to chaotic spatial arrangements, and lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. The goal is to transform verbose professional text into clear, logical diagrams efficiently.

Method: The method comprises four components: (1) a new large-scale dataset DocMeetSVG-100K for document authoring and meeting review scenarios; (2) curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively model complex structures; (3) reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics via reward signals; and (4) a generate-verify-repair agent loop providing explicit fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement.

Result: Extensive experiments show GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams.

Conclusion: GVR-Coder effectively addresses the data, layout prior, and visual feedback challenges in Text-to-SVG generation, achieving superior performance; code and data are publicly released.

Abstract: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

</details>


### [206] [Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28079)
*Tianyou Bai,Huan Wang,Mingchen Gao,Fangyue Lin,Pinze Ren,Zhenlin Zhao,Siming Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chem World is a comprehensive benchmark integrating 17 chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples for chemical property prediction, paired with Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge to improve prediction accuracy and robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing chemical property prediction benchmarks suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it difficult to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models in chemistry, materials science, and drug development.

Method: The authors introduce Chem World, a unified benchmark that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples covering properties such as density, electrical conductivity, and solubility. They also propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that embeds chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning to enhance prediction accuracy, robustness, and reliability.

Result: Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of Mixture-PINN compared with existing methods across multiple chemical property prediction tasks.

Conclusion: By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

Abstract: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

</details>


### [207] [From Expert Reduction to Behavioral Divergence: Tracing Numerical State through Sparse MoE Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28097)
*Tianyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders in DeepSeek-V4-Flash produce observable differences in sparse-MoE execution. The paper isolates this effect by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics, showing how operand representation and accumulator precision combine to create divergent continuation basins, and identifies post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether mathematically equivalent floating-point reductions—which differ only in execution order—can produce observably different behavior in sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, and to establish a numerical compatibility contract for MoE runtimes and hardware backends.

Method: The study freezes local MoE state in DeepSeek-V4-Flash and varies only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. Experiments compare 720 A-mode orders against 720 B-mode orders at a layer-5 fork, classify continuation basins, and run 192 persistent trajectories per scheme to assess bitwise and textual fidelity across native MoE and post-mHC states.

Result: A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins while B-mode yields 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Schemes P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts bitwise. A 192-trajectory check confirms C matches native MoE states exactly. Exact FP64 reconstruction of persistent state reproduces 301 downstream post-mHC states and trajectories over seven steps.

Conclusion: Post-mHC is an intra-token boundary while full persistent state serves as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens do not necessarily imply identical autoregressive state; divergence can survive token boundaries and manifest later. The findings establish expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order as part of a numerical compatibility contract, with C's order invariance limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

Abstract: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions. We isolate this effect in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. At one layer-5 fork, 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, the B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Across 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE, post-mHC, next-router, and LM states bitwise. For one controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the measured downstream trajectory. At the next decode boundary, exact FP64 reconstruction of the branch's full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 persistent-state checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps, given the same naturally generated next input. These controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state: divergence can survive a token boundary and become visible later. These results make expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. They establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; C's order invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

</details>


### [208] [Information Bottleneck Learning for Faithful Time Series Forecasting Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28124)
*Xu Zheng,Wei Cheng,Zhuomin Chen,Mo Sha,Jingchao Ni,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IB-Forecast is an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework that decomposes predictions into a learned periodic component and a residual component with explainable masks, enabling user-controlled explanation sparsity via a budget-constrained information bottleneck while matching black-box forecasting accuracy and providing faithful explanations at no extra inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures but cannot guarantee faithfulness to the underlying evidence, while faithfulness-oriented methods are mostly limited to post-hoc classification tasks. There is a gap for inherently interpretable forecasting that guarantees explanation fidelity.

Method: IB-Forecast decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. End-to-end optimization with a budget-constrained information bottleneck allows direct user control over explanation sparsity, and a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol is employed.

Result: IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Under a matched sparsity budget, its native explanations surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. It requires only 14-20% of observations to deliver low-error predictions.

Conclusion: Unlike existing interpretable forecasters whose native explanations exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity while using only a fraction of observations to achieve low-error predictions.

Abstract: As forecasts increasingly drive decisions in fields such as energy, transportation, and healthcare, understanding the historical data behind these predictions has become as crucial as the predictions themselves. Although existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures, they offer no guarantee that these structures faithfully reflect the underlying evidence driving the predictions. In contrast, while faithfulness-oriented methods explicitly verify model behavior, they are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose IB-Forecast, an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework. It decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. With a budget-constrained information bottleneck, end-to-end optimization enables users to directly control explanation sparsity. With a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol, extensive experiments demonstrate that IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Furthermore, under a matched sparsity budget, these native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. Ultimately, whereas the native explanations of existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity, requiring only 14-20% of the observations to deliver low-error predictions.

</details>


### [209] [LM-GRASP: Instance-Specific Language Models for Combinatorial Construction via Online Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28135)
*Mohand Mezmaz,Grégoire Danoy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LM-GRASP is a hybrid metaheuristic that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, training a decoder-only Transformer from scratch on each problem instance via behavioral cloning on elite trajectories, achieving performance gains on the Taillard PFSP benchmark comparable to GPU acceleration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural constructors for combinatorial optimization rely on reinforcement learning on large offline datasets, incurring high pretraining costs and poor generalization outside the training distribution. The authors propose an alternative that avoids offline pretraining and problem-specific feature engineering by learning construction policies online from the instance being solved.

Method: The framework reformulates GRASP's randomized constructive phase as online imitation learning. A local search procedure serves as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer acts as the constructive policy. The method follows an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories, interfacing with the domain only through the objective evaluator.

Result: On the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average, comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations.

Conclusion: Instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising and practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for optimization landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction, and avoid the high costs and generalization issues of offline-trained neural methods.

Abstract: Machine learning for combinatorial optimization typically relies on neural constructors trained via reinforcement learning on large offline datasets for a fixed problem class-incurring high pretraining costs and generalizing poorly outside the training distribution. We propose an alternative: a metaheuristic framework that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, trained from scratch on each problem instance. A local search procedure acts as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. Unlike classical GRASP, which relies on static, myopic heuristic rules based on localized scalar costs, our approach is fully data-driven: the construction policy emerges from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself, with no problem-specific feature engineering required.
  We instantiate this as LM-GRASP, a hybrid metaheuristic following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories-no external data or offline pretraining needed. The pipeline interfaces with the domain solely through the objective evaluator used by local search.
  Evaluated on the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), the most discriminating block due to half its optima being unknown, LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average-comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations. This suggests instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

</details>


### [210] [Search Strategies for Optimal Classification and Regression Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28170)
*Jacobus G. M. van der Linden,Mim van den Bos,Emir Demirović*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a general algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees (ODTs) that unifies existing search strategies and enables new ones, empirically evaluating 18 strategies. The best strategy outperforms state-of-the-art methods with significantly better anytime performance for classification and over an order-of-magnitude runtime improvement for regression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimal decision trees are compact and interpretable but suffer from scalability challenges. Although various search strategies have been proposed to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy is unclear, creating a gap in understanding and comparing these approaches.

Method: The authors propose a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that can instantiate previously used search strategies and supports the definition of new ones. This framework serves as a common lens for systematically understanding and comparing different strategies, which is used to empirically investigate 18 search strategies.

Result: The best search strategy identified through the evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification compared to state-of-the-art methods, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed unified framework clarifies the contribution of individual search strategies for ODTs and demonstrates that carefully selected strategies can yield substantial improvements in scalability and performance over existing approaches.

Abstract: Optimal decision trees (ODTs) are compact, interpretable machine learning models that globally optimize a given objective, but their scalability remains challenging. While recent work has proposed a variety of search strategies to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and enables the definition of new ones. This provides a common lens through which to understand and compare different strategies, which we use to empirically investigate the effect of 18 search strategies. Compared to the state of the art, the best strategy in our evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression.

</details>


### [211] [Multi-channel Uplift Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28182)
*Changjian Liu,Tianyu Wang,Xiaoxuan Deng,WenTao Zhu,Yuwei Xu,Jungqi Jin,Yong Gao,Chuan Yu,Jian Xu,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReAlloc is a fast-slow causal framework for allocating fixed marketing budgets across multiple e-commerce channels. It combines an Orthogonal Teacher for unbiased short-term gradient extraction and an Explanation-Guided Student for long-term marginal field distillation, enabling support-aware, conservative decisions. Validated on Taobao via simulations and online A/B tests, it improves both pay order and income.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in e-commerce budget allocation because of observational confounding and severe extrapolation in the compositional (simplex-constrained) allocation space. There is a need for a method that handles these challenges while capturing cross-channel substitutions.

Method: The paper formulates the problem as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and proposes ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. An agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, and an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This enables support-aware, conservative decisions.

Result: Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on the Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

Conclusion: ReAlloc effectively addresses the compositional budget allocation problem in e-commerce by combining short-term unbiased gradient extraction with long-term structured distillation, delivering improved business utility in real-world deployment.

Abstract: E-commerce platforms must allocate fixed marketing budgets across multiple channels to maximize business utility. However, standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in this compositional space due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation. We formulate this challenge as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and propose ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. Specifically, an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This design enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

</details>


### [212] [Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28185)
*Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proves that injecting independent Gaussian noise after each propagation step in recurrent GNNs prevents asymptotic oversmoothing by ensuring a positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both noise variance and graph spectral gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep GNNs where repeated message passing causes node representations to collapse toward a low-dimensional subspace, limiting effective depth. The paper seeks mechanisms that preserve representation diversity beyond existing deterministic approaches.

Method: The paper analyzes a recurrent GNN with independent Gaussian noise injected after every propagation step, treating it as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, it proves the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a unique invariant probability measure, and derives an explicit lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy.

Result: The main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both noise variance and graph spectral gap, guaranteeing stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear recurrent GNNs match theoretical predictions.

Conclusion: Persistent stochastic perturbations constitute a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing deterministic approaches like residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring.

Abstract: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

</details>


### [213] [TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28259)
*Md Joshem Uddin,Astrit Tola,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Topoformer introduces Topo-Scan, a parallelizable module that decomposes graphs into ordered sequences of topological tokens via node/edge filtrations, which are processed by a Transformer to yield expressive graph embeddings—matching or exceeding GNN and topology-based baselines on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks with superior compute efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional persistent homology pipelines for capturing topological structure in graphs are computationally expensive, require costly diagram computations, and integrate poorly with deep learning frameworks. The authors aim to provide a lightweight, scalable, and parallelizable way to encode topological inductive biases into attention-based architectures without the overhead of traditional topological methods.

Method: Topoformer encodes topological structure by using Topo-Scan, a module that decomposes a graph into short, ordered sequences of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These tokens capture multi-scale structural patterns and are fed into a Transformer to produce graph-level embeddings. The approach avoids persistence diagram computations, is parallelizable, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning pipelines.

Result: Topoformer achieves state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks, matching or exceeding strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. Theoretical stability guarantees for the topological encodings are also established.

Conclusion: The work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks, demonstrating that topological structure can be encoded efficiently and scalably within Transformer architectures.

Abstract: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

</details>


### [214] [HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28301)
*Tiangang Li,Xiangbo Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HARGO (Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization) is a reinforcement learning post-training method for LLMs on heterogeneous HPC tasks that uses confidence-modulated advantage with per-response importance weighting to outperform uniform-weight RL methods like GRPO across four HPC tasks and nine methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT alone equips LLMs with HPC domain knowledge but fails to produce task-appropriate behavior, and HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity—differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy—making uniform-weight RL methods like GRPO suboptimal.

Method: HARGO introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage. It computes a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulates the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels.

Result: Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals.

Conclusion: HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks, addressing the limitation that knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

</details>


### [215] [Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28304)
*Rasmus Tirsgaard,Laurits Fredsgaard,Marisa Wodrich,Mikkel Jordahn,Mikkel N. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that semi-supervised learning using ensemble consensus can improve predictive accuracy, robustness, and calibration across diverse molecular datasets and graph neural network architectures, without requiring label-preserving augmentations that are difficult to design in the molecular domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeled molecular data is expensive and time-consuming to acquire, while unlabeled molecular data is abundant. Standard semi-supervised methods require label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in molecular domains since small structural changes can drastically alter molecular properties.

Method: The authors employ semi-supervised learning based on ensemble consensus, training models with an ensemble consensus objective rather than relying on label-preserving augmentations.

Result: Training with an ensemble consensus objective boosts predictive accuracy across diverse molecular datasets, task types, and GNN architectures; increases model robustness; and produces individual ensemble members that outperform a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. The approach also reduces calibration error.

Conclusion: Ensemble-consensus-based semi-supervised learning is an effective alternative to augmentation-based methods in the molecular domain, offering improvements in accuracy, robustness, and calibration, with effects similar to knowledge distillation.

Abstract: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

</details>


### [216] [Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28308)
*Huiyuan Tian,Bonan Xu,Shijian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) and controlled experimental designs to separate three confounded quantities in sparse MoE language models: route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. Across six architectures and 39 factorial cells, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet selected experts explain token representations better than unselected rivals—though the actual prefix consistently narrows this advantage. Despite geometric narrowing, adding later experts still improves next-token prediction in most frozen-route comparisons and a controlled training study favors Top-2 over Top-1, a pattern termed "coherent overlap."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evidence on sparse MoE language models conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction, obscuring whether expert co-selection yields distinct representational directions and whether geometric similarity implies redundancy or pruning value.

Method: The authors propose an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) to quantify subspace overlap, use matched-route residuals to control for candidate quality, and a prefix-controlled 2×2 factorial design to isolate candidate-by-context interactions. They employ frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-k training study (Top-2 vs Top-1) to assess functional value across six MoE architectures (including OLMoE, Mixtral, DeepSeek) covering 39 factorial cells.

Result: Expert subspaces overlap substantially across all architectures, yet actual routes outperform matched alternatives in explaining token representations. In every one of the 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate explains more of the residual than the strongest unselected rival, but all interactions are negative (every 95% CI below zero). However, adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons (15 inconclusive), and Top-2 beats Top-1 in all three seeds of the controlled training study.

Conclusion: The authors identify a "coherent overlap" pattern: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood of overlapping subspaces, while useful multi-expert computation persists despite the lack of disjoint linear coverage. This implies geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning decisions; separating route coherence, candidate quality, and interaction is essential for evaluating MoE architectures.

Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

</details>


### [217] [Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28324)
*Jaume Ros,Alessio Arleo,Fernando Paulovich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that measures visual distortion in empty areas (gaps) of a layout by decomposing the space into empty triangles and comparing their deformation to high-dimensional counterparts. The GI is sensitive to small structural deformations with high visual impact, is fast to compute, and interpretable, unlike popular quality metrics that focus only on direct point relationships.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Popular quality metrics for dimensionality reduction projections focus on capturing distortions in direct relationships between points (distances or neighborhoods) but neglect distortions in empty areas of the layout, which often constitute visually relevant features of a 2D projection. This gap in metric coverage leads to incomplete assessment of visual fidelity in projections.

Method: The GI decomposes the projection space into empty triangles (triangulation of empty regions), compares these triangles to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute per-triangle deformation, and aggregates the deformation either into a single scalar value or overlays it on the projection to visualize regional distortion patterns.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact, which popular quality metrics fail to capture. Additionally, the GI is fast to compute and interpretable.

Conclusion: The Gap Index provides a novel and complementary quality metric for dimensionality reduction projections by quantifying spatial distortion in empty areas, filling a gap in existing metric coverage and offering both global (scalar) and local (overlay) assessment capabilities.

Abstract: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

</details>


### [218] [Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28338)
*Michael Ben Ali,Imen Megdiche,André Péninou,Olivier Teste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based Clustered Federated Learning as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure that restricts server updates to additive operations, enabling compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. This addresses the CFL trilemma by making metadata-based clustering encryption-compatible while preserving communication and computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CFL methods face a trade-off among privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency (the CFL trilemma). Metadata-based clustering approaches are efficient but incompatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms, limiting their practical deployment.

Method: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure. Server updates are restricted to additive operations, which makes the method compatible with practical secure FL schemes (e.g., encryption-based approaches) while retaining clustering efficiency.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, improving its position within the CFL trilemma.

Conclusion: FLAMECHE successfully resolves the CFL trilemma trade-off by achieving encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering without sacrificing the efficiency benefits of metadata-based approaches, thereby broadening the applicability of CFL in privacy-sensitive federated settings.

Abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

</details>


### [219] [LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28374)
*Enjun Du,Hange Zhou,Chenxu Du,Siyi Liu,Zirong Chen,Ziyu Zheng,Yongqi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG
