TL;DR: LedgerMind is a provenance-constrained framework for multimodal agent trajectories that uses a Structured Evidence Ledger as trajectory state, enforcing that reasoning and decision claims cite only tool-produced evidence. It introduces a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee, targeting four failure patterns that final-answer accuracy obscures. Experiments show improvements in both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal agents operate as multi-step trajectories (perception, retrieval, reasoning), yet evaluation is largely reduced to final-answer accuracy, which cannot distinguish whether a correct answer came from grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. The paper motivates a finer-grained evaluation and control of trajectory-level faithfulness.

Method: The paper models a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine. Tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that acts as trajectory state; downstream claims may only cite active ledger entries. Grounding is checked at entity and numeric levels. Repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. This is instantiated as LedgerMind, augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee.

Result: Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness, addressing four recurring failure patterns: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification.

Conclusion: Evaluating multimodal agents solely via final-answer accuracy is insufficient. By enforcing provenance constraints throughout the trajectory and adding verification-and-repair mechanisms with a non-amplification guarantee, LedgerMind improves both task accuracy and trajectory faithfulness, suggesting that provenance-constrained state machines are a viable design for trustworthy multimodal agentic reasoning.

Abstract: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

</details>


### [220] [Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28390)
*Ankur Naskar,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves the open problem of achieving order-optimal convergence guarantees for primal-dual actor-critic methods with neural critics in average-reward Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs). The authors introduce a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that debiases simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization, achieving the bias of a long optimization run with only logarithmic sample cost. This enables a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm achieving optimality gap and constraint violation of order O~(T^{-1/2}), establishing the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, without requiring knowledge of the mixing time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood for CMDPs, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained an open problem. The fundamental challenge is a bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation under NTK analysis: reducing critic bias substantially increases optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework.

Method: The paper introduces a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across two dimensions: trajectory sampling and critic optimization. This estimator achieves the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, the authors develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order O~(T^{-1/2}), establishing the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics. The results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

Conclusion: The work eliminates the fundamental bias-cost trade-off bottleneck in neural critic estimation for CMDPs via MLMC debiasing, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. This represents a significant theoretical advancement for safety-critical reinforcement learning with function approximation, with broader implications beyond constrained settings.

Abstract: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

</details>


### [221] [Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28399)
*Zihan Dong,Rui Qian,Qishi Zhan,Dongshen Peng,Kaixin Li,Yu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AAPT (Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees) is a method that eliminates decoding latency in computer-use agents by pre-constructing conditional policy trees during idle screen periods, allowing immediate action execution on transient GUI events without generating new text at decision time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents frequently fail on transient GUI events because the correct action is produced only after the relevant window has already closed. The root cause is expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path, which creates unacceptable latency.

Method: During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree containing observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree size is calibrated to cover the model's own decoding latency. At runtime, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text.

Result: In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window (p=1.8e-3) with no incorrect actions. Baselines achieve zero success. Ablations identify fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing as key requirements, with a pre-registered oracle probe revealing branch routing as the causal bottleneck. Results replicate on an independent model (p=4.9e-13) and match a reactive baseline on an external benchmark with complementary strengths.

Conclusion: AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot. The approach decouples planning from execution latency without modifying the underlying model.

Abstract: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

</details>


### [222] [On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28408)
*Imad Aouali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This thesis studies policy learning in large action space contextual bandits, covering both on-policy and off-policy paradigms. It introduces structured Bayesian methods (meTS and dTS) for efficient on-policy exploration, and for off-policy learning proposes structured direct methods, concave optimizable objectives, and differentiable pessimistic approaches based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large action spaces in contextual bandits pose major challenges in both on-policy and off-policy settings, including inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. Existing methods struggle to scale effectively to very large action sets.

Method: For on-policy learning: (1) meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and (2) dTS, which uses diffusion-inspired priors to model action dependencies. For off-policy learning: (1) sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, (2) concave policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives that are efficiently optimizable, and (3) differentiable pessimistic methods using exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds for regularized importance-sampling estimators.

Result: The proposed methods share information across actions and achieve regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions rather than the full action space size. The work also demonstrates that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces for off-policy learning.

Conclusion: Structured Bayesian priors and structured latent-variable methods, combined with concave objectives and differentiable pessimistic regularization, provide effective solutions to the key challenges of policy learning in large action space contextual bandits.

Abstract: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

</details>


### [223] [QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28422)
*Ran Miao,Rui Luo,Xiaohan Shan,Xiaoming Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction that captures local spatiotemporal syndrome correlations, sequentially adapts to evolving noise while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards residual syndrome to a global decoder. It reduces logical error rate by up to 5.79% and backend latency by 9.32% on Google's Willow benchmark data without target-domain fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing syndrome data. This is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, along with simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that degrades fixed neural decoders.

Method: QAdapt is a neural pre-decoding framework that captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder for final error correction.

Result: Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves up to 5.79% reduction in logical error rate and 9.32% reduction in backend decoding latency.

Conclusion: QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

</details>


### [224] [Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28428)
*V. S. Usatyuk,D. A. Sapozhnikov,S. I. Egorov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KSSE is a physics-inspired energy-based model that replaces dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding built on Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian principles, achieving 88.93% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1000 with only ~21M parameters—matching ViT-H/14 (632M) and outperforming Swin-L (197M) with 10-30× smaller footprints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense CNN classifiers are computationally heavy and parameter-inefficient. The authors seek a principled, physics-inspired alternative that replaces dense classifiers with a sparse spectral embedding framework, cutting model size dramatically while maintaining or exceeding state-of-the-art accuracy.

Method: KSSE maps pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs and constructs a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian. It solves D independent channel spectral problems in O(N log N + k²_mode N) via FFT on circulant blocks using Pontryagin self-duality, with low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized via star-domain surgery that builds local convexity around codewords while bounding frustration ρ(B_γ) ≤ 1+δ. Multi-scale fractal D₂ spectrum analysis certifies a landscape transition from rough (D₂>3) to star-domain basins (D₂<1). Six theoretical results are proven, including a generalized Ihara-Bass identity, trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence, additive channel separability with exchange-correlation bound, a surgery theorem with attractor width Ω(1/√d_min), quasi-stationarity perturbation and fixed-point convergence bounds.

Result: On ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792) in a transductive protocol, KSSE achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy using ~21.24M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4-87.3%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0-89.5%), with 10× and 30× reductions in model footprint respectively.

Conclusion: KSSE demonstrates that a physics-grounded spectral embedding approach can rival or surpass much larger transformer-based classifiers with dramatically fewer parameters, suggesting that principled energy-based and sparse-graph methods offer a viable path toward parameter-efficient high-accuracy classification.

Abstract: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

</details>


### [225] [Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28437)
*Jiannan Yang,Veronika Thost,Xiang Ling,Tengfei Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that uses an online graph neural surrogate to pre-screen candidate molecules before oracle evaluation. This improves molecular optimization under limited oracle budgets by spending queries more selectively, improving mean top-10 scores across multiple generators at no extra oracle cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular optimization is constrained by limited oracle budgets, so deciding which molecules to evaluate is as important as deciding what to generate. Existing methods focus on generation but not on smart selection of oracle queries under tight budget constraints.

Method: The authors propose a plug-in module called short-term graph memory that maintains an online graph neural surrogate. It pre-screens each round's candidate pool and prioritizes molecules with higher predicted utility for oracle evaluation. The module preserves the generator architecture and native update rule, making it broadly applicable.

Result: Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard benchmark, the module improves mean top-10 scores at no extra oracle cost and never underperforms the base on any oracle. The gain extends to all four tested generators at a tight budget of one thousand oracle calls. Analysis shows the benefit at larger budgets correlates with the backbone's search breadth and how effectively its native search exploits oracle feedback.

Conclusion: The short-term graph memory offers a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and the authors provide evidence on which generators benefit most from surrogate-guided selection.

Abstract: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

</details>


### [226] [Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28460)
*Amol Khanna,Manu Nandan,Cristian Viorel Popa,Joan Pujol-Roig,Diana Bolocan,Laura Vasilie,Alexandru Apostu,Chase Helwig,Mihaela Gaman,Michael Brautbar,Edward Raff,Chase Midler,Sven Krasser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) by training a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real Windows endpoint detections. It combines automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, and introduces a separately trained calibrator to estimate verdict confidence from the reasoning trace. The system achieves 82.6% test accuracy, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% at the high-confidence operating point, and demonstrates that a targeted fine-tuned 30B model outperforms frontier general-purpose LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SOC teams face alert fatigue because the volume of detections exceeds their triage capacity. Prior LLM-based approaches generate triage labels directly without training the model to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat, limiting both accuracy and explainability.

Method: The authors train a CoT reasoning-enabled triage classifier using a combination of automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, trained on real human-labeled Windows endpoint detections. Because CoT reasoning degrades label-token probabilities, they additionally train a separate calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace to estimate the probability that the verdict is correct.

Result: The system achieves 82.6% test accuracy. At the high-confidence operating point for automated triage, it improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. A trained calibrator is essential—an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero. A fine-tuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models.

Conclusion: Targeted training on domain-specific data (rather than relying on scale alone) is the key to effective and well-calibrated LLM-based triage; the combination of CoT reasoning training and a dedicated calibrator enables reliable high-confidence automated triage that meaningfully reduces SOC analyst burden.

Abstract: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

</details>


### [227] [Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28495)
*Alexander Boesgaard Lorup*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits the stage-replay assumption that reconstructing intermediate token prefixes with fresh prefill can substitute for continuation from the original decoder state. In a Qwen2.5-derived system, exact-token replay produces many divergent suffix/correctness labels under BF16, yet boundary K/V cache is shown to be a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory—transplanting all 48 key/value layers makes divergent continuations follow their cache donor in 24/24 and 43/43 tests. Numerical precision (BF16 vs FP32) moderates behavioral expression of this divergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stage-replay diagnostics assume that reconstructing intermediate token prefixes and re-prefilling is equivalent to continuing from the original decoder state. The paper aims to audit whether this assumption holds at whole reasoning-stage boundaries in production LLM systems, since unfaithful replay would undermine diagnostic validity.

Method: A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache vs one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens with exact replicas on both sides. A fixed-prefix 2x2 design holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction (live vs replay) and precision (BF16 vs FP32). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained caches bit-exact, plus an all-200 saved-ledger audit. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers is used to test causal sufficiency of the K/V cache.

Result: In BF16, replicas remain exact but constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; accuracy differs by only one point (95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). BF16 disagreements recur in the fixed-prefix 2x2, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (Wilson upper bound 1.88%). The bridge achieves bit-exactness on 12/12 rows, and the saved-ledger audit reproduces all trajectories. Transplants make 24/24 and 43/43 divergent continuations follow their cache donor.

Conclusion: Exact-token replay can be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. At the tested reasoning-stage boundary, the K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates how that divergence is behaviorally expressed.

Abstract: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

</details>


### [228] [The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28497)
*Srikanth Avasarala,Varun Gupta,Shahin Jabbari,Saber Salehkaleybar,Juba Ziani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes a failure mode in algorithmic recourse where actions flip classifier predictions without genuinely improving individuals' true qualifications, leading to strategic gaming and degraded model performance. The authors propose a causal performative framework that models how recourse actions propagate through structural causal models, characterize conditions for performatively stable solutions computable via iterative dynamics, and demonstrate on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets that causal recourse achieves stability and outperforms standard empirical risk minimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing algorithmic recourse approaches only aim to flip a model's prediction, ignoring whether recommended changes genuinely improve an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. This leads to behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and render deployed policies ineffective after model retraining.

Method: The authors introduce a causal performative framework for recourse, modeling how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model that captures feature interactions and effects on the true label. This induces a non-convex optimization problem; they characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be computed efficiently via simple iterative dynamics.

Result: The analysis shows that recourse policies ignoring causal structure induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria reducing gaming incentives. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate the approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining due to distribution shifts from strategic agent behavior.

Conclusion: Causal recourse is critical for achieving performative stability in algorithmic recourse settings; by accounting for causal structure, recourse policies can reduce incentives for strategic gaming, maintain predictive accuracy, and lower the frequency of model retraining.

Abstract: Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

</details>


### [229] [Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28525)
*Neelam Akula,Surbhi Kumar,Murat Kantarcioglu,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper formalizes same-graph cross-task transfer between node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP), proposes a leakage-free evaluation protocol with fixed splits and negatives, and shows transfer is strongly directional—NC→LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs while LP→NC is fragile. It introduces the CoTask Score (CTS) to quantify joint NC+LP utility and demonstrates that simple statistics like homophily can guide mechanism choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of cross-task transfer between NC and LP on the same graph use incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and inconsistent negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph transfer unreliable. A rigorous protocol and analysis are needed.

Method: The authors formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer, design a leakage-free protocol (fixed node/edge splits, shared message-passing graph excluding evaluated edges, fixed negatives for LP), evaluate across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), and introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility.

Result: Transfer is strongly directional: NC→LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC degrades accuracy under naive representation reuse except in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated. Simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, reliably guide mechanism choice.

Conclusion: Same-graph NC-LP transfer is predictable and direction-dependent, with LP acting as structural pretraining only under specific conditions; homophily can guide when and how to transfer, and the CTS provides a single metric for joint task utility.

Abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

</details>


### [230] [APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28553)
*Shentong Mo,Yatao Bian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: APO is a fully unsupervised alignment framework for flow-matching models in 3D atomic structure prediction. It replaces ground-truth coordinate supervision with a dual-reward mechanism combining eigen-decomposition-based latent structural mode reinforcement and thermodynamic stability, enabling self-correction without experimental labels. APO outperforms supervised baselines on crystal and antibody benchmarks while also improving inference efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised preference learning for flow-matching models in atomic structure prediction depends heavily on ground-truth coordinates, which are prohibitively expensive to obtain for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins, creating a bottleneck in data-scarce regimes.

Method: APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments with a dual-reward mechanism: (1) a reward that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (2) a reward that enforces thermodynamic stability. The framework performs self-correction by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups.

Result: On crystal and antibody structure prediction benchmarks, APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity. It also straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency.

Conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching, suggesting that unsupervised alignment leveraging physical priors is a viable and potentially better alternative for 3D atomic structure prediction.

Abstract: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

</details>


### [231] [$β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28582)
*Jiawei Xu,Minghui Liu,Juzheng Zhang,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies that vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a special case (β=1) of a broader policy-optimization family. It introduces β-OPSD, a general formulation with a tunable KL regularization parameter β that controls the trade-off between proximity to a reference policy and privileged teacher guidance. Instead of expensive RL, the method leverages the closed-form optimal policy as a distillation target through logit mixing, with return-to-go credit assignment for sequence-level alignment. β-OPSD outperforms vanilla OPSD on math reasoning benchmarks with improved stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vanilla OPSD is effective for improving reasoning language models but is brittle in practice, requiring substantial engineering effort to work reliably. The authors identify a structural source of this difficulty—vanilla OPSD corresponds to a fixed β=1 in a broader policy-optimization family—and seek to turn this implicit fixed value into a controllable regularization parameter for more robust optimization.

Method: The authors derive β-OPSD, where β weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. The optimal policy is derived as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Rather than optimizing the expensive RL objective directly, the closed-form solution is converted into a distillation target: each β selects a point along the reference-to-teacher path, implemented by mixing token-level logits. Return-to-go credit assignment aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining OPSD's simplicity.

Result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving both optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. The method demonstrates that inexpensive distillation can effectively approximate the solution of more expensive policy optimization.

Conclusion: The paper provides a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back, showing that by making β controllable, OPSD can be made more robust and effective without sacrificing the efficiency that makes self-distillation practical.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

</details>


### [232] [KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28608)
*Sparsh Roy,Samuel Girmachew,Nishita Chavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAISEN is a five-phase audit pipeline (stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, drift monitoring) stress-tested to failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes, and 3 intersections. Key findings: significance tracks min detectable effect; threshold optimization reliably reduces EOD while Platt scaling is inconsistent; mechanism diagnostics pass controlled but fail proxy-misspecified cases without warning; CUSUM threshold tuning does not transfer across cohorts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical risk models show good aggregate performance but uneven error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines exist to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested to failure, leaving it unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions.

Method: The authors build KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline, and evaluate it to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth: 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. They track four specific outcomes: significance vs. minimum detectable effect for disparity measurement, equalized-odds difference (EOD) under two post-hoc mitigation strategies, mechanism diagnostic accuracy under controlled vs. proxy-misspecified conditions, and CUSUM drift-monitoring failure/transfer properties.

Result: (i) Significance~EOD rank correlation is 0.56, rising to 0.78 when EOD is standardized by the minimum detectable effect. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48/48 held-out runs (delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]); group-wise Platt scaling improves only 19/48 runs (95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with near-zero mean effect. (iii) Mechanism diagnostics classify 144/144 controlled cases correctly but recover 0/48 proxy-misspecified cases without signaling failure. (iv) CUSUM failures/false alarms track cohort realization more than disease: all 27 false alarms and 7/8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p=0.002), so thresholds fail to transfer across cohorts.

Conclusion: Audit pipelines require component-level failure analysis to be trusted. Key implications: audits should report variance (not averages) for mitigation effects, mechanism diagnostics need robustness monitoring under misspecification, and drift thresholds must be recalibrated per cohort. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity.

Abstract: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

</details>

### [233] [OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27249)
*Bo Zhang,Ren Pan,Huan Chen,Xiang Song*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: OwlPath is an OWL2 reasoning layer built atop CodeGraph that encodes source code into a unified ontology, enabling lossless structural knowledge compression and efficient multi-hop code retrieval for LLM-based software engineering agents. It combines a transitive-closure engine using SPARQL property paths with a precomputed Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM), improving recall 2.06x, achieving 68.4% strict-apply rate (vs 66.7% baseline), and cutting token usage by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows (~100K tokens), and standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop structural dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) through slow trial and error.

Method: OwlPath encodes source code into a unified OWL2 ontology using tree-sitter parsing across multiple languages, then employs two complementary modules: (1) a transitive-closure engine that fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, and (2) OWL-SKM, a precomputed compact 3KB summary containing module trees, core APIs, and issue-related symbols to direct agents to target modules early.

Result: On 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath achieves 68.4% strict-apply rate vs 66.7% for CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval over 67 instances, recall improves 2.06x (0.464 vs 0.226) with 88.1% hit rate vs 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80% accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

Conclusion: OWL2-based lossless knowledge compression via OwlPath significantly improves structural code retrieval for LLM agents by capturing multi-hop relations that string-matching methods miss, while reducing both token usage and runtime, demonstrating the value of encoding code semantics into a formal ontology.

Abstract: LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows: roughly 100K tokens must store structurally relevant code  subsets to resolve bugs. Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies including subclass  chains, transitive callers and interface implementations through slow trial and error. We tackle this limitation with lossless knowledge  compression, encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology to answer structural queries using minimal relevant code fragments.
  We present OwlPath, an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph, a widely used code intelligence platform with 500K+ GitHub stars, offering a unified  CLI for structural code retrieval. Powered by tree-sitter parsing, OwlPath supports multi-language repositories (Python, JavaScript,  TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It adopts two complementary modules. First, a  transitive-closure engine fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed  by string matching. Second, the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) precomputes a compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs and  issue-related symbols, directing agents to target modules in the first query.
  Evaluated on 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath obtains a 68.4% strict-apply rate versus 66.7% for the CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage  by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06 times (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches  88.1% hit rate compared to CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80%  accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

</details>


### [234] [Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27250)
*Prakhar Khatri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A controlled ablation study across two frontier coding agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks, and 288 evaluated runs shows that persistent context files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) do not measurably improve correctness on either agent (bounded to ≤10-15pp via equivalence testing). Failure-mode triage reveals agents fail on implementation skill—not missing repository knowledge—and borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), explaining prior contradictory findings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent context files are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. The authors aim to resolve this contradiction with a controlled, systematic evaluation.

Method: Controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex) using 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), with 288 evaluated runs using gold-test evaluation, equivalence testing, failure-mode triage, and a manipulation probe.

Result: Context strategy does not measurably improve correctness on either agent (bounded to ≤10-15pp via equivalence testing). Agents fail on implementation skill rather than missing repository knowledge; manipulation probes confirm AGENTS.md never converts near-misses to passes. Borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75).

Conclusion: Persistent context files provide no measurable benefit for coding agent correctness within studied bounds. Prior contradictory results stem from single-agent studies drawing tasks from different agents' informative difficulty bands. All code, data, and analysis are released.

Abstract: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill---feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring---not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents' informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

</details>


### [235] [AgentS4D: Benchmarking Runtime Risks across the Execution Lifecycle of LLM-Based Workspace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27294)
*Jiajun Zhou,Zhaoxuan Ke,Jihang Ye,Xuanze Chen,Shanqing Yu,Qi Xuan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentS4D is a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation of LLM-based workspace agents, featuring a four-dimensional safety framework with six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, nine target harms, and seven lifecycle checkpoints. It includes 328 risk-injected cases, evaluated across 20 harness-LLM combinations (6,560 runs total). Results show 68.0% of runs trigger unsafe signals, and 66.22% of runs are unsafe yet complete, demonstrating that task completion cannot establish runtime safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM agent safety advance executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification but fail to provide a unified account of where risks enter, how unsafe behavior is induced, which harms are targeted, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. A lifecycle-wide, multi-dimensional runtime safety assessment framework is needed.

Method: The authors introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark with a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework: six risk-entry sources and six induction strategies guide case construction, nine target harms define risk scope, and seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. They construct 328 risk-injected cases and evaluate 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus), yielding 6,560 runs.

Result: 4,461 of 6,560 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Agent safety varies with both harness-LLM pairing and risk introduction method. Same induction strategy via different risk carriers yields different safety behavior, and the same target harm realized through different carriers and strategies elicits different responses. 4,344 runs (66.22%) are unsafe yet complete, showing task completion does not imply runtime safety.

Conclusion: Testing only one form of a risk can conceal important safety weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources, external tools, and persistent state. Their safety must therefore be assessed from actions, side effects, and state changes throughout execution. Although recent benchmarks have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification, they rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. We introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation. Its four-dimensional runtime-safety framework uses six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. AgentS4D contains 328 risk-injected cases. We evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.7-Plus) on these cases, yielding 6,560 runs. Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Across the 20 configurations, the observed safety of an agent system varies with both its harness-LLM pairing and how risk is introduced. Agent systems exhibit markedly different safety behavior when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers. They also respond differently to the same target harm when it is realized through different carriers and strategies. Moreover, 4,344 runs (66.22% overall) are unsafe yet complete. Thus, task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

</details>


### [236] [A Taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork Requirements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27302)
*Anastasia Mavridou,Hazel M. Taylor,Sandy Lozito,Louise A. Dennis,Michael Fisher,Marie Farrell*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper presents a two-level hierarchical taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements, derived from 361 requirements across 14 cross-domain sources, comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories. The taxonomy is validated through expert evaluation and a utility demonstration on an independent corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork are fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework addressing the complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks in safety- and mission-critical domains.

Method: The authors extracted 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources (academic literature, industrial standards, regulatory guidance), applied iterative classification and refinement to develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy with 6 high-level categories (information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, foundational system capabilities) and 21 low-level subcategories. Validation was performed via expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources across six HRT domains.

Result: A validated two-level hierarchical HRT requirements taxonomy was produced, confirmed through expert evaluation and demonstrated utility on an independent corpus spanning six HRT domains.

Conclusion: The proposed HRT requirements taxonomy provides a unified framework to structure and organize requirements for collaborative human-robot tasks, addressing the fragmentation previously present in the field and offering practical utility across multiple HRT domains.

Abstract: Autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical domains where humans and robots must operate as a team to complete complex tasks. Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork remain fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework that addresses complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks. We address this gap by presenting a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements derived from analysis of (academic and industrial) literature, standards and regulatory guidance. We extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources. Through iterative classification and refinement, we develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories that distinguish information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. We validate the taxonomy through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements drawn from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

</details>


### [237] [SIGIL: Compiling Agent Skills into Typed Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27309)
*Jayanaka Dantanarayana,Savini Kashmira,Lingjia Tang,Jason Mars*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Skill Compilation (SIGIL) compiles prose skill files into executable harnesses via the AG-IR typed intermediate representation, improving mandated-step compliance from 56% (prose) to 86% (compiled) across model generations while reducing token usage to 0.58x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents acquire capabilities from prose skill files loaded into context, but since skills are described rather than encoded, models re-derive control flow on every run and often skip mandated verification steps. Hand-writing executable harnesses solves this but is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills successful.

Method: The authors introduce Skill Compilation, realized in a system called SIGIL, which compiles prose skills into executable harnesses. The core is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation that separates model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism.

Result: Across 30 skills and two model generations, compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps (vs 56% for prose), complete the full procedure 2.3x more often, and require only 0.58x the tokens. The guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose varies from 56% to 68%.

Conclusion: Skill Compilation provides a robust alternative to pure prose execution by converting narrative skills into structured executable harnesses, yielding higher procedural compliance and efficiency that is stable across model generations, while preserving the authoring surface that made skills succeed.

Abstract: AI-Integrated agents increasingly acquire capability from skills: prose procedure files loaded into a model's context and run by a tool-calling loop. A skill is described to the runtime but never encoded in it, so the model re-derives its control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, a prose agent performs only 56% of the steps its own skill mandates, while producing artifacts that pass output checks. The remedy is known: write a harness, in which the procedure is program structure. However, hand-writing harnesses is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills succeed. To address this limitation, we introduce Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its center is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism. Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps, complete the full procedure 2.3x as often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Notably, the guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose swings from 56% to 68%.

</details>


### [238] [TrustChain-Review: A Risk-Adaptive Blockchain and Game-Theoretic Framework for Trustworthy AI-Assisted Code Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27310)
*Mohammad Naserameri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TrustChain-Review is a framework combining blockchain-based evidence, game-theoretic incentives, and risk-adaptive governance to support trustworthy code review. It uses a three-player model (developers, reviewers, platform) and was evaluated via simulation on the Diff Quality Estimation dataset across six governance configurations. Full-evidence governance yields the best reputation, trust, and detection but at the highest cost; risk-adaptive governance reduces cost and improves cost-efficiency while performing slightly worse on trust and detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted software development accelerates coding and review but undermines accountability: developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records are hard to audit. A framework is needed to restore trustworthy code review.

Method: The framework comprises three components: (1) a blockchain-based evidence layer for verifiable records, (2) a three-player game-theoretic model involving developers, reviewers, and the platform, and (3) a rule applying stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. Evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset, comparing six governance configurations over 30 independent runs across metrics including reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious/superficial review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency.

Result: The full-evidence configuration achieves the strongest reputation, trust, and detection performance but incurs the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers cost and improves cost-efficiency by selectively applying stronger controls, though its trust and detection results are inferior to the full-evidence setting.

Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most suitable for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes, while selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost for routine or lower-risk contributions.

Abstract: Context: AI-assisted software development can speed up coding and review, but it also makes accountability harder to establish. Developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records may be difficult to audit. Objectives: This study introduces TrustChain-Review, a framework that combines verifiable evidence, strategic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support more trustworthy code review. Methods: The framework includes a blockchain-based evidence layer, a three-player game-theoretic model for developers, reviewers, and the platform, and a rule that applies stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. The evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset. Six governance configurations are compared over 30 independent runs using reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency. Results: The full-evidence configuration produces the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results, but it also has the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers this cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, although its trust and detection results are lower than those of the full-evidence setting. Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes. For routine or lower-risk contributions, selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost.

</details>


### [239] [PROGRESS: Property-Guided Regression Search for Semantic Falsification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27359)
*Davis Tocheuk Mo,Noshin Ulfat,Matthew B. Dwyer,Soneya Binta Hossain*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: PROGRESS integrates intent-driven properties from language models into coverage-guided search-based test generation, combining property-based testing's independent semantic oracles with search-based testing's structural exploration to detect bugs and reach deep program states. It detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) on 25 large-scale Java systems, versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Search-based regression-test generation achieves high structural coverage but inherits faults as expected behavior since oracles derive from the system under test. Property-based testing provides independent semantic oracles but depends on high-quality properties and lacks guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions. Neither approach alone addresses both structural exploration and independent fault detection.

Method: PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences.

Result: On 25 large-scale Java systems, PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik, and preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties.

Conclusion: Integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided search-based test generation successfully combines the strengths of both paradigms: PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions, demonstrating that property-guided search can significantly improve bug detection in real-world Java systems.

Abstract: Search-based regression-test generation effectively explores complex program structures, yielding high structural coverage, but its oracles are derived from the system under test: faults already present are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles, but depends on high-quality properties and gives little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions.
  We present PROGRESS (PROperty-Guided REgression Search for Semantic Falsification), integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided, search-based evolutionary test generation to reach deep program states and detect violations of intended behavior. PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; and (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward coverage and bug-detection goals.
  We evaluate PROGRESS on 25 large-scale Java systems against regression-test generation, standalone property-based testing, and context ablations. PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions; we release a comprehensive artifact package.

</details>


### [240] [From Backlog Items to Security Guidance: Towards Continuous Security Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27374)
*Ignacio García Núñez,Florian Angermeir,Fabiola Moyón Constante*

Main category: cs.SE
