TL;DR: The paper presents an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements, using a security-relevance classifier combined with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Evaluated in a large enterprise in regulated domains, the system achieves substantial inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' κ=0.787), a recall-oriented classifier with F2=0.774 in-distribution and ~0.65 mean zero-shot G-measure across five benchmarks, and preliminary positive results from a RAG pipeline retrieving security requirement clauses (12/24 rated ≥4/5 relevant).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Engineering teams in regulated domains struggle to address security throughout the development lifecycle because security requirements are rarely explicit in backlog items. Engineers must infer security relevance from brief free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable security requirements, creating a gap between continuous development practices and security compliance.

Method: The approach combines two components: (1) a security-relevance classifier trained on 288 labeled backlog items from nine security practitioners to detect security-relevant backlog items, and (2) a four-stage retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in security requirements documents (company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks) that links detected items to relevant security requirement clauses. The classifier's zero-shot performance was benchmarked against five established datasets.

Result: The labeled dataset achieved substantial inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' κ=0.787). The classifier achieved F2=0.774 in-distribution and a mean zero-shot G-measure of ~0.65 across five benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. In the RAG pipeline evaluation with two practitioners, 12 of 24 retrieved clauses were rated at least 4/5 for relevance.

Conclusion: The findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can assist engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process, thereby facilitating continuous security compliance through the proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

Abstract: Continuous software engineering in regulated domains requires engineering teams to address security throughout the development lifecycle. Yet making security requirements explicit in backlog items is still problematic. Engineers must instead infer security relevance of backlog items from brief, free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable requirements. We present an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements. The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents. The approach was developed and evaluated in the context of a large enterprise in highly regulated domains. We present three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 288 backlog items labeled for security relevance by nine security practitioners, with substantial agreement (Fleiss' $κ=0.787$). Second, a recall-oriented classifier achieving $F2=0.774$ in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure $\approx 0.65$ across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. Third, we preliminarily evaluated a four-stage security requirements document-grounded RAG pipeline with two practitioners on industrial backlogs using company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks. Of the retrieved 24 clauses, 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance. Our findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process. With this work we aim to facilitate continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

</details>


### [241] [SWE-NFI: Studying and Benchmarking Coding Agents for Non-Functional Improvements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27409)
*Pengyu Xue,He Yang Yuan,Xin Wang,Junkai Chen,Haonan Zhang,Boyuan Chen,Zishuo Ding,Zhenhao Li,Weiyi Shang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces SWE-NFI, a benchmark with 188 tasks built from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects to evaluate coding agents on non-functional improvements (NFIs). It operationalizes developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation. Findings show that while the best agent achieves 70.0% functional correctness, all agents fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability, particularly in structural code improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing coding agent benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness, leaving non-functional improvements (e.g., code quality, maintainability, performance) underexplored, despite being a core part of real-world software development.

Method: The benchmark contains 188 tasks derived from real merged pull requests, defines 92 executable rules for developer-oriented NFIs, and uses an evaluation suite combining functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI assessment.

Result: The best-performing agent achieves 70.0% functional correctness, but all evaluated commercial and open-source agents fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability, with structural code improvement NFI scores ranging from 0.0 to 1.3 versus 1.5 for the human reference.

Conclusion: SWE-NFI provides a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness, highlighting a significant gap between agents and humans in non-functional improvement tasks.

Abstract: Although coding agents have achieved impressive performance on correctness-oriented benchmarks, their ability to make behavior-preserving non-functional improvements (NFIs) remains underexplored. In real-world software development, developers continuously improve software quality without changing observable behavior, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate functional correctness and provide limited support for assessing these non-functional improvements.
  In this paper, we present SWE-NFI, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on NFIs beyond functional correctness. Our benchmark contains 188 tasks constructed from real merged pull requests in open-source Python projects. We operationalize developer-oriented NFIs into 92 executable rules and develop a comprehensive evaluation suite that combines functional correctness testing with rule-based NFI evaluation.
  We evaluate state-of-the-art commercial and open-source coding agents. Although the best-performing agent achieves a 70.0\% functional correctness rate, all evaluated agents generally fall short of human developers in overall NFI capability. The gap is particularly evident for structural code improvements, where agents' NFI scores range from 0.0 to 1.3, compared with 1.5 for the human reference. Our benchmark and findings provide a reproducible foundation for evaluating and advancing coding agents beyond functional correctness.

</details>


### [242] [LimICE: Integrating LLM into ICE Framework for Efficient Loop Invariant Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27606)
*Kai Fan,ShiWen Yu,GuangSheng Fan,HaoAng Chi,WanWei Liu,Ji Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental loop invariant synthesis that integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the ICE learning framework. It introduces LimICE, an LLM-based tool that generates ordered sequences of lemmas with ICE-DT as a fallback. Experiments on 417 benchmarks show LimICE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, solving 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Loop invariant synthesis is fundamentally undecidable and challenging. Existing machine learning-based methods adopt a monolithic approach that cannot strictly constrain the learning process, making it difficult to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants for complex problems. This is because a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas rather than a single formula.

Method: The paper proposes Incremental ICE, a learning framework that integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the ICE invariant learning framework. It defines a lemma-specific learning objective and introduces a counterexample filtering mechanism to enable sound incremental learning. The framework instantiates LimICE, which uses LLMs to generate ordered lemma sequences and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence.

Result: On 367 linear benchmarks, LimICE solves 349 problems averaging 15.2 seconds; on 50 nonlinear benchmarks, it solves 47 problems averaging 8.8 seconds. Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, it solves 12-24% more instances while being 36-63% faster. It also outperforms strong non-LLM baselines, solving at least 86 and 27 additional instances on linear and nonlinear benchmarks respectively.

Conclusion: The incremental synthesis framework is effective for loop invariant generation, demonstrating that decomposing invariants into ordered lemma sequences significantly improves both completeness and efficiency compared to monolithic learning approaches.

Abstract: Loop invariant synthesis is a fundamental problem in program verification, yet the inherent undecidability makes it highly challenging. Recent studies have increasingly employed various machine learning techniques to generate loop invariants. However, most of these methods adopt a monolithic approach. Due to the inability to strictly constrain the learning process, learning-based methods struggle to simultaneously consider all necessary conditions and generate complete invariants when tackling complex problems. In fact, a loop invariant is often an ordered sequence of lemmas, rather than a single invariant formula. This motivates us to propose Incremental ICE, a novel learning framework for incremental synthesis. Our framework integrates the incremental philosophy of IC3 into the general invariant learning framework ICE. By defining a lemma-specific learning objective and introducing a counterexample filtering mechanism, we can achieve sound incremental learning. Under this framework, we instantiate a loop invariant synthesis tool, LimICE, which leverages LLMs to generate the ordered sequence of lemmas and incorporates ICE-DT as a fallback mechanism to complement the lemma sequence. Experiments on 367 linear benchmarks and 50 nonlinear benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. LimICE solves 349 (out of 367) linear problems on an average of 15.2 seconds and 47 (out of 50) nonlinear problems on an average of 8.8 seconds. Compared to the state-of-the-art LLM-based baseline, our approach solves 12-24% more instances while running 36-63% faster across linear and nonlinear benchmarks. LimICE also consistently outperforms strong non-LLM baselines and solves at least 86 and 27 additional instances on the linear and nonlinear benchmarks, respectively.

</details>


### [243] [Not as Sweet by Another Name: An Empirical Study of Format Robustness in LLM Document Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27648)
*Xiaoyu Zhang,Xianyun Cheng,Tianlin Li,Yuwei Zheng,Yue Yang,Yang Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes a format-aware metamorphic testing framework to evaluate the robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows when content is delivered in different document formats. A large-scale empirical study across four workflows, four tasks, and four formats (48,000 executions) reveals that format changes cause accuracy drops of up to 53.63% and decision drift in over 41% of instances, while lightweight user-side mitigation strategies can recover up to 44.21% of format-induced drift without model retraining. The study concludes that document format is a critical, non-neutral factor affecting LLM software system reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing testing work for LLM-driven systems focuses on robustness and reliability when the input is a single prompt string, but ignores document-centric end-to-end workflows where the same semantic content can arrive in different document formats (e.g., CSV) via file upload. The paper addresses the critical unanswered question of whether these document workflows maintain robust behavior when content is delivered in different formats.

Method: The paper proposes a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to evaluate format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. It conducts a large-scale empirical study spanning four LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, totaling 48,000 workflow executions.

Result: Format variation poses a systematic and serious threat: merely switching formats can cause accuracy drops of up to 53.63% and trigger decision drift in over 41% of instances. Lightweight mitigation strategies from a user perspective recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in real-world high-stakes deployment scenarios.

Abstract: LLM-driven software systems are rapidly evolving from plain-text conversations to document-centric end-to-end workflows, where the same semantic content can be delivered in diverse document formats (e.g., CSV) through file upload interfaces. Yet existing testing work focuses on the robustness and reliability of models and systems whose input is a single prompt string, leaving a critical question unanswered: Can these document workflows maintain robust behaviors when the same content arrives in a different document format? To fill the gap, in this paper, we propose a format-aware metamorphic testing framework with three metamorphic relations to comprehensively evaluate the format robustness of end-to-end LLM document workflows. Based on this framework, we conduct a large-scale empirical study spanning four representative LLM workflows, four real-world tasks, and four document formats, comprising a total of 48,000 workflow executions. Our findings reveal that format variation poses a systematic and serious threat. Merely switching formats can cause accuracy to drop by up to 53.63% and trigger decision drifts in over 41% of instances. We further design lightweight mitigation strategies from the users' perspective that recover up to 44.21% of format-induced decision drift without model retraining. Our study demonstrates that document format is not a neutral wrapper but a critical factor affecting the reliability of LLM software systems, calling for corresponding testing and safeguards in the deployment in real-world high-stakes scenarios.

</details>


### [244] [Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27674)
*Bowen Shen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper builds an LLM-based merge conflict solver using a generate-validate-retry agent with only inference-time signals, and evaluates it using a two-metric suite: a calibrated LLM-as-judge (G-Eval) for developer-match and a deterministic structural-validity check. On 292 human-labeled cases, the judge achieves 100% precision at 64.6% recall. LLM solvers match developer resolutions on ~55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), beating the best traditional tool (AutoMerge at 36.7%) by 18-22 points, with the edge coming almost entirely from coverage. The paper also finds that the LLM judge accepts 4 of 5 structurally invalid resolutions, arguing structural correctness must not be delegated to LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost in collaborative software development. Traditional structured/semi-structured merge tools frequently abstain from resolving conflicts when their heuristics don't apply. LLMs can propose resolutions for almost any conflict, but evaluating whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is difficult because human judgment doesn't scale.

Method: The authors build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent using only inference-time signals (conflict markers, Java parser, duplicate-declaration checks). They evaluate with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as G-Eval, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels; (2) a deterministic structural-validity check using no LLM.

Result: On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's resolution on ~55% of true conflicts (conservative floor). Under coverage-fair comparison, LLMs (55-59%) beat AutoMerge (36.7%) by 18-22 points, the edge coming almost entirely from coverage (tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts, LLM on none). The LLM judge accepted 4 of 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check.

Conclusion: LLM-based solvers provide substantially better coverage than traditional merge tools while matching developer resolutions on a conservative majority of true conflicts. The calibrated LLM-as-judge can reliably validate resolutions with zero false accepts. However, structural correctness must be verified deterministically, not delegated to LLM judges, as evidenced by the judge accepting 4 of 5 structurally invalid resolutions.

Abstract: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost of collaborative software development, and the traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools that address them frequently abstain: when their heuristics do not apply, they leave the conflict unresolved. Large language models (LLMs) can instead produce a candidate resolution for almost any conflict, but measuring whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is hard, because obtaining human desirability judgments for every model output does not scale. We study both problems together on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench. We first build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. We then evaluate its resolutions with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric and, crucially, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every acceptance is trustworthy and every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under a coverage-fair comparison the LLMs (55-59%) beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by roughly 18-22 points; the edge comes almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy, since the tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Finally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, evidence that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.

</details>


### [245] [A comparative analysis of automated techniques for security bug report identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27893)
*Muhammad Laiq*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A comparative analysis of automated techniques (traditional ML, transformers, LLMs, and few-shot learning) for identifying security-related bug reports, finding SetFit achieves the best overall performance (F1=0.80), with RoBERTa competitive and GPT-5.2 performing poorly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature on automatically identifying security-related bug reports is fragmented, with studies using different techniques, baselines, and experimental setups, making it difficult to compare results and determine which approaches are most effective. This lack of systematic comparison leaves researchers and practitioners without clear guidance.

Method: The authors conducted a comparative analysis of seven techniques—Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit—evaluated on benchmark datasets for security-related bug report identification. They also performed cross-project experiments to assess transfer learning effectiveness.

Result: SetFit achieved the best overall performance with an F1-score of 0.80, outperforming other techniques on three of four datasets. RoBERTa was competitive and approached SetFit on some projects. Traditional ML, especially Logistic Regression, remained a strong baseline in certain contexts. GPT-5.2 performed poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Cross-project transfer learning improved performance for data-limited projects but degraded results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

Conclusion: SetFit is the most suitable technique overall for identifying security-related bug reports, while traditional ML approaches like Logistic Regression still hold value in certain scenarios. Transfer learning is beneficial for projects with limited data but can be detrimental for projects with strong idiosyncratic traits, underscoring the need for context-aware technique selection.

Abstract: Timely identification of security-related bug reports is essential to minimize the window of vulnerabilities in software systems. Manually screening incoming bug reports to identify security-related issues is time-consuming, error-prone, and non-scalable for large-scale software systems. Thus, a variety of automatic techniques, including traditional machine learning (ML) techniques and large language models, have been proposed to facilitate this task. However, the literature remains fragmented. Most studies introduce or optimize a particular technique and evaluate it against a limited set of baselines, often under different experimental setups. As a result, it is difficult to compare their results and draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of existing approaches, leaving researchers and practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most suitable for the task.
  To address this gap, we conducted a comparative analysis of several promising automated techniques to identify security-related bug reports using benchmark datasets. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework).
  Our results indicate that SetFit achieves the best overall performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming other techniques on three of the four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively and approaches SetFit in some projects, while traditional ML techniques, particularly Logistic Regression, remain a strong baseline in certain contexts. In contrast, GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. In addition, cross-project experiments demonstrate that transfer learning can improve performance for projects with limited data, but may degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

</details>


### [246] [The Case for Vibe Modeling: A Missing Step in AI-Based Trustworthy Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27923)
*Shalini Chakraborty,Michael Mittermaier,Judith Michael*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that AI-based software development focuses too much on direct code generation and proposes "vibe modeling" as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language and code generation to preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. A student survey study examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the usefulness of vibe modeling across AI-assisted development scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-based development practices overemphasize direct code generation from natural language prompts, lacking intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. This creates challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust in LLM-generated software artifacts.

Method: The paper presents a conceptual argument for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation, supported by a student survey study examining perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios.

Result: The study provides empirical insights from students regarding LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across AI-assisted development scenarios, intended to inform future research on trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering.

Conclusion: Vibe modeling holds potential as a lightweight intermediate abstraction to address understanding, validation, traceability, and trust challenges in AI-assisted software development; the survey results lay groundwork for future studies on trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software artifacts from natural language prompts. While this enables rapid prototyping and lowers the barrier to software creation, it also introduces challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. In this paper, we argue that current AI-based development practices focus too heavily on the direct generation of code and insufficiently on intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. We argue for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation. To explore its potential, we present a student survey study that examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios. Our results are intended to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

</details>


### [247] [Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27964)
*Yang Li,Ping Hou,Nobuko Yoshida*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Syntropy is a framework that combines multiparty session types (MPST) with large language models to synthesize protocol refinements that are guaranteed to preserve behavioural correctness, achieving 95.6%-99.5% validity while producing diverse, non-trivial refinements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distributed software systems require protocol refinement—safe substitution of protocols preserving correctness and compatibility—but LLMs lack mechanisms to reliably produce behaviourally correct outputs, and formal approaches like MPST offer deadlock-freedom guarantees but limited support for automatically constructing refinements.

Method: Syntropy is a framework that synthesises protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs, incorporating refinement constraints directly into the generation process to ensure the produced variants satisfy correctness and compatibility guarantees.

Result: The comprehensive evaluation shows Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

Conclusion: Combining formal MPST specifications with LLM-based generation can effectively and reliably synthesise protocol refinements that preserve behavioural correctness while remaining syntactically sound and diverse.

Abstract: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

</details>


### [248] [Advancing Awkward Arrays for High-Performance CPU and GPU Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28145)
*Ianna Osborne,Manasvi Goyal*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents recent developments in the GPU backend of Awkward Array, a Python library for nested, variable-length data widely used in high-energy physics. The work includes CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CCCL, optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, preserving the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, yet nested and variable-length data structures are difficult to accelerate on GPUs due to indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. Efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential for the Awkward Array library.

Method: The authors present CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management strategies, and segmented reduction algorithms specifically designed for ragged arrays. They also describe the backend architecture and an automated validation framework to ensure correctness of the GPU implementations.

Result: The developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. Benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations are provided.

Conclusion: The Awkward Array GPU backend enables efficient execution of nested, variable-length data on accelerator hardware, making it well-suited for HL-LHC analysis workloads while maintaining the familiar Python interface.

Abstract: Awkward Array is a Python library for representing and processing nested, variable-length data that is widely used in high-energy physics. As HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential. While dense numerical arrays map naturally to GPUs, nested and variable-length data structures remain significantly more difficult to accelerate because they require indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. We present recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays. These developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. We describe the backend architecture, automated validation framework, and benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

</details>


### [249] [Integrating AI into Requirements Quality Learning in Software Engineering Education: A TPACK-Guided Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28176)
*Hansika Ekanayake Mudiyanselage,Rohan Jai Dharmaraj,Malik Abdul Sami,Zheying Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study investigates a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level requirements engineering (RE) assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using mixed methods with 100 students (72 submissions analyzed), it finds that structured assignment design led to selective AI use as support rather than automation, improved alignment on structurally concrete quality dimensions (value articulation, testability) but mixed effects on negotiability, and fostered conditional trust and active refinement while surfacing usability challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in software engineering practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects like requirements engineering where understanding, not just task completion, matters.

Method: A TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool was embedded into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. A mixed-methods design was used (N=100; 72 submissions analyzed) to examine how structured assignment design shaped AI use, understanding of user story quality criteria, and perceptions of AI benefits and limitations.

Result: Students used the AI tool selectively, primarily as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete quality dimensions like value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, increased awareness of quality criteria, and moderate usability challenges.

Conclusion: TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

Abstract: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in software engineering (SE) practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects such as requirements engineering (RE). This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analysed), we examine how structured assignment design shaped students' AI use, affected their understanding of user story quality criteria, and influenced their perceptions of AI's benefits and limitations. Results show that students used the AI tool selectively, mainly as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete requirements quality dimensions, such as value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges. The findings show that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

</details>


### [250] [Agentic Metaverse Services: A New As-a-Service Paradigm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28242)
*Xiaofei Xu,Quan Z. Sheng,Zhongjie Wang,Boualem Benatallah,Xiao Wang,Ruipeng Han*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper systematically overviews Agentic Metaverse Service (AMServ) and its realization approach Meta-AaaS (Agent-as-a-Service in the metaverse), covering their evolution, principles, forms, application examples, and future research directions in the context of GenAI-empowered agentic services.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI has created a new service paradigm, and combining agentic services with the metaverse raises the need to formalize and understand this new form of metaverse service—namely AMServ and its implementation via Meta-AaaS—and to chart its principles and research agenda.

Method: The paper provides a conceptual and systematic overview: it reviews the evolution and new features of GenAI-empowered agents and services, characterizes the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse, defines the forms, characteristics, and principles of AMServ and Meta-AaaS, and presents typical application examples before outlining research directions.

Result: The paper defines and formalizes AMServ as a new form of metaverse service for business processing, introduces Meta-AaaS as the realization paradigm, catalogs its forms, characteristics, and principles, demonstrates representative application examples, and identifies emerging research tendencies.

Conclusion: AMServ and Meta-AaaS represent a transformative service paradigm in the AI era, promising significant opportunities for human society and services while driving the growth of future emerging service industries.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reconstructing the digital virtual world, upgrading agents through enhancing their abilities in autonomous learning, multi-modal interaction, content generation, and collaborative decision-making. In particular, the shift from conversational chatbots to agentic AI, the most recent significant technical breakthrough of GenAI, has brought a new form of services, agentic services and Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS), in which the agent's abilities are encapsulated, such as perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration, and content generation, to provide the customized agent services to users. The metaverse is a virtual ecosystem for human life, work, creation, and entertainment, supported by the new generation of digital technologies. Through combining agentic services and the metaverse, an Agentic Metaverse Service, denoted as AMServ, is produced for metaverse business processing, as a new form of metaverse service. The AaaS in the metaverse environment, denoted as Meta-AaaS, as an approach to realize AMServ, has become a new paradigm of agentic services and service computing. This paper overviews the evolution and new features of agents and services empowered by GenAI, reveals the roles and principles of agentic services in the metaverse environment, presents the forms, characteristics, and principles of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, discusses the typical application examples of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS, and finally points out the new tendencies and research directions of the AMServ and the Meta-AaaS. The AMServ and the Meta-AaaS will bring great opportunities to human society and services in the AI era, and promote the rapid development of emerging service industries in the future.

</details>


### [251] [Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28271)
*Andras Ferenczi,Jordan Docherty,Mariya Bessonov,Matthew Findlay,Krishna Lingamneni*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes "Locksmith Loop," a novel agentic test-synthesis method for validating COBOL-to-Java migrations. It uses dual instrumented runtime environments (COBOL source and Java target), an iterative agentic loop that performs Witness Search over input mocks with parity-preserving mutations, and an analyzer that identifies "Locked Paragraphs" blocking deeper branch exploration. Across three case studies (430-4,114 SLOC), it improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching near-complete coverage on open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on a production-like COBOL program, with all accepted test cases matching the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legacy COBOL-to-Java migration requires extensive testing that is complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. Existing approaches plateau at limited coverage due to insufficient input exploration.

Method: The method prepares two instrumented runtime environments (COBOL source and generated Java target, executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware with mocks). An iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, applies parity-preserving mutations, and when routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a "Locked Paragraph" — a condition preventing deeper exploration.

Result: Across three COBOL-Java case studies (two open-source, one internal production-like; 430 to 4,114 source lines), Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, achieving nearly complete coverage on open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the production-like program. All accepted test cases passed deterministic parity checks against the COBOL reference.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle, showing that agentic test synthesis with locked-paragraph analysis can effectively validate COBOL-to-Java migrations even in the absence of pre-existing test data.

Abstract: Migration of legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure correct functionality. This effort is often complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. In this paper we propose a novel agentic test-synthesis method, the "Locksmith Loop," which is initiated by preparing two runtime environments: the COBOL source and the generated Java target are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware, then an iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a Locked Paragraph: a condition preventing deeper exploration. Across three COBOL-Java case studies, spanning two open-source programs and one internal production-like COBOL program and ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines, Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. The generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases. Through these findings we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle.

</details>


### [252] [From Textual Requirements to Microservice Architectures - A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLM-Based Design Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28307)
*Danyllo Albuquerque,José Renan,Guillermo Rodríguez,Guillermo Rodríguez,Emanuel Dantas,Ademar França,Mirko Perkusich,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This study evaluates whether an LLM (OpenAI o3) can synthesize complete microservice architectures directly from natural-language requirements, using zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems. FS prompting yields higher agreement with reference architectures (service F1=0.97 vs 0.79; communication F1=0.82 vs 0.61) and is perceived as more modular and plausible by experts. Results are promising but context-specific to small systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microservice decomposition remains a largely manual and code-centric process, limiting applicability during early design stages when only textual requirements exist. Despite advances in LLMs, there is limited empirical evidence on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures (services and their interactions) directly from natural-language requirements.

Method: A mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 with zero-shot and few-shot prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated via (i) quantitative comparison against reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for both service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility with open feedback synthesis.

Result: FS prompting improves service identification agreement (F1=0.97 vs 0.79 for ZS). Communication recovery is harder: ZS yields dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1=0.61), while FS improves to F1=0.82 and reduces unsupported dependencies. Expert assessment corroborates these results, with FS architectures rated as more modular, coherent, and plausible.

Conclusion: OpenAI o3 demonstrates potential for requirements-driven microservice architecture synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. However, results are model- and context-specific, derived from two small systems, and do not constitute model-independent proof of general capability.

Abstract: Microservice architectures have become dominant for modernizing monolithic systems, yet identifying appropriate services remains challenging and largely manual. Existing decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, including service definitions and inter-service interactions. This study investigates whether an LLM can bridge requirements engineering and architectural design, generating architectures solely from textual requirements and evaluating structural agreement and perceived quality of results. We conduct a mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated through (i) comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis. OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.79 for ZS versus = 0.97 for FS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement, reaching F1 = 0.82 and reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs. OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. Results are model- and context-specific from two small systems, not model-independent proof.

</details>


### [253] [Structural Validation of LLM-Generated Microservice Decompositions Using Source-Code Dependencies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28331)
*Daniel Silva,Renan Alves,Emanuel Dantas Filho,Ademar Sousa Neto,Mirko Perkusich,Danyllo Wagner Albuquerque,Kyller Gorgônio,Angelo Perkusich*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 from textual requirements preserve the structural dependencies present in the original source code of the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. Using an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis, the authors compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting with dependency preservation (TPD) and violation (TVD) metrics, and find that after normalizing for class-to-service mapping coverage, both prompting strategies yield equivalent structural adherence (TPD: 68.0% PetClinic, 83.3% Bookstore).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can generate semantically plausible microservice decompositions from textual requirements, it is unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies actually implemented in the source code. The paper addresses this gap by evaluating structural adherence of LLM-generated decompositions.

Method: The authors propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis. They evaluate OpenAI o3-generated decompositions for PetClinic and Bookstore systems, comparing zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies using TPD (dependency preservation) and TVD (dependency violation) metrics, and perform a robustness analysis to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage.

Result: After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% for PetClinic and 83.3% for Bookstore.

Conclusion: Structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for class-to-service mapping coverage, since apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise stem from methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

Abstract: Decomposing monolithic systems into microservices is a key activity in software modernization. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate semantically plausible decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the source code. This paper evaluates the structural adherence of microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. We propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis and compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis was conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage. After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). The findings demonstrate that structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage, as apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise reflect methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

</details>


### [254] [Demystifying Solana Bots: From GitHub Blueprints to On-Chain Fingerprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28424)
*Xiaoye Zheng,Yujing Chen,Minghao Wu,David Lo,Difan Xie,Daoyuan Wu,Xiaohu Yang,Zhiyuan Wan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary perspectives—586 GitHub repositories and 200 on-chain bot addresses with over 44 million transactions—deriving a taxonomy of 15 bot categories across five domains, identifying a shared five-stage operational pipeline, and uncovering systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Solana's high throughput and low fees make it vulnerable to bot spamming and financial exploitation, yet there is no systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how those implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints.

Method: The study analyzes 586 bot repositories from GitHub (implementation view) and 200 bot addresses on Solana with over 44 million on-chain transactions (execution view), deriving a taxonomy through a two-view empirical methodology.

Result: The study produces an implementation-grounded taxonomy of 15 Solana bot categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and finds systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors across different trading platforms and assets.

Conclusion: The findings highlight future research directions and provide practical recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

Abstract: Solana is an emerging blockchain platform designed for high throughput and low transaction fees, making it inexpensive to submit transactions at scale and, consequently, increasing exposure to bot spamming and related financial exploitation. Solana bots are typically off-chain software systems that operate in a competitive on-chain execution environment by constructing and submitting transactions, and the bot-related transactions on the decentralized exchanges exceed 250 million dollars in daily trading volume in January 2026. Prior studies on Solana have examined system performance, smart-contract security, and specific on-chain phenomena. However, we still lack a systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints. To address this gap, we performed a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: (i) 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) 200 bot addresses on Solana, with over 44 million on-chain transactions. Our study derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots comprising 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, and On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors of Solana bots across diverse trading platforms and assets. Based on our findings, we highlight future research directions, and provide recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

</details>


### [255] [Emerging Challenges in Threat Modeling for GenAI-Augmented Systems: A View from the Trenches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28431)
*Nicolás E. Díaz Ferreyra,Manish Mahesh Kumar,Nohemí Villarreal,Pankaj Pantel,Immo Brueggemann,Riccardo Scandariato*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods applied in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) context, comparing three shortlisted techniques on a GenAI-augmented industrial case study. Results show each method identifies different threats, with limited coverage of GenAI-specific risks related to software supply chains and human-centered security, along with practitioner feedback on usability and adoption challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional threat modeling methods like STRIDE are insufficient to assess the emerging GenAI-specific security risks in systems that increasingly incorporate Generative AI. There is a need to evaluate whether existing GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques are practical and effective, particularly in resource-constrained SME settings.

Method: The study conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques, then systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system in an SME. Practitioner perceptions on usability, effort, and integration were also collected.

Result: The three selected methods identified different sets of threats, indicating variation in coverage. Notably, all methods showed limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, especially those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. Practitioners reported usability and integration challenges, including perceived effort and adoption barriers in SME workflows.

Conclusion: Current GenAI-aware threat modeling methods offer partial coverage of GenAI-specific risks and face practical adoption challenges in SME settings, highlighting the need for improved techniques and better integration support for smaller organizations.

Abstract: Threat modeling remains a central task in secure software engineering, as it enables the identification of security issues from system architectures. As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly pervasive across software systems, traditional threat modeling methods (e.g., STRIDE) are insufficient to assess emerging GenAI-specific risks. In this work, we present the first results from an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. For this, we conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant techniques and systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study involving a GenAI-augmented system. The results highlight differences in the threats identified by each technique and reveal limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. We further report practitioners' perceptions of the usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, including their perceived effort and adoption challenges.

</details>


### [256] [CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28529)
*Minghao Hu,Lannan Luo,Allen Roush,Phillip Howard*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CoGate is a confidence-gated co-decoding approach for secure code generation that controls a security expert model's influence based on its confidence, outperforming existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) by up to 12.6% on Func-Sec@10 across multiple benchmarks and LLM backends.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing co-decoding approaches for secure code generation do not consider the security expert model's confidence. When the expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution contexts, its guidance can be misleading, leading to insecure code generation.

Method: CoGate is a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert model's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence level. It is evaluated across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, CWEval).

Result: CoGate outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

Conclusion: Incorporating the expert model's confidence into the co-decoding acceptance rule improves secure code generation, addressing the limitation of existing co-decoding approaches that ignore expert uncertainty and thereby reducing misleading guidance in out-of-distribution contexts.

Abstract: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can therefore be misleading. To address the challenge, we propose CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. We implement our approach and evaluate it across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval). Our approach outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

</details>


### [257] [PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28587)
*Manyi Wang,Junjielong Xu,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper systematically studies PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks, finding 13.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances exhibit misalignment across five patterns and eleven fine-grained scenarios. The authors propose PAIChecker, a three-phase multi-agent system for detecting PR-Issue misalignment, which achieves up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used but their PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned due to the inherent complexity of large repository development and maintenance. This misalignment undermines the reliability of these benchmarks for evaluating LLM issue resolution capability, motivating the need for systematic detection and scalable construction of more accurate benchmarks.

Method: The authors first systematically analyze SWE-bench Verified instances to categorize misalignment into five patterns across eleven fine-grained scenarios. They then propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system with a three-phase design: (1) specific pattern identification, (2) cross-agent label synthesis, and (3) code-level validation, enabling accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection.

Result: Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show PAIChecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% binary accuracy on SWE-Gym and 91.67% on SWE-bench Multilingual. The analysis also reveals that 13.6% of SWE-bench Verified instances exhibit misalignment.

Conclusion: PR-Issue misalignment is a significant problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks, and PAIChecker provides an effective multi-agent solution for detecting such misalignment, enabling reliable and scalable benchmark construction in the future.

Abstract: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. In this work, we systematically study SWE-bench Verified instances, finding that 13.6% exhibit misalignment across five patterns in eleven fine-grained scenarios. To enable reliable and scalable construction of those benchmarks in the future, we propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for checking PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Specifically, PAIChecker adopts a three-phase design that combines specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, thereby enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection. Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show that PAIchecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy, respectively.

</details>


### [258] [Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28591)
*Haomin Qi,Xingliang Wang,Xuanqi Gao,Baihui Sang,Xin Zhang,Minghua Ma,Pengfei Gao,Yu Kang,Qingwei Lin,Saravan Rajmohan,Dongmei Zhang,Qi Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Change2Task is a system that converts merged pull requests from repository history into verified, executable coding-agent tasks on healthy modern revisions, achieving 79.6% verified task construction success across five task families (Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, API Migration, Security Repair) and recovering 29.2% more verified tasks than a pull-request-based baseline while reducing environmental setup costs by 10.8%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling coding agents requires a continuous supply of executable data (for training, benchmarking, and evaluation), where each task must pair a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. The scarcity of such data motivates the need for a system that can systematically generate verified tasks from existing repository history.

Method: Change2Task processes merged pull requests to create tasks on healthy modern repository revisions. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states using three strategies—Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, and Agent Reconstruction—and validates the full lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and to a restored state, ensuring each derived task is grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments.

Result: From 1,130 eligible source changes, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across five task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a pull-request-based construction baseline. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, and reuse of modern bases reduces pipeline expenditure by 10.8%.

Conclusion: Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation by deriving multiple verified tasks from repository history, while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort—demonstrating that repository-history-grounded task construction is an effective, scalable approach.

Abstract: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states through Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and a restored state. By deriving multiple tasks grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments, Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort. We evaluate the system through five common and widely adopted coding agent task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, Application Programming Interface Migration, and Security Repair. Starting from 1,130 source changes eligible for construction, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across these task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a construction baseline based on pull requests. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, while reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%.

</details>

### [259] [Multi-Head Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27230)
*Cheng Luo,Zefan Cai,Junjie Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MHAR reshapes the routing query in attention residuals into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over depth history, enabling block-diagonal reads without added parameters. It improves validation loss over standard Transformers at 100M, 350M, and 1B scales, achieves the best result among four methods, and supports 8B mid-training with GSM8K and GPQA improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Transformers propagate information through a single additive residual stream where every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this but use a single query shared across the entire width, forcing all feature subspaces to read depth history through one distribution. This compromise becomes increasingly costly as subspace disagreement grows with model width.

Method: MHAR reshapes the routing query into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. This makes the read block-diagonal, adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and reduces to attention residuals when H=1. Training uses a deduplicated, quality-filtered Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is STEM- and code-heavy. Fused Triton routing kernels boost throughput. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals enables mid-training on 8B models.

Result: MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B scales (improvements of -0.061, -0.149, and -0.140), achieving the best result among four methods in every setting. Validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H=4 or H=8. H=8 is adopted for large-scale models. Fused Triton kernels improve throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of baseline. 8B mid-training yields +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

Conclusion: The head count H is a real design axis rather than a free knob, with over-splitting (H=16) consistently giving back part of the gain. A direct probe confirms learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. MHAR provides an efficient, parameter-free mechanism to let different feature subspaces read different depth histories, improving performance across scales and enabling effective large-scale mid-training.

Abstract: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

</details>


### [260] [KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27231)
*Peiyu Zang,Jian Tao,Jialing Zhang,Yichen Yuan,Wentao Zhang,Guang Liu,Yonghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KernelGenBench is a unified benchmark for evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across multiple operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two sub-benchmarks (Multi-Source and Multi-Chip) and, through a large-scale evaluation consuming 15 billion tokens, reveals that agent-based methods outperform pure LLM sampling, cross-platform performance degrades severely, and autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have increased demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains specialized and labor-intensive. Despite progress in automated kernel generation via LLMs and agents, there is no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms.

Method: The paper introduces KernelGenBench, a benchmark with two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) covering 210 operators from three sources beyond PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens was conducted.

Result: (1) Agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, with cuBLAS operators being the most challenging; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaching 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling.

Conclusion: KernelGenBench provides a systematic framework for evaluating LLM- and agent-based kernel generation, highlighting that while agents improve generation quality, significant challenges remain in cross-platform portability and computational cost efficiency.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

</details>


### [261] [RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27235)
*Frank Li,Bardia Khosravi,Mohammadreza Chavoshi,Theo Dapamede,YoungSeok Jeon,Janice Newsome,Hari Trivedi,Judy Gichoya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library providing a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets (primarily chest radiographs, with early support for CT and MRI). It standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets, wraps MONAI datasets for deep-learning-ready delivery, supports multiple annotation types (classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, report text), includes an interactive visualization tool, and introduces an AI-agent skill for streamlined dataset integration. The authors demonstrate its utility with RadHarmony-ViT, a vision transformer pretrained on three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets without dataset-specific code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training deep learning models on radiological images is hampered by the heterogeneity of data across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. There is a need for a tool that unifies these diverse datasets to lower the barrier for reproducible radiological deep learning research.

Method: RadHarmony provides a unified API that (1) standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, (2) wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, (3) supports multiple annotation modalities through a single interface, (4) offers interactive visualization for dataset exploration, and (5) introduces an AI-agent skill to automate the dataset integration workflow including raw data inspection, code generation, and testing.

Result: The authors pretrained RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline, by combining three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets using RadHarmony with no dataset-specific code, demonstrating the library's utility in enabling large-scale multimodal training from diverse radiological sources.

Conclusion: RadHarmony offers a practical, extensible solution for harmonizing heterogeneous radiological datasets, and its open-source availability (code and pretrained weights) promises to support reproducible research in medical imaging. The AI-agent skill further reduces the integration barrier for new datasets.

Abstract: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing.
