We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

</details>


### [262] [Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27240)
*Aarnav Choudhary,Matheus Fonseca Rocha,Jiwon Seo,Vasu Sharma,Maheep Chaudhary*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Standard model merging methods (Linear, SLERP, TIES, DARE-TIES) preferentially transfer refusal behaviors over safety classification accuracy when merging two safety fine-tunes on Gemma-3-1B-IT. Merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates but classification accuracy drops to at most 12.9%, due to larger task-vector magnitudes in the refusal fine-tune rather than opposing task-vector directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model merging combines capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods can preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously.

Method: A controlled case study merging two Gemma-3-1B-IT fine-tunes (CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal) using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES. Evaluated on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance, with weight-space task-vector analysis (cosine similarity and per-layer magnitudes).

Result: All four merging methods transfer attack resistance significantly better than classification accuracy: 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates retained while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011), so asymmetry is not from opposing directions. The refusal fine-tune yields consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates.

Conclusion: Standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale, indicating that merging methods need to account for task-vector magnitude disparities to preserve multiple safety behaviors.

Abstract: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

</details>


### [263] [HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28375)
*Xiangbo Wang,Jiasheng Zhang,Xingtong Yu,Luoqiang Lei,Delvin Ce Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperClaim is a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level video misinformation detection that models higher-order cross-modal interactions among query tokens, evidence text, and short temporal frame spans, achieving 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV under the FactGuard temporal protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global multimodal fusion and free-form reasoning both tend to under-represent localized authenticity cues arising from coupled multi-way interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short frame sequences. Since these interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graphs fail to capture them fully, motivating hypergraph-based modeling.

Method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames. It applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units, performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration, and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states via a discrepancy-aware readout.

Result: HyperClaim achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV respectively under the FactGuard temporal protocol, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal token- and frame-level structure.

Conclusion: Hypergraph-based higher-order modeling with adaptive incidence reasoning and discrepancy-aware aggregation preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion flattens, all without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, yielding superior video misinformation detection and interpretable token/frame-level evidence.

Abstract: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

</details>


### [264] [Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27248)
*Yimi Wang,Hao Li,Shuo Yang,He Cao,Dechen Zhang,Ziang Wu,Zhiyuan Yan,Fanyang Mo,Li Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Divergence Decoding is a training-free framework that fuses generalist and specialist LLM capabilities by monitoring Jensen-Shannon divergence between their token-level distributions and adaptively routing control to the generalist when the specialist shows significant divergence, outperforming both model types on scientific benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models face a dilemma: generalists excel in reasoning but lack specialized scientific knowledge, while domain specialists are knowledgeable but suffer from side-effects such as diminished logic and reduced robustness. There is a need for a method that combines the strengths of both without training.

Method: Divergence Decoding reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. It uses Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor distributional disagreement between the specialist and generalist at each token. When the specialist shows significant divergence (indicating a potential reasoning risk), control is instantaneously routed to the generalist, enabling inference-time policy composition of the two models.

Result: Evaluated on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench) across Qwen and Llama model families, Divergence Decoding outperforms both domain-specialized and general-purpose models, surpassing most single-model baselines.

Conclusion: Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration, effectively combining domain expertise with general reasoning.

Abstract: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

</details>


### [265] [PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27287)
*Amir Hossein Sharafi,Alireza Shahbazi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces PIE, a unified framework with two modules (PIE-Abducer and PIE-APT) for reasoning and planning over dynamic knowledge graphs represented as Description Logic theories. It handles incomplete information via direct-derivation abduction (avoiding minimal hitting set enumeration) and employs Generate-and-Test recursive planning with A* search and temporal projection validation, showing qualitative and quantitative superiority over classical planners and MHS baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reasoning and planning over dynamic knowledge graphs with incomplete information is challenging due to decidability issues in action formalisms, the Ramification Problem, and the combinatorial explosion of structural abduction (MHS enumeration). The authors aim to unify reasoning and planning within an expressive, decidable Description Logic framework while bypassing expensive syntactic search for missing knowledge.

Method: The framework models state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. PIE-Abducer injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences, avoiding MHS enumeration. PIE-APT uses a recursive Generate-and-Test architecture interleaving backward-chaining A* search with PIE-Abducer up to bounded causal depth, followed by forward-chaining Temporal Projection for strict validation. Actions are represented natively in OWL without external modal operators, treating the incremental reasoner as a black box to preserve decidability.

Result: Evaluation on four OWL benchmarks (parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting) demonstrates qualitative superiority over classical planners. The direct-derivation approach also quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

Conclusion: The PIE framework provides a decidable, expressive, and scalable solution for abductive planning over dynamic knowledge graphs with incomplete information, effectively circumventing the combinatorial bottlenecks of traditional MHS-based abduction while preserving logical semantics through native OWL action representation.

Abstract: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

</details>


### [266] [PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27354)
*Haoyu Chen,Xirui Shi,Yuyao Wang,Jerry Chen,Di Niu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments, showing that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic settings where agents must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services.

Method: PAUSE benchmark captures core challenges of real-world deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state and authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. It incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework (semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics for open-ended tasks; deterministic, state-based verification for constraint-intensive tasks), and presents a user-centric synthesis pipeline for scalable benchmark generation.

Result: State-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns.

Conclusion: PAUSE provides a principled and reproducible evaluation framework for personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated settings, with a scalable synthesis pipeline supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

Abstract: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

</details>


### [267] [SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27360)
*Xiaoyi Bao,Yuanzhen Xie,Yunzhi Tan,Jinghang Gu,Zhongqing Wang,Chu-Ren Huang,Bo Hu,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillMentor trains a separate Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to perform blind-spot diagnosis—generating diagnostic tasks, identifying recurrent failure modes, and curating corrective skills—thereby improving executor performance by an average of 44.2% on AppWorld and BFCLv3 without updating executor weights or using human supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent self-evolution has focused on learning to act but overlooked learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches assume failure discovery is given and only address repairing failures after identification. The paper asks whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned as a capability separate from execution.

Method: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to: (1) generate diagnostic tasks, (2) identify recurrent failure modes, and (3) curate them into reusable corrective skills. The setup excludes executor adaptation and human supervision, ensuring all improvements originate from the learned diagnostic capability.

Result: Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%, demonstrating that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

Conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability distinct from execution. By learning to diagnose failures, agents can self-evolve through improved diagnostic skills rather than updated execution weights or human-annotated examples.

Abstract: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

</details>


### [268] [Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27386)
*Saurabh Yadav,Badri Narayana Patro,Vijay Srinivas Agneeswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates the robustness and calibration of Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) against autoregressive (AR) baselines using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B, Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. DLMs show natural resistance to gradient-based adversarial suffixes due to stochastic loss landscapes but remain vulnerable to natural noise, exhibit systematic overconfidence, and mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption—isolating fragility to a decoder routing failure that cannot be fixed by prompt patching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While Diffusion Language Models offer advantages over autoregressive generation via bidirectional context and iterative refinement, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored, creating a critical knowledge gap for deployment safety.

Method: The authors use parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) to isolate architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors, evaluating across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses.

Result: DLMs exhibit a nuanced robustness profile: stochastic loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes but provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise; DLMs show systematic overconfidence posing deployment hazards; mechanistic probing reveals all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility to decoder routing failure; prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines.

Conclusion: DLM robustness cannot be patched on at the surface level—it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop, as robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

</details>


### [269] [Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27415)
*Xu Zheng,Chaohao Lin,Zhuomin Chen,Weijieying Ren,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAMER is a novel framework that bridges inference-time scaling and episodic memory for LLM agents by modeling historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph, decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, and using dual-stream Temporal Difference learning to estimate positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes for bi-directional decision optimization during inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference-time scaling approaches for LLM agents operate in a stateless manner and engage in redundant search processes, while existing memory mechanisms rely heavily on LLM reasoning capabilities, leading to prohibitive computational costs.

Method: The framework models historical reasoning as a dynamic Action-Centric Graph, decouples the memory mechanism from LLMs to save token/money usage, and employs a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate positive (suggestion) and negative (avoidance) values of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During inference, the learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally—positive values provide action suggestions while negative values indicate high-risk actions—and efficient graph searches improve inference scaling efficiency.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate GAMER achieves superior performance with 20.81%/6.17% improvement in success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

Conclusion: By bridging inference scaling and episodic memory through a graph-based, LLM-decoupled memory mechanism with dual-stream value estimation, GAMER significantly improves both the efficiency and effectiveness of inference-time scaling for LLM agents.

Abstract: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

</details>


### [270] [Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27420)
*Mayank Sharma,Savira Nadela,Tyler Matteson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HLE measures a single general reasoning factor, not eight distinct domain-specific capabilities, and its measurement precision is poor at the high ability levels where frontier models cluster.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HLE's eight subject-domain category subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct model capabilities, but no study has validated whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs or whether the benchmark can differentiate between models of similar ability.

Method: Evaluated 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE (428 items) and applied psychometric methods: fitted a two-parameter logistic IRT model to assess dimensionality, and analyzed the test information function to evaluate measurement precision distribution.

Result: Convergent evidence of a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's ω_h = 0.998, domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's d = 0.016), and domain-specific ability estimates correlate ≥ 0.81 with the total score. Measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above θ = 0.

Conclusion: HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations, and the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

Abstract: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

</details>


### [271] [Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27443)
*Xu Zheng,Zhuomin Chen,Chaohao Lin,Hua Wei,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Trajectory Graph Copilot, a framework that acts as a proactive "copilot" for LLM-based agents by diagnosing potential action errors before execution. It models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify failure-prone action patterns, enabling early warnings and self-correction. Experiments across four benchmarks with three LLM agents show a 14.69% average pass ratio improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks (e.g., embodied AI) due to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory and exhaust the limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. The goal is to overcome this without costly fine-tuning.

Method: The proposed Trajectory Graph Copilot framework contains a Graph Debugger that models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns frequently leading to failure. It functions as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, providing early warnings on potentially flawed actions before execution, prompting the agent to self-correct pre-action.

Result: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a 14.69% pass ratio improvement on average.

Conclusion: Pre-action error diagnosis enables LLM agents to avoid costly mistakes and significantly enhances their ability to complete long-horizon interactive tasks, providing a training-free approach inspired by software debugging principles.

Abstract: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

</details>


### [272] [VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27453)
*Joshua Meyer,Sahar Shayegan,Ritiz Tambi,Ali Khan,Sun Kim,Victor Shih,Mehdi Jamei,Andi Partovi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces VAmoS Bench, a benchmark for evaluating complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful credit-card customer-support domain, measuring "containment"—the share of calls an automated system resolves without human handoff. It uses 100 scenarios with simulated callers, a seeded PostgreSQL backend, five SQL-executing tools, and binary assertions graded against full interaction traces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing voice-agent benchmarks focus on component quality (word error rate, latency, naturalness, turn-taking) but rarely measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers use "containment" to measure this, and current benchmarks fail to address this gap.

Method: VAmoS Bench places the agent as "Riley," a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank, in 100 scenarios with simulated callers (each with private goals and seeded backend state), ~1/3 involving adversarial pressure. Agents can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Binary assertions are graded against the complete trace of dialogue and agent actions (tool invocations, arguments, returned rows).

Result: The benchmark captures correct call outcomes, catching both agents that falsely claim database changes and agents that make correct database changes while disclosing protected information. The evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard for comparing additional voice agents.

Conclusion: VAmoS Bench is the first version focused on financial services, measuring end-to-end voice-agent performance in a stateful task; its design allows successive benchmark versions to expand tasks and scenarios while the current evaluation protocol supports ongoing evaluation of new voice agents.

Abstract: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

</details>


### [273] [Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27484)
*Jinwei Hu,Yi Qi,Xinmiao Huang,Youcheng Sun,Yi Dong,Xiaowei Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework and benchmark (BACKROOMBench) to detect the "Reasoning Backroom"—a systematic gap between stated skill use by language agents and intervention-measured causal influence. Experiments reveal pervasive provenance failures: stated skill use often diverges from actual causal reliance and signed utility, observational detectors fail to identify genuine skill-dependent decisions, and multi-agent systems exhibit both skill influence surviving source loss and phantom attribution of never-supplied skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluations of skill-augmented language agents infer skill use from visible reasoning traces or the agent's self-attribution, which only show what the agent appears to use rather than whether the skill actually changed its decision. This motivates the need for an intervention-based evaluation framework to measure genuine causal influence of skills on agent behavior.

Method: The BACKTRACE framework pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. This is instantiated as BACKROOMBench across controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families.

Result: The evaluation finds pervasive provenance failure across models and domains: stated skill use remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary (producing silent uptake and performative use). Behavioral effects track procedural content more than skill identity, while attributions respond to artifact availability. Observational detectors (direct claims, text mentions, trace similarity, LLM judge) fail to identify genuinely skill-dependent decisions. In multi-agent settings, skill influence can survive communication after source loss, while no-skill teams still name nonexistent skills and sources.

Conclusion: The Reasoning Backroom is established as a general AI provenance problem requiring intervention-based audit; observational signals are insufficient to determine whether skills actually influence agent decisions.

Abstract: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

</details>


### [274] [INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27487)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INCLAIR is a framework for anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles that scores observations against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. It uses U-statistic theory for variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation to control computational cost, plus validation-selected top-k pooling to mitigate attenuation of localized anomalies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important yet challenging due to sparse abnormal evidence, unequal patient history lengths, and costly expert explanations.

Method: INCLAIR (1) scores each observation against multiple historical contexts; (2) aggregates evidence at the profile level; (3) generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-l U-statistic form, enabling a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independent of profile length. Mean aggregation is shown to attenuate localized anomalies by a factor dependent on anomaly support and profile length, motivating a validation-selected top-k pooling strategy.

Result: Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. A case study on longitudinal steroid profiles validates practical relevance, with predictions and explanations compared against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis.

Conclusion: INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision, producing both accurate detections and grounded explanations validated against expert judgment.

Abstract: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

</details>


### [275] [MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27490)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Asim Ahmed,Mihan Mohagheghzadeh,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedLLM is an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained via a three-phase fully open pipeline. At sub-billion scale, medical competence splits by task type: it performs well on context-grounded QA (within 2.9pp of a 7B medical model), but on knowledge-recall QA, performance is capacity-constrained, revealing a task-type dissociation that is masked at 7B scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open medical language models have converged on 7B parameters or larger, leaving the sub-billion parameter regime uncharacterized. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating how medical competence behaves under extreme model compression.

Method: A fully open three-phase training pipeline: (1) general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, (2) domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb (a reference-guided medical corpus selected from general web data via embedding similarity to medical QA data), and (3) preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO).

Result: On context-grounded QA, MedLLM comes within 2.9pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines. On knowledge-recall QA, it stays near the floor on MedQA but significantly exceeds all 7B and sub-7B baselines on MedMCQA. This task-type dissociation is masked at 7B scale.

Conclusion: At sub-billion scale, medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type: context-grounded reasoning survives compression well, while knowledge-recall is limited by model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is only observable at small scales, highlighting a fundamental constraint of tiny models for closed-book medical knowledge.

Abstract: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

</details>


### [276] [A dataset of rated conceptual arguments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27499)
*Emery Cooper,Caspar Oesterheld,Linh Chi Nguyen,Alexander Kastner,Ethan Perez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a novel benchmark for evaluating large language models on "conceptual questions"—questions without verifiable ground truth where progress is made through reasoned debate—using a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts across topics from AI safety to politics, rated by six expert raters along dimensions like centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity, with proposed scoring functions and benchmarking of various models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs have shown rapid improvement on verifiable tasks (math, programming), little is known about their ability to reason about conceptual questions—questions lacking ground truth and consensus methodology but amenable to reasoned debate. The authors argue that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be assessed far more reliably, motivating a new evaluation approach.

Method: The authors construct a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts spanning philosophy-relevant topics (AI safety, decision theory, ethics, politics). Six expert raters provided 1,458 ratings along four dimensions: centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. Two scoring functions are proposed to aggregate these ratings, and a range of LLMs are benchmarked against the dataset.

Result: The benchmark reveals that model performance on evaluating conceptual arguments tracks general capability rankings—i.e., stronger overall models perform better on this task, suggesting that reasoning about conceptual debates correlates with general model capabilities rather than requiring specialized adaptation.

Conclusion: This work provides a principled framework for evaluating LLM reasoning on conceptual questions by decomposing them into evaluable argument-level components, offering a benchmark that could guide progress on AI safety, decision theory, and other domains where verifiable answers are unavailable.

Abstract: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

</details>


### [277] [Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27518)
*Jeff Mohl,Nelson Gardner-Challis,Magda Dubois,Harry Coppock,Benjamin Allan-Rahill,Kaelan Yim,Damian Sójka,James Mann,Justin Olive*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The authors developed automated "AI scanners" to detect four types of validity issues (ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity) in agentic benchmark transcripts, evaluated them against human labels on Inspect Evals benchmarks, and found they surfaced verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, though performance varied and several challenges remain for broader quality assurance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual audits of agentic benchmarks like SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered validity issues, but manual review does not scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably identify flaws that compromise benchmark validity.

Method: Developed AI scanners targeting four validity issue types: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. Created grading rubrics for each type to guide human labeling, then evaluated scanner performance against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks.

Result: Scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. However, not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria, and models. Open challenges include standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance.

Conclusion: Automated transcript analysis can serve as a proof of concept for auditing benchmark quality at scale, but improvements are needed—particularly addressing standardization gaps—to enable stronger quality assurance claims.

Abstract: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

</details>


### [278] [AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27547)
*Brady D. Lund,Zoë Abbie Teel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper redefines AI literacy as a critical practice that fosters epistemic agency, moving beyond technical competency and responsible-use frameworks. Drawing on Foucault, Freire, and digital literacy scholarship, it proposes a three-part framework—contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance—to equip individuals to evaluate, resist, and shape AI systems rather than merely consume them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI literacy frameworks are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles that enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI, failing to foster genuine epistemic agency among users.

Method: A theoretical reconceptualization grounded in Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, synthesized into a three-part framework comprising contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance.

Result: A reconceptualized AI literacy framework that addresses structural epistemic inequities and positions individuals as epistemic agents rather than competent consumers of AI-generated information.

Conclusion: AI literacy must be reoriented from consumer training toward empowerment, accounting for unequal access to AI tools and enabling individuals to critically evaluate, resist, and participate in the governance of AI systems.

Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

</details>


### [279] [Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27553)
*Lennart Meincke,Karan Girotra,Gideon Nave,Christian Terwiesch,Karl T. Ulrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper compares AI-generated (GPT-4) new product ideas against human-generated ideas for products targeting college students under $50. AI ideas outperform human ideas in average purchase intent and are seven times more likely to rank in the top 10%, but are perceived as less novel and more similar to each other, particularly with few-shot prompting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether large language models can effectively generate high-quality new product ideas, and to understand the trade-offs between AI and human creativity in the context of new product development.

Method: Three idea pools were compared: (1) human-generated ideas from university students in a product design course, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot generated ideas, and (3) GPT-4 few-shot generated ideas. Quality was assessed via standard market research techniques predicting average purchase intent probability, text mining for idea similarity, and human raters for novelty evaluation.

Result: AI-generated ideas outperformed human ideas in average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting slightly better than zero-shot. However, AI ideas were perceived as less novel and exhibited higher pairwise similarity. AI ideas were seven times more likely to rank in the top 10% of ideas, a conservative estimate that doesn't account for AI's greater productivity.

Conclusion: Despite lower novelty and diversity, AI creativity provides a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development, suggesting LLMs can serve as valuable tools in ideation despite certain limitations.

Abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

</details>


### [280] [Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27556)
*Phuc Pham,Truong-Son Hy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework to assess the scientific credibility of LLM-based biological agents by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory—rather than architecture or final output—as the primary unit of analysis. The authors apply FEV to map 109 agentic systems and 28 benchmark resources across 128 publications spanning genomics, single-cell/spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics. They find that planning and tool-mediated execution have outpaced replayability, provenance, validation, and prospective testing, and argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed via workflow correctness, not final-answer correctness alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing reviews of biological agents organize systems by application, architecture, and capability but fail to jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. Fluent responses, successful tool calls, and strong benchmark performance do not sufficiently establish scientific credibility, motivating a new framework centered on the inspectable workflow trajectory.

Method: The authors propose the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework, which decomposes agent assessment into three dimensions: demonstrated workflow operations (Function), traceable support for actions and claims (Evidence), and use-case-specific validation (Validation). They apply FEV to systematically map 109 agentic/agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark/evaluation resources across 128 unique publications spanning six bioinformatics domains.

Result: Across all domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. This asymmetric development reveals a critical gap between technical fluency and scientific accountability in agentic bioinformatics.

Conclusion: Agentic bioinformatics should be evaluated through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and for designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

</details>


### [281] [DeepResearch Agent System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27562)
*Yong Huang,Yulu Huang,for the team Collaboration*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeepResearch Agent System is a sparse-activation LLM (30B total, 3B activated per token) designed for deep information retrieval and autonomous research, achieving state-of-the-art results on agent benchmarks with 3.2x faster inference, 128K context with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning (ReAct and IterResearch), multi-tool coordination, GRPO-based RL optimization, and an automated data synthesis pipeline. It is fully open-sourced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To build an efficient, capable large language model system specialized for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks that overcomes the limitations of dense models in terms of inference speed, long-context handling, and iterative reasoning capability.

Method: The system employs: (1) sparse activation architecture (30B total, 3B activated) for efficiency; (2) 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention; (3) dual-mode reasoning engine combining ReAct for basic tasks and IterResearch for iterative deep research with up to 20 steps; (4) multi-tool coordination for retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing; (5) GRPO-based reinforcement learning with token-level policy gradients; (6) automated data synthesis via seed-based expansion.

Result: Achieves 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. Demonstrates 3.2x faster inference than dense counterparts, 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches, 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines, 92.1% tool-use accuracy, 35% training stability improvement, 42% faster convergence, and 92.5% data usability rate.

Conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System demonstrates that sparse activation combined with hierarchical attention, dual-mode reasoning, and GRPO-based optimization can deliver state-of-the-art agentic search and research performance while maintaining computational efficiency, and is fully open-sourced to support academic, business, R&D, and educational applications.

Abstract: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

</details>


### [282] [What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27578)
*Sandeco Macedo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a formal, operational definition of "prompt graph engineering" — treating prompts as nodes in explicit, executable, improvable graphs — through conceptual analysis of persistent sources and grey literature. It reconstructs the genealogy of the idea, states four constitutive conditions, provides an inclusion/exclusion test validated against six real systems, and outlines a research agenda along four design tension axes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While industry practice has converged on graphs (e.g., LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow) to structure prompt-driven systems, the vocabulary lags behind: "prompt engineering" still implies writing a single string, and terms like "graph" ambiguously refer to reasoning topologies, multi-agent conversations, or orchestration artifacts. There is no reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable graph.

Method: Conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. The authors reconstruct the genealogy from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and thought topologies (chain/tree/graph), to compiled and optimized graph artifacts. They then propose four constitutive conditions (explicit structure, separation of structure and content, executable semantics, graph as first-class artifact) operationalized as an inclusion/exclusion test applied to six real systems.

Result: The paper produces an operational definition and inclusion/exclusion test that consistently includes and excludes the six examined systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents), and it delineates boundaries against six neighboring concepts.

Conclusion: The contribution is an operational definition and shared vocabulary for prompt graph engineering — a practice industry already exercises daily but lacks precise terminology for. The paper closes with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes.

Abstract: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

</details>


### [283] [From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27579)
*Oliver Guidetti,Reza Ryan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study adapted the Implicit Association Test to examine whether ChatGPT (GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, GPT-4T) exhibits sentiment differences across racial categories in open-ended text. Using 126 prompts crossed with eight racial categories and a control, the authors found only a small, analysis-dependent main effect of racial condition (partial-eta squared = .044) that did not survive rank-transformed sensitivity analysis or Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons. Evidence for sentiment differences was weak and the authors argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit complex, non-linear decision-making that is difficult to interpret, yet they are increasingly used in government and healthcare. Psychological methods developed to probe unobservable mental processes may help detect and measure bias in LLM behaviour, particularly subtle racial sentiment differences in open-ended text generation.

Method: Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 responses). Sentiment was scored via categorical labels and source scores (positive labels kept source score, negative labels negated, neutral coded zero). A two-way ANOVA plus a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, Tukey-corrected comparisons, and post hoc analysis were performed.

Result: A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044; no model effect or interaction was found. The effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis (F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145), and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant but post hoc and hypothesis-generating only.

Conclusion: Evidence for sentiment differences across racial conditions in ChatGPT was weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by prompts. The authors outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

</details>


### [284] [Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27598)
*Jason Lo,Mohammadnima Jafari*

Main category: cs.AI
