TL;DR: This paper presents a theory of gluing wiring diagrams that enables iterative (incremental) Hasse clustering to be applied to sequential data, overcoming the combinatorial explosion that occurs when the number of expected clusters grows. The approach is validated on figure skating jump video classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hasse clustering is a useful algorithm for extracting common patterns in sequential data, but it becomes computationally infeasible due to combinatorial complexity as the number of expected clusters increases. The authors aim to make the algorithm scalable.

Method: The authors develop a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, which allows Hasse clustering to be applied iteratively (in smaller, manageable steps) while producing the same result as a single monolithic application. This decomposes the problem to avoid combinatorial blow-up.

Result: The proposed iterative approach via gluing wiring diagrams is tested in the domain of classifying videos of figure skating jumps, demonstrating the practical utility and correctness of the theory.

Conclusion: The theory of gluing wiring diagrams enables scalable, iterative Hasse clustering that matches the result of a single application, making the method feasible for larger cluster counts and real-world sequential data classification tasks.

Abstract: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

</details>


### [285] [World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27599)
*Xiangcheng Zhang,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: World Action Planner is a robot planning system combining Vision-Language Models for reasoning with a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model for physical grounding, enabling agents to propose and iteratively refine action plans via optimization and search over imagined rollouts, outperforming end-to-end policies like VLAs and WAMs in compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments but fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks, limiting their applicability across diverse real-world applications.

Method: The system combines VLM reasoning capabilities with a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. It proposes initial action plans and iteratively refines them through optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts.

Result: Superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs.

Conclusion: Combining VLM-based reasoning with physically grounded world model rollouts enables better generalization for robot planning compared to end-to-end policy models.

Abstract: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

</details>


### [286] [CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27615)
*Yunfeng Zhao,Qingfeng Chen,Yue Tan,Shiyuan Li,Yili Wang,Yixin Liu,Shirui Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes CORE, an in-context reconstruction approach for unified tabular anomaly detection that aligns heterogeneous features via a decorrelated feature alignment module and reconstructs samples using contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified tabular anomaly detection faces two key challenges: (1) aligning heterogeneous data across datasets often relies on distance-based unified feature construction that obscures original feature semantics, and (2) formulating anomaly detection as binary classification overlooks diverse anomaly patterns and may be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies.

Method: CORE introduces two modules: (1) a decorrelated feature alignment module that directly aligns heterogeneous features into a unified representation space while preserving semantic information, and (2) an in-context reconstruction module that reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, where reconstruction errors indicate deviation from normality.

Result: The proposed method enables unified tabular anomaly detection on arbitrary unseen datasets without requiring labeled or synthesized anomaly samples, using reconstruction errors derived from contextual normal samples as the anomaly signal.

Conclusion: By formulating unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem with decorrelated feature alignment, CORE addresses the limitations of existing distance-based alignment and binary classification approaches, offering a more robust and generalizable solution for unified tabular anomaly detection.

Abstract: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

</details>


### [287] [Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27617)
*SiYuan Ma,Yiqin Luo,Zhangji,Canran Xiao,Albert Gao,Wei-Hsing Huang,Wei Wang,Qiwei Wu,Xinran Li,Jinfeng Wei,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "forked futures," a method for probing latent-language-model interfaces by sampling future operations after a prefix state forms and comparing states through induced response distributions. It derives an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without researcher-specified labels, and evaluates four interface hypotheses (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) under prequential causal description length. Shared interfaces win in held-out description length on Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3-8B, survive a five-backbone sweep, dominate transplantation analyses, and recover 14/16 organisms in a blind four-class test, supporting an economical reusable causal interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current-answer probes only establish correlations between hidden states and outputs, not reusable internal interfaces—two states can produce identical answers yet support different future computations. The authors want a causal, empirical method for mapping the functional structure of hidden states without relying on researcher-annotated latent labels, enabling principled comparison of interface architectures.

Method: The paper samples future operations only after a prefix state forms ("forked futures"), then compares hidden states by the response distributions these operations induce. This constructs an empirical causal quotient over states. Four interface models—Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed—compete under prequential causal description length with constraints on future-signature fidelity and matched capacity. Evaluations include detailed model analysis, a five-backbone sweep, figure-aligned transplantation analysis, and a blind four-class model-organism test.

Result: Shared interfaces achieve the lowest held-out description length: gains of 0.216 nats (Qwen2.5-1.5B) and 0.294 nats (Llama-3-8B) over alternatives while keeping mean future-signature distortion tightly clustered. The five-backbone sweep retains a positive Sharedness Gain direction. Transplantation analysis shows Shared has the strongest joint profile across target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite measures; API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for null paths. In the blind test, 14/16 architectures are correctly recovered, with one non-Shared-to-Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms.

Conclusion: The results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, but the claim is explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures examined. The forked-futures framework offers a label-free causal methodology for characterizing internal interface structure in language models.

Abstract: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

</details>


### [288] [SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27630)
*Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet,Nguyen Huu Duc,Le Cong Bang,Tran Cong Dao,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE is a general framework for black-box combinatorial optimization that learns a set of synthetic conditional objectives from search history to evolve diverse search policies, with an outer loop adaptively selecting objectives and an inner loop returning a portfolio of top policies, consistently improving search performance under limited evaluation budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In black-box combinatorial optimization, the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where to explore next under a limited evaluation budget, making it difficult to systematically identify high-quality solutions.

Method: SCOPE learns synthetic objectives conditioned on accumulated search history, where each objective exposes a distinct preference over candidate solutions. These objectives evolve search policies generating diverse candidates, which are assessed via black-box evaluations. An outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives based on effectiveness, while an inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to mitigate reliance on a single surrogate preference.

Result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

Conclusion: SCOPE reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces.

Abstract: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

</details>


### [289] [HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27636)
*Taewoo Park,Kyeonghyun Yoo,Kiseok Kim,Seunghyun Yoo,Hwangnam Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HALO is a runtime admission protocol for agentic AI systems that selectively preserves supported components from heterogeneous responses while rechecking actions before dispatch and enforcing dependency prerequisites.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems return heterogeneous responses containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions whose components may not remain mutually supported when conditions change before external use. Whole-response rejection discards useful components, while independent component checks can leave a dependent without its prerequisite.

Method: HALO (Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations) is a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates.

Result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay it retained 248/248 supported components (including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes) versus 0/248 for a whole-response policy. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

Conclusion: HALO provides a fine-grained admission control approach that substantially outperforms whole-response rejection, preserving useful supported components while ensuring stale or unsupported actions are blocked and recoverable.

Abstract: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

</details>


### [290] [ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27631)
*Zhenrong Zhang,Fei Wu,Jun Du,Jianshu Zhang,Si Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReDiPPO is a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework that improves mathematical reasoning in LLMs by using reference answers as privileged signals during training to provide more accurate token-level value estimates, and by quantifying the discrepancy between the reference-guided and standard critics to reweight token-level advantages at difficult reasoning states.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In mathematical reasoning tasks with long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, standard PPO critics fail to provide reliable token-level credit assignment because they cannot accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, leading to noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates.

Method: ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that leverages reference answers as training-time privileged signals for more accurate value estimation, while retaining a standard critic. The framework quantifies the token-level discrepancy between the standard and reference-guided value estimates, using this discrepancy as an indicator of difficult reasoning states to reweight token-level advantages during PPO optimization.

Result: Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.

Conclusion: Reference-guided value estimation combined with discrepancy-aware advantage reweighting significantly enhances token-level credit assignment in PPO for mathematical reasoning, establishing ReDiPPO as a superior alternative to existing policy optimization methods.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

</details>


### [291] [Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28187)
*Marco Alecci,Francesco Marchiori,Iyiola Emmanuel Olatunji,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé,Jacques Klein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates three commercial multimodal image-moderation APIs under simple, model-agnostic image transformations and finds all can be bypassed without gradients or knowledge of the target system, concluding that foundation-model-based moderation APIs are not a reliable standalone security boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional task-specific classifiers for content moderation offer limited policy coverage and contextual understanding. Commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models promise broader, more capable safety filters, but it is unclear whether this shift yields more robust image moderation.

Method: Large-scale black-box evaluation of three commercial image-moderation services using seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities.

Result: (1) All three commercial services can be bypassed via inexpensive transformations requiring no gradients, surrogate models, or target-system knowledge; (2) even fixed transformations like color inversion and grayscale cause unsafe-to-safe decision flips while content remains human-recognizable; (3) robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm showing pronounced vulnerabilities.

Conclusion: Replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not by itself provide a reliable security boundary. These systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

Abstract: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

</details>


### [292] [HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27635)
*Xiaotong Yu,Joshua Y. Kim,HaeJin Lee,Kalina Yacef*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HealthCAT is a framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token to provide class-specific, time-step-level interpretations of wearable sensor data. It outperforms deep learning baselines (up to 17% F1-score, 12% accuracy) on two real-world datasets (306 participants total), and its identified time steps carry significantly more predictive value than random selection in masking experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data prioritize predictive accuracy over interpretability, which limits their application in health research where understanding when and how behavioural patterns occur is critical.

Method: HealthCAT integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations that can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles (e.g., time-of-day) for individual-level analysis.

Result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy on both datasets (p<0.05). Masking experiments showed the identified time steps carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all conditions (p<0.05).

Conclusion: HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns by coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, enabling accurate health indicator prediction while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur.

Abstract: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

</details>


### [293] [Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27686)
*John L. Turner-Smith,Zimeng Huang,Yuhan Fu,Yihang Zhang,Tonghan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the challenge of measuring click-through intent for LLM-driven advertising by constructing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, distilling it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent and ad quality as differentiable estimates, then building a pricing mechanism on top of these estimates where truthful bidding is the unique optimal strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As search shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is embedded in generated responses and must be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is that click-through intent signals are unavailable: behavioral logs are missing, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. This creates a compounding problem where pricing requires a continuous intent signal, but generating such a signal requires supervision that does not exist.

Method: The authors construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework and distill it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent alongside three companion dimensions of ad quality as smooth, differentiable estimates. They then build a pricing layer on top of these estimates, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations.

Result: The evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalizes without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgments across five annotators, with agreement rising with evaluator confidence.

Conclusion: The differentiable intent signal generated by the evaluator enables principled pricing through a derived payment rule where truthful bidding is optimal, and also stands ready as a training objective for ad generation, closing the loop between evaluation, pricing, and generation in LLM-driven advertising.

Abstract: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

</details>


### [294] [Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27687)
*Jiazhen Ji,Shouhong Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies the "confidence cliff" in autoresearch loops—where an LLM judge's ability to predict whether a code modification will improve the metric degrades substantially as successful changes accumulate (selective accuracy dropping from 82.8% to 56.9%). The authors introduce Rehearse, a lightweight skill that proposes multiple ideas, compares them before execution, and uses a focused memory of similar past attempts. This raises late-loop selective accuracy to 83.5% and improves endpoint performance across 4,000 budgeted training runs on three benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In autoresearch—an iterative loop that proposes machine-learning code changes, runs full training jobs, and keeps improvements—efficiency depends on judging whether a modification is likely to work before spending a training run. The authors investigate how reliable this pre-execution judgment is and find it degrades sharply late in the loop ("confidence cliff"), motivating a method to counteract this decline.

Method: The authors first analyze public AutoSOTA logs showing the fraction of helpful modifications drops from 70% (first two iterations) to 43% (iteration 6+). They construct a 366-pair benchmark from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks where each pair contains one beneficial and one harmful modification, with outcomes hidden, and measure an LLM judge's selective accuracy. They then introduce Rehearse, a loop skill that proposes several ideas, compares them before execution, runs the most promising, and judges using a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes to improve late-loop accuracy.

Result: The LLM judge reaches 79.5% accuracy on strict-consensus pairs without prior-attempt history. However, late in the loop, selective accuracy falls from 82.8% to 56.9% while the judge remains confident—the confidence cliff. Rehearse's focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

Conclusion: Pre-execution judgment of code modifications in autoresearch exhibits a "confidence cliff"—accuracy degrades while confidence persists as successful changes accumulate. A lightweight skill (Rehearse) that incorporates focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes restores late-loop accuracy and improves overall autoresearch efficiency, suggesting that outcome memory is crucial for sustaining the quality of idea selection in iterative ML research loops.

Abstract: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

</details>


### [295] [Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27698)
*Yuan Tian,Yi Mei,Mengjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a novel reverse-direction knowledge transfer framework where knowledge extracted from genetic programming (GP)-evolved priority rules is used to guide an online large language model (LLM) decision maker in dynamic multi-mode project scheduling. Four injection mechanisms (Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, Rule Follow) are evaluated, showing that GP-derived guidance improves LLM scheduling performance, stability, and rationale quality, with Feature Selection being most token-efficient and Rule Follow achieving the strongest performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs provide a flexible interface for scheduling decisions but suffer from lack of domain knowledge, high token consumption, and decision variability in zero-shot settings. Meanwhile, GP hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve high-quality scheduling rules but require domain expertise to design. The authors propose using GP-evolved rules as a source of scheduling knowledge to guide LLMs, reversing the typical LLM-GP hybrid direction where LLMs support heuristic evolution.

Method: The authors extract knowledge from high-quality GP-evolved priority rules and inject it into an online LLM decision maker through four mechanisms: (1) Feature Selection - simplifying the decision context by selecting key features; (2) Feature Hint - highlighting important features to the LLM; (3) Rule Reference - referencing GP rules as context; and (4) Rule Follow - supplying explicit decision logic from GP rules for the LLM to follow. These are evaluated on scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and feature focus in generated rationales.

Result: GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but representation matters. Simplifying the decision context (Feature Selection) or supplying explicit decision logic (Rule Follow) is more effective than merely highlighting important features (Feature Hint). Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, while Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

Conclusion: Knowledge transferred from GP-evolved rules can effectively guide LLM decision-making in dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, with the representation of that knowledge being critical to its effectiveness. The findings provide practical guidance on how to structure GP-derived knowledge for LLM integration, balancing performance, token efficiency, and decision stability.

Abstract: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

</details>


### [296] [SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27703)
*Yang Zhou,Zixuan Huang,Sunzhu Li,Zhuo Yang,Chen Zhang,Shunian Chen,Caijun Yan,Jianyao Xu,Shunyu Liu,Weijie Fu,Peiliang Li,Xiaozhi Chen,Yuxiang Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpatialCLI is a three-stage framework (Call, Learn, Internalize) that teaches vision-language models to use specialist spatial vision tools and progressively internalize their perceptual capabilities, raising Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% on MindCube and introducing a 516-example benchmark (SpatialCLI-Bench) for compositional spatial perception.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General VLMs can reason about overall tasks but miss critical visual details, while specialist vision models capture details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. This capability mismatch limits VLM performance in embodied agents that require both high-level reasoning and precise spatial perception.

Method: SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models (localization, segmentation, depth, pose) as spatial tools to augment VLM perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start Supervised Fine-Tuning and agentic Reinforcement Learning to improve tool use; (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to progressively internalize specialist perceptual capabilities into the VLM without external tools.

Result: On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization. A new benchmark, SpatialCLI-Bench, with 516 examples covering localization, segmentation, depth, and pose is introduced.

Conclusion: SpatialCLI demonstrates that VLMs can effectively leverage specialist spatial tools and progressively internalize those capabilities, achieving strong performance both with and without tool access, suggesting a promising paradigm for bridging general reasoning and specialist perception in embodied agents.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

</details>


### [297] [Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27705)
*Ting Gong,Michael Ruofan Zeng,Yong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Albilich is an open-source agentic harness for mathematical autoresearch that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management. It solves 10/10 RealMath problems with CAS, 9/10 without, produces a counterexample to Kourovka Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem 20.2, and demonstrates 32.0% token reduction with CAS enabled.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, but long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce.

Method: The system integrates long-horizon reasoning agents, computer algebra system support, literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management in an open-source agentic harness. It includes an advisor agent and enables human steerability.

Result: Albilich solved 10/10 RealMath problems with CAS and 9/10 without CAS. On Kourovka open problems, it produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem 20.2. Ablations showed 32.0% token reduction with CAS enabled, and demonstrated that removing the advisor agent leads to higher verifier-rejection rates and failure to synthesize proof routes.

Conclusion: Albilich serves as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

Abstract: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

</details>


### [298] [MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27709)
*Wentao Long,Yunfei Zhang,Chenyi Li,Zaiwen Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MECA is a multi-agent framework that constructs mathematical conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms, transforming broad research directions into precise, well-specified conjectures with substantive mathematical support that remain challenging for automated provers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many existing open problems and conjectures are too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies, making automated mathematical conjecture construction a central challenge.

Method: MECA uses a multi-agent framework where Explorer agents propose mechanisms (inequalities, invariants, decompositions, or reductions) and test their applicability while revising candidate conjectures, and Critic agents assess mathematical validity and research value. Feedback iteratively guides changes to assumptions, scope, and conclusion.

Result: MECA was evaluated in two settings: (1) reconstructing target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials versus a generate-and-revise baseline; (2) constructing 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and evaluating them via independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Mechanism-centered refinement produced well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

Conclusion: Mechanism-centered refinement is effective at producing well-specified and research-worthy mathematical conjectures that remain unresolved and challenging for current automated proving systems.

Abstract: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

</details>


### [299] [New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27720)
*Francisco Requena-Domínguez,Rafaela Benítez-Rochel,Ezequiel López-Rubio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a new synchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks, called SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter), which updates multiple neurons simultaneously per time step to reduce processing time while guaranteeing convergence and maximizing energy decrease at each step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The original Hopfield network uses asynchronous (sequential) updates, processing only one neuron per time step, which is slow. The authors aim to reduce processing time by enabling simultaneous updates of multiple neurons while maintaining convergence guarantees.

Method: The authors introduce a new tool called Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) to solve the combinatorial optimization problem of determining the next network state that yields the maximum energy decrease while ensuring convergence. Based on this tool, they develop the SD-DDF synchronous dynamics that updates one or more neurons simultaneously per time step.

Result: The paper provides theoretical justification for the new synchronous dynamics and presents four computational experiments to empirically assess the speed-up in processing time compared to the original asynchronous dynamics.

Conclusion: The proposed SD-DDF synchronous dynamics offers a faster alternative to the original asynchronous Hopfield network by leveraging simultaneous neuron updates that guarantee convergence while maximizing energy decrease at each step.

Abstract: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

</details>


### [300] [Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27726)
*Dhruv Agarwal,Rishitha Guttapalle Mohan,Aarti Kumari,Ashi Sinha,Athulya Anil,Kavitha Srinivas,Horst Samulowitz,Andrew McCallum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Baikal is a framework that frames deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem, clustering heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and adaptively balancing exploration and exploitation via policies like Bayesian ε-greedy and UCB, improving report quality by 28-36% over strong baselines on HybridQA and TAT-QA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent methods for deep research over data lakes perform iterative retrieval and generation where accumulated context determines next steps, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget.

Method: Baikal (1) clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, (2) treats research as budgeted search over these regions, (3) generates region-grounded subquestions within selected regions, (4) uses finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates, and (5) guides search using policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian ε-greedy and UCB.

Result: Evaluated on 15 queries each over HybridQA (10,993 tables) and TAT-QA (2,757 tables) with 227K Wikipedia and 13K financial passages, Baikal's best configuration improves report scores by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA over the strongest baselines (DeepSearcher and OpenCode research agent variants). Analysis attributes gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, improving groundedness and diversity with more useful findings under the same subquestion budget.

Conclusion: Structured semantic exploration over clustered evidence regions is valuable for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes, outperforming context-driven iterative retrieval approaches.

Abstract: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

</details>


### [301] [VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27733)
*Changguo Jia,Tianqi Zhao,Zhiyou Xiao,Weiming Zhang,Minghui Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for LLM-agent-based program verification that attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills—accepting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. It outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires reusable skills for generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations. While skill self-evolution (distilling and refining skills from trajectories) is a natural remedy, existing methods fail on program verification because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback.

Method: VeriSkill (1) attributes verification failures to specific skill deficiencies, (2) distills diagnostic signatures from failures into reusable lessons, and (3) iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that demonstrably improve verification performance while preserving program semantics.

Result: VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

Conclusion: VeriSkill effectively addresses the limitations of prior self-evolution methods in program verification by providing reliable failure attribution and actionable feedback extraction, leading to consistent improvements across diverse verification settings.

Abstract: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

</details>


### [302] [SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27788)
*Yixuan Chen,Bo Liu,Yusen Tan,Guokun Yang,Wenjie Du,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpecCal is a training-free, model-agnostic candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction that improves molecular reconstruction by re-ranking candidate molecules and introducing structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency, without requiring parameter updates to base models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inferring molecular structures from IR spectra is fundamentally ambiguous because different molecules can share similar functional groups and vibrational patterns, producing highly similar spectra. Existing IR-to-molecule models generate ranked candidate sets that reflect the model's learned generation preference rather than fully covering structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints, limiting reconstruction accuracy.

Method: SpecCal is a plug-and-play, training-free framework that operates on candidate outputs from existing base models. It improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while adding structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework requires no parameter updates and is model-agnostic.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models, demonstrating that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity is a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra.

Conclusion: Candidate-set calibration under spectral ambiguity provides a practical and effective approach to improving molecular reconstruction from IR spectra, offering a plug-and-play enhancement compatible with diverse base models.

Abstract: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

</details>


### [303] [Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27792)
*Subinay Adhikary,Dwaipayan Roy,Debasis Ganguly,Shouvik Kumar Guha,Kripabandhu Ghosh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces LeDA, a web-based Legal Data Annotation system designed to annotate and adjudicate concepts within legal case proceedings. It allows dynamic creation of new tags when no pre-defined ontology exists, enabling annotators to discover concepts as they review documents. The system was used by three assessors to annotate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings, producing bag-of-concepts representations for downstream tasks like prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal documents benefit from structured representations (bags of concepts) over flat bag-of-words text representations to enhance processing. The paper aims to find concepts/topics from legal case proceedings and support scenarios where no pre-defined ontology of concepts exists, requiring dynamic discovery during annotation.

Method: LeDA is a web-based system providing generic annotation and adjudication of entities/concepts within documents. A key feature is the dynamic creation of new annotation tags, allowing annotators to discover and define concepts on-the-fly while examining more documents. The system was applied by three assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

Result: LeDA successfully supported annotation of legal concepts from Indian Supreme Court proceedings, producing semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts suitable for downstream tasks such as prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.

Conclusion: LeDA demonstrates an effective approach for legal data annotation, especially in domains lacking pre-defined ontologies, by enabling dynamic concept discovery. The resulting concept-based document representations can facilitate various legal NLP downstream applications.

Abstract: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

</details>


### [304] [MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27798)
*Weihang Wang,Kainan Tu,Jielei Zhang,Run Yang,Boheng Sheng,Yuchen He,Yu Xie,Pengyu Chen,Peiyi Li,Huyang Sun,Longwen Gao,Zhouhui Lian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemeBench is a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with VIKR annotations (Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, Reasoning mechanisms). Across 26 LVLMs, all models perform better on visible content than on background knowledge, with the strongest model retaining a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. The paper introduces KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase that improves VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% across four controlled models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate image descriptions do not guarantee correct meme interpretation, since memes rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions that go beyond pixels. Existing meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, which obscures exactly where an explanation breaks down.

Method: The paper introduces MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. VIKR decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. They also propose KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase, and evaluate across 26 LVLMs.

Result: Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and the strongest model still retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% across four controlled models and repairs more answers while breaking fewer compared to generic retrieval. However, both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison.

Conclusion: MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap, serving as a diagnostic tool that tests if and how LVLM meme comprehension can be improved through targeted retrieval.

Abstract: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

</details>


### [305] [STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27824)
*Farane Jalali Farahani,Corina Dima,Mojtaba Nayyeri,Raphael H. Heiberger,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STEREODISCO is a framework that adapts the semantic differential method to systematically discover and recover stereotypical semantic axes in LLM internal representations, using ~2,000 WordNet antonym-derived axes probed in activation space. Applied to social group stereotypes in LLAMA-3-8B and MISTRAL-7B, it finds LLMs agree more with each other than with humans on social group ratings, and uncovers novel stereotypical axes (e.g., humble vs. proud, cowardly vs. brave) not previously studied, which human annotators confirm.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior computational research on stereotypes in LLMs focuses on a small set of semantic axes from social psychology and only operates on word embeddings, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes.

Method: STEREODISCO constructs ~2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes using a statistical test over concept projections. A case study applies it to social group stereotypes in LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT.

Result: The two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, indicating LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from social psychology documentation. The framework also discovers stereotypical axes not previously investigated, including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

Conclusion: STEREODISCO enables systematic, scalable discovery of stereotypical semantic axes in LLM internal representations, revealing that LLM stereotype content diverges from human-documented stereotypes while also surfacing novel axes that humans validate.

Abstract: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

</details>


### [306] [Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27826)
*Shiwei Gan,Lichen Wang,Xiao Liu,Yafeng Yin,Kuizhuang Liu,Sanglu Lu,Lei Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA), a new task that evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. The authors construct two SignQA benchmarks (based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily) covering five question categories, and propose a baseline model with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and in-domain knowledge transfer, which outperforms representative vision-language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SL understanding tasks (continuous SL recognition and SL translation) use predefined objectives with fixed mappings from videos to glosses or sentences, providing only limited assessment of whether a model truly comprehends the semantic content of SL videos. A more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework is needed.

Method: The paper (1) proposes the new SLQA task; (2) constructs two SignQA benchmarks from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily using template-based automatic generation of question-answer pairs from existing gloss/sentence annotations, covering five question categories (position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, translation understanding); (3) proposes a baseline with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy.

Result: Extensive experiments show the proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all five question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future SLQA research.

Conclusion: SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework for sign language understanding, and the constructed benchmarks and baseline establish a solid foundation for future research in this direction.

Abstract: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA.
