Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

</details>


### [307] [MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27834)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Fanshuai Meng,Qianli Ma,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTxn is a governance layer for persistent memory in LLM agents that provides transaction boundaries for memory updates, using Ordered PatchTest for validation, a Temporal Resolver for version selection, and a durable snapshot journal for fault recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory in long-running LLM agents enables reuse across sessions, but errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems focus on storage and retrieval but lack a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery.

Method: MemTxn is a governance layer external to the answer model. It verifies whether an update is supported by its source, selects the visible version when facts conflict via a Temporal Resolver, and restores application-visible state after faults using a durable snapshot journal. It uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes.

Result: On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it fully restores the declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, it achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations, outperforming Dense by 17.06-24.07 points in five representative settings.

Conclusion: MemTxn demonstrates that adding a governance/transaction layer for persistent memory improves reliability and performance of LLM agents, enabling accurate fact consolidation and fault recovery while being model-agnostic.

Abstract: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

</details>


### [308] [Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27836)
*Xiangyu Yin,Jiaxu Liu,Zhen Chen,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Large language model unlearning is fragile under relearn attacks, and the paper traces this to a "margin cliff" where post-hoc unlearning methods converge to a narrow per-token answer-margin band above the retain reference due to token-saturating losses. The authors prove this cliff follows from retain coupling, propose Margin Calibration (MC) as a plug-in polish that restores forget-side pressure via a non-saturating margin hinge and KL probe, and demonstrate that a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and reduces post-attack ROUGE-L from 0.41 to 0.18 across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing large language model unlearning methods are consistently fragile under relearn attacks—fine-tuning on just twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set performance for every evaluated method. The paper aims to understand this systematic fragility and develop a solution that is robust to relearn attacks.

Method: The paper analyzes the optimization geometry of unlearning, identifying a "margin cliff" where 41 of 42 method-size cells converge to a narrow per-token answer-margin band. It proves this cliff follows from retain coupling and token-saturating losses at stationarity. The proposed Margin Calibration (MC) is a plug-in polish that adds a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus. A gradient-dominance condition with an on-trajectory signature is stated, and its stationary set is shown to lie on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on relearn margin lift.

Result: Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen MC configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells, reducing panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L from 0.41 to 0.18. It lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14 cells, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant achieves the same gains without a retain-trained reference.

Conclusion: The margin cliff is a fundamental cause of unlearning fragility under relearn attacks, and Margin Calibration effectively addresses it by restoring forget-side pressure where native losses saturate. The method is robust across diverse model sizes and benchmarks with a single configuration, though reduced retain-side utility remains the primary trade-off.

Abstract: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

</details>


### [309] [Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27840)
*Lukas Kubelka,Alexander Bott,Frank Döhner,Saksham Kiroriwal,Georg Zeeb,Julia Butte,Julius Pfrommer,Jürgen Beyerer,Tobias Käfer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that captures workflow provenance for multi-stage manufacturing. It makes datasets FAIR and distinguishes data generated during individual workflow steps, with contributions including an ontology, a provenance framework, and a user interface.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Downstream AI-based optimization tasks in multi-stage manufacturing require the ability to distinguish between datasets generated during individual workflow steps, yet existing data catalogues do not capture this level of workflow provenance explicitly.

Method: VPD consists of three components: (1) a VPD ontology serving as the semantic core of the catalogue; (2) a provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) a user interface providing human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. Both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance are made explicit, and datasets are provided in a FAIR manner.

Result: The paper reports the development of VPD and makes the ontology and code publicly available at the provided GitHub repository, though specific quantitative evaluation results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: VPD addresses the need for FAIR data cataloguing with integrated workflow provenance in multi-stage manufacturing, enabling AI-based downstream optimization through explicit prospective and retrospective provenance tracking.

Abstract: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

</details>


### [310] [Simplifying Neural Networks During Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27854)
*Lorenzo Sciandra,Samuele Fonio,Roberto Esposito*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper combines Neural Collapse and Tunnel Effect insights to propose a training framework that simplifies deep networks by monitoring representation dynamics via the Inverse Fisher Criterion, identifying the optimal split point between feature extraction and classification, and replacing trailing layers with a lightweight head. Results across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show substantial parameter reduction with maintained accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding the training dynamics of overparameterized deep networks remains challenging; the authors aim to bridge the Neural Collapse and Tunnel Effect perspectives to achieve network simplification during training without sacrificing performance.

Method: The framework monitors representation dynamics using the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a proxy for variability collapse, to identify (1) the split point between feature extraction and classification layers and (2) the training stage at which simplification is viable. Trailing layers are then replaced with a lightweight classification head and training continues on the reduced model.

Result: Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures demonstrate substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the full model.

Conclusion: The proposed NC-inspired framework enables efficient network simplification during training by exploiting geometric structure in representation dynamics, offering a practical approach to reduce model complexity without significant accuracy loss.

Abstract: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

</details>


### [311] [Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27861)
*Minwoo Yu,Young-guk Ha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Negative sampling in continuous-time dynamic graph link prediction benchmarks is not neutral: the choice of negative distribution and candidate-set size changes model rankings and measured ablation effects. The authors recommend all-entity ranking over the full fixed destination catalog to eliminate sampler-induced bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard evaluation protocols for next-destination prediction in CTDGs rank observed interactions against a small set of sampled negative destinations. The authors demonstrate that this practice introduces uncontrolled variance and bias: non-uniform negative distributions shift the Bayes-optimal ranking, and even uniform sampling destabilizes model ordering and module-effect measurements.

Method: The authors (1) theoretically analyze how non-uniform negatives alter the Bayes-optimal ranking and how finite uniform candidate sets destabilize ranks; (2) construct a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership to expose the transmission mechanism; (3) run a factorial evaluation crossing repeated/new positives with seen/unseen negatives; (4) perform controlled representation interventions; (5) evaluate six models across LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia under Uniform-20 and full-catalog ranking.

Result: On three of four datasets, at least one model pair changes relative order between the Uniform-20 metric and full-catalog ranking. The measured effect of the same module changes in magnitude and direction depending on candidate-set size and training objective.

Conclusion: Model-superiority and ablation conclusions drawn from sampled-negative benchmarks are contingent on the candidate configuration. All-entity ranking over an enumerable fixed catalog eliminates negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original scorer, and is recommended as primary evidence for architecture comparisons on such benchmarks.

Abstract: Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

</details>


### [312] [Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27867)
*Gerrit Großmann,David A. Selby,Sebastian J. Vollmer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Orca extends structural causal models to continuous-time settings with irregular observations and feedback loops by using neural operator learning, where each causal node is a function of time and each mechanism maps between function spaces, enabling counterfactual reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard structural causal models only handle static variables, forbid cyclic dependencies, and cannot naturally represent systems that evolve continuously in time with irregular observation patterns and feedback loops, such as patients, climates, and economies.

Method: Orca proposes a framework where each node in the causal graph is a time-dependent function and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. Neural operator architectures are extended to express causal mechanisms by taking multiple parent functions as input, respecting temporal causality (arrow of time), and treating latent exogenous noise as an inferable function reusable for counterfactuals.

Result: The model class is formalized and counterfactual reasoning is demonstrated on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is released publicly.

Conclusion: Neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in continuous-time dynamical systems with feedback loops and irregular observations, enabling counterfactual queries in this setting.

Abstract: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

</details>


### [313] [Search as Computation Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27871)
*Alexander Tuisov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems, where computational resources are spent internally (producing observations that update beliefs) and matter only through terminal decision loss. It provides Bellman equation characterizations for optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification; connects value of computation (VOC) to information theory via mutual information and knowledge-gradient quantities; and demonstrates that maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A* as a special case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many algorithms consume computational resources internally (e.g., bandit pulls, tree simulations) but are only evaluated by the quality of their final output. There is no unified formal framework to characterize how computation should be allocated to minimize terminal decision loss across different computation topologies.

Method: The paper formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems and derives Bellman equations for optimal allocation under three settings: fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. It establishes theoretical relationships between value of computation (VOC) and information-theoretic quantities—showing mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss and that VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity under simple regret. It also provides a one-sided upper bound relating information gain to VOC. The framework is applied to bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions, and is shown to recover weighted A* (with A* and greedy best-first search as limits) under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Bellman equations characterize optimal computation allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification; (2) mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, but information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly under simple regret, while still providing a one-sided upper bound on VOC; (3) the framework unifies diverse computation topologies including bandits, trees, and node expansions; (4) maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A* with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases.

Conclusion: The framework identifies a shared decision problem underlying seemingly disparate acquisition rules (e.g., information gain, knowledge gradient, A*-style search) without claiming any single acquisition rule is universally optimal. It provides a unifying theoretical lens for computation allocation across different algorithm families.

Abstract: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

</details>


### [314] [An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27877)
*Yanyu Ren,Yunfeng Bai,Xizheng Wang,Li Chen,Dan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSEval is a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world, full-stack projects, featuring a LegoGent execution engine that tests 10 collaboration topologies with native CI/CD deployment, and a TAgent automated grader measuring functional success, latency, and cost. Results across 100 runs show organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping speed-cost-quality trade-offs, with structured pipelines performing best and heavy oversight degrading performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore real-world time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion rather than practical software development outcomes.

Method: MSEval evaluates multi-agent coding on 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains, scoring performance via hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. Its execution engine LegoGent tests 10 collaboration topologies with periodic sync intervals and native CI/CD pipelines, while the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost.

Result: Across 100 runs, varying collaboration topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time for identical tasks and models. Structured pipelines converge fastest with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance, demonstrating that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed-cost-quality trade-off.

Conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, addressing the gap between synthetic benchmarks and real-world software engineering practice.

Abstract: Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

</details>


### [315] [Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27888)
*Qiangqiang He,Zhongheng Wu,ZiJian Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether privileged self-teacher signals in on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provide reliable answer-aligned token-level supervision for long-CoT reasoning. The authors find that privileged shifts are unreliable as direction indicators and that their magnitudes reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than learning value. They propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a GRPO extension that downweights highly sensitive tokens, which consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline on long-CoT math reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Critic-free RL methods like GRPO broadcast response-level rewards uniformly across all tokens, ignoring unequal token contributions to the final outcome. OPSD provides dense distributional supervision via forward KL divergence against a privileged self-teacher, but implicitly assumes these likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. The authors aim to test this premise and develop a more principled token-level credit assignment method.

Method: The authors test OPSD's premise by re-scoring fixed sampled trajectories under two opposing outcome conditions (correct vs. incorrect) and analyzing token-level shift directions. They find limited sign reversals and that large shifts concentrate on substitutable surface-form tokens. Based on this diagnosis, they propose CSCR, which reduces credit for highly counterfactual-sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction.

Result: CSCR consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates on long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Targeted ablations confirm that privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

Conclusion: Privileged self-teacher shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned token-level directions, and their magnitudes reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. A simple credit reallocation based on this diagnosis—downweighting sensitive tokens while preserving the credit budget and direction—yields consistent gains over GRPO, validating a more conservative and interpretable approach to token-level credit assignment in RLVR.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

</details>


### [316] [Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27891)
*Yan Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), a temporal graph learning method that treats the spectral filter coefficients themselves as recurrent temporal states, allowing the graph propagation mechanism to evolve over time rather than just node states or interaction histories. DSF achieves competitive accuracy on three temporal link-prediction benchmarks while dramatically reducing parameter count, GPU memory, and training time compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal graph learning methods focus on evolving node states or encoding interaction histories, but overlook whether the graph propagation mechanism itself should evolve over time. The authors study this operator-centric question and propose that adapting the filter explicitly as a recurrent state may serve as a useful temporal inductive bias, especially when computational efficiency matters.

Method: DSF represents the propagation at snapshot t as a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These compact multi-order coefficients are explicitly treated as recurrent temporal states, updated by a recurrent branch while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate the magnitude of updates. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes, keeping the method scalable.

Result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs achieve AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K-133K trainable parameters, 68-182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6-2.1 seconds training per epoch. Compared to DEFT, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3-8.6x fewer parameters, 25-33x less GPU memory, and 5-19x less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3-38.6x less GPU memory.

Conclusion: Results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement. DSF demonstrates that evolving the propagation operator itself can be both accurate and highly parameter- and memory-efficient.

Abstract: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

</details>


### [317] [MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27895)
*Jinpeng Hu,Erqiang Wang,Shan Wang,Zhuo Li,Peipei Song,Xun Yang,Meng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MMHBench is a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding in long-form videos, featuring 268 videos and 2,184 questions across third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking settings. A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework synthesizes questions from diverse social roles, and evaluation of 22 MLLMs shows the task remains highly challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mental health understanding benchmarks reduce the task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. There is a need for a benchmark that evaluates nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states in long-form videos.

Method: The benchmark introduces two evaluation settings: (1) third-person assessment with 605 questions focusing on observable behaviors and multimodal evidence interpretation, and (2) first-person perspective-taking with 1,579 questions requiring perspective-conditioned reasoning. A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives, refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization with expert-guided verification.

Result: Evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

Conclusion: MMHBench reveals that current MLLMs struggle with nuanced, multi-perspective mental health understanding in long-form videos, highlighting a significant gap in existing models and providing a rigorous benchmark for future progress in this domain.

Abstract: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

</details>


### [318] [A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27910)
*Xiangyu Yin,Tora Bodin,Rohan Menon,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper compares five inference-time direction-based defences against VLM jailbreaks across 15 model-layer cells from four architectural families, using a magnitude-controlled protocol with random controls. No single defence dominates; image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B with minimal utility loss, prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, and attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction-specific but architecture-specific and non-transferable, and CMRM/text-only and image-conditioning refusal geometries show partial overlap (mean cosine 0.35).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously evaluate and compare candidate inference-time defence directions for VLM jailbreaks under a controlled protocol, and to understand whether text-only refusal geometry transfers to multimodal settings and across model families.

Method: Five defence candidates (mean image conditioning shift, CMRM-style refusal direction, ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, prompt instruction to ignore image, random control) are compared across 15 model-layer cells from four architectural families. A magnitude-controlled protocol matches intervention size per prompt and pairs each direction with a random control of identical norm. Refusal recovery and utility preservation are measured, and cosine alignment between CMRM and image-conditioning directions is analyzed.

Result: No single defence dominates both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B, with utility loss at the measurement noise floor in every family. Prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL; attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction-specific in 13/15 cells but architecture-specific and non-transferable between the only compatible pair (LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B). CMRM direction positively aligns with image conditioning shift in all 15 cells (mean 0.35, range 0.17-0.65, 15-25x random null, sign test p≈3e-5).

Conclusion: Direction-based defences recover partially overlapping geometry between text-only (CMRM) and multimodal (image conditioning) refusal mechanisms, but should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family due to architecture specificity and non-transferability.

Abstract: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

</details>


### [319] [IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27912)
*Yuetian Mao,Chunyang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IFHierBench is a new hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts across four constraint-tree depths and 35 constraints, each with deterministic scope-aware checkers. Evaluation of seven leading LLMs shows that even the strongest model barely exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, with accuracy sharply degrading as constraint depth increases, revealing that nested constraint following remains a major gap for current LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as a flat list applied uniformly to the entire response, failing to capture real-world scenarios where constraints are scoped to specific sections or nested fields of a structured output. This limits the ability to measure and improve fine-grained instruction-following ability in modern single-call LLM deployments.

Method: The authors construct IFHierBench, a benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints. Each prompt specifies a layered output (overall artifact, structural sections, nested fields) with constraints scoped to particular parts, paired with deterministic checkers that verify constraint satisfaction at every hierarchical scope. Seven proprietary and open-weight LLMs are evaluated on this benchmark.

Result: Even the strongest model among the seven evaluated only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy. Accuracy degrades sharply as constraint-tree depth increases, indicating a systematic failure in handling nested or scoped constraints.

Conclusion: Reliably following nested, scope-specific constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs. The findings motivate future training methods that account for constraint adherence at finer granularity to improve instruction-following capability.

Abstract: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

</details>


### [320] [One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27917)
*Enyi Shi,Fei Shen,Chuancheng Shi,Linxia Zhu,Shuyi Miao,Jinhui Tang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework that identifies modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons) in large vision-language models, and updates only ~0.03% of parameters to defend against compound multilingual and multimodal attacks while preserving general utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety defense methods for LVLMs isolate language and modality defenses, and suffer from scarce safety data and high fine-tuning costs, making it difficult to defend against compound attacks combining multilingual instructions and visual information.

Method: The framework works in four steps: (1) identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful vs. benign samples using activation strength and downstream impact; (2) intersect unimodal neurons within each language to extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) bridging visual and textual risks; (3) use English as a semantic anchor to intersect MS-Neurons across languages, yielding modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons); (4) update only this minimal neuron subset (~0.03% of parameters) to transfer English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios.

Result: Extensive experiments show the method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

Conclusion: The identified MLS-Neurons provide an efficient and effective cross-dimensional safety alignment for LVLMs, enabling defense against compound attacks with minimal parameter updates.

Abstract: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

</details>


### [321] [Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27929)
*Zhihong Pan,Jiyuan He,Kai Zhang,Yupeng Han,Ze Liu,Yuze Zhao,Yongcong Ye,Zhaohua Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Meta-Task is a framework that reframes terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself, where an agent iteratively generates, executes, and verifies tasks in a real container environment. This ensures internal consistency and executability within the generation loop. Fine-tuning on only 3,221 synthesized trajectories achieves state-of-the-art results on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively), outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality trajectories, but acquiring such data is challenging. Existing synthesis methods suffer from (1) weak reliability due to the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability from dependence on existing repositories.

Method: Meta-Task redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates in a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, ensuring components are checked for consistency and executability within the generation loop. It decouples task requirements across multiple dimensions, uses a multi-phase mechanism to dynamically design novel task specifications before producing tasks, incorporates optional external material support for diversity/realism, and applies LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure data quality.

Result: On Terminal-Bench 2.0, fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

Conclusion: Meta-Task demonstrates that treating task synthesis itself as a terminal task, with in-loop execution and verification, yields high-quality, diverse, and scalable training data for terminal agents, achieving competitive or superior performance with far fewer training trajectories.

Abstract: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

</details>


### [322] [The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27933)
*Ziyang Rao,Yiren Zhao,Weiyu Guo,Ben Fei,Yandong Guo,Hui Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes "denoising acceleration" (accel), a cost-free uncertainty proxy for Flow Matching-based action heads in embodied models. It measures the bending of the denoising trajectory in a single forward pass, based on a geometric interpretation that FM uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Accel matches or outperforms costly resampling- and training-based baselines in online failure detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow Matching does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks when it misinterprets scenes or encounters OOD inputs. Existing uncertainty estimation methods suffer from extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. Determining when FM-generated actions can be trusted is essential for safe deployment.

Method: Provides a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Introduces denoising acceleration (accel), a single-forward-pass uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling.

Result: Theoretically and empirically demonstrates that accel is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty. In online failure detection, accel identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or outperforming resampling- and training-based baselines under realistic deployment budgets.

Conclusion: Denoising acceleration provides a highly-generalizable, cost-free uncertainty estimate for FM-based action heads, enabling safer deployment of embodied models with effective online failure detection.

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

</details>


### [323] [Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27934)
*Bente Gortworst,Cem Okulmus,Magdalena Ortiz,Anni-Yasmin Turhan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies automatic SHACL shape learning, specifically the fitting problem: given positive and negative example nodes, compute a SHACL shape expression that validates positive and rejects negative examples, using recursive shape catalogues under well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. The authors focus on the core fragment equivalent to Description Logic ELI, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, and identify polynomial-time special cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language) is used to validate knowledge graphs, but writing shape expressions manually is labor-intensive. Automatic shape learning is therefore essential for practical knowledge graph applications.

Method: The paper formalizes the fitting approach: given positive (P) and negative (N) example nodes from an input graph, compute a SHACL shape expression C (potentially using recursive shape names defined in a catalogue). The fragment corresponds to the Description Logic ELI, and the authors consider three semantics for the catalogue: well-founded, stable, and supported. They analyze computational complexity of fitting existence and most specific fitting.

Result: Tight exponential-time upper bounds are established for both fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, with polynomial bounds derived for relevant special cases.

Conclusion: The fitting problem for SHACL shape learning in the ELI fragment is computationally characterized, establishing its intrinsic complexity bounds while identifying tractable special cases.

Abstract: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

</details>


### [324] [From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27937)
*Xu Xia,Jinghua Piao,Min Yang,Xiaochong Lan,Jiaju Chen,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OVCSD is a self-distillation method for LLM agents that uses outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories to internalize agentic skills, achieving significant success-rate gains on ALFWorld and WebShop with minimal privileged interaction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OPSD methods supervise students by scoring actions along student trajectories, but teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes and action-level scores underutilize information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship.

Method: OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, retains only outcome-verified successful continuations, applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence, and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales, OVCSD outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

Conclusion: Outcome-verified teacher supervision combined with comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories provides a more effective mechanism for capability internalization in LLM agents than action-level scoring approaches.

Abstract: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

</details>


### [325] [MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27967)
*Dawei Wang,Di Zhao,Xinyuan Liu,Marci Chi Ma,Xiaoyang Liu,Chengming Zhou,Gary Ushaw,Richard Davison*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MARS-RA is a framework that reformulates credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons from large multimodal models, converting these into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping, with theoretical guarantees and demonstrated effectiveness on embodied AI tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit assignment is challenging in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, especially in embodied AI settings with limited/delayed feedback and dynamically changing numbers of active agents. Absolute credit estimation is fragile under noise and dynamic participation, motivating a more robust alternative.

Method: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem. It uses large multimodal models to generate contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents, then aggregates these relative rankings into contribution scores that are used for potential-based reward shaping. Shapley values serve as an interpretive reference for the resulting scores.

Result: The framework provides theoretical justification for convergence and robustness. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types demonstrate that MARS-RA effectively guides agents toward cooperation.

Conclusion: Shifting from absolute to relative credit estimation (via rank aggregation) offers robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation in cooperative embodied AI, and the resulting framework successfully improves cooperative behavior across diverse tasks while being theoretically grounded.

Abstract: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

</details>


### [326] [Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27984)
*Weining Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper asks whether domain specialization for AI evaluators should be embedded in the model weights or in the rule that decides when to trust the model's judgment. Using 99,952 rubric-conditioned examples, the authors find that splitting training among expert LoRA judges degrades accuracy (losing 10.05 points) and audited coverage, while concentrating capacity in a shared judge—augmented with learned deferral rules—is far more effective. On RewardBench 2, a correctness-routing cascade (0.6B-4B-8B) achieves 89.40% accuracy versus 84.75% for 8B alone at 0.415 normalized compute, suggesting a design rule: share judgment learning until enough data justifies a split, and place specialization in an audited release boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic systems increasingly produce candidate outputs faster than they can be reviewed, widening the gap between generation and evaluation. The paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be baked into an evaluator's weights (via expert adapters) or into the rule that decides when a judge's output can be trusted (deferral/release boundary)?

Method: The authors conduct controlled experiments on 99,952 public rubric-conditioned examples. They compare (a) supplying correct vs. unrelated rubrics to a locked test, (b) splitting the training corpus into eight criterion-family LoRA judges vs. a single rank-64 adapter of the same capacity, (c) initializing family adapters from a shared trained judge vs. scratch, and (d) on RewardBench 2, routing examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade using learned correctness heads that decide deferral without altering reward scores. All runs are audited via exact one-sided 95% risk tests across 20 locked repartitions.

Result: Correct rubrics improve locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over response-only, while unrelated rubrics cost 2.66 points. Splitting into eight LoRA judges loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%, an effect not explained by capacity, learning rate, or steps. Initializing from a shared trained judge recovers 76.85% accuracy (19.94 points above scratch). On RewardBench 2, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy vs. 84.75% for 8B alone at 0.415 compute; margin-based rules stay near 84.8% using at least 0.94 compute.

Conclusion: The paper's results support a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary (deferral rules) rather than in the evaluator's weights.

Abstract: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

</details>


### [327] [SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27994)
*Jia Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework where agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement, combining embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Evaluated on six reasoning benchmarks, it substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but yields limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks, with non-monotonic agent-count scaling and most gains arising in the first refinement round.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents increasingly depend on large skill libraries, effectively selecting, combining, and maintaining these skills remains a significant challenge that needs addressing.

Method: SKIMIX employs three key mechanisms: (1) embedding-based skill retrieval to locate relevant skills, (2) submodular anti-dilution routing to allocate tasks to agents with diverse skill portfolios while preventing dilution, and (3) adaptive skill evolution for maintaining and improving skills over time. Agents collaborate through iterative refinement rounds.

Result: Across six reasoning benchmarks, SKIMIX substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but shows limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements occur during the first refinement round.

Conclusion: Task characteristics fundamentally determine whether skill-level ensembles provide benefits. The findings offer practical guidance for scalable agent design, particularly regarding when to employ multi-agent collaboration and how to allocate refinement rounds.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

</details>


### [328] [MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28006)
*Xianpeng Zhang,Jiahua Yang,Dongyu Chen,Lei zhang,Jian Ma,Xu guohuan,Haonan Lu,Tianhuang Su,Chuangchuang Wang,Kai Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, and MMLDSum-LLM, a two-stage training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with specialized weighted losses and GRPO with a multi-objective reward, demonstrating significant improvements in key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal long documents contain sparsely distributed critical evidence across paragraphs and modalities, causing key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in multimodal LLM summarization due to attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and inter-modal alignment gaps.

Method: The paper proposes MMLDSum-Bench (a benchmark across multiple domains, context lengths, and visual-textual modality distributions) and MMLDSum-LLM, a two-stage training framework: (1) supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by (2) GRPO with a multi-objective reward incorporating keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control. Evaluation uses a unified protocol with LLM-as-a-judge, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE.

Result: Extensive experiments against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol demonstrate that MMLDSum-LLM significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency in multimodal long-document summarization.

Conclusion: The proposed benchmark and training framework effectively address attention drift and inter-modal alignment gaps in multimodal long-document summarization, yielding improved summarization quality in terms of key information retention and cross-modal consistency.

Abstract: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

</details>


### [329] [MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28030)
*Farzaneh Seyedshahi,Kai Rakovic,Adalberto Claudio Quiros,John LeQuesne,Ke Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer that models tissue architecture in multiplexed imaging by framing it as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens, achieving performance comparable to foundation ViT models with substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost across multiple clinical downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for modelling tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging rely on handcrafted features (e.g., marker intensity statistics, cell-type proportions) that fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels.

Method: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer that frames tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. It learns contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, capturing higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient.

Result: Across core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model with substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

Conclusion: MUL-T demonstrates that a lightweight, self-supervised transformer over discrete cell tokens can effectively model tissue architecture, providing a scalable and generalisable alternative to handcrafted feature-based approaches for multiplexed imaging analysis.

Abstract: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

</details>


### [330] [DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28033)
*Debin Meng,Jiaming Yang,Zefang Zong,Tengyue Xu,Haining Xie,Yang Li,Peng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI
