TL;DR: DataClawEval is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating autonomous agents on end-to-end data engineering tasks, comprising 100 tasks across five execution engines (PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, FlinkSQL) built on production-grade code, with deterministic rule-based grading in isolated sandboxes. Evaluation of 16 frontier agents reveals no single model excels uniformly (best achieves 74.9 overall), demonstrating that autonomous data engineering remains an unsolved challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or basic data analysis, leaving the complex domain of end-to-end data engineering unexplored. The authors identify a gap in evaluating LLM agents on real-world, production-grade data engineering workflows.

Method: The benchmark is built from production-grade code written by professional enterprise data engineers, comprising 100 end-to-end tasks across five execution engines. Each task runs in a case-specific isolated sandbox and is scored by deterministic rule-based scripts rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge. Sixteen frontier agents are evaluated.

Result: The strongest model achieves only 74.9 overall score. No single model dominates; each excels on a different engine, indicating strict domain specialization. This reveals significant limitations in current agents for autonomous data engineering.

Conclusion: Autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. The benchmark, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts are publicly released to facilitate further research.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

</details>


### [331] [SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28048)
*Qiming Shi,Yibo Dou,Jiawen Zhu,Yulong Tao,Linbo Jin,Zhaolu Kang,Yunfan Zhou,Di Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILL-KD is a contrastive skill distillation framework that extracts actionable textual "skill patches" from the discrepancy between a student LLM agent's failure and a teacher's success on the same task, iteratively refines patches by re-running the student, and uses Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation to update a skill library without causing skill drift. It improves frozen student agents across five benchmarks and two student settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing skill acquisition methods treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or summaries of successful demonstrations, which creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: failed trajectories may lack evidence of missing behavior, and teacher trajectories may be too implicit to internalize as reusable guidance. Skills should serve as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities.

Method: SKILL-KD distills the actionable discrepancy between a student failure and teacher trajectory on the same task into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines it if the student still fails. It prevents skill drift via trace-linked edit histories and Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, which decides whether each patch should add a new rule, delete/modify an existing rule, or be skipped.

Result: Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

Conclusion: Treating skills as an explicit distillation medium via contrastive discrepancy extraction, iterative patch refinement, and drift-aware consolidation is an effective mechanism for improving weaker student agents without modifying their parameters.

Abstract: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

</details>


### [332] [IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28050)
*Nianchen Deng,Jiaxin Ai,Tao Hu,Shu Zou,Yurui Dong,Siqi Li,Xinyu Cai,Xuemeng Yang,Licheng Wen,Hongbin Zhou,Hairong Zhang,Pinlong Cai,Botian Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IndustryForge-27B is a multimodal foundation model built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B, fine-tuned on six industrial-CAD sub-corpora (~52k samples) covering CAD visual QA, parametric CAD code, assembly-level CAD code, and Windows COM API operations for Inventor/SolidWorks. It improves CAD-domain benchmark performance by +33.65 pp on average (outperforming GPT-5.4 on all four CAD benchmarks) while maintaining and slightly improving general capabilities (+1.56 pp), serving as a unified substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose multimodal models fail on specialized industrial CAD tasks (engineering drawing comprehension, parametric modeling, COM API scripting, parts-to-assemblies coverage), while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to serve the diverse calls issued by upper-layer agents. There is a need for a unified multimodal model spanning the full industrial CAD pipeline.

Method: IndustryForge-27B is constructed by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora (~52k multimodal samples): CAD-VQA (visual QA), text2cadquery (parametric CAD code), text2cadquery-assembly (assembly-level CAD code), and three COM sub-corpora (com_2d/com_3d/com_assembly) for Inventor and SolidWorks automation. The model is trained with a unified multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipe on top of the Qwen3.5-VL-27B base model.

Result: Across four CAD-domain benchmarks, IndustryForge-27B improves the base model by +33.65 pp on average and outperforms the closed-source GPT-5.4 on all four. Across eleven general-capability benchmarks, it retains and slightly improves base model performance (+1.56 pp mean), demonstrating no catastrophic forgetting.

Conclusion: IndustryForge-27B provides a unified foundation model for full-stack industrial agents, spanning CAD design to industrial-software operation, single parts to assemblies, and single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement, serving as a common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects.

Abstract: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

</details>


### [333] [SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28069)
*Hui Xie,Peng Xiao,Yutong Deng\textsuperscript,Shuoran Dou,Jian Yang,Jinyang Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer via behavioral distillation to compile native per-layer document KVs for reliable position-independent caching, while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. It introduces KV Gradient Checkpointing for memory-efficient training. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 from 0.53 (KV Packet) to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, and position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed.

Method: SemPIC trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation, keeping the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. The paper also introduces KV Gradient Checkpointing to reduce peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs.

Result: Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

Conclusion: By adapting the document representation itself—rather than only conditioning on boundaries—SemPIC makes position-independent caching more reliable, narrowing the gap to full recomputation while preserving the standard KV interface and decode path.

Abstract: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

</details>


### [334] [Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28074)
*Yash Pandya,Sahil Gupta,Sarthak Harne,Archana Yadav,Kavyansh Chourasia,Hussein Mozannar,Vibhav Vineet,Sara Abdali,Corby Rosset,Yash Lara,Ahmed Awadallah,Ece Kamar,Akshay Nambi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications with database-graded tasks, and uses a co-evolution loop that reads graded rollouts as both environment repairs and training signal. A 9B model trained on twelve such environments improves from 36.5% to 67.1% across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger teacher model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Computer-use agents need applications they can act on, break, and reset for training, but the most important applications are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments are used as stand-ins. The bottleneck has shifted from environment quantity to quality—specifically behavioral depth, targeted interaction difficulty, and the ability to improve alongside the model.

Method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database. It employs a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: once as repairs to the environment, its tasks and verifier, and once as training signal for the model. Additionally, it serves as a reinforcement-learning environment with a reward combining the grounded verifier and a dense per-step judge.

Result: A 9B model improves from 36.5% to 67.1% across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the larger frontier model that taught it. Deep environments raise live-site accuracy (80.0→85.0 and 48.0→65.0) while shallow ones lower it (80.0→75.0). Drilling one interface control transfers to held-out widget families and the open web. Repairing a single environment lifts the model from 16.2% to 38.5%. The RL reward raises held-out score from 58.8% to 68.0%.

Conclusion: The quality of synthetic environments—measured by behavioral depth, targeted interaction, and co-evolution—is the key driver of computer-use agent performance. Four environments are released as a benchmark with applications, seed data, and grounded graders.

Abstract: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

</details>


### [335] [Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076)
*Binbin Zheng,Zijun Xie,Guanqun Zhao,Enlei Gong,Xing Ma,Xiaoliang Fu,Zeyu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRSD is a group-reflective self-distillation method that uses a policy's own verified rollouts to generate capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance for RLVR, improving agentic LLM training and generalization to unseen tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR only provides coarse terminal rewards that entangle successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices in a single trajectory-level signal. Existing self-distillation methods that enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills either retrieve skills externally or extract them from single trajectories via stronger models, which may mismatch current experience, exceed policy capability, or remain path-specific.

Method: GRSD has the policy reflect on each verified trajectory within an on-policy group, then uses a stop-gradient snapshot to contrast reflections from successful versus failed rollouts, constructing group-level privileged guidance. A self-teacher then refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction.

Result: Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales show GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

Conclusion: Deriving guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts (rather than external or stronger-model sources) provides capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative supervision, yielding better performance and generalization than existing baselines.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

</details>


### [336] [Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28086)
*Nelson Higuera Ruiz,Markus Hofmarcher,Claudiu Leoveanu-Condrei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether LLMs can autonomously distill complete, correct ASP theories for visual question answering (VQA) tasks using a neurosymbolic approach with a solver in the loop. Using a dataset-agnostic protocol with a 1-hour time limit, nine models of varying scale are tested on CLEVR, GQA, and CLEVRER benchmarks. Three of four frontier models achieve near-perfect results on CLEVR and strong performance on GQA/CLEVRER, with GPT-5 showing inconsistent performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Writing ASP theories from scratch is difficult and time-consuming. The authors aim to determine whether a model can automatically distill complete and correct ASP theories given a fixed agent harness with a solver in the loop, removing the need for hand-crafted theory engineering.

Method: A dataset-agnostic neurosymbolic protocol is used where the model starts from an empty file with a single prompt and is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete ASP theory. The solver is kept in the loop as part of a fixed agent harness. Nine models spanning frontier, mid-tier, and open-weights categories are evaluated on three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER).

Result: Three of four frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek V4 Pro) reach 100% on CLEVR, 92.8%-98.8% on GQA, and 92.7%-95.3% on CLEVRER. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and 86.7% on CLEVRER. Providing handwritten reference theories only marginally changes frontier model performance (±3.4 pp) except for GPT-5, which degrades by 3-19 pp.

Conclusion: Frontier models are capable of autonomously distilling complete and correct ASP theories for VQA benchmarks when given solver-in-the-loop feedback, demonstrating that modern LLMs can effectively automate theory induction for neurosymbolic systems. However, model capability varies significantly, and the task appears to require frontier-scale models.

Abstract: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

</details>


### [337] [Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28087)
*Rui Xu,Yunke Wang,Linwei Tao,Wenjie Xuan,Yong Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization in AI-assisted research ideation. It extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions, and reduces redundancy across the community portfolio while preserving researcher-direction fit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-assisted research ideation systems optimize individual suggestions in isolation, leaving two blind spots: (1) coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream but poorly-grounded directions, and (2) independent recommendations concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes, causing homogenization.

Method: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline: (1) extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, (2) generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, (3) scores candidates along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and (4) surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio.

Result: On a benchmark of 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, it reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score.

Conclusion: DivAlign effectively addresses community-level homogenization in AI-assisted research ideation without sacrificing researcher-specific alignment, offering a principled approach to balance diversity and fit in research direction generation.

Abstract: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

</details>


### [338] [PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28090)
*Panpan Cui,Yiqi Liu,Wenhao Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PerturbMap predicts missing single-cell perturbation effects in unseen recipient contexts by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with transported source-context responses via source-to-recipient ridge experts, weighted by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma data, it improves full-effect MSE by 4.1% over the low-rank base and outperforms all controls while staying within 2.82e-6 MSE of a centralized reference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-cell perturbation atlases are incomplete—queries are often measured in some contexts but missing in the recipient context where the effect is needed. Existing approaches either discard measured responses (losing query-specific evidence) or naively copy/calibrate them across contexts (risking transferring spurious signal). A principled method is needed to leverage source-context measurements for cross-context prediction.

Method: PerturbMap combines a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the query's measured source responses into the recipient context via source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations. Proposal weights are determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors.

Result: On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1% over the low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It stays within 2.82e-6 MSE of a centralized token-matched pooled reference. Same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5% (base) to 80.5% (PerturbMap).

Conclusion: PerturbMap effectively transfers query-specific perturbation evidence across cellular contexts, yielding more accurate recipient-context effect predictions than baselines and controls, and approaching a stronger centralized reference—demonstrating that source-context information can be reliably leveraged without discarding query-specific measurements.

Abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

</details>


### [339] [An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28094)
*Paulo Carvao,Claudio Mayrink Verdun,Isabel Adler,Jeffrey Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals, using empirically grounded multi-attribute rubrics to surface tradeoffs and normative assumptions without prescribing outcomes. It employs a mixed-methods approach combining expert qualitative insights with computational text analysis, and benchmarks commercial LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. There is a need for a systematic, transparent framework that structures policy analysis around multiple attributes and allows users to surface priorities and tensions without dictating outcomes.

Method: A mixed-methods approach integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to design policy attribute rubrics. The framework uses rubric-based assessment with explicit analytical assumptions (attribute selection, rubric construction, weighting schemes), quantifies policy objective emphasis, and presents comparative visualizations. Commercial LLMs are benchmarked against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model.

Result: The framework enables interpretable cross-policy comparison through quantified emphasis of policy objectives and comparative visualizations. Benchmarking commercial LLM outputs against the domain-trained rubric-calibrated model evaluates LLM suitability for rubric-based policy analysis. The framework is jurisdiction-agnostic and focuses on relevance and alignment across policy attributes.

Conclusion: By making analytical assumptions explicit, the framework allows users to assess whether its embedded priorities align with their own normative commitments. It supports policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments, offering three contributions: empirically grounded multidimensional policy assessment, a transparent hybrid methodology, and a benchmark for comparing general-purpose LLMs against a rubric-calibrated domain model.

Abstract: This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

</details>


### [340] [SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28098)
*Jiyong Rao,Yicheng Qiu,Chi Zhang,Chunfeng Song,Runkai Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm where LLM agents navigate hierarchical scientific data repositories, interpret heterogeneous files, execute analyses, and integrate cross-file evidence. The authors present SciDataSailor, a framework that uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms to synthesize tool-interactive training trajectories, and construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation (627 meta-information summarization and 586 scientific QA tasks across 27 datasets in life, earth, and physical sciences).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific datasets are organized as hierarchical repositories with heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and highly dependent on domain expertise. Although LLM agents have advanced in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments.

Method: The authors propose SciDataSailor, a framework that synthesizes tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. It instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) enhanced with four task-specific mechanisms: (1) difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, (2) dual-feedback first-play urgency, (3) hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and (4) entropy-guided branching. These are used to construct a fine-tuning dataset (SciDataSailor-SFT-2K) and an evaluation benchmark (SciDataSailor-Bench).

Result: The framework produces SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a new agentic task paradigm for deep scientific data exploration and provides both a trajectory synthesis framework (SciDataSailor) and associated training/evaluation resources to enable LLM agents to interact with real scientific datasets through executable environments.

Abstract: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

</details>


### [341] [MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28103)
*Dongyi Liu,Haixing He,Xiaobao Wu,Jia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MIND is a lightweight defense framework against memory injection attacks on LLM-based agents, using an intent-aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact representations and detect poisoned memories while preserving task accuracy and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks where poisoned memory retrieved from attackers diverts agent behavior from user intent, causing task failure. Existing defenses either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts.

Method: MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck (IB) to extract compact intent-behavior representations from the initial user intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector classifies malicious memories from these representations, avoiding repeated LLM auditing overhead.

Result: Extensive experiments show MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. On ReAct-StrategyQA, it reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3% respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

Conclusion: MIND effectively mitigates memory injection attacks in a lightweight manner by exploiting distinguishable relationships between initial user intent and subsequent behavior in benign versus poisoned trajectories, striking a favorable balance between security, task accuracy, and inference efficiency.

Abstract: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

</details>


### [342] [Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109)
*Jiawen Tao,Miao Peng,Yaoming Li,Xiaokun Yuan,Mengzhou Wu,Wenhan Yu,Guoan Wang,Nuo Chen,Tong Yang,Maxm Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether organizing synthetic pre-training content into coherent book-level documents (rather than just content quality or rewriting style) improves language model performance. The authors build a scalable pipeline producing 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines, and controlled comparisons show book-level organization yields +1.02 to +1.17 mean gains over content-matched, length-matched, and retrieval-matched baselines on downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on synthetic pre-training data treats improvements as stemming from generated content or local rewriting style, but the authors hypothesize an understudied factor: whether related content is organized into coherent, book-level documents with hierarchical structure (TOC, chapters, sections).

Method: The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (Full setting). Controlled ablations include: Split (same text/tokens, each section independent), RandomConcat (sections from different books joined, length-matched), and Rephrase (independent rewriting of retrieved documents without clustering/TOC/assembly). Evaluation on downstream tasks including Llama3-8B.

Result: Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with the synthetic corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Full outperforms Split (+1.02, isolating document packaging), RandomConcat (ruling out length alone), and Rephrase (+1.17, demonstrating value of structured synthesis). On Llama3-8B, Full also outperforms RandomConcat and Natural Books.

Conclusion: Book-level organization is a distinct and valuable axis for synthetic pre-training data design, beyond generated content quality or local rewriting style. Coherent, hierarchically structured documents yield measurable downstream gains over other synthetic data configurations.

Abstract: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

</details>


### [343] [BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28110)
*Ruslan Khrulev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces BlueprintRepair, an interface that lets LLMs repair Lean proof blueprints (dependency graphs) via ten schema-checked local operations, and BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 failure trajectories. Typed repair matches free-form patching/rewriting in solving localized failures but is significantly cheaper, especially as token budget becomes tight.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly represent proofs as blueprints (dependency graphs of formal statements), but there is no controlled interface for repairing a blueprint or a benchmark to evaluate such repair approaches.

Method: Constructs BlueprintRepair with ten schema-checked local operations targeting named nodes, with Lean verifying every change and requiring declared use of blueprint lemmas. Builds BlueprintTrace with 142 failure states including accepted and rejected repair trajectories. Compares typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget using DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash.

Result: With DeepSeek-V4-Flash all three interfaces solve nearly the same number of localized failures. Typed repair is cheapest per solved state (patching 1.30x, rewriting 2.06x more expensive) and reaches nearly full final coverage within 10,000 tokens, while free-form lag. Qwen3.6-Flash solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, ahead on proof-authoring states.

Conclusion: Typed blueprint repair is the most cost-effective interface for localized proof failures: it matches free-form approaches in solving ability while being substantially cheaper and faster to converge in token budget, and this advantage generalizes across models.

Abstract: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

</details>


### [344] [ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28126)
*Bingchen Liu,Yuanyuan Fang,Lei Liu,Guangyuan Dong,Xing Fu,Yuanyuan Gao,Shuyue Wei,Xin Li,Xiangtian Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted long-horizon steel-equipment inspection that segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, uses Shapley-style estimation to score each unit's diagnostic value, and retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. It achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% vs. naive 8K-context LLM baselines, and successfully retains weak early seal-wear signals across three inspection cycles in real-world deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems for long-horizon steel-equipment inspection treat historical inspection logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, thereby failing to surface early-risk signals that could prevent equipment failure.

Method: ConMem consists of three stages: (1) segmenting inspection logs into functional evidence units, (2) estimating each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis via Shapley-style valuation, and (3) retaining high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget within a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system.

Result: ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy on a real-world dataset, outperforming the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces average input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies confirm that functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation help prioritize weak degradation signals. Real deployments show early-stage seal-wear alerts retained across three inspection cycles.

Conclusion: A contribution-aware, budget-constrained memory framework can substantially improve the efficiency and early-risk detection capability of LLM-assisted equipment inspection, outperforming static-corpus RAG baselines while retaining weak early warning signals across multiple inspection cycles.

Abstract: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

</details>


### [345] [AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28175)
*Zixuan Jiang,Binghao Qiang,Jiaying Chi,Yanqiao Zhu,Kai Yu,Xie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgenticASR introduces Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), a task transforming audio into clean, intent-preserving text by removing disfluencies and resolving self-corrections in real time. It uses an ASR–Refiner architecture with continual emission and revision over streaming audio, plus AASR-Bench for evaluation, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple ASR front ends.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verbatim ASR output retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that hinder readability and obscure the speaker's final intent. Existing spoken-to-written methods process complete audio/transcripts and cannot revise previously emitted text when later speech changes interpretation, motivating a real-time, continual revision approach.

Method: The paper formulates AgenticSR as an audio-to-clean-text task and proposes AgenticASR, an ASR–Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as new audio arrives, enabling continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. A bilingual benchmark, AASR-Bench, with fine-grained atomic rubrics is introduced for evaluation.

Result: Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR achieves the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human–AI agreement study shows rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality–latency trade-off between online and offline inference.

Conclusion: AgenticASR is established as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech, with code, benchmark, and demo to be released.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

</details>


### [346] [Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28227)
*Hanzhang Zhou,Panrong Tong,Xu Zhang,Quyu Kong,Chenglin Cai,Tianyu Xia,Gongjie Zhang,Jianan Zhang,Long Li,Long Chen,Lei Wang,Gaole Dai,Pengxiang Li,Liangyu Chen,Yue Wang,Steven Hoi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Qwen-UI-Agent is a real-world centric foundation GUI agent that spans mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments, combining diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. It uses a unified action space interleaving GUI and CLI operations, an AutoResearch-style data flywheel, and online RL with over 10,000 concurrent environments. It achieves state-of-the-art results on mobile-use benchmarks and competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models like Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to advance GUI agents toward real-world use by envisioning agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI with CLI execution, handle long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate services, and autonomously improve with minimal human effort.

Method: The approach combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime, uses a unified action space that interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn, employs an AutoResearch-style data flywheel where agents construct tasks, diagnose failures, and plan iterations, and applies online RL supporting trajectories exceeding 100 turns with over 10,000 concurrent environments for rollout acceleration. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows.

Result: Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks: 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. It achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2 for computer use, and 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro for browser use and GUI grounding, with competitive results against frontier models including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol.

Conclusion: Qwen-UI-Agent demonstrates that a real-device-centric, multi-environment foundation GUI agent with unified actions, scalable data flywheel, and online RL can achieve state-of-the-art mobile performance while remaining competitive on computer- and browser-use tasks, advancing toward general-purpose real-world digital device execution.

Abstract: GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent, a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL supports training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
  Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively.

</details>


### [347] [CDAE: Enhancing Perturbation Robustness in Pretrained Language Models with Contrastive Denoising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28236)
*Sina Heydari,Amirreza Abbasi,Mohsen Hooshmand,Majid Ramezani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) to refine pre-trained BERT embeddings by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objectives, making sentence representations more robust to semantic-preserving perturbations like synonym substitution, masking, and word dropout. Experiments show CDAE achieves higher embedding similarity under perturbations than both original BERT and SimCSE.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models produce sentence embeddings that are sensitive to semantic-preserving textual perturbations (e.g., synonym substitution, masking, word dropout), which undermines representation stability. The paper aims to address this by learning perturbation-invariant representations.

Method: The proposed Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) refines pre-trained BERT embeddings by jointly optimizing two objectives: (1) a contrastive loss that pulls representations of perturbed and original sentences together, and (2) a reconstruction loss from a denoising autoencoder framework. Multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths are used for evaluation.

Result: CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations compared to original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Improvements become more pronounced with stronger perturbations, demonstrating enhanced representation stability while retaining semantic information.

Conclusion: Perturbation-invariant learning is a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings, and the CDAE framework provides an effective lightweight solution that enhances representation robustness against textual perturbations.

Abstract: Pre-trained language models have significantly improved sentence representation learning, yet their embedding remain sensitive to semantic preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking and word dropout. This work proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embedding by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objective to learn perturbation-invariant representation. We evaluate the proposed framework using multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths and compare it against the original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations, with the improvements becoming more pronounced as framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information, highlighting perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ComputationIASBS/CDAE

</details>


### [348] [AI and Authenticity in Islamic Research: A Critical Evaluation of Generative AI Reliability, Hallucination, and Source Fidelity in Quranic, Hadith, and Fiqh Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28237)
*Muhammad Sajjad Akbar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study empirically evaluates six leading generative AI systems against fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions across Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Using a mixed-method framework examining accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation, the study concludes that current AI systems are useful as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the growing adoption of generative AI by Muslims for religious guidance, there is limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts. This gap motivates a comprehensive empirical evaluation.

Method: Six leading generative AI systems were evaluated using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering six domains (Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics). Responses were collected from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom under real-world conditions and analysed using a mixed-method framework assessing domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation. Four research questions structured the analysis.

Result: Current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but are not sufficiently reliable as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research. The study identified issues with hallucinations, incomplete citations, unverifiable references, and inconsistencies in handling jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty.

Conclusion: AI-generated Islamic knowledge requires verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise before being used for religious rulings, education, or research. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by Muslims for religious guidance, Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith explanation, jurisprudential rulings, and Islamic education. Despite its growing adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts. This study evaluates six leading generative AI systems using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analysed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
  The study addresses four research questions: (1) How accurate and authentic are AI-generated responses across major Islamic knowledge domains? (2) To what extent do AI systems produce hallucinations, incomplete citations, or unverifiable religious references? (3) How consistently do models handle jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty? (4) Are current AI systems sufficiently reliable for religious guidance, Islamic education, and scholarly research?
  Overall, current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

</details>


### [349] [Operationally Guided Placement-Aware Learning for Industrial Online 3D Bin Packing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28257)
*Dheeraj Poolavaram,Aanchal Rajesh Chugh,Sebastian Dorn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPAL is an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D bin packing that combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space (OG-EMS) generator, an xLSTM-based placement encoder, and a masked ranking policy trained with PPO. It achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49 on the BED-BPP benchmark, with gains of 15.1% from candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior learning-based methods for online 3D-BPP focus almost exclusively on optimizing the placement policy, while candidate generation and representation remain geometry-driven and neglect operational requirements such as stability, compactness, and balance that are critical in industrial settings.

Method: OPAL comprises three components: (1) OG-EMS, a candidate generator that evaluates multiple anchors within free-space regions and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements; (2) an operational representation encoding geometric and operational attributes of each candidate placement; (3) an xLSTM-based Placement Encoder that models dependencies among candidate attributes, coupled with a lightweight recurrent core that combines embeddings with current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions via a masked policy trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO).

Result: On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49. Operationally guided candidate generation contributes a 15.1% improvement, while learned ranking adds a further 6.3%, all while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

Conclusion: Jointly improving candidate generation and representation alongside the ranking policy yields substantial gains over prior geometry-driven approaches, demonstrating that operational guidance is a key enabler for effective online 3D-BPP in industrial palletizing contexts.

Abstract: The online three-dimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP) is a longstanding challenge in logistics and industrial palletizing. Recent learning-based methods use a learned policy to select among feasible candidate placements. Performance depends on the candidate generator and representation, especially in industrial settings where packings must be space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced. However, prior work has mainly optimized the policy, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. We address this gap with OPAL, an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D-BPP which combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS), an operational representation for each candidate placement, and a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization. OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements. An xLSTM-based Placement Encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes, while a lightweight recurrent core combines the resulting embeddings with the current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions. On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

</details>


### [350] [LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Constraint Model Reformulation to Improve Solver Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28268)
*Kostis Michailidis,Dimos Tsouros,Nguyen Dang,Tias Guns*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented reformulation of constraint models. Using an evolutionary framework inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design, the authors introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance to runtime vectors to retain behaviorally diverse attempts. Experiments on eight CSPLib problems show substantial held-out speedups, with diverse-context retention outperforming recency- or performance-only strategies, and validation-based selection improving all strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While LLMs can produce correct constraint models from natural language, even correct models can be computationally expensive to solve because performance is highly sensitive to modeling choices. The authors aim to automate performance-oriented model reformulation to improve solver efficiency without manual expertise.

Method: The authors use an evolutionary framework inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), where an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against a user-defined baseline. They compare AHD-adapted search strategies controlling which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. They introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which uses Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) on instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviorally diverse attempts.

Result: On eight CSPLib problems: (i) iterative reformulation produces substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep retained context diverse outperform those retaining only recent or fastest attempts; (iii) validation-based selection improves held-out speedup for every strategy.

Conclusion: LLMs can effectively automate performance-oriented constraint model reformulation via evolutionary search. Diversity in retained context is a key factor for success, and validation-based model selection provides consistent improvements across all search strategies.

Abstract: Combinatorial problems appear in numerous industrial applications. A common approach is to formulate these problems as declarative constraint models that can subsequently be compiled to and solved by a range of back-end solvers. Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce correct models from natural language, but even a correct model can be expensive to solve because performance remains sensitive to modelling choices. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented model reformulation. Inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), we use an evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against the user-defined baseline model. We compare AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance, but do not explicitly diversify the context. To cover this gap, we introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. We systematically evaluate the strategies on eight CSPLib problems using validation-based final model selection. The results show that: (i) iterative reformulation can produce substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep the retained context diverse outperform those that retain only recent or the fastest attempts; and (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy.

</details>


### [351] [MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28272)
*Rong Wu,Daocheng Fu,Licheng Wen,Xuemeng Yang,Shu Zou,Jianbiao Mei,Yuxin Wang,Hairong Zhang,Yu Yang,Tao Hu,Cong Zhang,Botian Shi,Pinlong Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemHarness is a framework that enables LLM agents to actively reconstruct and adapt retrieved past experiences to the current context rather than replaying them verbatim, outperforming static memory-augmented baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, ignoring the gap between abstract stored experience and concrete current states, which frequently causes negative transfer. Humans, by contrast, reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context.

Method: MemHarness uses a unified policy model that critiques and reconstructs retrieved experiences conditioned on the current state at each decision step, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. The reconstructive ability emerges through end-to-end training using GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, with strong robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios. Analyses reveal the reconstruction objective prevents negative transfer and serves as latent guidance during training, improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

Conclusion: Reconstructing rather than replaying past experiences is a more effective paradigm for memory-augmented LLM agents, as it aligns adaptive memory use with human cognitive processes and fundamentally enhances reasoning capabilities during training.

Abstract: Retrieving past experiences has become a common strategy to enhance large language model agents. However, most existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, injecting them into the context regardless of whether they align with the agent's current situation. This ``replay'' paradigm ignores the gap between the abstract, general nature of stored experience and the concrete, ever-changing states encountered at decision time, frequently causing negative transfer. In contrast, humans rarely recall past experiences verbatim; instead, they reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context. Inspired by this, we propose MemHarness, a framework that equips LLM agents to actively harness and reconstruct past experiences based on the present context. At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability emerges naturally through end-to-end training with GRPO.
