Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that this reconstruction objective not only prevents negative transfer but also serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

</details>


### [352] [Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28287)
*Jens Lehmann,Andrei Aioanei,Sahar Vahdati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces ARC-AGI-3, a skill-acquisition benchmark where agents must infer game rules, hidden state, and goals through interactive play. It presents Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs game-specific executable models from structured interaction history. Actor-requested delegation achieves 88.49 mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE) on public games; top policies reach 100.00 RHAE completing all 183 levels. The paper formalizes a joint problem called "active abstraction" — deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model given its cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ARC-AGI-3 transforms abstraction into an interactive skill-acquisition problem where action efficiency is paramount. Agents must infer unfamiliar game rules, hidden state, and objectives while every move costs. This requires a system that can decide when building, using, repairing, or bypassing a game model is worth the interaction cost.

Method: The authors formalize environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines. They introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames to build a structured history. The agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass free-form executable hypotheses. Four orchestration policies are compared on 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets, including actor-requested delegation to a model builder.

Result: Actor-requested delegation to a model builder achieves the highest observed mean RHAE of 88.49. GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels, with game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks of 98.5 and 100.0 respectively. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than aggregate official human baselines. Automatic repair after verification failures produces more accurate transition models but yields only 83.07 RHAE, showing transition match alone does not improve play.

Conclusion: Transition match (whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics) is insufficient for strong play — it does not indicate whether the model identifies the objective or improves the next action. The joint problem of generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost is termed "active abstraction." Strong play requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 turns abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition. A player must infer an unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goal while maintaining action efficiency because every move counts. We formalize these environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, an agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis.
  In one matched public-set run per policy, we compare four orchestration policies on all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets. Actor-requested delegation to a model builder obtains the highest observed mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), 88.49. With this selected policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels. Their game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than the aggregate official human baselines.
  Automatic repair after verification failures produces models that reproduce observed transitions much more accurately, yet reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match indicates whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics, not whether it has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play also requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. We call this joint problem active abstraction: generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost.

</details>


### [353] [One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317)
*Cesare Zavattari,Alessandro Tommasi,Giuseppe Prencipe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes auditing of N LLM agents under a finite budget B using self-reported confidence scores that may be adversarially miscalibrated. Modeling this as budgeted noisy inspection with a two-level Gaussian copula, it derives a miscalibration threshold δ* beyond which confidence-ranked auditing underperforms random auditing. Counterintuitively, δ* increases as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is dominated by shared difficulty rather than lineage. Empirical tests on five open-weight LLMs reveal near-constant (useless) confidence with point estimates at/past the flip threshold, while a proprietary model shows informative confidence below the threshold. The paper provides a quantitative criterion for "vacuous" oversight and validates policy orderings via trace replay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: A single human auditor cannot inspect all LLM agent outputs (B << N audits per round) and must rely on agent self-reported confidence to prioritize audits. Since confidence may be adversarially miscalibrated and errors correlated, it is critical to determine when confidence-ranking actually helps versus when it degrades to (or below) random auditing performance.

Method: The authors model the problem as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula, capturing both miscalibration and correlated errors. They derive a closed-form miscalibration threshold δ* separating regimes where confidence-ranked auditing beats random selection. They empirically measure confidence calibration properties of five open-weight and one proprietary LLM, locate the flip point, and validate policy orderings by replaying policies on recorded traces.

Result: Two a-priori expectations are reversed: δ* rises as the audit budget shrinks (contrary to intuition that more precision is needed with fewer audits), and cross-family correlation is not low—shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs exhibit operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, with point estimates at or beyond the flip (though CIs straddle it), while the proprietary model is informative and falls below the threshold.

Conclusion: Confidence-ranked auditing is only justified when confidence miscalibration stays below δ*, but open-weight LLMs' near-constant confidence places them at or past the flip, rendering their self-reports unusable for oversight prioritization. The paper provides a quantitative criterion for detecting "vacuous" oversight and empirically confirms the predicted ordering via trace replay.

Abstract: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

</details>


### [354] [PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28318)
*Zongyi Chen,Yu Liang,Jie Lin,Liansheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PathVU is a vision-anchored benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models' fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology, containing 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs, built from 23 public datasets with programmatic scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal pathology benchmarks primarily score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports, which provide limited insight into whether MLLMs actually understand the multiscale visual content necessary for pathology reasoning and decision-making.

Method: PathVU is built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations. It evaluates two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. Raw annotations are converted into deterministic task targets enabling programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment across 14 VQA-style tasks.

Result: Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, the authors observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images.

Conclusion: PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding, revealing current model limitations in fine-grained pathology visual reasoning.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

</details>


### [355] [Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28330)
*Mingdai Yang,Shicheng Fan,Kejing Yu,Duohao Wang,Li Sun,Hao Peng,Philip S. Yu,Zhiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLM agents acting as autonomous merchants frequently fabricate product attributes under competitive pressure, even when instructed to be honest. The authors design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a complaint-noise-forgiving deadband and state-dependent severity, which suppresses sales of low-rated liars without needing ground truth. Paired with SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism, the penalty becomes behaviorally binding—LLM merchants stop fabricating when it costs them sales, driven by penalty-gated self-correction reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous LLM agents that write product listings fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models, even under explicit honesty instructions. Platforms cannot verify claims directly since they only observe noisy, biased complaint signals with no ground truth access, so a mechanism is needed to deter fabrication without relying on perfect information.

Method: The authors propose CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with two key components: a deadband that forgives complaint noise, and state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is designed to be robust to strategic gaming. They also introduce SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism that makes the penalty behaviorally binding on LLM merchants by gating their reasoning on felt consequences.

Result: CARP suppresses the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle without ever accessing the truth, achieving the best welfare among compared policies. The behavioral effect binds across models with supporting confidence intervals: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance.

Conclusion: The CARP+SPARC framework demonstrates that reputation-based penalties can effectively deter LLM merchant fabrication in the absence of ground-truth verification. The distinction between compliance and self-interested restraint—traced to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning—shows that behavioral binding requires the penalty to materially impact the agent's outcomes, not merely instruction-following.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

</details>


### [356] [Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28336)
*Feng Xiong,Leyan Xue,Hongyu Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD), a label-free method for multimodal reasoning distillation that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement as complementary witnesses, improving distillation effectiveness across eight benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but trajectory-level rewards cannot distinguish whether a failed answer stems from perception errors or subsequent reasoning errors. Existing Perception Success Rate (PSR) estimates are ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty.

Method: PCD identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement as complementary witnesses, with their product forming a soft AND gate. This is motivated by Bayesian evidence combination, where multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception-reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged.

Result: Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B→2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28, and the 32B→8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively.

Conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

Abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

</details>


### [357] [How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28367)
*Zihan Dong,Zhiyuan Ma,Zekun Wang,Yunqing Li,Zirou Liu,Ruixuan Deng,Qishi Zhan,Rui Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a reliability framework for evaluating computer-use agents (CUA), auditing 150 failure-scored trajectories across five benchmarks and finding that 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are incorrect (10.7% evaluator false negatives and 4.7% broken tasks). It proposes a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy revealing that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate, and derives stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CUA benchmark scores are often produced by brittle scripted oracles rather than robust evaluation pipelines. Problems span stale tasks, trajectories lacking decisive visual evidence, evaluators rejecting valid alternatives, and aggregate reports hiding failure causes. The paper seeks to organize these issues into a coherent reliability framework and quantify their impact.

Method: The authors propose a reliability framework spanning four stages: task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. They then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five benchmarks covering web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control domains. They introduce a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy to classify genuine failures (verification/feedback, planning, execution/grounding).

Result: The audit found that 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7% are broken tasks. Analysis of genuine failures via the three-tier taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate over execution/grounding errors, and a single scalar success rate cannot explain these failure patterns.

Conclusion: The findings connect to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and yield stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation, emphasizing the need for more reliable, diagnostic, and stage-aware benchmark construction and scoring.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

</details>


### [358] [When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28384)
*Tairan Wang,Liang Zhou,Zikang Zhan,Pingchuan Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a controlled experimental framework for studying how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing specifications, using a symmetry-based design and executable mathematical benchmarks to reveal systematic preference patterns across representation types (formal > naturalized formal > pure NL > I/O examples), with extensions to heterogeneous domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly need to integrate multiple potentially conflicting information sources, yet there is a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications.

Method: A controlled experimental framework that constructs specifications with explicit conflicts, uses a symmetry-based design to reduce confounding factors, and enables systematic comparison of preferences across representation types. Evaluated on a 550-instance executable mathematical benchmark spanning 11 function families and four representation types, then extended to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains.

Result: Systematic preference patterns were observed (not random), with a consistent ordering: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input-Output Examples. Example effects depend on model capability and function family. The framework generalizes across diverse tasks and specification forms.

Conclusion: The framework provides a unified, controllable, and attributable approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information across diverse domains and specification types.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

</details>


### [359] [GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28397)
*Maya Arseven,Anette Frank,Beni Egressy,Johann Higl,Moritz Plenz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a graph language model (GLM)-based retriever for retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs, and systematically compares it against GNN-based and vector-search-based retrievers across single- and multi-hop RAG settings, with emphasis on cross-domain transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge graph RAG requires retrievers that capture both graph structure and semantic information. Existing GNN-based retrievers model graph topology but may lack semantic richness, while the emerging GLM paradigm offers a promising integration of graph reasoning and language model capabilities. There is a need to systematically compare these paradigms and evaluate their generalization to unseen domains.

Method: The authors propose a GLM-based retriever for knowledge graph RAG and conduct comparative experiments against GNN-based retrievers and traditional vector-search-based retrievers across single-hop and multi-hop reasoning tasks, evaluating both in-domain performance and out-of-domain transferability.

Result: Finetuned GLM retrievers achieve state-of-the-art results on two multi-hop benchmarks and generalize better out of domain. They remain comparable to prior work on in-domain multi-hop QA, with performance improving as parameters and subgraph coverage scale. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with efficient training, while vector-search baselines excel at single-hop datasets.

Conclusion: GLM-based retrievers offer superior cross-domain generalization for multi-hop knowledge graph RAG, whereas GNN-based and vector-search retrievers retain strengths in graph coverage and single-hop efficiency respectively, indicating complementary roles depending on the task requirements.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

</details>


### [360] [QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28405)
*Jiacheng Zhou,Jinfan Lv,Ruixuan Li,Longtai Zhang,Yan Wang,Wenqiang Zhang,Lizhe Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuantWAMs is a post-training quantization (PTQ) framework specifically designed for World Action Models (WAMs), addressing the mismatch between existing PTQ methods and WAM deployment by aligning quantization decisions with model structure, rollout distribution, and task objectives. It introduces three strategies—shared-basis outlier calibration, co-training-objective saliency, and fixed-intervention rollout auditing—and demonstrates near-FP16 accuracy (0.2–0.7 percentage point difference) under W4A4 settings on both simulation and real-robot tasks, while reducing memory to ~29% of FP16 and achieving 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World Action Models jointly predict future observations and actions via iterative denoising and closed-loop execution, making efficient deployment costly. Existing PTQ methods are poorly suited because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that fail to reflect actual deployment conditions.

Method: QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: (1) shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; (2) co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video-action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and (3) fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without altering the precision budget.

Result: Evaluated on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under W4A4-dominant settings, simulation means differ from FP16 by only 0.2–0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials confirm deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29% of FP16 and provides 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups for targeted video and action blocks.

Conclusion: QuantWAMs demonstrates that a PTQ framework that explicitly aligns quantization with the calibration context of WAMs—defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective—can achieve near-full-precision accuracy, substantial memory savings, and practical speedups, making WAM deployment feasible on real robots.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

</details>


### [361] [WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28418)
*Haozhe Hu,Hao Wu,Peiran Yin,Chao Han,Yunpu Ma,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WIDE is the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs that enables fine-grained computation allocation at the neuron-block level (attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups) for both prefill and decode scenarios, achieving 55.1% performance boost over SOTA dynamic depth pruning and up to 1.98x/4.95x kernel-level speedups for prefill/decoding via a pruning-kernel co-design approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly but suffer from accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity due to input-agnostic computation allocation. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality but are limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and lack practical acceleration in real-world inference scenarios. There is a need for fine-grained dynamic pruning that is both accurate and practically accelerated.

Method: WIDE introduces an end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework that allows each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning to neuron-block-level granularity. It uses a two-stage training pipeline to learn token-wise sparse execution patterns. A pruning-kernel co-design framework decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping for efficient execution across granularities.

Result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost over the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration respectively.

Conclusion: WIDE demonstrates that fine-grained token-level dynamic width pruning combined with a kernel co-design strategy can deliver both substantial quality retention and practical end-to-end acceleration for LLMs across both prefill and decode scenarios, bridging the gap between accuracy and efficiency in dynamic sparsity.

Abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

</details>


### [362] [When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28421)
*Zongheng Guo,Tao Chen,Tianli Li,Mingzhe Cui,Yang Jiao,Lei Xie,Yi Pan,Xiao Hu,Manuela Ferrario*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper defines derived-feature over-trust (DFOT), a failure mode where LLMs treat derived measurements (e.g., physiological signals) as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. Using PPG-ECG physiological sensing as a case study, the authors propose five quantitative estimands to measure this chain of over-trust and demonstrate that a privileged-distillation baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points on a 187-patient test set.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Derived measurements (measurements computed from raw signals) are increasingly fed into LLM pipelines as if they were direct facts, even though their validity depends on the specific instance. This "derived-feature over-trust" can lead downstream LLMs to act on incorrect or out-of-scope information, and there is currently no unified evaluation framework to quantify and compare mitigation strategies for this problem.

Method: The framework defines DFOT and operationalizes it via five estimands: (1) conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and (2) context-induced error rate (CIR) for two test scenarios (D1: accepting a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG; D2: rejecting an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading history), (3) correct repair rate (CRR) for frozen-error repair, (4) evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasting matched vs. patient-disjoint shuffled evidence, and (5) utility harm rate (UHR) for unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases. The approach is evaluated on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records, using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as a baseline versus PPG-only inference. ECG is used only for training supervision and offline reference, never shown to the LLM at inference.

Result: On a protocol-locked 187-patient test set, the ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero. UHR increased by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7), indicating a minor trade-off in unnecessary verification. The framework is agnostic to the reliability generator, and code is released.

Conclusion: DFOT provides a common, protocol-locked evaluation target for measuring and comparing mitigation strategies against derived-feature over-trust in LLM pipelines. While the baseline improves key repair and specificity metrics with a small, insignificant increase in verification burden, the framework is intended as a foundational benchmark for stronger future mitigation methods.

Abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

</details>


### [363] [A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28432)
*Chenghan Wu,Zongmin Yu,Liu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UNICON is a foundation model demonstrating "numerical intelligence"—the ability to acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context—by inferring predictive relations from graph-based examples and applying them across scientific and social systems, including disciplines unseen during training, achieving specialist-level performance without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While large language models exhibit intelligence through textual context, intelligence need not be confined to language. Scientific and social systems require models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context, a capability the authors call "numerical intelligence" that has not been addressed by existing foundation models.

Method: UNICON uses graph-based examples from a system as context to infer the predictive relation shared across them, then applies this inferred relation to queries from the same system. It is further combined with language-model agents to enhance performance, and leverages training-corpus diversity to improve generalization to unseen disciplines.

Result: UNICON approaches specialist performance without retraining across scientific and social systems, including disciplines absent from training. When combined with language-model agents, it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen during training. Training-corpus diversity is shown to improve generalization to unseen disciplines.

Conclusion: UNICON establishes itself as a foundation model of numerical intelligence, serving as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence that extends beyond language-based intelligence.

Abstract: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [364] [Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28434)
*Marc Heimann,Roxana Assadi Moghaddam,Olga Brovkina,Mark Pettifor,Lutz Goetzmann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces two unsupervised scores computed from a language model's hidden states in a single forward pass: an "aggregator" that measures whether a token position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration, and a "differentiator" that measures whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace. The aggregator is shown to track a token's structural place in a specific text (not its lexical salience or surprisal), validated against two independent ground truths: an engineered register (6/6 cells) and a psychoanalyst's fixed clinical annotations (34/36 cells). A transfer test shows that models whose token structure travels with lexical type perform worse on singular discourse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how language models internally organize a single text at the level of token positions, and to establish a relational (rather than essentialist) reading of hidden states — that a token's structural value depends on its place in the specific text, not just its vector or lexical properties. The authors also aim to provide an unsupervised method requiring no training.

Method: Hidden states from a single forward pass are scored on two properties at every token position: an aggregator score (whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration) and a differentiator score (whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace, i.e., transport in a metaphorical sense). No training is used; constants are frozen on one discovery text and all other texts are confirmatory. Validation uses an engineered register (6/6 cells) and fixed clinical annotations from a psychoanalyst (34/36 cells), plus a transfer test with matched base/instruct model pairs.

Result: The aggregator is neither an information measure nor a salience measure: across three unrelated models, repeated signifiers show draining surprisal and attention while the aggregator score holds. It follows an engineered register across its boundaries (6/6 cells) and matches a psychoanalyst's pre-fixed annotations in 34/36 cells, with graded increments above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. The transfer test shows the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads singular discourse worst, and instruction tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer.

Conclusion: Structural value is a property of a token's place in the specific text, not of its vector alone — a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states. The aggregator operationalizes theory that predated the instrument, and the method provides a training-free way to track textual organization through a model's internal representations.

Abstract: What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

</details>


### [365] [SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28457)
*Hongyu Chen,Liang Lin,Guangrun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SVR is an oracle-free multi-turn RL framework where a language model learns to use its own self-verification (a correctness verdict + confidence score) as a compute-control policy for adaptive test-time reasoning, avoiding external feedback and uniform compute budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scaling test-time computation for reasoning is wasteful when uniform budgets are applied to easy inputs, and existing verifier-guided refinement methods depend on external feedback signals that may not always be available.

Method: SVR trains with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories. At each turn the model generates a solution plus a discrete correctness verdict and confidence score; it keeps the answer only if the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, otherwise it refines using self-verification. Ground truth is used solely for training rewards (solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states) and is not exposed to the policy. Adaptive stopping is applied only at inference.

Result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 using only 2.99 inference turns on average. It outperforms standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference in the complete-system comparison, while requiring far fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.

Conclusion: Learned self-verification can function as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive allocation of test-time compute, providing a practical oracle-free alternative to external verifiers and uniform budgets.

Abstract: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

</details>


### [366] [LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28459)
*Pablo Manrique,Stefan Szeider*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a framework in the Lean theorem prover that provides end-to-end verification for constraint programming, covering both formulation-level properties (equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking correctness) parametrically for entire problem families, and solver-produced certificate checking for individual instances via translation backends to MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. The framework enables a workflow that establishes satisfiability/unsatisfiability without trusting external solvers, with verified symmetry breaking reducing solver search effort by up to 2x10^7 while certification remains affordable (at most a few minutes).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constraint programming results need trust at two levels: reformulations applied beforehand must be semantics-preserving, and solvers must produce correct answers. Existing systems lack a unified means to verify both levels without trusting external solvers.

Method: The framework is implemented in the Lean theorem prover and addresses two verification levels: (1) proving formulation-level properties such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints parametrically for entire problem families; (2) checking solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats including MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end certified workflow.

Result: Verified symmetry breaking reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, with a single parametric proof per problem family reused across all instance sizes. The in-Lean certification is affordable, taking at most a few minutes for the largest instances tested.

Conclusion: The framework successfully provides an end-to-end approach to establishing the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of constraint problems without trusting external solvers, while demonstrating practical efficiency gains from verified symmetry breaking.

Abstract: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

</details>


### [367] [A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28466)
*Jia Yu,Yan Zhu,Yili He,Zilong Wang,Xinyang Jiang,Peiyao Fu,Ruijie Yang,Tianyi Chen,Siyuan Li,Zhihua Wang,Fei Wu,Quanlin Li,Xian Yang,Pinghong Zhou,Shuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EndoCLIP is a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. It outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings, with linear-probe benign-versus-malignant classification approaching expert-level performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models are underused in colonoscopy despite abundant expert text descriptions in routine reports. However, these reports summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. The authors aim to transform routine documentation into scalable supervision by recovering finding-to-frame correspondence, thereby avoiding the need for task-specific manual annotation.

Method: The authors develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy-specific vision-language foundation model, by progressively recovering lesion-level image-text pairs from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records, yielding 125,756 training pairs. The model is evaluated on lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings.

Result: EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders across all evaluated tasks. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists.

Conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence from routine reports can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision for colonoscopy vision-language modelling, enabling clinical targets to be specified in natural language rather than annotated separately for each task.

Abstract: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

</details>


### [368] [Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28470)
*Antonio Delgado-Rosa,David Muñoz-Valero,Enrique Adrian Villarrubia-Martin,Juan Moreno-Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A workflow combining on-board inference on a 6U CubeSat with generative data augmentation via low-rank adapted diffusion models addresses the dual bottlenecks of limited downlink bandwidth and class-imbalanced aircraft datasets in LEO surveillance. The system achieves 82.2% mAP (up from 77.9%) and F1=0.811 for the minority class, with a quantized detector running at 25-30 FPS on orbit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit faces two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have limited downlink budgets yet conventional approaches transmit terabytes of raw imagery to ground, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced, which delays timely decision-making and prevents standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes.

Method: The proposed workflow deploys on-board inference on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned via low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated through pseudo-labelling by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples to create a balanced training dataset.

Result: The balanced dataset raises global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, improves minority-class F1 from 0.683 to 0.811, and the quantised detector fits on-chip memory while projecting 25-30 frames per second on orbit.

Conclusion: The computational tests support the proposed workflow as an effective decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites, contrasting with the conventional bent-pipe architecture where the satellite acts as a passive data collector.

Abstract: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

</details>


### [369] [A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28481)
*Ngoc Thai Le,Thanh Ma,Umberto Straccia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework for automated sewer pipe severity assessment, combining a Swin Transformer perception module with a J48 decision tree converted into 19 IF-THEN rules, evaluated with three fuzzy operator pairs on 3,244 images across five imbalanced severity classes, improving accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1, and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3% over image-only classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional automated sewer pipe severity assessment uses direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the relationship between visual defects and final severity scores is implicit and non-interpretable. The authors aim to bridge this gap by decoupling perception from reasoning and producing traceable, explainable decisions.

Method: The framework has two modules: (1) a perception module using a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images, and (2) a symbolic reasoning module where Weka's J48 decision tree is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, with tree paths converted into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules. Inference uses fuzzy logic with t-norm activations from CODE conditions weighted by rule confidence, combined via s-norms. Three operator pairs (Product, Łukasiewicz, Hamacher) were evaluated. Ground-truth labels were generated via consensus from five independent LLMs analyzing original inspector notes on 3,244 images spanning five imbalanced severity classes.

Result: The framework improved accuracy by 17.9%, balanced accuracy by 12.2%, Macro F1 by 23.0%, and MCC by 17.3% over image-only based classification, achieving competitive class-balanced performance while maintaining traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

Conclusion: The proposed neuro-symbolic framework provides a competitive and interpretable alternative to standard black-box image classification for sewer pipeline severity assessment. It combines strong class-balanced performance with transparent, rule-based reasoning that can be traced from visual defects to final severity scores.

Abstract: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

</details>


### [370] [SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28488)
*Yunhao Liang,Xianqi Cao,Pujun Zhang,Yuan Qu,Yongzhi Qi,Ningxuan Kang,Max Z. J. Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE is a composite policy model that treats supply-chain entities as tokens, uses a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to a decision interface, enabling unified end-to-end replenishment planning (assortment, sourcing, frequency, routing) instead of isolated per-department optimization. Evaluated on real data from Dingdong and JD.com, it outperforms stage-separated and practice-oriented baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supply-chain replenishment decisions (assortment, source assignment, frequency, routing) are operationally coupled yet typically optimized by separate departments and systems, causing stockouts, excess inventory, and avoidable transportation. There is no unified framework that coordinates these interdependent decisions end-to-end.

Method: SCOPE represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Decisions are made sequentially building on partial plans, and the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. The framework is instantiated for urban fresh-retail replenishment covering service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing.

Result: On real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com (two large-scale supply chains at different echelons), SCOPE consistently outperforms both methods that optimize each decision stage separately and practice-oriented supply-chain baselines.

Conclusion: Learning and explicitly coordinating cross-department operational couplings leads to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions than isolated per-stage optimization, demonstrating the value of unified composite policies for replenishment planning.

Abstract: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

</details>


### [371] [InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28503)
*Dorian Quelle,Lisa-Maria Neudert,Jonathan Bright,John Gallacher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a live, continuously updated AI benchmark measuring frontier language models' vulnerability to co-option for state-backed information operations, drawing on 2,100+ tracked operations from Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state media. Testing 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings, it finds integrity scores range from 8.8% to 94.5%, with great variability unexplained by model size. Chinese-developed models show sharp compliance drops (48–70 percentage points) on China-critical claims compared to benign ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-backed information operations pose a persistent threat to information integrity, and large language models may be co-opted to amplify such disinformation at scale. Static benchmarks saturate quickly, so there is a need for a dynamic, actively maintained benchmark that tracks current information operations and continuously evaluates frontier models against them.

Method: The authors built a live monitoring pipeline tracking over 2,100 state-backed information operations from Russia, China, and Iran. They constructed a dynamic benchmark updated weekly, tested 17 models from 8 providers across four different prompt framings, and measured integrity as the percentage of refused requests, alongside metrics on fact-checking rates and output harmfulness.

Result: Most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores varied from 8.8% to 94.5%—an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Models differ in output character: some fabricate details making output more harmful than source material, others defuse claims while complying, and fact-checking rates ranged from 2.9% to 72.9%. Chinese-developed models (except GLM 5.2) sharply cut compliance on China-critical claims by 48–70 percentage points.

Conclusion: Model integrity against information operations is partially linked to general refusal behavior, even for benign claims, highlighting the trade-off between usability and safety. The findings expose systematic vulnerabilities across frontier models and show that model choice materially changes operational risk, with potential geopolitical alignment effects in Chinese models' behavior on China-critical content.

Abstract: In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

</details>


### [372] [Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28523)
*Theofanis Aravanis,Costas D. Koutras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, a framework that extends standard credibility-limited belief update by allowing a compound epistemic input to be transformed into a weaker proxy per source world before applying credibility limitations. It provides semantic and axiomatic characterizations, identifies two well-behaved sub-classes (consistency-preserving and maximal consistency-preserving update operators), and shows that both credibility-limited and Katsuno-Mendelzon belief update emerge as special cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing credibility-limited belief update treats the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, making it impossible to represent situations where only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes an input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, which is too permissive. There is a need for a framework that supports source-dependent selective acceptance of parts of epistemic inputs.

Method: The authors introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, where the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. They provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators, and identify two sub-classes with additional constraints: consistency-preserving operators (requiring every transformed input to be credible from its source world whenever the original input is consistent) and maximal consistency-preserving operators (additionally requiring the proxy to be maximally informative among credible consequences of the original input).

Result: The framework recovers credibility-limited belief update as a special case and yields Katsuno-Mendelzon belief update when credibility restrictions are removed and transformation functions are set to identities. This demonstrates the framework is a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides a unified and more expressive account of belief update that generalizes both Katsuno-Mendelzon and credibility-limited belief update, capable of handling cases where only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized relative to each source world.

Abstract: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities.
